The Duke of Grafton, and the Forest Officers ap- ber-pointed by his Grace, inform us, that the Commoners enjoy this Right without Stint, as to the Number of their Cattle. The Right however, which by the ancient Forest Laws the Commoners had in the Forests, was only to the Surplus Herbage, after a full Supply for the Manwuod, Deer, of which any Number may be kept without Pa. 229. Limitation.

The Cattle allowed to depasture in the Forest are Horn Cattle and Horses only. No Sheep or Swine are admitted. The Forest is driven Once a Year, or oftener, to examine whether there are any Cattle belonging to Persons not having Right of Common; and when any such are found they are impounded, and a small Fine is imposed on the Owner; the rest are marked as belonging to Commoners, and turned again into the Forest. The Numbers which commonly depasture in the different Walks are stated in the Answers of the Keepers.

In the Reign of Charles the Second the Office of Warden, or Master Forester, was held by the Earl of Northampton, under a Grant from Charles the First, for his Life, with an antient Fee of Five Pounds per Annum for himself, and certain small Salaries for the Under Foresters, and other Officers appointed by him, amounting together to 23/. 6 s. 8 in

Money; and those Officers had also certain Allowances of Wood, amounting to 231 Loads a Y~ear, as specified in a Claim preferred by Lord Northampton, lathe Tower, at a Justice Seat held for this Forest, in the 11th of Charles I.

In the 32d of Charles II. that King, by Letters Patent, reciting the Grant of the Office of Warden, for the Life of the Earl of Northampton, granted the said Office in Reversion, after his Death, to Henry Earl of Arlington for Life, and after his Decease to Henry Duke of Grafton, and the Heirs Male of his Body, for ever.

But both the Earl of Northampton, and Henry Duke of Graf ton, dying before the Queen Dowager, it appears that Doubts arose as to the Validity of the Grant of the Wardenship, by reason that the Settlement of the Forest on the Queen Dowager was not recited in it; and on this Account, after the Queen Dowager’s Death, which happened in 1705, Charles Duke of Grafton applied by Petition to Queen to grant new Letters Patent, to ratify and make good the former Patent of 326 of Charles II. The Woodwardship of this Forest is held by Mr. Smyth, the Deputy Ranger, and Keeper of Sholbrook Walk, by Letters Patent during His Majesty’s Pleasure, with a Salary of Five Pounds per Annum, paid out of the Land Revenue; an Allowance of 20 /. per Annum in lieu of Poundage on Wood Sales, formerly received by the Woodward from the Buyers of the Wood; and a Fee of Four Pence per Tree for every Tree marked for felling, which is received from the Purchasers of the Wood and Timber. The Allowance in lieu of Poundage, which is paid by the Surveyor General out of the Produce of Wood Sales, was directed by Warrant from the Treasury, in the Year 1762, to be paid, from Time to Time, into the Hands of the Lord Warden of the Forest, to be paid over to the Woodward.

The Number of Loads of Timber is not stated in this Survey; but the Account of the Value of the Trees enables us, in some degree, to supply that Defect. The common Price of Oak Timber at that Period being about 10$.* per Load, the 51,046 Trees then valued at 25,755/., must have contained, one with another, about a Load of Timber; and, making reasonable Allowances for the Tops and Branches of the Trees, there must have been in the Forest from 40 to 50,000 Loads of Timber, Girt Measure, or from 60 to 75,000 Loads, Square Measure. It is necessary, however, to observe, that the Seven Coppices in Hasleborough Walk, now belonging to Earl Bathurst, and which contain 418 Acres, appear to have been the Property of the Crown at that Time, and were, consequently, included in the Survey of 1608. A

proportionable Deduction must therefore be made from the 51,046 Trees comprised in that Survey, and there will then remain 45,568 Trees, as the Number growing on the Lands in which the Crown is still entitled to the Timber; and that Quantity is not more than should be expected to grow on such an Extent of Wood Land, of a Soil so favourable for Timber, under proper Management; for as the Coppices in which the Timber now belongs to the Crown contain 3.447 Acres, if w'e suppose only the same Number of Trees to have been standing in the Lawns and open Parts of the Forest in 1608, as were reported to be growing in them on a Survey of the Tirpher in 1783, being 191 Trees, of 30 Feet and upwards, and that the remaining Number grew within the Coppices, the Proportion would hot be more than Thirteen Trees to an Acre.

The First Proceeding that we have met with relative to the felling any Timber in this Forest for the Navy, during the present Century, was in the Year 1771, when the Navy Board having written, to the Surveyor General of the Woods, acquainting him that their Purveyor had surveyed about 1,300 Loads of Timber fit for the Navy, in the Twro Forests of Whittlewoodand Salcey, and desiring that it might be felled as soon as possible, the Surveyor General applied to the Treasury for Directions on that Subject; and expecting, probably, that a Warrant would forthwith be issued for felling that Timber, as the Navy Board had desired, he immediately sent an Agent into the Forest to make Preparations for felling the same: But the Lords of the Treasury having thought it proper

to communicate the Proposal for cutting Timber in Whittlewood Forest to the Duke of Grafton, before making any Order upon it, and the Surveyor General’s Agent having, in the mean rJ’ime, proceeded to mark Trees for felling in all the Coppices, without regard to the Age or Growth of the Underwood, instead of confining the fall to those Coppices which had been cut the preceding Season, the Duke of Grafton remonstrated to the Lords of the Treasury against that Proceeding, as injurious to his Property; in consequence- of which the felling of any Timber that Year was suspended, and Directions were given by the Board of Treasury, that the Naval Timber in the Forest should not be felled, until the particular Coppices in which it grew should come in course to be cut.

22d March 1G68. A Warrant was issued for felling 1,000 Trees in Forest for the Use of the Navy; which Warrant

states, that the Earl of Oxford, Chief Justice in Eyre, had certified, that though considerable Quantities of Timber had been felled there by the late Lord Treasurer’s Order, yet the Forest was so well stored, that 1,000 Trees might be spared without defacing the same.

here, both for securing the Annual Supply to the Public, and guarding against the Possibility of a profuse and wasteful Cutting of the Timber by a future Possessor of the Forest.'

An Arrangement of this Nature, we apprehend, would prove advantageous both to the Crown and to the Grantee: The Duke of would have it in

his Power to pursue that Plan of Management which he should think the most for his own Interest, and by which the Property might be best improved: A less Number of Officers might, perhaps, be found sufficient for a Forest of this Extent; and certainly the Repairs of Lodges and Fences would be performed with more Oeconomy than they have been by the Officers of the Crown; and all the Profit to be derived from Care of the Forest, or Saving in the Expenditure, or from any Plan of Improvement, either for the Increase of the Timber or Underwood, would be entirely his own.

The authentic Proofs we have given of what this Forest formerly produced while the Interest in the Timber and the Underwood belonged wholly to the Crow’n, shew the Value to which it might again be brought, if it should be freed from the Mixture of Rights created by the Grants under which the various Interests are now held; for it can hardly be doubted, that under the watchful Care of the Grantee, if he were the Sole Proprietor, the Forest would be at least as productive as it formerly w as, under the Disadvantages attendant on public Management.

The Crown would, at the same Time, be freed from the difficult Task of protecting Property mixed with that of others, who have opposite Interests; and of guarding against the misconduct of its own Servants; as well as from the Charge of paying a Number of Officers, not of its own Appointment; and of supporting and repairing of Lodges, at an Expence which cannot easily be ascertained or regulated; and the public Object would, at the same Time, be attained, of securing a Supply of Timber for the Dock Yards.

But previously to the carrying this Plan into Execution, it would be extremely desirable that such a Settlement should take Place between the Crown, the Duke of Grafton, and the Commoners, as we have recommended in our Report on the Forest of Salcey, by which, if it shall be agreed on the Part of the Crown and the Duke of Grafton to discontinue the keeping of Deer in the Forest, or to confine them to an inclosed Part of it, the Commoners should consent to the Coppices being kept a longer Time inclosed after each Cutting of the Underwood, in Consideration of their having the entire Enjoyment of the Pasture of the uninclosed Parts of the Forest for their Cattle (instead of having, as at present, only a Share of it, in common with the Deer) and of their being wholly freed from the Damage done to their Lands, by the Deer straying upon them, for which they are at present without a Remedy; and the ascertaining of that additional Term of Inclosure should also be submitted to Commissioners.

Besides the great Advantage to the Saplings and Underwood from the Coppices being kept a longer Time inclosed, and protected from the Cattle, there would be a considerable Saving in the making of Fences; which would not require to be of so expensive a Kind, if the Deer were either removed; or confined

to an inclosed Part of the Forest: And the Browse Trees might then be wholly cut and disposed of, which would give Room for more Underwood, or better Trees, to grow' in their Stead.

If the Benefit to be derived to the Woods and Timber, from such an Agreement with the Commoners shall be extended to the Coppices belonging to Earl Bathurst, an adequate Consideration should be allowed by him to the Crown and the Duke of,

proportioned, as we conceive, to their respective interests in the Deer, in return for the Advantage which his Property will receive from the Woods being longer inclosed; but if no Alteration shall take place with respect to those Coppices, the additional Pasturage within them for the Cattle, in consequence of the Removal of the Deer, will form Part of the Compensation to the Commoners for keeping the other Coppices a longer Time inclosed.

Objections have been suggested to us, by the Duke of Grafton, to the Proposal for a Rent Charge in Timber, both on Account of the Risk to the Public, and to the Grantee; from the Possibility that some future Possessor of the Forest may dispose of the Whole of the Timber, to the Injury of the Public, which might be disappointed of the Supply expected for the Navy, and of his Successors, who would remain burthened with the Rent Charge, though deprived of the Stock from which it was to be furnished: And wc can propose no other Means to guard against this Danger than what occurred to his Grace, and are stated in our Report on Salcey Forest, and the usual Restrictions to Seventh Represent Waste in entailed Property. port> pa>

If, however, neither of the Plans on which we have proposed a Transference of the remaining Rights of the Crown to the Grantee, shall meet with the Approbation of the Legislature, and of the Duke of Grafton, it remains for 11s then only to recommend a more regular and attentive Management of the Property which the Crown now has in the Forest; and that more effectual Checks may be put on the Conduct of the Officers to whom the Care and Management of it shall be intrusted.

With this View' we think that a new Survey should be taken of all the Timber and other Trees and Saplings belonging to the Crown; and that Regulations

similar to those which we have suggested m our Report on the Forest of Salcey, for the Care of the Interests of the Crown there, during the Continuance of the present Grant of the Wardenship of that Forest, should be established here.

E!§llth RepoJl be advisable, that, as the Crown will be freed from the LandVeveuue ° Pa)’ment of Officers, and from the Repairs of Lodges, '/ or other Expences, within the Part of the Forest to be allotted to the Duke of Grafton, that Part should be rendered Fee Simple, instead of being held, as it now is, only during the Continuance of Heirs Male of the Family of Grafton. The Terms agreed on for such Exchange should be laid before Parliament; and if approved, an Act should be passed for carrying the Agreement into Execution.

As the great Object for the Public, in the future Management of the Woods to be then allotted to the Crown, will be the Increase and Protection of Timber for the Navy; and as the young Trees are often destroyed, and even the Underwood considerably injured by the early Admission of Cattle, it may be further advisable that, in the same Act, Provision should be made for an Alteration in the Mode of enjoying the Right of Common; by which, instead of the Coppices being thrown open to the Cattle at the End of 9 Years, the Crown should be empowered always to keep a certain Proportion of the Forest inclosed, until the Trees shall be past Danger from Cattle; and that on throwing

uarii. A. 1792.

open those Inclosures, or any Part of them, an equal Portion of the Residue should be inclosed for Timber, in the same Manner as is provided in the Acts for Dean and New Forests, and as we have proposed for the 20 Cha. ir. Improvement of others. 9 & 10W.III.

By such a Settlement with the Commoners, though the Crown will be entitled to increase the Quantity inclosed, in consequence of the Removal of the Deer, the Interest of the Commoners will not be injured, because they will have the entire Use of the Herbage of the Part left open for their Cattle; and though that Part will be of smaller Extent, the Pasture will not be less valuable.

The Officers who may be appointed for the Care of Salccy Forest may, as we have suggested in the Report on that Forest, have the Superintendance of both, which would in some degree obviate the Second Objection.

An ACCOUNT of the Coppices* Lodges, Lawns, and other Lands, within the Forest of extracted from a Survey thereof, made by Order of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue, by Richard Davis, in 1787.

Whittlewood Forest,

Is situate in the Parishes of

and Passenham, or Denshange (which is a Hamlet to

Passtnham) in the County of Northampton, and a small Part in the Parish of Lillings in the County of Buckingham.

This Forest is divided into Five Walks, namely, Hasleburrou', Sholbrook, W Hanger, and Shrob

Walks; and there is a Keeper to each Walk, appointed by his Grace the Duke of Grafton. Those Keepers have each a separate Lodge, and have their respective Page Keepers to* assist them.; -

Hasleburrou>

Is situate in the ! Parishes of TVhitfield and Silslone, in the county of ; Northampton, at the South End of lVhittleumd Forest, and is bounded on Parts by the Parishes of Whittlebuty, Bid-

dlesden, and Siresham.The Turnpike Road from Oxford to Northampton passes through the Middle of this Walk, which is not encompassed by a Ring Fence on every Part as the other Walks are, but is in Places open, so that the Deer and Common Cattle often stray into the Village of Silstone, and other adjacent Places. '

This Walk contains Ten Coppices, which are in the Parish of Whitfield, where the Timber is the Property of the Crown, and the Underwood is the Property of his Grace the Duke of ftnd

Seven Coppices which are in the Parish of Silslone, where both the Timber and Undefwood belorlg to the Right honourable Earl Bathurst.

The Soil is in general good, consisting of a Red Loam, and Sand mixed w'ith Clay, in that Part of the Walk which is in the Parish of though

the Underwood, from having been neglected many Years ago, is of the least Value here of any other Walk in the Forest, there being more Plains and open Places in these Copses than are tnet with in general, which makes the Feed to the Deer and Common Cattle to be of the greater Value. 1 '

Sholbrook Walk,

Is situate in the Parish of Whetween Lord Bathurst's Coppices and Walk, and is

bounded on Parts by the Parishes of Lillingstone-Lovell, Lillingstone-Durcll, Silstone, and other Lands within the same Parish of Whittlebury. _

This Walk contains Sixteen Coppices, on which the Common Cattle and the Deer ‘depasture when open, and Three Copses, where the Deer are excluded, being only connected to the Forest by ai narrow Neck of Land, which would make it expensive to have a proper Mound to contain the Deer. —

The Soil is in general a strong deep Clay, with a little Exception; of Sand and Loam. The Underwood is for the most Part thick, and the Oaks appear healthy.

In this Walk is Sholbrook Lodge, the Residence of the Lieutenant and Deputy Ranger, Joseph Smyth, Esquire; Maggots Moor Lodge, in the Occupation of William Lovell, Page Keeper; ind another Lodge, in the Occupation of William Savage, the other Page Keeper. 1

Vo I.. 47.

Wakefield Walk, Eighth n^rt

J of the Hoani

Is situate in the Parishes of Whittlebury, Potters-Pury, La„d Revenue.

and Passenham, or Fknshanger (which is a Hamlet to v ----- ---, ——

Passenham) in the County of Northampton, and a Part in the Parish of Lillingstone-DareU, in the County of Buckingham, laying between Sholbrook and Hanger Walks, and is bounded on Parts by the Parishes of Paulers-Pury, Lillingstone-Lovell, and Wick

There are in this Walk Twenty Coppices, on all of which the Common Cattle and Deer depasture when open, and several open Plains and Ridings, particularly a large Plain open at all Times, called Holy-brook Plain, a Part of which used to be inclosed as a Coppice a few Years ago, but is now thrown open in Consequence of an Agreement with the Commoners, in lieu of an Inclosure which is at no Time thrown open, adjoining to Wakejield Great Lodge, called The Pheasantry.

In this Walk is Wakefield Great Lodge, the Seat of his Grace the Duke of Grafton, with suitable Otlires,

Garden, and the Pheasantry above mentioned laid out in the Style of a Pleasure Ground. Also Little Lodge, in the Occupation of Mr. Charles Ileath;

The Gullet Lodge, in the Occupation of Thomas Oakley,

Page Keeper; and Sutfield Green Lodge, in the Occupation of William Waterman.

Wakefield I mud,

Is a large Tract of Land, on which no Cattle arc admitted but the Deer and Horses, Cows and Oxen, belonging to the Ranger. The Common Cattle are excluded by Rails, a Round of near Three Miles, which are kept up both in Stuff and Workmanship at the Expence of the Crown, rough Timber for that Purpose being cut in the Forest.

The Soil is various, but for the most Part is good Land (especially the Lawn) and consists more of a sandy Loam and less of the Clay that is prevalent in this Forest. There are many good Coppices of Underwood, and much line Oak Timber.

Hanger Walk,

Is situate in the Parish of Passenham, adjoining to Wakefield Walk, at the South-east End of that Part of the Forest which lays connected together.

There are in this Walk Eight Coppices, on all of which the Deer and the Common Cattle depasture when openand several Ridings, as Arell as a small Plain called Hanger Hoi loirs, open at all Times.

There are also Two Lodges: Hanger Lodge, in the Occupation of Mr. William Taylor, Keeper of the Walk, and another Lodge in the Occupation of George Taylor,

Page Keeper.;

- The Soil, most of it, is strong deep Land, and produces in general some of the best Navy Timber, and ( good Underwood; fewer Browse Trees in this Walk than the last, and, where the Ridings are ploughed, ‘ produces good Crops of Corn.

Shrob Walk,

Is situate in the Parish of Passenham, being encom-: passed with a Ring Fence by itself, and detached for near the Distance of a Mile from any other Part of the Forest, in an Eastward Direction from This Walk nearly adjoins to the Town of Stony Stratford, and is bounded on one Side by the West Chester Road, called The Walling Street Road.

There are in this Walk Five Coppices, which are, as well as every other Part of this Walk, entirely exempt from Rights of Common at all Times; nor are there any Deer in this Walk, they having been driven hence to the other Part of the Forest, about Twelve Years ago, by Order of his Grace the Duke of Grafton.

156 13® Februarii. . 1792.

Eighth Report The Underwood and Timber are consequently of the of the Board of most Value of any of the Copses, and the Vicinity Land Revenue. to Stony Stratford and the Turnpike Road occasions ----- ----- -' the Underwood to fetch a superior Price.

There is but One Lodge in this Walk, which is occupied by Mr. Reuben Capes, the Keeper of the Walk, who is also the Deputy Surveyor of the Forest; and there is a greater Quantity of Land in the Occupation of the Keeper of this Walk than any of the others, because there are no Common Cattle nor Deer to partake of the Feed of the Plains and open Ridings.

The Ring Mound of this Walk has not been kept up with so much Care and Strength since the Deer are gone; and is moreover liable to many Depredations from being stolen, by laying near a great Town.

The Soil is of a mixt Nature, in general Loam and Mould, with some Clay, and is of that Kind as might be converted to almost any Purpose: Such as in Woodland produces good Underwood and Timber; the Meadow produces good fair Crops; and the other Parts, which are now pastured, would, if ploughed up, produce good Crops of Corn.

OBSERVATIONS.

The Underwood in the inclosed Coppices cannot rightfully be cut, except at Twenty-one Years Growth; and, after the Two Verderors of the Forest have taken the Second best Half Acre of Woodland each in every Copse, the Remainder is the Property of his Grace the Duke of Grafton.

When a Copse goes to Sale, it is inclosed with a strong Hedge and Ditch, made at the Expence of his Grace the Duke of Grafton, on such Parts as are not the Outer Boundary of the Forest. If an Outer Boundary, it is inclosed mostly with Posts and Rails, at the Expence of the Crown, and that Hedge is continued Nine Years, in order that the Underwood and Saplings may grow out of the Reach of the Cattle and Deer, and then must, by Prescription, be thrown open to admit the Deer and Common Cattle for Twelve Years.

AH Timber Trees growing in this Forest are reserved to the Crown. There are very few Trees of any other Sort than Oak and Ash; the latter are of no considerable Value, because of the immemorial Custom practised of cutting off their Heads, and making them Dottrells or Pollards, in order that they may bear more Lop for browsing the Deer.

In the greatest Part of the Coppices in this Forest, the young Oaks stand tolerably thick, and as near to one another as they ought, to come to Perfection, and not injure the Underwood; but in some of the Copses there is little or no Succession of young Oaks, which may be attributed to this Cause. If it is a plentiful Year of Acorns when a Copse goes to Sale, then the Cattle and the poor People, collecting them together, tread them together into the Ground, and there is a Voi. 47.

plentiful Spring of young Oaks; but if, on the other Hand, it is not a Year for Acorns, then there are few or no Saplings, and by a Copse going to Sale Twice or Thriee in a scarce Year, the Succession of Oaks is entirely lost. There are a few Copses of this Description, as well as some where the young Oaks stand, in particular Spots, as thick as possible (too thick even to grow Twenty Years without injuring one another).

I am informed these particular Spots are Places where the Keepers have had Skirmishes with poor People, who make a Practice of collecting Acorns to sell, and have cut their Bags, by which many of the Acorns have been trod into the Ground.

To remedy the Evil of losing the Succession of Oaks, as before mentioned, would it not be advisable to plant the vacant Places with Acorns thick enough ? The best and most promising might be selected, and saved at proper Distances, and the worst taken out at different Intervals; and perhaps Thirty Trees of Navy Timber would be as many as should be left to come to Maturity on an Acre or more, depending on their Size, and the Number of young Trees in Succession.

In th’ose Copses where the Saplings of Oaks stand too thick to come to Maturity, and are of a proper Age, an earlier Stock might be procured by transplanting some of them to the vacant Places in the same Copse, or in any other Copse where the Succession was lost, than by planting Acorns.

There are many ancient Oaks, in every Copse, called Browse Trees, which are the only Oaks that are suffered to be lopped: These are very unequally divided, some Walks having many more, in Proportion to the Quantity of Ground, than others , Some of

these

N* 4.

To the Queen’s Most Excellent Majestie.

The Humble Peticon of Charles Duke of Grafton;

Sheweth,

That King Charles the 2d, by his Letters Patents under the Great Seale of England, bearing Date the 12th Day of January, in the Thirty-second Year of his Reign (reciting Letters Patents'granted by King Charles the First to Sir Christopher Hatton, Knight of the Bath, whereby he was constituted and appointed Warden of the Forest of Whittlewood, in the Count’ys of Northton and Bucks, with all Fees, Profits, and Perquisites thereunto belonging, IN TRUST for and dureing the Life of James Earle of Northton) grants to Henry Earl of Arlington, for the Terme of his Life, the said Office of Warden of the Forrest of Whittlewood, from the Death of the said Earle of Northton, or Surrender of the said Letters Patents above recited.

The said King Charles the 2d, by the same Letters Patents, grants to Henry Duke of Grafton, Your Pet" Father, and the Heires Males of his Body issueing, the said Office of Warden of Whittlewood Forest, with all Fees, Profitts, Perquisites, and Emoluments, thereunto belonging, from the Death of the said James Earl of Northton, and Henry Earl of Arlington.

That all the Interests granted precedent to the Estate granted to the said Henry Duke of Grafton, are long since determined.

That dureing the Life of the late Queen Dowager the said Forrest, being granted to her Trustees in Trust for her said late Majestie, dureing her Life, Your Petitioner is Son and lleire Male of the Body of the said Henry Duke of Grafton, was hindred from the enjoying the Benefitt of the said Grant; and since her Majesties Death, some Question hath been made touching the Validity of the said Letters Patents, on Pretence of some Want of Forme in the same, and Your Petitioner is kept out of the said Office by some Persons who have not any Right in themselves, by any Grant from Your Majestie, or any of Your Royall Predecessors.

In regard therefore that by the said Grant Your Majestie’s Royall Uncle King Charles the Second's Intentions appear to be, that the Heire Male of the said Henry Duke of Grafton should enjoy the said Office of Warden of the said Forrest;

Your Petitioner humbly beseeches Your Majestie, by Your Majestie’s Letters Patents, to ratifie and make good the said Letters Patents to Your Petitioner, and the Heires Males of his Body, and thereby to supply the Defects therein, if any such be, that Your Petitioner may enjoy the said Office, according to his said late Majestie’s gracious Intentions, Your Petitioner being advised that it is in Your Majestie’s Power so to do, Offices being no Part of the Land Revenue of the Crown.

And your Petitioner (as in Duty bound) shall ever pray, &c.

Whitehall, Treary Chambers,

9"' Xber, 1710.

To the Right HonWe the Lords Com" of Her Matie’s Treasury.

’May it. please your Lordships,

In Obedience to Your Lordships Comands signi-fyed to me by Mr. Lowndes, I have considered of y* annexed Petition 6f Charles Duke of Grafton, whereby he represents to Her Majesty, that King Charles the 2d, by his Letters Patents bearing Date the 12th Day of Jan,r, in the 32d Year of his Reign, granted to Henry Earle of Arlington, for the Term of his Life, the Office of Warden of the Forest of Whittlewood, in the County of Northampton, from the Death oif James Earl of Northampton, for whose Life that Office was before granted; and by the same Letters Patents did grant the said Office to Henry Dukie of Grafton, the Petitioner’s Father, and the Heirs Male of his Body, to hold from the Death of the said Henry Earl of Arlington, and James Earl of Northton, both long, since dead. That the Petitioner is Son and Heir Male of the Body of the said Duke of Grafton, but could not enjoy the Benefit of the said Grant during the Life of the late Queen Dowager, the said Forest being granted to Trustees for her during her Life, and since her Death hath been kept out of the said Office by some Persons who have not any Right in themselves, by any Grant from her Majesty, or any her Royal Predecessors; and the Validity of the said Letters Patents have been questioned on Pretence of some Want of Form in the same. And the Petitioner thereby prays, that in regard the said King Charles the 2nd’s Intentions appear to be, that the Heirs Male of the Body of the said Henry Duke of Grafton should enjoy the said Office, that Her Majesty would be graciously pleased to ratify and make good the said Letters Patents to the Petitioner, and the Heirs Male of his Body, and thereby to supply the Defects therein, if any such there be, the Petitioner being advised that ’tis in Her Majesty’s Power so to doe, Offices being no Part of the Land Revenue of the Crownand I doe must humbly certify Your Lordships, that long before the 32d Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, the Forest of Whittlewood, in the Countys of Northton and Bucks, was granted for a Term of Years, in Trust for the late Queen Dowager during her Life, and after in Trust for the Crown. That on the 12th of Janrr, in the 32d Year of King Charles the 2nd, the said late King, by Letters Patents, reciting therein a Grant made by King Charles the 1st to Sir Christopher Hatton, at the Nomination of James Earl of Northton, of the Offices mentioned in the Petition for the Life of the said Earl, in Trust for him, did grant the said Office to the said Henr. Earl of Arlington for his Life, when void by yc Death of the said Earl of Northton, and after both their Deceases to the said Henr. Duke of Grafton, and the Heirs Males of his Body issuing; and therein is contained a Clause declaring the said Grant shall be good and effectual, notwithstanding any Statute, Act, Ordinance, Provision, Proclamation, or Restriction, or any other Matter, Thing, or Cause, whatsoever, to the contrary. That the said Earl of Northampton and Henry Duke of Grafton, dying in the Life of the Queen Dowager, in Trust for whom the Forest was granted during her Life, and She being enabled to nominate to the said Office for her Life, Her Matr did appoint the late Earl of Feversham to the same for his Life, and he

surviving

32 Geo. III. 13 ° Februarii. 161

surviving the said late Queen, under Colour thereof, tho’ his Grant determined by her Death, kept Possession of the same during his Life, and the respective Rights of the Petitioner and the Lord Feversham were by their severall Petitions humbly laid before her Majesty, but no Determination was thereon. That the Objection made to the said Grant of King Charles the 2nd to the late Duke of Grafton was, that the Term of Years of the Queen Dowager’s Trustees in the Forest was not recited, as it ought to have been, and for that Reason the Grant wa3 void, unless made good by the Gen" non obstante therein, which I doubt will not supply that Defect, although the Petitioner is advised by his Councell that it will. The Patent is very ill drawn, which was not the Fault of the late Duke of Grafton, but the Neglect of those who had the preparing and passing it; and the Intention of the late King is fully therein expressed to be, that that Office should be enjoyed by the said Duke, and the Heirs Males of his Body; and I am of Opinion it is in her Maty’’ Power to supply that Defect, by granting the Office as the Petitioner desires, the Restraint which her Majesty hath been pleased to submit to by the Act of the Civil List extending only to Grants of Lands, &c. for which Rents might be reserved, and not of Offices.

All which is most humbly submitted to Your Lordship’s great Wisdoms.

EDWD NORTHEY.

To the R* Honw‘ Robert Earle of Oxford and Earle Mortimer, Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain.

In Obedience to Your Lordship’s Comands signified by Mr. Lowndes, that Applicacon having been made to the Queen, by the Duke of Grafton, for confirming his Grant of the Office of Master Forester of the Forest of Whittlewood in the Counties of Northton. and Bucks, your Lordship was pleased to direct me to propose (in case such Confirmacon should be made) what Cautions or Clauses I think necessary to be incerted for preserving the Queen’s Timber.

I humbly represent to Your Lordship, that in order thereto, I have read over that Grant, and do not find any Allowances menconed therein, but all referred to former Grants; I have therefore (that I might be able to give Your Lordship a true State thereof) searched the Records at the Tower, and find, that at the last Justice in Eyre’s Seat, held by the Earle of Holland, in Anno 1636, the following Claimes were allowed to Spencer Earl of Northton. then Master Forrester; (viz.)

The Office of Master Forrester, and Master of the King’s Wild Beasts of the said Forrest, and all other Wild Beasts and Coneys within the same, during his Life, with a Fee of Five Pounds per Annum.

Power to name a Deputie, and to constitute all the Under Forresters and Page Keepers, and at his Pleasure to remove them, and constitute others, with the several Yearly Allowances following:

To the Master Forrester all Windfalls, dry and withered Trees called Dotards, and the Roots of Trees cutdowne, and One Acre of Underwood, cutt and sold in each Copice every Year.

I am humbly of Opinion, that the onely Way to preserve the Queen's Timber in that Forest, -which is at present very considerable, and will increase, is to take off the Allowance of Wood, and in lieu thereof to pay them 10#. per Load, in Money, which will amount to 115/. io#. 0 pr Ann. and added to the Allowance of 231. 6 8 d. payable out of the Exchequer, makes in all 138/. lbj. 8 which may be raised Yearly by Sale of Trees already rendered unfitt for the Use of the Navy, by browseing and unlawful Methods used to make dead Trees, and the same may be paid to the respective Officers, in Vol. 47.

Proporcon to their severall Claims of Wood and Money.

That they may be allowed Windfall Wood, such as dead and rotten Boughs, blowne down by ordinary Winds, and the Rootes of Trees cutt downe.

It may be objected, that in hard Frosts and Snow the Deer will want the Browse for Sustenance, though in several Forests none is allowed; but in such Case the Keepers may be suffered to lopp some Trees that have been lopped before, and will' afford such Browse as the Deer will feed on, but those not without the Assignment of the Surveyor of the Woods or his Deputy, and some of the Regarders, if there be any, and that, together with Hay that may be made in the Grounds laid to each Lodge, as it’s reasonable to believe for that Purpose, by the Allowance of 3 /. 6. 8. pr Ann. for making Hay for tire Deer, &c. will be sufficient.

N° 7.

The Answer of his Grace the Duke of

to the Precept of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue.

1 hold the Office of M ai den or Ranger of the Forest of // 'hitllciicod (viz'.) the Superintendency of the Whole, with the Powers and Duties common to all Rangers of Forests, together with that of Master of the Game in the same, by Grant under the Great Seal of Charles 1IJ, after the Life of Catharine Queen Dowager. The Office is Hereditary, hut determinable on Failure of llcirs Male from myself, and of Lord Southampton, when the same would revert to the Crown. As Chief Ranger, or Master of the Game, I am entitled to 20/. i6j. 8 from the Exchequer; besides which I was entitled to a certain Number of Loads of Timber by virtue of the aforesaid Grant, which specifics the Quantities to each Head Keeper and Page Keeper; in lieu of which the 't reasury, on my Grandfather’s Representation, altered it to a fixed Sum to each Person above Go Years ago. He always gave his Share, as I have constantly done mine, among the Keepers; therefore I will not speak t5 the precise Sum, but 1 believe it to be about 401, per Ann. and paid by the Deputy Surveyor of the Woods. I receive no Fees or Emoluments whatever, but such as arise from the pleasurable Consideration of the Place, &c. on which I cannot set the Value for another, but feel how estimable these are to me. I kill for my own Table what Deer I want, and give the rest that is killed among my Neighbours. The Messuage, &c. which I live in as Ranger, reverts to the CrownWhen the Office does; till then it belongs not to the Crown, but is my Property, and that of my Heirs Male. My Grandfather and myself have laid out

full 10,000l. upon it. ----- --- The Land I hold as

Ranger is 52 Acres of Meadow, Tythe free - - - - 104

About 300 Acres in a Fine Lawn, but where the Deer are also admitted - - 200

Value per Ann. - £. 304

Resides a large Lake, near 40 Acres, made at my Grandfather’s Expence. — There are Five Walks, each

of which have a Head Keeper. There are Eight Under or Page Keepers besides, to all which my Grant gives me the Appointment. They are paid by the Deputy Surveyor of the Woods, as above; and you will have received from them the Amount of their Salaries. They have each a Habitation suitable for a Keeper, and no better; with a pretty Meadow. They are removeable at my Pleasure. I receive no Rents or other Sums of Money for the Use of the Crown. Prosecutions of Deer Stealers, Poachers, and Mood Stealers, &c. have been carried on at the Expence of my Grandfather and myself, without troubling the Treasury with them, though we have never considered that Charge to be incumbent on us to defray. There are Brow se Trees, so called, or Pollards, having been set out as such many Years before my Time, under a Treasury Warrant. These in their Turns are lopped for the Deers browsing, and in the Summer are faggotted up for the Keepers Fire, for which it seldom is sufficient. My Share of this is no larger than that of the Under Keeper. — None is allowed to be sold. No Timber Tree is touched or used for any Repairs, unless by Order of the Treasury. The Keepers can best answer the Question concerning the Number of Deer kept, and the Number killed, and I conclude have done so. What Hay is given to the Deer is made, &c. at my sole Expence, except One Stack, put upon his Lawn by the Lieutenant of the Forest, Joseph Sim/th, Esquire, w hose Name

and Office I omitted before. The Tenure of his depends on my Pleasure, as well as the Offices of the other Keepers. 1 lis Meadows and Lawn are very valuable. I know of no Intrusions or Encroachments on the Rights of the Crown within the Forest, or at least so inconsiderable as hardly to be mentioned as such. Three or Four poor Cottagers may have very lately got, among them all, Half an Acre for Potatoes, adjoining to their Dwellings. Even those are told perpetually that they may expect to have them taken from them. All the M'ood in Whittlewood Forest (Timber Trees only excepted) is my Property, by virtue of another Grant of Charles IP. I hope and believe that no Timber on any private Estate was ever more carefully attended to than that in this Forest, from the Time our Family have held it, but it has suffered greatly by being left to grow too close and thick, and in many Places weakened thereby. The Soil is peculiarly kind to the Growth of M’ood. The Right of Common is without Stint, being bond side the Property of the Inhabitants of the many In and Out Parishes who have that Right, of which the Keepers will have sent you the Names. Horse and Cow Stock only are admitted; no Swine are allowed at all; and the Cattle are considered by us Foresters as belonging to the Common from Jllay 1st to All Saints l)ay (O. S.) The Forest is not cleared of Cattle during the Fence Month. During the Winter Ilaining the Ground is too wet and bare to keep Cattle, even if they could prove a Right. No Payments are made by Persons having Right of Common. The Forest Cattle are usually drove fas the Expression is) Once a Year, by One of the Verderors and Keepers; and if any unlawful Cattle are found, these are pounded, and a few Pence paid on letting them out, which never can pay the Charges of Driving. The rest of the Cattle are branded. I know of nothing that can be done to improve Four of the W’alks in the Forest; for the fine State of the Wood and Timber in those Four M'alks would surprize any one who is a Judge of the Effects to be expected from the Right that the Deer and Cattle have to go into the Coppices at Nine Years Grow th, feeding in and upon them for Twelve Years, till the Age of Twenty-one Years, at which, by long Custom, they are to be cut, and not sooner.

Hasteborough, the Fifth Walk, (as I have been told by old People) was little inferior to any, till the Timber

was,

165

32 Geo. III. 13° Februarii.

was, illegally in my Opinion, taken down by the Crown, in the standing Coppices of this Walk, towards the Building of Blenheim. The dying Interest of the Queen Dowager did not move her to stir in the Business; and the Perquisites of certain Officers were too tempting to expect them to start Objections in Defence of the Interest of others. The sad Consequence is, that both Timber and Underwood are miserable in that Walk; even one or Two Coppices left without the Means of inclosing the m. I have endeavoured to redeem One, a large one, which had not been inclosed for Eighty-four Years; I flatter myself that the Expence I have been at in mounding it, &c. will answer to me, if so it must of course to the Crown, to whom the Timber will belong, and without Cost.

I should have mentioned, that on One of the Five Walks, called Shrob Walk, there is no Right of Common at all.

On the Whole, I am of Opinion that, except Hasle-borough Walk, the whole Forest is in an excellent State for the Growth of Underwood, and of Timber; and I have greatly my Doubts whether, if sold Tomorrow, the greatest Part would not be kept in Wood, as likely to pay in that State best. Fuel and Hedging Stuff, &c. are so scarce, and so much demanded, and of course so dear in those Parts, that the Country for Twenty Miles around would feel the Distress, if such a large Tract was to be converted to Pasture or Arable; not to mention the Want which the vast Number of Hands would find, and which this populous Neighbourhood sends now into the Forest to Wood-work all Winter, in a Country which by the Nature of it has not the Advantages to employ its Labourers at that Season, which many others have, and where the Poor’s Rates come up to, if they do not exceed, those of any other Place unconnected with Manufactures, &c. These Circumstances I am persuaded will never escape your Consideration, nor that of the Legislature.

I ought perhaps to have added to my Answer to your Third Question (respecting the Tenure on which my Office is held) that I have Seven Sons, Three of them grown up, One married. My Brother has as many, at least, Two of whom are married. The Male. Descendants of every of these having their Rights prior to the Expectancy of the Crown, I will leave it to you to calculate the present Value of such a Reversion, for lam unable.

Grafton,

Ranger of the Forest of January 30th 1790.

Board of Green Cloth, 11th May 1790.

Gentlemen,

In Answer to your Letter of the 6th Instant, I send you the Particulars of the Venison ordered to be served to the Household, by Warrants of 1st Queen Anne. 1st Geo. I. 1st Geo. II. and 1st Geo. III. Ido

not find any Entry of any prior to that of the 1st James II. which was sent in a Letter from this Board, the 5th of February last.

I am,

Gentlemea,

Your most humble Servant, To John Call, and J.

After my hearty Commendations: Whereas her Majesty, by Letters Patents under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing Date the 19th Day of July 1712, in the Eleventh Year of her Reign, hath given, granted, and confirmed unto his Grace Charles Duke of Grafton, and the Heirs Male of his Body issuing, the Office of Master Forester of her Majesty’s Forests and Parks of Whittleuood, in the County of Northton, and Master Conductor of the Wild Beasts of the said Forest, with several Powers, Authorities, Liberties, Privileges, and Advantages therein particularly mentioned, and all and singular Wages, Fees, Rewards, Allowances, Commodities, Rights, and Emoluments whatsoever, to the said Offices, or any of them, belonging or appertaining (except as in the said Letters Patents are excepted): And whereas in the said Letters Patents it is specially recited, that the Claims heretofore Annually allowed to the Master Forester, and the rest of the Officers of the said Forest, were as followeth; vis.

Allowances.

And whereas her Majesty by the same Letters Patents (for the Causes and Considerations therein mentioned) hath declared that in all Times coming for the firture the said Claims or Allowances of Wood shall be absolutely abolished, discharged, and made void; but that nevertheless the said respective Officers and Ministers, heretofore having and receiving the said Allowances of Wood, shall have and receive in lieu thereof, for the future, an Allowance in Money, after the Rate of Ten Shillings for every Load of Wood, so that there now becomes payable to the said several and respective Officers and Ministers, on their former Allowances in Money, the Yearly Sum of Twenty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, and for and in lieu of their former Allowances in Wood, which amounted to Two hundred Thirty-one Load, the Yearly Sum of One hundred and Fifteen Pounds Ten Shillings, computing the same at the Rate of Ten Shillings a Load as aforesaid: These are therefore, by virtue of the said Letters Patents, to direct, authorize, and require you, in the Presence and with the Assistance of the Master Forester, or his Deputy for the Time being, and any Two or more of the Under Foresters there, Yearly and every Year, to mark, fell, and cut down, or cause to be marked, felled, and cut down, at the most fitting and proper Season for dqing thereof, so many dotard and decayed Trees, or other Trees, within the said Forest, not fit for the Service of her Majesty’s Navy, as by the Sale thereof, and of the Lops, Tops, and Offal Wood of the same (which Sale you are hereby authorized and appointed to make) shall be sufficient to raise the said several and respective Yearly Sums of Twenty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, and One hundred and Fifteen Pounds Ten Shillings, and thereupon to pay unto the said respective Officers and Ministers for the Time being, Yearly and every Year, their several and respective Parts and Shares thereof in Manner aforesaid, and take Receipts, specifying therein that the Money so paid is not only in full of all former Allowances in Money for the respective Years so to be paid,

Whereas We are given to understand, by a Report of Charles Wither, Esq. Surveyor General of Our Woods, bearing Date the 22d of June last, which you have laid before Us for Our Pleasure to be signified therein, that the Great Lodge, Outhouses, and Buildings thereunto belonging, at Wakefield, in Our Forest of Whittlcwood; in the County of Northampton, which are held and enjoyed by Our right trusty and right entirely beloved Cousin and Councellor, Cha' Duke of Grafton, as Ranger in Fee of the said Forest, are at present in so ruinated a Condition that the estimated Charge of putting the same into substantial Repair does amount to the Sum of Three thousand Five hundred Pounds, which the said Charles Duke of Grafton proposes to perform and defray at his own Cost and Expence, in case One hundred and Fifty Loads of rough Timber growing within the said Forest be assigned him towards the same, to which We, being graciously pleased to condescend and agree, Our Will and Pleasure is, and We do hereby authorize, direct.

and require you to give Warrant unto the said Sur- Eighth Ibport veyor General, in the Presence and with the Assistance iievenuc*^ of such Officers of our said Forest as should or ought \ \

to be present in Cases of this Nature, to mark, fell, and cut down, or cause to be marked, felled, and cut down, in such Part and Places of the said Forest where the same may most conveniently be spared, so many Trees, not fit for the Service of Our Navy, as may be sufficient to produce the said One hundred and Fifty Loads of rough Timber, and to deliver the said One hundred and Fifty Loads of rough Timber, when felled, to the said Charles Duke of Grafton, or his Order, to be employed in and about the said Buildings and Repairs; and you are to direct and require Our said Surveyor to take Care that the Bark, Lops, Tops, and Offal Wood of the Trees to be felled, be sold, and disposed to the best Advantage for Our Service, and the Monies arising thereby be brought to his Account of Woodsales, within such Space of Time as you shall think fit to direct and appoint And whereas W e are further given to understand, by the said Report, that the Under Foresters, Under Keepers, or Page Keepers, and other Under Officers within the said Forest, have, instead of Allowances of Wood heretofore claimed and taken by them, to the great Waste and Destruction of the Timber and Trees within the said Forest, Allow ances in Money made to them Yearly by Our said Surveyor out of Woodsales; and that it will be for the Service of the Crown, and the Encouragement of the Keepers to be vigilant and active in their Duty and Attendance, in case the Suihe of Ninety-eight Pounds by the Year, over and above the present Allowances, be allowed and made payable to them in Manner following; that is to say,

The Answer of Joseph Smyth, Esquire, Lieutenant and Woodward of the Forest of and

Keeper of Sholbroo/c Walk, in the said Forest, to the Precept of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue.

The said Joseph Smyth saith, That he holds, by virtue of Letters Patent from the Crown, the Office of Woodward of the Forest of Whittlexvood, during His Majesty’s Pleasure. That he receives as Woodward a Yearly Fee or Salary of Five Pounds, which is paid by the Receiver General of the Land Revenue, by virtue of a Debenture from the Auditor; and a Yearly Allowance of Twenty Pounds, paid by Reuben Capes, Deputy to the Surveyor General of the Woods, from the Sale of dotard and decayed Trees, in lieu of a Fee of Twelve Pence in the Pound, formerly received by the Woodwards of the said Forest, from the Buyers of Wood or Timber there; and he has also a Fee of Four Pence for every Tree felled there, which is paid by the Purchasers of the Timber and Wood.

That he holds likewise the Office of Lieutenant or Deputy Warden of Whittlexvood Forest, and Keeper of Sholbrook Walk there, by Appointment of his Grace the Duke of Grafton, Lord Warden of the said Forest, during his Grace’s Pleasure. That, as Lieutenant, he has the Superintendance and Care of the whole Forest under the Lord Warden; and, as Keeper of Sholbrook, he has the particular Charge of that Walk. That he receives Annually from the Surveyor General of the Woods, or his Deputy, the Sum of Ninety-seven, Pounds Ten Shillings for the several antient Fees and Allowances following; vis.

That the Time allowed for the In-Towns to turn in their Horses and Cows, is about the Fifth of April, and to take them out on the Twelfth of November; and for the Out-Towns to turn in about the Fourth of May, and take out the Twenty-fifth of September Yearly. of Strangers, is by a Forest Drift. Those that are com- v monable and branded, pay One Penny for the Drift.

Those that are commonable, and not branded, pay Four Pence per Head, and One Penny for the Drjft. And when any Cattle are found belonging to any one who has no Right of Common, a Penalty of Ten Shillings per Head is demanded; which Monies are usually divided among the Keepers of the respective Walks where the Drift is made. The planting of Acorns in particular Parts of the Forest would be of great Use.

The Examination of John Hammond, Keeper of Haslcborough Walk; taken upon Oath, the Oth Day of December 1790. The Examination of William Taylor, Keeper of Hanger Walk; taken upon Oath, the 6th Day of December 1790. The Examination of Charles Heath, Keeper of Wakefield Walk; taken upon Oath, the 6th Day of December 1790. The Examination of Reuben Capes, Keeper of Shrob Walk; taken upon Oath, the 6th Day of December 1790.

Appointment. Saith, That he is Keeper of boroughWalk, in Forest, appointed by his Grace the Duke of Grafton, during his Pleasure. That he is Keeper of Hanger Walk by the like Appointment, during Pleasure. That he is Keeper of Wakefield Walk, by the like Appointment, during Pleasure. That he is Keeper of Shrob Walk, by the like Appointment, during Pleasure.

Duty. That the Duty of his Office is to take Care of the Woods, Deer, and Game, within the said Walk, and to assist in other Parts of the Forest, when required. That his Duty is to take Care of the Woods Timber, Vert, and Venison, and to kill or assist in killing the Deer when required. That the Duty of his Office is to look after the Deer, Woods, and Game, and to assist in killing the Deer in this Walk, or in other Parts of the Forest, if required. That the Duty of his Office is to take Care of the Woods, and Game within the said Walk, and to assist in killing Venison when required, in any Part of the Forest.

Salary. That he is paid by Reuben Capes, Deputy to the Surveyor General, the Yearly Salary of 25/. 6s. 8 out of which is deducted, for the Surveyor’s Poundage, the Sum of 1 /. 5 4 d. TI.3 like Salary, and Deduction for Poundage. That his Salary is 26/. per Annum, paid by Joseph Smyth, Esquire, Lieutenant of the Forest. That his Salary is 25/. 6 s. 8 per Annum (One Shilling in the Pound deducted to the Surveyor’s Use) payable out of Monies arising by Wood Sales, by virtue of Warrants from the Treasury.

Fees on Venison. That the Fees received by him for Venison killed within this Walk, including the Value of a Fee Buck and Fee Doe, amount to about 30/. 6 s. 6d. per Annum, or more, which Fees are paid by the Receivers of the Venison, and he receives about 23/. 17 s. 6d. per Annum, by Sale of the Skins and Offal. That the Fees received by him for Venison, amount, on an Average, to about 10/. 3 s.4 d.per Annum, and the Emoluments from the Skins and Offal to about 10/. i6j. per Annum, and he has also a Fee Buck and Fee Doe yearly, which he sells for 61. \6d. That the Fees which he receives for Venison killed in Wakefield Walk, amount, on an Average, to about 50/. per Annum, which are paid by the Receivers of the Venison, and the Profit from the Skins and Offal of such Venison to about 651, per Annum, or more, arising by the Sale thereof. That he has a Yearly Allowance of Six Guineas, paid by the Duke of Grafton, in lieu of a Fee Buck and Fee Doe, no Deer being kept within this Walk.

Lodge and Land. That he occupies a Lodge worth 51. per Annum, and about 14 Acres of Sweard Ground, worth 14/. per Annum, out of which he pays for the Land Tax, and House and Window Tax, 1 /. 18 s. 3 d.per Annum. That he occupies a Lodge and Offices, and about 11 Acres of Land, worth 15/. ioj. per Annum, subject to the Payment of the House, Window, and Land Tax, amounting together to 2/. 1 6s.a d.a Year. That he occupies a Lodge worth about 5 I.per Annum, and 6 Acres of Land, worth about 5/. 1 per Annum, subject to the Payment of 1/. 14$. for House and Window Taxes. That he occupies a Lodge in Shrob Walk, with 19 Acres of Pasture, worth about 30 I.per Annum, subject to the Payment of Land and Window Tax.

c That he has about 1,200 Faggots - Yearly, from the Wood cut for browsing the Deer, within W

worth 20 s.per Hundred, after Payment of the Expences of cutting.

That no Timber is cut Annually for the Forest Officers, except for Payment of their Salaries; and when any Timber is wanted for Repairs, it is cut by Authority of the Surveyor’s Warrant to his Deputy.

That there are about 360 Head of Deer of all Sorts in Hasleborough , as nearly as he can ascertain.

That about 15 Brace of Bucks and 8 Brace of Does are Annually killed within his Walk, for the Use of Noblemen and Gentlemen, whose Property sustains Damage by the Deer, and 6 Brace of Bucks and 6 Brace of Does are Annually sent from other Walks of the Forest; but as to other Warrants he refers to the lieutenant of the Forest, and his Deputy.

That no Timber is allowed to the

Keepers; but Browse Wood is cut for the Deer, according to the Severity of the Winter, and when the Deer have done with it, alter Lady Day, it is gathered up for Fuel, for the Use of the Keepers, of which this Examinant hath about 8 or 9 Loads, worth about 20 per Load.

That the Number of Deer kept in the Forest, or in any particular Walk, cannot be ascertained, but this Examinant thinks there may be about 100 Head of all Sorts in Hanger Walk.

Of which on an Average are killed 5 Brace of Bucks and Brace of Does Yearly, exclusive of the Keeper’s Fee Buck and Fee Doe: All Venison Warrants, and Orders for Venison, are directed to the Lieutenant of the Forest, or his Agent, to whom he refers for an Account thereof.

L

That he has Annually about 1l Loads of Fuel Wood, from the Wood cut for browsing the Deer in Wakefield IValk, worth about 20 s.per Load, after paying the Expences of cutting, &c.

That no Timber is Annually cut for Repairs; but when any are wanted, they are done by the Surveyor of the Woods.

That the Number of Deer in Wakefield Walk, cannot be well ascertained,

but have been computed to be about 1,000 Head of all Sorts.

That the Number killed Annually on an Average, is about 37 Brace of Bucks and 29 Brace of Does, of which 6 Brace of Bucks, and 6 Brace of Does, are returned to the Warrants of the Board of Green Cloth, 5 or 6 Brace of Bucks, and about 5 Brace of Does (as they can be spared) to the Cofferer’s Warrants. The Chief Justice in Eyre, his Secretary, the Verderors and Purlieu Ranger, each have Fee Venison. Some are ordered by his Grace the Duke of Grafton for his own Use, and some to his Friends, and the rest are disposed of by the Lieutenant to the Gentlemen and others round the Forest, that sustain Damage by the Deer.

That he has the Browse Wood of the Oak and Ash Trees in this Walk, (such as have heretofore been browsed) and cuts Annually about 700 of Faggots, worth about 71, per Annum; but that no Timber Trees are cut down for Fuel in this Walk, or in any other Part of the Forest, for the Use of the Forest Officers.

Not Annually for Repairs, but occasionally by Warrant from the Lords of the Treasury.

That about 1,500 Weight of Hay, worth about 21. 5 s.is Annually provided for the Deer within JVa Ik, as the Severity of the Season requires, at the Expence of the Keeper of the said Walk.

That the Townships of and Slapton pay as each Yearly, to the Keeper of Hasleborough , which they call Fence Money, or Hen Money, and the Townships of and

Crofield pay about 155. Annually, more or less, which is collected from House to House, and divided between the Keeper and Page of Hasleborough Walk.

That to prevent the Forest being surcharged by Commoners, or the Admission of Cattle of Strangers, the Cattle are driven to a convenient Place, and there kept, till Notice is sent to the different Parishes to which the Cattle are supposed to belong, for the Owners to take them away; and if any be found that have no Right of Common, the Commoners that do appear generally put a Fine of ioj. per Head on each Beast. The Money collected on that Day is mostly expended; the Residue is divided between the Keeper and Page of the Walk where the Drift is made.

That the last Drift but One, the Number of Cattle driven amounted to 96 Horses, and 191 Cows, in all 287; and the Cattle la9t driven were 124 Horses, and 205 Cows, in all 329.

That the Cattle belonging to Persons having Right of Common, and which are branded, pay One Penny for the Drift for Horses and Cow s separate, be the number more or less, of each Sort, and those not branded, pay per Head, which Money is likewise divided as aforesaid.

That no Notice is taken of the Fence Month; and the In-Towns are apt to encroach on the Time of Winter Haining.

That the Cattle admitted to depasture in the Forest, are Horse and Cow Kinds only; and all others are excluded.

That when any Imposition is suspected in regard to the Cattle turned into the Forest, a Drift is made, and the Owners of such Cattle as have Right of Common, and are branded, pay only One Penny for the Drift; those unbranded pay per Head, and One Penny their Drift; and those that have no Right pay a Penalty according to their Trespass, sometimes as high as 105. per Head: Which Money is divided among the Keepers of the Walk where the Drift is made.

Memorandum:

This Return is from the best Account we can collect of the Numbers of Cattle of each Sort from each Parish turned into the Forest of Whittlexvood by the Commoners last Year, which we think near upon an Average the Stock turned in Annually: But as the Pasture upon the Commonable Parts of the Forest is some Years mud) better than others, the general Stock is uncertain. — Some Years a Common will turn in several, other Years few, or none, according as is most convenient to themselves, therefore the general Stock of Cattle, as we have before observed, is variable.

The Answer of J. Frederick fVillesy Esquire, One of the Verderors of the Forest of Whittlezeood, to the Precept of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue; dated January 18th, 1790.

The Duty of my Office in Whittlcwood Forest is to inspect the Vert and Venison. I was appointed by the Freeholders of the County of Northampton; my Appointment is for Life. My Allowance is by no Means certain, but depends upon the Sale of Underwood. Since I have enjoyed the Office, which has been about Seven Years, I have never received Yearly more than Seventeen Pounds, or less than Nine Pounds. The only certain Fee I have is a Buck and a Doe. I occupy no Messuage or Lands belonging to the Crown, receive no Rents, nor make any Disbursements by virtue of my Office. No Timber is cut for Forest Officers, but to pay their Salaries. None of the Timber has been destroyed, that I know of The Poor in the Neighbourhood have trespassed to pick up Acorns, and upon the Keepers applying to Justices they could meet with no Redress. Fifteen Forest Towns and Hamlets have Right of Common on all the Commonable Lands of the Forest. Six are In-Towns; viz*. Whitfield, Whittlcbury, and Silvcrston, Potter spury, and Yardley Gobion, Passenham and Daneshanger. Nine Out-Towns; viz*. Syresliam and Crasfield, Paulerspury and HcathencotCy Graf tony Alderton, fVieken, Lillingstone-Lovell, Lillingstone-Dayrell, Wappenham, and Slapton, without Stint. The Cattle Vol, 47.

The Answer of Humbo Rigby, Esquire, Purlieu Ranger of the Forest of fVhittlcuood, to the Precept of the Commissioners of the Land Revenue; dated 16th December 1789.

My Office in the Forest of Whittleuood is that of Purlieu Ranger, to hunt out and protect the King’s Deer in the Purlieus. I was appointed by the Duke of Grafton, and my Warrant signed by the King. My Appointment is for Life. My Annual Salary is

Twenty

180 130 Februarii.A. 1792.

Eighth Report Twenty Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence (Sur-of the Board of veyor’s Poundage deducted) and is paid by Mr. Land Revenue^ Capes, Deputy Surveyor. I have no other Fee or Emolument than a Buck and a Doe. I occupy no Messuage or Lands belonging to the Crown, receive no Rents, nor make any Disbursements, by virtue of my Office. I have no Allowance of Fuel Wood, or Timber for Repairs. I do not know of any Spoil, Waste, or Destruction having been committed of the Woods and Timber, nor of any existing Abuses injurious to the Rights of the Crown, in the said Forest. I can give no Answer to the Inquiries concerning the Right of Common on the Forest, the Times the Cattle are admitted, or when turned in, or taken out, not living within the Forest, nor having any Business to inquire into them.

Whereas Our right trusty and right entirely well-beloved Cousin and Councellor Augustus Henry Duke of Grafton, who holds to himself, and the Heirs Male of his Body issuing, the Office of Master of Our Forest and Parks of Whittlewoo in the Counties of Northampton and Bucks, did by a Writing under his Hand and Seal, dated the Ninth Day of March 1766, by virtue of the Powers vested in him by the Letters Patent or Grant under which he holds the said Office, appoint Humbo Rigby, Esquire, to be Purlieu Ranger of the said Forest; and We are graciously pleased to give and grant unto the said Humbo Rigby the like Salary and Allowances, in respect of his said Office, as are made and given to the Under Foresters there; that is to say,

After our hearty Commendations. Whereas you, y* Surveyor Generali of their Ma'* Woods on this side Trent, did in your Presement of ye 8th Instant (amongst other Things) sett forth, that in the Forrest of Whittlewood, in y* County of Northampton, there are great Quantityes of Pollard and decayed Trees titt onely for Country Uses and Firewood, and that you conceived it would be for their Ma'1 Service to cause Sales thereof to be made Annually, not exceeding y* Value of One thousand Pounds in any one Yeare: That there are sevall Walkes and Lodges in y* sd Forrest, in respect whereof y* Keepers or Pages do claime great Quantityes of Fuell Wood, which are usually taken without any Assignement, & thereby many Thousands of good Trees are lopped & polled, & sometimes topped, wch is y' Occasion that so many become dotard and decayed, & that you have forbid y* Keepers to comitt any of the like Spoiles for y* future, or take any Firewood excepting such moderate Quantityes as may be spared from old Trees that have been formerly lopt, and such onely to be taken by Assignin' of the Woodward or his Deputy, with some of the Regard, & not otherwise: And have therein further certifyed, that (the Revenue of ye Coppices in y° s'1 Forrest of Whittlewood being granted away, and the Timber Trees onely reserved to ye Crowne) it is convenient y* s" Coppices should be carefully Surveyed every Yeare before'any of them be cutt; and that where the Growth of the Underwood will admitt thereof, so many Trees may be nuinbred and markt up as are fitt to grow to Timber, & given in Charge to y* Woodward & Keeper of the Walke: And have therein also proposed that no Trees for Gates, Railcs, &c. be felled for encloseing of the said Coppices, until a Certificate be returned by you or y* Surveyor for the Time being of such Survey taken, & also of what old Trees are fitt to be cutt. All which his Ma‘r haveing been pleased to approve of, these are, pursuant to their Ma'* Letters of Privy Seale in this Behalfe, bearing Date the 28<l> of this Instant A prill, to direct & authorize you the sd Surveyor Gen11 noiv being, and ye Surveyo' for the Time being, in y* P'sence & with the Assistance of some of the principal Officers of y* sd Forrest of Whittlewood, to cause so many Pollard or decayed Trees as aforesaid (not being any of those that are or may be in any wise fitt for Shipp Timber) to be felled & cutt downe at seasonable Times within the said Forrest, & sold Yearly, as by the Sale thereof shall or may raise any Sume not exceeding One thousand Pounds p Ann. for so long Time as the same may be done without P'judice to y* said Forrest, or that Orders be given to y* contrary: And also that you ye sd Surveyor Gen11 now and for y* Time being doe take Care that y* Orders lately given by you ye said Surveyo' to the Keepers of the said Forrest as aforesaid, touching their Browse & Fuell Wood, be duely comply’d with, and that y* Regulations for felling the said Coppices, &c. be likewise duely observed.

And whereas in y* said Presenlm* of ye said Surveyo' Gen" it is conteyned, That in ye Forrest of

Lund Revenue.

Salsev, in y* said County of Nortftton the Revennuc W'"'1 Report of y* Coppices therein are all granted from the ll,c Boar'1 Crowne (the Timber Trees onely excepted) and ye immoderate Browsing in y* sd Forrest, &. Firewood taken by the Keepers there, is very prejudicial! to their Ma" Woods therein Ami you did therefore,

That as to y* cutting of the Coppices Yearely, and Allowances for Browse Sc Firewood, this Forrest, and the Keepers thereof, might be under the like Regulations as are above proposed & directed for Whittle-wood aforesaid: That y*. three Keepers Lodges are very old, and much out of Repairc, & to make the same conveniently habitable would require at least Sixty Pounds for each of the said Keeper's Lodges,

& Twenty-five Pounds for y* Page Keeper’s Ix)dge; and that the Charge thereof might be defrayed by Sale of some of the old & most defective Trees in the said Forrest of Salsey; And also, that the Keepers, after such Reparations made, should enter into Bonds to keep the said Lodges, at their owne F.xpences, in good and sufficient Repairc dureing their Abode therein, which his Ma‘r haveing also approved of.

These are, by vertue of ye sd Letters of Privy Seale, to authorize and direct you, ye Surveyo' now being, and y° Surveyo' for the Time being, to take Care that the Keepers of ye s* Forrest of Salsey doe observe in the like Orders for Browse Fuell Wood as is above ordered and directed for Whittlewood Forrest; And that ye cutting of ye Coppices therein be under the same Regulation with those of Whittlewood: And you sd Surveyo', now and for ye Time being, are hereby Further authorized Sc directed, in the P'sence & with yc Assistance of some of the principall Officers of y* said Forrest of Salsey, to fell, or cause to be felled & cutt downe, and to their Ma" best Advantage, so many of the old and most defective Trees in the said Forrest of Salsey (not being such as are or shall be fitt for Shipping) as by y* Sale thereof will raise the Surae of One hundred and Eighty Pounds towards repairing the Three Keepers Lodges; and also the Suiiie of Twenty-five Pounds for Repaive of the Page Keeper’s Lodge there; and that you expend ye same in repairing the said Lodges, and take Bond from the said Keepers respectively for maintaining the same so repaired during their Abodes therein as is above proposed: And lastly, you the said Surveyour are hereby directed to receive all yc Moneys arising by the Sales aforesaid, and to pay the same into the Receipt of y* Excheq' (except such Part thereof as is directed to be expended in the said Repaire); and you are also to render an Acco' of your Proceedings herein before their Ma" Auditor of the said County, as often as you shall be thereunto required, and least Once in every Yeare. And for so doing this, being first entered with the said Auditor, shall be your sufficient Warrant.

Ninth Report To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of the Board of in Parliament assembled.

Land Revenue.

' The Ninth Report of the Commissioners appointed to enquire into the State and Condition of the Woods, Forests, and Land Revenues of the Crown, and to sell or alienate Fee Farm and other Unimproveable Rents.

The Forest of Rockingham is situated in the Northern Part of the County of Northampton, and is esteemed to have been antiently One of the largest Forests in the Kingdom.

A.D. ia86, in In a Perambulation dated 14th of Edward the the Chapter First, it is described to extend from the Town of minster. Northampton to Sta, being in Length about Thirty-three Mile«, and from the River Nene, on the South-East, to the Rivers Welland and on the North-West, being a medium Breadth of about 1299. Eight Miles. But on a subsequent Perambulation, In the Twer, in the 27th of the same King, those Limits were

163®*

Ibid.

1642 16 Cha* .1.

much contracted by the Reduction of many new Afforestations which had been made after the Accession of Henry the Second. In the 13th of Charles the First (near 340 Years afterwards) an Attempt was made, by a new Perambulation, to revive the extensive Limits described in that of the 14th of Edward the First; but the Bounds of the Forest were finally settled by an Inquisition taken 27th September, in the 17th of Charles the First, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament passed in the preceding Year, by which it was enacted, That the Meets and Bounds of the Forests should be the same as they were com- C. »6. monly known and reputed to have been in the 20th Year of King Janies the First.

This Forest consists of Three separate Districts, called the Bailiwicks of Rockingham, Brigstock, and Clive or Cliff, situated at the Distance of Two to Four Miles from each other. Their Bounds are minutely described in the Inquisition or Perambulation of 17 th Appendix, of Charles the First, of which a Copy is annexed to ** 1.

this Report; and each Bailiwick is divided into several Walks, the Keeperships of which are held in Fee, by the Officers under named;

The Three Bailiwicks were formerly under the Superintendance of One Warden, or Master Forester, of the whole Forest; which Office was granted in the 1st of James the First to Thomas Lord Burleigh, for Three Lives. Charles the First divided, or rather abolished that Office, and constituted Three Master Foresters of separate Districts. The Master Forester-

unconnected in respect to their Government or Management. The Election of Verderors is still continued, though their Office is become little more than nominal.

A very considerable Part of the Woods and Lands in all the Three Bailiwicks heretofore belonged to the Crown; but the greatest Part of those Possessions have ship of Rockingham Bailiwick, with Geddington Woods, been granted in Fee. ROCKINGHAM BAILIIVICK.

The Bailiwick of Rockingham comprises divers extensive Woods in the Parishes of Cottingham,

Great and Little Oakley, GLittle and

Corby, reputed to contain about 3,500 Acres, a large open Plain called Rockinghamshire, and several smaller

Plains, containing together about 560 Acres, and an inclosed Lawn, called Benefield Lawn, containing about 384 Acres.

The Woods and Plains within this Bailiwick belong to the Earls of Harcourt and Cardigan, Lord Sondes, George Finch Hatton, Esquire, and other Proprietors; and are subject to the Feed of the Deer, and Commonable to the adjacent Towns and Parishes.

The Lawn of Benefield, and the Keeperships of the several Walks, are held by Mr. Hatton, by virtue of a Grant in Fee to Sir Christopher Hatton, in the 25th of Queen Elizabeth, of The Custody of her Lawn of Benefield, and the Office of Page and Groom Keeper of that Lawn, and of her Deer within the same; the Offices of Keeper of the Outwoods called Thornhawe, haxve otherwise Wadehawe, and Corby Woods, and of Gretton Woods, and the West Bailiwick, within the Bailiwick of Rockingham; the Custody and Governance of the Deer within the said Lawn, Woods and Bailiwicks; and all Wages and other Profits thereto belonging; and the House called The Lazcn Lodge-, but reserving Power for the Warden of the Forest to occupy the same so long as he should remain there to superintend the Forest, and not otherwise: And also the Herbage and Pannage of the said Lawn of Benefield, with divers Privileges and Powers mentioned in the Grant, of which a Copy is annexed to this Report; and the Grantee covenanted to pay all Keepers Fees, and perform all necessary Repairs of the Premisses for ever.

The Lawn of Benefield is a Tract of Pasture Land in the Nature of a Park, inclosed and set apart for the Feeding of the Deer, and not subject to any Right of Common. The Grant of the Herbage and Pannage thereof entitled the Grantee to the Surplus Herbage above what might be necessary for the Sustenance of the Deer; and it appears to have been possessed in that Manner by the Hatton Family until about the Year 1718; when Lord Hatton presented a Petition to the King, representing that the Lawn produced no Profit to the Crown, except a small Number of Deer, and praying a Grant to disafforest the same.

In Consequence of that Petition a Commission was issued under the Great Seal, and an Inquisition taken on Oath, by which it was found that the said Lawn contained 237 Acres of Pasture Land, Forest Measure, (which at 21 Feet to the Pole is equal to about 384 Acres Statute Measure) " And that the Issues and

" Profits Annually accruing to the King from every N* 5.

" Acre thereof (Forest Measure) were of the clear " Annual Value, beyond Reprizes, of F'our Pence, and " no more."

And in the following Year a Grant was made to 14 April,

Henry Hoar, Esquire, in Trust for Lord Hatton, of 1721'"

" All the Annual and other Issues and Profits accruing to the Crown out of the said Lawn," for a Term of 31 Years from the Date, under a Rent of 3/. 19 j. per Annum, being the Amount of the estimated Value of Four Pence per Acre; with Clauses, authorizing the Grantee to inclose the La\vn with Hedges and Ditches, and convert it to Tillage or any other Uses; and declaring that it should, during that Term, be wholly disafforested; and that the Grantee should hold it free from all Custody and Depasturation of Deer and Wild Beasts whatsoever, by the King, or any claiming under him.

This Grant expired in the Year 1751, and has not been renewed; but the Rent of 3/. ipj. was paid to the Crown until the Year 1783, and was then discontinued.

Mr. Hatton informs us that the Powers given by this Grant to cultivate the Lawn, were not carried into Effect, it being found of more permanent Value remaining as Pasture Land. The Lawn, however, has been divided, and fenced with Quickset Hedges; and is stocked with Cattle and Sheep, by Mr. s

Tenants, but the Deer are not excluded.

We are not enabled to state what Stock of Deer are kept within this Bailiw'ick, nor how' many are Annually killed; nor are we informed what Keepers are employed, or what Wages, or other Charges, are paid by the Grantee, Mr. Hatton having declined answering our
