21. 8 s.!yd. per Annum, being One Third Part of the estimated Value of One Penny per Acre, of Forest Measure, and less than a Farthing per Acre Statute Measure: And Clauses were inserted in the Grant, exempting the Woods and Lands from all Forest Rights, Liberties, and Privileges; declaring them Free Hay during the Term, and granting all the Deer and Wild Beasts to the Earl of Westmorland, without Account, on Condition of exonerating the Crown from all Forest Charges concerning the Premisses.

On a Review of this Proceeding, the Circumstances attending it cannot but appear extraordinary. The Earl of Westmorland represented to the Crown, that the Charge of paying Keepers, and other Expences concerning the Forest, had been a great Burthen on him and his Family, and that they had a Right to be reimbursed; though the Offices were granted to his Ancestors on the express Condition of paying the Wages of the Keepers, and were accompanied with Grants of Woods and Lands of very great Value. Nor is it easy to discover on what Grounds the Herbage and Deer Browse were valued at only One Penny per Acre. It could not have been proportioned to the Damage done by the Deer, for Lord Westmorland represented his Woods to be almost entirely destroyed; nor to the Supply of Deer served for the Use of the Crown, for it hardly amounted to the Value of a single Brace of Bucks. One Consideration of the Grant was the discharging the Crown from all Forest Charges, from which the Crown was, in Fact, exempted by former Grants: And though the Suggestions of the Officers to whom Lord Westmorland’s Memorial was referred were followed, so far as was necessary for complying, in Appearance, with the Requisitions of the Act of the 1st of Queen Anne, in reserving a Third Part of the Annual Value as a Rent, yet the Advice they gave, to make the best Advantage of His Majesty’s Dem'esnes, was not attended to; and the valuable Lawns of Moorhay and Sulekay, containing near 400 Acres of Pasture Land, not subject to any Right of Common, and reserved for the Feeding of the King’s Deer, became discharged of that Incumbrance, and the full and undivided Possession of them was transferred to the Grantee, for the Consideration of less than a Farthing an Acre, Statute Measure.

The serving of Deer from Moorhay and Sulehay was of course discontinued from the Time of obtaining that Grant, which was afterwards successively renewed to the Earls of Westmorland, to make up the Term

to 31 Years, until the Year 1782, when Lord Westmorland surrendered the Term then in being, and obtained a Lease of the Herbage and Deer Browse for the «ame Three Lives for which the Office of Master Forester is '-Id.

In Consequence of these Grants, the Crown receives the Walk3 of Moorhay and Sulehay no other Return tw,n the sman Rent Qf 2l. 8$. 5 a Year; but when the '..gt mentioned Grant shall expire, we apprehend ,"lfc lights will revert again to the State they were in before >. a passing of the first Grant of the Herbage and Deer x-owsej in the Year 1719.

We know not what Stock of Deer is maintained within those Walks, nor how many Keepers are employed, or what Expence is incurred, in the Care of them. Lord Westmorland, considering the Deer to be his absolute Property, as undoubtedly they are during the Continuance of that Grant, has declined answering our Enquiries on those Subjects.

From the Account we have given of the State of each Bailiwick, so far as regards the Forest Offices, and Forestrial Rights, it appears that the Offices of Forester or Keeper of the several Walks are granted in Fee, and the Crown exonerated from the Payment of Wages to the Keepers; and that those of Master Forester of Clijfc Bailiwick, and Farming Woods, which are held for Lives, are now little more than honorary; that the Walk of Geddinglon Woods is disafforested, atul granted in Perpetuity, without Exception or Reservation of any Kind to the Crown; that the Walks of Moorhay and Sulehay (except Earl’s Woods in Moorhay,) are in Effect disafforested for Three Lives, for the Consideration of 2/. 8 s.5d. a Year; and that the Deer supplied from the other Walks for the Use of the Royal Household, are only Eight Brace of Bucks, and the same Number of Does, Yearly;

It farther appears, from the foregoing Statements, that some of the Hereditary Officers of this Forest, possess Lands of considerable Extent and Value in Right of their Offices. In Rockingham Bailizcick, Mr. Hatton holds the Lawn of Benc/ield, containing about 384 Acres, under the Grant of the Keepership; f Herbage and Pannage thereof in Fee. In

Bailizcick, Lord Ossory holds the Lawn of Farming Woods, mentioned to contain about Two hundred Acres, as Keeper in Fee; and the Herbage and Pannage for Three Lives. In Cliffe Bailizcick, the Lawn of Moorhay, containing 316 Acres, and that of Side-hay, containing 51 Acres, are held by Lord Westmorland as Keeper in Fee of those Walks; and the Herbage and Deer Browse of those Lawns for Three Lives; and there are some small Inclosures occupied by the Under Keepers in each District. Those Lawns being inclosed, and appropriated to the Feeding of the Deer, and not subject to any Right of Common, seem to us to be in the Nature of Parks; and, as the best Explanation we can offer of the Nature of the Interests appertaining to the Crown and the Grantees in those Lands, we shall state what appears to have been, the Construction formerly put on Grants of a similar Nature.

None of the Grants under which the Offices in this Forest are held contain any Condition, which abridges the Power of the Crown, either to increase the Stock of Deer, or to disafforest the same. The Grants were made subject to those Powers; and the Case of dington Woods is an Instance of the Exercise of them.

The Acceptance by Lord Hatton, and the Earl of Westmorland, of Grants of Disafforestation for Terms of Years or Lives, are farther Admissions of the Right; and the Lands being subject to the Exercise of those Powers, we humbly apprehend, that on a fair Estimation of the Rights of the Crown, and of the Grantees, those Considerations would have material Influence.

We have found no Account of any Timber being felled in those Woods for the Use of the Crown, prior to the Year 1704; and there is reason to believe that none had been cut for a very long Time before the Commencement of the present Century, as it appears that the Existence of the Right to that Timber was then unknown to any of the Officers of the Crown.

The First Mention we find of it is in the Entries th the Office of the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, of the Date-of 1702, where it appears that an anonymous Information was given to the Lord Treasurer Godolphin, " That the Lady Westmorland was " in the Possession of Grounds in Rockingham , " which a certain Gentleman had made it his Business " to look into the Titles of, and found them to be the " Queen’s; and that the Land and Timber was worth a£ 50,000l.*’ .

This Information having been given at a Time when, as we observed in former Reports, Attention was still shewn by Ministers to the landed Property of the Crown, and when different Officers co-operated in the Management of the Royal Forests, the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, with the Surveyor General of the Woods and Forests, and a Purveyor of the Navy, were immediately directed by the Lord Treasurer to enquire into the Matter, to view those Woods, and make a Survey of the Timber.

In pursuance of this Order, a Survey was taken, and

Appendix, there were found to be growing in them 5,389 Timber N° 20. B.

Trees, whereof 778 Trees, containing 940 Loads, were esteemed then fit for the Service of the Navy; 1,634 Trees, reckoned to contain 1,828 Loads, were looked upon to be defective or decaying, and fit to be sold in the Country; and the remaining 2,977 Timber Trees were young and flourishing, and ought to be preserved for the Navy: Besides which, there were 8,691 thriving Oak Saplings, standing at such convenient Distances, that they conceived they might all grow up to Timber, and ought very carefully to be preserved for the Use of the Crown.

Those Officers, on taking their Survey, observed several Stools, where large Oak Trees had been cut,

which they were informed were felled by the Direction of the late Earls, or the then Countess of Westmorland, who, they were told, had frequently made Falls of Timber, upon the Sales of the Underwood; and they found large Boughs lopped from divers Trees, which had prejudiced them very much for the Service of the Navy. To prevent the Continuance of those Practices, a Clause was inserted in the Grant of the Office of Master Forester, which was renewed shortly afterwards, to restrain the Grantee from lopping, topping, or cutting down auy Tree in Sulehay , unless it should be first certified by the Surveyor of the Woods, that the same should not be prejudicial to the Timber.

The Accounts of the Surveyor General of the Woods, remaining in the Office of the Auditor of the Land Appendix, Revenue, shew what Timber was felled for the Use of the Crown, after the Discovery of the Right in 1702.

Another Warrant was issued in April 1741, for raising 191/. 6s. by Wood Sales in this Forest; but no Timber was felled in pursuance thereof.

In the Year 1764, the Earl of Westmorland, upon an Application for Renewal of the Grant of the Office of Master Forester, requested that the Clause which restrained him from lopping or cutting any Trees in Sulehay Walk, might be discontinued.

The Lords of the Treasury referred the Consideration of that Request to Sir Edmond Thomas, then Surveyor of the Woods, and directed him to report the Value of the Timber in Sulehay Walk, with his Opinion what might be fit to be done thereupon; and Sir Edmond Thomas reported, that he found, on a Survey which he had caused to be made, " that " there were no more than 2,750 Timber Trees " standing on the Premises, besides Saplings, likely " to become Timber;" and that very few of those Trees were fit for the Service of the Navy, or likely to be so; and he was of Opinion that they might be valued to the Earl of Westmorland at about 1,710/.

Upon this Report, the Lords of the Treasury thought proper to sell that Timber to the Earl of Westmorland, for the Sum of 1,710/.; and the restraining Clause, prohibiting the lopping, topping, and cutting down of the Trees in Sulehay , was left out of the Grant of the Master Forestership, as Lord Westmorland had desired.

Appendix, We have inserted in the Appendix, a Copy of ** the Report of Sir Edmond Thomas, which we found in the Office of the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands: And we cannot avoid observing, that though the Report recommended the Sale of the Timber standing, to the Owner of the Underwood, it did not advise, any Limitation of Time for taking it away, nor suggest any Regulations for distinguishing the Trees to be sold from those which were to be left standing, or for securing the Succession of young Timber, for the Benefit of the Crown. If the Interest of the Crown had been properly attended to, and the Right to the future Growth of Trees, in the Place of those sold, had been considered, the Purchaser should have been obliged, by the Conditions of the Sale, to remove the Trees immediately, which were growing in the Parts of the Walk not encop-piced; but the best Time for felling Timber growing in Coppices, being the Spring next after the cutting of the Underwood, and those Woods being divided into Sixteen Sale9, and One of them cut each Year, the Term of Sixteen Years would have been the proper Time to be allowed for taking away that Part of the Timber, and the Purchaser should have been obliged to clear away what was growing in each of the Sales, as they came in Course of Cutting; and an Agent for the Crown should have taken an Account of the Trees remaining in each Coppice, after what were sold had been taken away.

Had Regulations to this Effect been adopted, the Whole of the Timber sold would have been cleared away by the Spring 1780, and no Ground of Difference with the Purchaser could have subsisted, nor any Doubt remained with respect to what belonged to the Crown: But the Timber having been sold, without marking either the Trees to be felled, or those to be left standing, and without any Limitation of Time, or other Condition, for taking it away, the Purchaser has thought himself at Liberty to cut it when and in what Manner he pleased.

Though the Grant of the Master Forestership with which this Sale of Timber was connected, in the Manner we have described, was afterwards renewed in the Year 1772, and again in 1776, no Enquiry appears to have been made whether the Timber purchased had been felled, or what Part of it remained standing, nor any Endeavours used to dis-

Crown.

Finding that nothing had been done in consequence of that Representation, and that though more than Twenty-two Years had elapsed since the Sale of the Timber, Lord Westmorland claimed to be entitled to a considerable Quantity still standing, but without specifying what Number of Trees had been cut, or how many were wanting to make up the Number purchased — we thought it a necessary Step, preparatory to the settling so complicated a Matter, to have a Survey taken of all the Trees growing in those Woods, above Ten Inches Square, Three Feet from the Ground; and we directed our Surveyor to endeavour to obtain Information what Number of Trees had been felled since the Time of the Purchase.

From that Survey, of which an Abstract is annexed to this Report, it appeared that the whole Number of the Trees of that Description, when the Survey was taken, was 3,253, which were valued by our Surveyor at 3,679/. 9$. ic)d.

It also appeared, that the Sixteen Sales into which the Woods are divided, had all been cut Once, and Seven of them a Second Time, since 1764; that Timber had been felled in all of them at the time of cutting the Underwood; and that in the Sales which had been cut a Second Time there remained a very small Quantity of Timber, or of Saplings likely to become Timber; but the Surveyor found it impracticable to get any certain Account of the Number of Trees felled, the Timber having been sold to various Persons, some of whom were dead, and Information from others impossible to be obtained; and no Stools, or other Remains of the Trees, being visible, from which the Number could be ascertained.

The present Earl of Westmorland, being the Third successive Proprietor since the Purchase of the Timber, and many of the Coppices having been cut before he came into Possession, it is hardly to be expected that he should give an Account of all the Trees which have been cut for Twenty-seven Years past, more especially as there was not any Condition in the Sale which obliged the Purchaser to keep such an Account. It was certainly the Business of the Officers of the Crown to provide all necessary Checks; but that not having been done, Recourse must be had to some other Method of drawing a Line between the Claims of the Purchaser and the Rights of the Crown.

Lord Westmorland says, it has always been considered by him, and his Family, that the Purchase included all the Trees which were then Ten Inches Square; and the Proceedings for the Sale undoubtedly seem to authorize that Construction. The Directions given by the Treasury to the Surveyor of the Woods in 1764 were, to report the Value of " the Timber in tc Sulehay Walk."* In the common Acceptation of that Term, all Trees of Ten Inches Square and upwards are considered to be comprised under the Denomination of Timber; And as the Report of Sir Edmond

3 E Thomas

of the Board of " Timber Trees standing on the Premises," besides Land Revenue^ Saplings likely to become Timber, it seems natural to' suppose that all the Trees of Ten Inches Square and upwards were included in his Survey. There is no Mention of the Size of the Trees in any Document that we have met with.

On the Supposition that all Trees down to Ten Inches Square were included in that Purchase, the Object is to discover, from the present Size of the Trees now growing in Walk (no other Evi-

dence, that we know of, being obtainable) which of them probably were of that Thickness in 1764, and having been then sold, must still belong to Lord Westmorland. We have accordingly taken some Pains to inform ourselves to what Size Trees of that Dimen-

sion might be expected to arrive in the Course of 23 Years (our Survey having been taken in 1787); and it has been suggested to us by several Surveyors* and other Persons of Experience, that they would probably increase, one with another, to about 20 Feet of Timber.

If that Opinion be a just one, it follows, that all the Trees in the Survey made in 1787, containing more than 20 Feet of Timber in each, still belong to Lord Wzstmorland; and that all which had then only Twenty Feet or less, and were of the Thickness of Ten Inches Square, belong to the Crown.

£ 3,679 9 10

Besides the Trees last mentioned, all such as are become of the Thickness of Ten Inches Square since 1787, are to be added to the Number now belonging to the Crown.

If it should be thought adviseable that the Rights of the Crown and Lord Westmorland should remain unaltered, all that in that Case is necessary, in order to bring the strange improvident Transaction in 1764 to a Conclusion, is, that all the Trees of more than Twenty Feet Contents, according to that Survey, should now have a particular Mark with Paint put on them, to shew that they are Lord Property; and in the Annual Sales of the Underwood to be made by Lord Westmorland, each Coppice should be cleared of those Trees, leaving all others, as belonging to the Crown, according to the Terms of the Grant.

By Means of this Arrangement, the Remainder of the Trees sold to Lord Westmorland in 1764 will be taken away gradually, and the Whole will be completely removed in 16 Years; and the Rights of the Crown, and of Lord Westmorland, will be gradually brought back, during the same Period, to the State in which they were prior to that Transaction.

By thus removing the Trees in each Division, only when the Underwood is cut, Lord Westmorland's Property will not be injured by the Removal.

This Arrangement which we have suggested is, no Doubt, favourable to Lord Westmorland. It is admitting that all the Trees belonging to the Crown were bought by his Predecessor in 1764, which, though probable, is not certain; — it is admitting, that a considerable Part of the Trees, though sold in 1764, are still growing the re, though during that Time the Underwood in all the Sixteen Sales has been once cut, and in Eleven of them cut a Second Time; — and it is making no Claim for any Trees belonging to the Crown, which may possibly have been taken down along with those cut by Lord Westmorland since 1764, nor for the Injury done to the Crown, by occupying the Ground with the Trees then sold, from 28 to Years (being the Distance of Time between the Sale and the final Removal of the Timber) to the Prevention of the Growth of other Trees, which would have come up in their Place, and would now have been considerably advanced; though it cannot well be supposed that it was intended to allow so much Time for the Removal of that Timber.

But it is to be considered, that these are the Consequences of a very unwise Transaction, made by the Officers of the Crowd, which it is desirable to bring

ft,

to some speedy Settlement without Litigation, and which there does not appear to us to be any more equitable Mode of bringing to a Close.

For the future Protection of the Property reserved by the Crown, it must seem obviously necessary, if those Rights are to remain unaltered, that some Officer should attend at every Cutting of the Underwood, to take Care that no Saplings be cut. — The Trees of such an Age as to admit of it should be marked with Paint, and numbered: Returns should be made, and kept in the Office intrusted with the Care of the Forests; and the Woods should be frequently visited, and their Condition reported from that Office.

But if, on the other Hand, it shall be thought that the Effects naturally to be expected from such a Mixture of Rights as have been created in this Forest, are so destructive, that no Care which can be bestowed will be sufficient for the Protection of the Trees and Saplings, without an Expence beyond what the Advantages from so small an Extent of Ground will ever be found to bear; and if Government shall, on that Account, judge it proper to sell, and Lord Westmorland shall be disposed to purchase, not only all the Trees belonging to the Crown, which are now growing in Sulehay Walk, but the Right to all which shall grow hereafter- we should in that Case, think what follows a just Mode of estimating that Right of the Crown.

According to the Extract we have given from the Survey taken in 1787, it appears that there were 2,530 Trees growing in Sulehay Walk, which belonged to the Crown, and were worth at that Time 2,0491- 3 s- 5 d.

To these are to be added all Trees which have become Ten Inches Square since the Survey was made, which may be ascertained at little Expence by a Surveyor.

No Mention is made in the Grant to Lord Westmorland’s Ancestors, of the Saplings which would afterwards grow to Ten Inches Square: But in the Report of Mr. Travers, Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, upon the Discovery in 1703, he says, " he Appendix, " had consulted the Attorney General on the Ex- N*20ception in the Grant, who agreed with him in " Opinion, that the same must be construed for the " Benefit of the Crown, and the Growth and Increase <c of Timber;" and we cannot doubt of its being incumbent on the Grantee, to leave at least as many Trees as are required to be left in Woodlands, by the Act of 35 of Henry the Eighth, or, in other Words,

199

that the Meaning of Parties, when the Grant was made, should be explained by that Law, no Explanation being contained in the Grant.

By that Act, the Owners of Coppices cut at Twenty-four Years Growth,' or under, must, in cutting the Underwood, leave Twelve Standils of Oak on every Acre, of the most likely to become Timber; which Standils are not to be felled before they become Ten Inches Square, Three Feet from the Ground; or, if there be not so many Standils at the first Cutting, the Numbers must be made up at the next, and he is obliged to preserve them.

Lord Westmorland has no Right to take Firebote from those Trees, which is forbidden by the Grant, nor to take Housebote, &c. for that is only allowed 35 Hen. to be taken by the Owners of the Timber; and here VIII. C. 17. the Crown is the Owner.

If therefore it shall be deemed expedient to part with this Right of the Crown, it cannot, we think, be difficult to put a just Value on it; and the Crown may receive the Price or Value, either in a Sum of Money to be immediately paid, or by a Rent Charge in Money, or an Annual Delivery of a certain Quantity of Timber fit for the Navy, to commence at such Time as the Trees belonging to the Crown may be computed to become fit for Naval Use. We cannot avoid adding, that, from the present State of Oak, Timber in this Country, and the Convenience of Water Carriage by the River Nene, from situated within less than a Mile the

Annual Delivery of a certain Quantity of Timber appears to us the most for the Advantage of the Crown, and of the Public.

As the best of the Saplings would be left, and the Trees would have full Room to grow, it cannot, in our Opinion, be thought unreasonable, in such a Transaction, to presume, that in 50 Years after Trees have grown to be Ten Inches Square, Three Feet from the Ground, they will, one with another, be found to contain a Load of Timber; so that Twelve Loads on the Acre may be reasonably expected at that Time, on the Ground on which the Crown possesses the Right to the Timber of that Description. The Extent of the Ground will naturally be ascertained by actual Admeasurement, before any such Treaty shall be concluded.

The 2,530 Trees already stated to have become Ten Inches Square since 1764, must come gradually to be in Course of felling in 50 Years from that Time; and the Whole should be felled in Twenty-three Years from 1791, by equal Portions in each Year.

At every Fall of Underwood since the Survey was made, Lord Westmorland should have made up the Number of Trees left for the Crown to Twelve at least of Ten Inches Square on every Acre, and probably has done so; which wall shew what Number of Trees he ought to deliver Annually, after Fifty Years from the Date of that Survey.

What we have now suggested will establish the

Principles of a very easy Computation of the Value of Ninth Report the reserved Right of the Crown to the Timber in the Board of Sulehay Walk, and of the Quantity of Timber which v ao ^venue-J should be Annually delivered, in consequence of the Sale of it to Lord Westmorland.

We would therefore farther propose, that the same Commissioners or Trustees should be empowered to treat and agree with Lord Westmorland for the Sale to him of that Right, leaving any Difference which may be, between their Estimation of it and Lord Westmorland's, to be determined by Arbitration.

By the Settlements we have proposed, all the Parties interested would, as we apprehend, be benefited.

A Forest in a Situation so distant from any Residence of the Royal Family, with an Establishment of Offices, either granted in Perpetuity or esteemed of little Value by those who possess them, and in which so little of the Right to Timber has been reserved, can neither contribute much to the Amusement of the King, the Dignity or Profit of the Crown, or the Advantage of the Public.

Lord Ossory informs us, That " the Expences attending the Renewal of his Grant of the Office of " Master Forester of Farming Woods (for the adding of every new Life) is about 200l., the Whole of " which is distributed at the different Offices through " which the Patent passes, and no Part is paid into " the Treasury, upon Account of the Crown or the " Public." Lord Westmorland in like Manner pays merely the Fees of the different Offices, on the Renewals of his Grant of the Master Forestership of Cliffe Bailiwick; and no Fine or Consideration, on Account of either, goes into the Exchequer.

And though the antient Forest Laws, and the 50 Clra. II. Courts, when regularly held, have been found by Experience to conduce very much to the Increase and Preservation of Timber, in Forests thinly inhabited, and set apart as Nurseries for the Navy, and have therefore been, very properly, kept in Force by special Statutes in Dean and New Forest; yet in Rockingham Forest, where the Crown has little Property left, where a considerable Part of the Land is already in Tillage or Pasture, and the Country pretty fully inhabited, it cannot be desirable that those Laws should be continued. The Inconvenience and Counteraction occasioned by a Mixture of Rights, and a divided Management in the same Property, would be removed by the Disafforestation and Settlements we have proposed; and a valuable Part of the Country would be freed from Restraints and Burthens, which, by impeding its Improvement, must be a Loss to the Public, as well as to the Proprietors.

The 21st March 1674. Robert Lackston, aged about Forty-four Years, Keeper of a Walk within his Majesty's Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, called Wood Walk, doth depose, That he having been Keeper of the said Walk for above Five Years last past, and born within the Parish of Gretton, where he has lived all his Life Time, doth very well know the Lawn called Benefield Lawn, lying within the said VOL, 47.

Of the Manors of Apelhorpe, Wood Nezclon and well, and the Park of Apelhorpe, with their Appurtenances.

Of the Office of Forester and Keeper of Sulthay Fct'ius and Shorluood, within the Bailiwick of Clijj'e.

Of divers Woods and Coppices within the Walks of Sulchay Farms and Shorlu ood, except all Oak Trees Ten Inches Square, Three Feet above the Ground, and sufficient Browse for the Queen’s Deer, and other wild Beasts there.

Of divers Lands, called Bushrobs, Springhaxve, ats Bringhazce, Caldey, and Dicks, within the

Bailiwick of Cliff'e.

Of divers Lands, called East and West Bodlaus, Long Hedges, Monk's Dick, and many others, in the Manor and Parish of Sonthuick, in the Bailiwick of Cliff'e.

Of certain Coppices, called Great and Little Tollcnhoe Coppices, Old Sale Coppice, Coppice, and divers

others, containing together 1,52.5 Acres within the Walks of Moorkayand except all Oaks Ten Inches square, Three Feet from the Ground, and the Lops and Tops of all Oaks, being Timber; and all Mines; and the Herbage of the said W’ood-lands for Hie King’s Deer, and other Wild Beasts; also the Office of Forester, or Keeper of the Lawn of Moorhay.

Of all the Timber Ti ees, Lops and Tops, See. except and reserved by the last mentioned Grant.

Forest, which he conceiveth may contain about Three Hundred and Fifty Acres of plain Ground Statute Measure, without any Trees upon it, not commonable to any Parish. And also the West Bailiwick or West Walk lying within the said Forest, which he conceiveth may contain about Two hundred and Sixty Acres of Wood Ground, Forest Measure, to which there is about Sixty Acres of Plains adjoining, commonable for all Cattle. And also the W oods called alias Wadehaxc, and ThornehawWoods, lying within the said Forest, which he conceiveth may contain about Three hundred Acres of Forest Measure. And 3 G a!,u

Ninth Report also the Woods, called Corby Woods, in the said Fo-Land'iFfT*!^ rest, which he conceiveth may contain about Four v n 'j hundred and Ten Acres of Forest Measure; to which

there is a Plain adjoining, called Rockinghamhire, containing, as he conceiveth, about Three hundred Acres, commonable for all Cattle. And also the Woods, called Gretton Wood Walk, within the said Forest, consisting of several Parts, whereof One Part, called Gretton Woods, he conceiveth may contain about Six hundred and Sixty Acres of Forest Measure; and One other Part, called Little Welden Woods, about Two hundred Seventy-five Acres of like Measure; and another Part, being Part of Corby Woods, within the said Walk, he conceiveth may contain about Four hundred and Fifty Acres of Statute Measure: All which said Wood Grounds, called The West Walk, Woodhaw ats Thorn-haw Woods, Corby Woods, and the said Woods in Gretton Woods Walk, are Coppice Woods, and commonable by the Great Cattle of the adjacent Towns at the End of Seven Years after the Fall of any of the said Coppice Woods. And there is also Three Plains, called BloxvesPlain, Fulling Plain, and Middle Plain or Straights, containing together about a Hundred Acres; and another Plain, Part also of Rock-inghamshire, containing about a Hundred Acres more, all lying within the said Walk, called Gretton Woods Walk; the First Three Plains being commonable to the Great Cattle of Gretton Parish, and the aforesaid Part of Rocking hams hire being commonable for all Cattle within the said Parish of Gretton.

That the Premises are divided into Five Walks, to every of which there is a Keeper’s Lodge, and about Two Acres of Ground inclosed to every one of them.

That these Walks lie all contiguous and adjoining together, and do now maintain about Four hundred Deer in the Whole, whereof there is usually served, upon His Majesty’s Warrants, about a Brace of Bucks, and a Brace of Does, Yearly, out of each Walk.

And this Deponent likewise saith, all the said Walks and Premises do lie distinct from the Residue of the said Forest, the nearest Part being about Two Miles from Farming Woods, and as far from Geddington Woods, and about Four Miles from Westy and Moory Walks, being all Parts of the said Forest of Rockingham.

William Jones, aged about Eight-and-Forty Years, Keeper of the West Walk above mentioned, for about Nine Years last past, and born in the Lodge belonging to it, where he hath lived all his Life, do testify the Truth of the above Deposition of Robert Lackston.

JuranV 2i° Die Martij Rob. Laxton.An° 1676. Coram me,

William Jones. B. Bertie.

Whereas by an Inquisition taken at Kettering, in the County of Northampton, the 17th Day of August last past, by virtue of his Majesty’s Commission under the Great Seal of Great Britain, to certain Commissioners in that Behalf directed (of which Commission and Inquisition the aforegoing are certified to be true Copies, as the same do remain of Record in Chan-ceryj It is found by the Oaths of good and lawful Men that the Launde of Benefield, within the Forest of Rockingham, in the County aforesaid, in the same Commission mentioned, as to Statute Measure, contains 384 Acres of Pasture, and no more, but as the Forest Measure contains 237 Acres, and no more, and that the Issues and Profits Annually accruing to the King from every Acre thereof, according to Forest Measure,

are of the clear Annual Value (beyond Reprises') of Four Pence and not above, which Quantities and Values of the Premises being so ascertained by the said Inquisition, These are to direct and require you to make forth a Constat of the said Premises from the said Commission and Inquisition, and rate the same, in order to the passing a Lease thereof, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, unto William Viscount Hatton, his Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, for the Term of 31 Years, or Three Lives (at the Option of the Lessee) reserving to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, an Annual Rent of Four Pence upon each Acre, Forest Measure-, and you are to advise on the said Constat a Clause for discharging the Premises so to be leased of and from all Forest Duties for and during the said Term, as also all such other Clauses, Provisoes, and Covenants and Agreements, as you shall think advisable to be inserted in the said Lease, for rendering the same effectual as well with respect to the Lessee as to his Majesty’s Interest therein; and for so doing this shall be your Warrant.

Treasury Chambers, 16 December 1719.

J. Wallop.

To our very loving Friend, Geo.

Hugh Cholmley, Esquire, Wm,

His Majesty’s Surveyor General.

N* 8.

Copy of an Antient Paper in the Office of the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, intituled, " A State " of the Forrest of Rockinghamwithout Date, but

appearing to have been written prior to the Disafforestation of Geddington Woods Walk, in the Year 1676.

If it bee Examined, it will appeare that Woodes Walk differeth from the rest of the Walkes in Rockingham Forrest, for it lyeth on the Outside of the Forrest, by it self, and the Coppices thereof lye distinct by themselves, and not intermixed w'h any other Woodes of the same Forrest, but Separate there-from by the Common feildes of Stanyon and

little Oakcly; and in regard that all the Coppices and plaines are Comonable to ffive Townes, & nothing severall for the Deere but a small Bushey Lane of 13 Acres, affording no Hay for the Deer, so that no considerable Number of Deer can be maintayned, & if the Lord Montagu, who hath the Kecpership in fee, had not constantly, in the Time of Snow, or hard Weather, sent them Hay for their reliefe, out of his owne Groundes adjoyning to it, it would have had much fewer Deer in it.

For the rest of the Forrest it standes thus; the Lord Hatton hath the Kecpership of severall W’alkcs in Rockingham Baylyuick, and the Lord Rockingham one Walk, called Corby Woodes. The Woodes of Corby Walke are the Lord Cardigans; One Coppy amongst the Lord Rockingham. Almost in the midest of these Woodes, the Lord Hatton hath the Keepership of Benefeild Lawne, about 400 Acres 6f severall Groundes, wherein the Deer feed, & affordeth every Year soe great a Quantity of Hay that it doth not only serve the Deer, but severall Loadcs of Hay is sold to Neighboures of the Countrey every Year; of wth Woodes the Lord Hatton hath the Keepership, many of them belonging to others, as to Mr. Brent, Colting-ham & Middleton Woodes, to Mr. Brookes, of great Oakcly, a Wood called SoiCatlshcad to Mr. Donne hall, some Coppices in Welden Woodes to the Lord Rockingham, ffor farming Woods, wch are S' John Robinson's, and he hath the Keepership of them; there belongeth to that Walk a great Lawne about 200 Acres in Scveraltie, where the Deer doe feed; & a fair house upon it, & a great Quantity of Hay is got every Year for the Deer.

For Westhay Walk, in Cliff Bailiwick, the Woodes are the Lord Westmorelands's, & the Keepership belongeth to the Earle of Exeter; Moorehay, where are severall Walkes, the Lord Westmoreland hath the Keepership in fee, & most of the Woodes; The rest are the Lord Halyfaxes; there is a great Lawne in Morehay, about 300 Acres, where there is a great Herd of Deer, & a great quantitie of Hay got every Year for the Deer; Sulehay Walk, the Lord Westmoreland hath the Keepership in Fee, & a large Lawne in it; The Underwood belongeth to him, but the Great Oakes, of such a bignesse, are the King’s, and not

granted; the Sizes of small Oakes, or Saplings, that he may fell, is set downe in the Grant to his Ancestors. I think it was granted in Queene Mary's time.

A true Copy — Examined by

Wm Harrison,

Acting Surveyor General.

To the King's Most Excellent Majesty.

The humble Petition of Edward Lord Montagu, of Boughton, in the County of Northampton.

Humbly Sheweth,

That whereas Your Majesty’s Royal Father, by Letters Patent bearing Date the 26th Day of February, in the Third Year of His Reign, for the Consideration of 850/. did grant unto Your Petitioner’s Father, and his Heirs, all the several Coppices of Wood and Underwood lying in Geddington Woods, within the Bailiwick of Brigslock, within the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, and the Soil thereof, under the Yearly Fee Farm Rent of 10/., excepting the Timber Trees, and the Herbage for the Feed of the Deer, and all Mines therein; And by the said Letters Patent did also grant unto Your said Petitioner's Father, and his Heirs, the Office of Under Forrester of the said Woods called Geddington R oods. And whereas Your Majesty’s Royal Father, by other Letters Patent bearing Date the 20,h Day of August, in the 4th Year of his Reign, for the Consideration of 1,000l. did grant unto Your Petitioner’s Father, and his Heirs, the said Timber Trees so formerly excepted; which said Woods is one of the Walks of the said Forest of Rockingham, and is mentioned in the said Letters Patents by Estimation to contain 708 Acres, One Rood, and besides the Herbage and Mines so excepted as aforesaid, in the said First Letters Patents, there is still remaining the re to Your Majesty, the Deer, the Lodges, a little Lawnd of Ten Acres in Severalty, and the Ridings and Plains which are Commonable, but all of an inconsiderable Value, and nothing of Revenue or Profit. — Now whereas the said Walk lieth very near the Chief Mansion House of the said Petitioner, and the said Walk, and the Coppices thereof, lie distinct by themselves, and not intermixed with any other Woods of the same Forest, but separate therefrom by Common Fields; and that it will be a great Grace and Favour from Your Majesty, and an Accommodation of much Pleasure to Your Petitioner and his Family, to have the same made a Chase, and to remain to them so, yet, nevertheless, subject to the Common and Interest of the Commoners:

Your Petitioner most humbly beseecheth that Your Majesty, of Your Grace and Favour, will be pleased to grant unto Your Petitioner, and his Heirs, the said Game of Deer, Herbage, Lodges, Lawnd, Ridings and Plains, and that the same, together with the said Woods and Coppices, may be turned into a

N° u.

The Earl of Upper Ossory, by virtue of his Grant, dated August 28th 1772, claims to hold for 99 Years, or during the Lives of himself, the Marquis of,

and Richard Fitz Patrick, Esquire, and the Survivor of them, the Office of Master Forester and Keeper of Farming Woods, in the Forest of Rockingham, and Supervisor of Vert and Venison of the said Woods, Receiver of Fines and Amerciaments therein, the Office of Bailiff of Brigstock, except Geddington Woods, the Herbage and Pannage of the New Land of Farming Woods, also the Hundred of Orlingbury and Mellescy, in the County of Northampton, the Rents of Aid of the Sheriff within the said Hundred, and all Rights, &c. together with all Wages, Fees, Profits, Commodities, Advantages, and Allowances, to the same Offices belonging, and all Courts, Fines, Amerciaments, Jurisdictions, within the said Hundred, also the Wages of

3 /. 6s. id.a Year, and 3d. a Day Ranger’s Fee, to

be paid out of the Issues of the Forest of Rockingham, and the Castle and Demesne Lands thereof, and the Castleward Rents, also a Power of constituting a Ranger of the said Woods, and of appointing a Clerk or Steward of the Court of the Forest; his Lordship also claims under the said Grant, all Deer-fallen and Wind-fallen Wood, Vermin Trees, and Coppice Hedges, Within the said Woods.

Under Two Grants, or rather Purchases, from the Crown, dated 30th May, and 23d July, 4th Charles the First, Lord Ossory is entitled in Fee to all the Timber Trees and Underwood in Farming Woods. Farming Woods is supposed in those Grants to contain about 800 Acres, the Woods or Coppices after cutting are in Band, or fenced against the Deer for Four Years, and against the Commoners Cattle for Seven, both of which Terms are too short for the tolerable Preservation of either Underwood or Timber, according to the present Mode of Stocking by the Commoners, who turn in larger Beasts, and more in Number, for Want of due Regulation by Forest Courts, than formerly.

It is evident that the Succession of Timber in all Rockingham Forest cannot be kept up under the present Usage of Commoning, which in so large a Tract is a National Consideration.

The Parish of Br'igstock, in which Farming Woods lies, being included in the Perambulation of the Forest, made in the Reign of Charles the First, claims, and has always enjoyed, a Right of Common in the Open Woods there. The Parish of Sudborough has also Cattle usually Commoning the re, though it is apprehended they can have no Right, not being a Forest Town, and expressly excluded in the Perambulation; and no Part of the Parish being within the Bounds of the Forest, it is considered only as an Escape Common.

All Cattle ought to be taken out of the Forest from Martinmas to Lady Day, and during the Fence Month; but these Regulations, for Want of Forest Courts, are not enforced.

Upon a fair Calculation in Money, taken upon the Number of Beasts and Horses usually Commoning upon Farming Woods, it is worth about 501, per Annum to those who enjoy it, and the Cattle do Damage to a much greater Amount to the Timber and Underwood.

Brigstock, and all its Open Fields, lying within the Perambulation of the Forest, it is contended that the Deer ought not to be molested when found ranging over them, but the Occupiers of the Fields may exclude them, by keeping up the Forest Fence, and stopping the Gaps, for which they are allowed to cut Wood out of it.

This Privilege of the Deer ought to be set against that of the Right of Common in the Woods.

The following is a Statement and Valuation of the Heads of Lord s Grant.

Office of Master Forester, &c.

Under this Head Lord Ossory has the Benefit of the Management and Disposal of the Deer, the Number of which vary, but the present Average enables him to kill 34 Bucks, and as many Does, Annually.

The following necessary Deductions of Profit must be made: — To the Crown, by Warrants from the Board of Green Cloth or Master of the Household, 4 Bucks and Does, One of each to the Forest Ver-deror, and there is also a Claim of another.

Composition Venison allowed to the Proprietors of neighbouring Grounds and Purlieus, for Liberty to hunt back the Deer, without which Permission the

The Profits of Lord Ossory’s Grant may be therefore said to be none; standing thus:

The Hundred of Orlingbury and Mellesey, consists of Rents called Sheriff’s Aid, amounting Annually to 6$. 17$. 6d. collected with Difficulty, and the Expences of Collection and holding Courts are equal to the Value; — therefore of no Value.

Though the Earl of Upper Ossory s Grant is of no Value in Point of Profit, it is not denied to be very eligible to him, and has been enjoyed by his Ancestors since the 22d of Charles 11"*, when it was granted to Sir John Robinson, from whom Lord Ossory immediately derives.

The usual Mode of renewing is, when a Life drops, for the Grantee in Possession to present a Memorial to the Lords of the Treasury for a Renewal, and to surrender the subsisting Grant, upon which invariably a new one is made out, without any Fine whatever. The Expences attending the Renewal are about 200l.; the Whole of which is distributed at the different Offices through which the Patent passes, and no Part is paid into the Treasury, upon Account of the Crown or the Public.

It is evident from the above Statement, that the Reversion of the Grant in Question, after Three Lives at present in being, cannot be of any considerable Value; but Lord Ossory, in order to be released from the Claims of the Crown, and admitting that if he was so, he might be enabled to improve his Property in the Woods, and have the Means of making some Agreement or Composition with those who claim a Right of Common, which he has not at present, is desirous, whenever the Commissioners are enabled to treat with him, to purchase, at a fair and reasonable Price, the whole Rights and Interests of the Crown now granted to him by Lease, and whatever Price he pays will be an entire Gain of so much to the Public, who it does not appear have ever derived or are likely to derive any Advantage from this Grant, or the Renew’al of it.

N° 14.

The Earl of Exeter, under a Grant dated 4th 4th Charles I*1, claims to hold in Fee the Office of Forester or Keeper of the Lawnd of within the Bailiwick of Cliff', in the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, and all the Deer for Hunting, or other Y\7ild Beasts, within the Lawnd of Westhay, and all Lodges, Profits, Fees, Advantages, Deer-fallen Wrood, See.

And under a Grant of the 23d July, 4th Charles I", he claims to hold in Fee the Timber in Westhay.

Westhay is supposed to contain about 800*, of which about 700 are Wood Land, the rest open.

The Woods are divided into 18 Sales, one of which is cut every Year; after cutting, the Sale is band from the Deer Years, from the Commoners Cattle Seven Years.

The Parishes of King's Cliffe and claim

a Right of Common in Westhay, they usually stock from A lay Day to Old Martinmand have near 250 Head of Cuttle in Westhay.

JJrcsthaybordering upon the open Fields of Duddington and King's Cliffe, the Farmers and Cottagers of those Parishes fence against Westhay at their own Expence, to keep in the Deer, and to preserve their Corn from the Deer; but if the Deer do get into the Fields they cannot run a Dog at them.

The open Places in Westhay, containing about 100* are open to the Commoners at the same Time with the YY oods not in band.

The Earl of Exeter pays his Keeper 40/. a Year in Addition to which the Keeper has the usual Fees from Presents of Venison made by his Lordship.

Lord Exeter also finds Hay for the Deer in the Winter, which costs him, upon an Average, Annually about 60/.

His Lordship serves the Crown Annually with 3 Bucks and 3 Does. He kills in the Year, on the Average, about 40 Bucks and 3C Does.

The Deer delivered by Lord Exeter to the Crown has been Time immemorial unvaried; to be discharged from the further Claims of the Crown as to Deer (which he conceives to be the only Claim the Crown has upon him) and from the Claim of Common, in order to hold the Estate in Severalty for ever, he expects he must pay the Value of the 3 Bucks, and 3 Does, and the Value of about 60/. a Year in Land, to the Two Parishes of King's Cliffe and

To the Right Honorable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury.

May it please Your Lordships,

We have considered the annexed Petition of the Earl of Westmorland, who by virtue of several Grants and Westhay, in the aforesaid Forest; and from the Crown is intitled to several Parcels of Wood also the Ground and Soil of the aforesaid Woods, Ground, and other Lands, lying within and Parcel of Underwoods, and Woodlands, afore granted (except the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of North amp-all great Oaks, in Height Three Foot from the ton, which he now desires to be declared Free, as other Ground, and in Breadth Ten Inches of Assize Square, Free Hays are; and also to have the Deer granted and except all Boughs and Lops and Tops of all Oaks him that are upon the Premises, and to be discharged and Trees in the Premises, being Timber, which, by the Custome of the Forest, ought not to be lopt and topt; and all Mines; and also, except the Herbage of the said Woodland, for the King’s Deer, and other Beasts, to feed on, as before was wont) And also all Boughs, Lops and Tops of Oaks and Trees, w hieh, by the Custom of the said Forest, are wont to be lopped,

from the Privilege reserved to the Crown. We find her late Majesty Queen Elizabeth, by Letters Patterns bearing Date the 3d of Augin the 13th Year of her Reign, Granted to Walter Mildmay All those Woods, Underwoods or Woodlands, or Coppices of Wood, called TrampouleSayle, BayurdSale, Morton Sale,

Nashington Spires, WhispitSale, alias The Queen's Sale, are granted to the said Fay and Bellamy: To hold the Old Sale, Fresh Lease; also One Parcel of Wood same to them, their Heirs and Assigns, for ever, Ground adjoining to Fresh Lease, containing Two paying Yearly too/.

Acres; also Lord Montjoy's Sale, Lady Sale Coppice, The said Fay and Bellamy are also empowered to Shorluood Coppice, Poiton Yate, Quarter Coppice, and inclose all and singular the Premises, and to cut and Four Acres thereto adjoining, and Sulchay Coppice, carry away all Woods, &c. (except as before is ex-Jaclc Close Coppice', which Premises lie within the cepted) at Pleasure. There is a Covenant on the Forest of Rockingham, in the County of Northampton, Lessees Part, that they shall so keep the Woods, that and within the Precincts or Walk called Sulehay Farm, there shall be sufficient Convenience for the Preserva-or Shortzcood, within the Bailiwick of Cliffe or Cleeve, tion of the Deer, and other Beasts remaining on the

Premises;

221

Premises; and also leave sufficient Staddell. There is also granted to the said Pay and Bellamy the Office of Keeper of the Laund of Morekay, in the said Forest of Rockingham, together with Keeper of the Deer and other Beasts within the said Laund, To hold to them and their Heirs for ever.

We find also, That his said late Majesty King Charles the First, by Letters Patents bearing Date the 23d Day of July, in the Fourth Year of his Reign, at the Nomination of the Earls of Westmorland and Peterborough, in Consideration of 2,000l. Granted to the aforesaid Pay and Bellamy, and Francis Pickering and Edward Stanton, their Heirs and Assigns, for ever, amongst other Things, all the great Trees, Oaks, Ashes, and Elms, being Timber, or reputed so; and all Saplings of Oak, Ashes, and Elm, and all manner of Woods and Trees, which were excepted and reserved to his said late Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, by the Letters Patents bearing Date the 30th of May, in the 4th Year of his Reign, which are before recited, and all Timber then growing, or that should happen to grow, or be, within the Laund, Riding, Limitt, & Boundary of y* Hayes or Walkes called Morehay or West hay, in Rockingham Forest, in the County of Northampton.

The late Earl of Peterborough, Pay, Bellamy, Pickering, and Stanton, by Indenture dated the 31st Octor, in the 4th Year of King Charles the First, assigned to the then Earl of Westmorland, his Heirs and Assigns for ever, all the Timber in the last recited Letters Patents, and before expressly mentioned to be granted to them.

We take Leave to observe to your Lordships, that by the Letters Patents of the 13th of Queen Elizabeth, afore-recited, all the Timber growing on the Premises lying within the Precincts of the Hay or Walk, called Sulehay or Shoriwood (thereby granted) is reserved to the Crown; and the Browse for the Deer does now belong-to his Majesty; but the Wood, after the Deer have browsed, belong to the Earl.

And also, by the Letters Patents bearing Date the 30th of May, and the 23 July, Car. the Timber and Coppice Wood growing and to grow within the Hay or Walk called Morehay or Westhay, therein described, containing 1526 Acres (being granted away) there is reserved to the Crown Herbage of the said Woodlands for the King’s Deer and other Beasts to feed on as before was wont

And if his Majesty shall be graciously pleased to grant to the said Earl of Westmorland, the Petitioner, the Deer within the Precincts of the Hay or Walk called Sulehay or Shoriwood, and within the Hays or Walks called Morehay, and Laund of within the Forest of Rockingham, and shall be pleased to grant the Woodlands aforesaid, and other Lands of the said Earl, to be ffreehay (which is desired) for such Term as his Majesty is impowered to do, by an Act passed in the First Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, we are of Opinion that an Inquisition ought to be taken of the Premises, to know the Value of the said Reservations, in order to reserve to his Majesty, upon such Grant, such Rent as is required by the said Act; and we think it adviseable that if the Deer be granted away, as is desired, that the best Advantage ought to be made of his Majesty’s Demesne (if any there be ungranted within the said Hays or Walks) and that his Majesty should be discharged from paying any Keepers or other Officers "Wages, or other Allowances, on Account of the Vert or Venison within the Hays or Walks aforesaid.

30th Oct' 1718. II. S. G.

May it please Your Lordship,

Mr. Attornye’s Report) As to the L4 -

upon Lord Willough- > bids Interest in Bestwoud bye's Peticon. J Parke, 1 finde, upon pu-sall of the Copy of the Letters Patents, that the late King granted to the now L4 , by the

riame of William Willoughby, Esq^ the Custody of that

Park, with the Fees, &c.; and by the same Patent did further grant to him the Herbage and Pannage of and within the Park, to hold from the Determination of the former Grants then in being during his Life, & the Life of John Carey, Esq. And it being fallen in Poseon it is affirmed by the L4 Willoughby (but I have not seen it) that the now King hath granted his Lot,\ a Lysence to plow the whole Parke during the said two Lives.

I conceive that by this Grant the Lord Willoughby hath an Interest in the Office of Keepship, with all the casual Fees belonging to it, and hath an Interest in ye Surplusage of the Herbage, over and above the Sustenance & feeding of the Game, so long as the Parke continues a Parke, but the King may increase the Deere; and if there be no Surplusage, hee that hath the Herbage cannot put in any Beast: And if the King do dispark the Parke (as he may) both the Office of Custody, and the Interest in the Herbage, will thereby determine; yet in such Cases it hath been held reasonable to give Compensation for the Custody and Herbage, wherein the Libty of plowing (if any such there be) is to be also considered.

All which is humbly submitted, &c.

29 Jan. 1666. J. Palmer.

EXTRACT from a Report of Sir Charles Harbord, Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, to the Lords of the Treasury, on a Petition of William Lord Willoughby and John Carey, Esq', for a Lease of Beslwood Park, in the County of Nottingham.

The Custody and Herbage of the said Park was granted by his late Majesty, by Letters Patents, dated 20 Octr 1638, to these Petitioners for their Lives successively, with a Fee of four pence p and

my Lord Willoughby hath plowed up a great Part thereof, by Warrant from his Majesty, as he pretends, which otherwise W'ould have been a Forfeiture of his Interest.

I do not find that the Lord Willoughby hath rccT-d the said Fee of Four pence p diem, nor do I conceive it to be due to him, being a Fee for his Keep-ership, which, by destroying of the Deer, is of no use.

I do not conceive that a Grant of the Custody of a Park, with the Herbage and Pannage thereof, doth amount to a Right to all the Profits in case the Deer be destroyed, but ought to be apportioned, as hath been done, in some such Cases, to a third part; and under the late usurpacon, to a fifth part only of the whole, as in the Case of Clarendon Park, &c.

And in some Cases, where the Park hath been dis-parked and disfranchised, the Interest of the Herbage hath been lost without any Recompence given to the Grantee, as in some of the Parkes of the Hono' of Amplhill,&c. But in some of the Parks

of the Hono' of Grafton, the Grantees of y* Custody, and Herbage & Pannage, have been allowed more than the Moyety of the full Yearly value, in Re-

15th March 170^.

To the Right Honbl® the Lord High Treasurer of

England.

May it please your. Lordship,

Pursuant to your Lordship's Directions by Mr.

Lowndes's Letter of the 15th March last, I have revised my Report made to your Lordship 18th of concerning Timber fit lor her Majesty’s Service in the Forest of Rockingham, on Lands in the Possession of the Lady Westmorland, and find the Facts therein laid down to be true, That all 'l imber formerly belonging to the Crown, within the Hays or Walks called West hay, and Farming Woods, were, by the Grant in that Report recited, made to Sir Nicholas Pay, Clement Belamy, and others, granted away in I ce.

Having taken some Time to answer your Lordship’s Commands, I have made particular Enquiry into the Situation and Title of those several Parcels of Woodlands, which were mentioned in a Memorial delivered to your Lordship as belonging to her Majesty, whereby I find the same are situate within the Mays or 'Walks of Side farms, and Shortwood, within the Bailiwick of Cliff, in the said Forest of Rockingham; and I find a Grant, passed 3d August, Anno 13th Elizabeth, of all the Woods and Underwoods belonging to the Crown, within the said Hays or Walks, and "of the Soil thereof, to Sir Walter Mildmay, her then Majesty’s

Chancellor of the Exchequer, his Heirs and Assigns for ever, under a Fee Farm Rent of 30/. u. 10 per Annum, which is now Parcel of the Queen Dowager’s Jointure, and paid to Michaelmas last. But out of this Grant is excepted and reserved to the Crown all Oak Trees zchich then did, or aft should, exceed the Scantling of Ten Inches Square, a Yard above Ground: And the Grantee covenants to discharge the Crown of the Sum of 3/. 6 s. 8 per Annum Salary, payable to the Keeper or Forester of the said Walks, and to find sufficient Erowsewood for the Deer from Time to Time, which Erowsewood the Grantee is afterwards to take to his own Use, together with all Topps and Lopps of the Trees above mentioned to be excepted, which anciently have, or by the Customs of the Forest may be topped or lopped.

I have advised with Mr. Attorney General upon this whole Matter, and particularly upon the Exception in the Grant, by Reasons some Persons had informed nie that the same was understood, as if the Grantee had a Right to cut all young Trees under the aforesaid Scantling; and Mr. Attorney agrees with me in Opinion, that the same must be construed for the Benefit of the Crown, and the Growth and Increase of Timber; and I am assured by an Agent of the Earl of Westmorland's, that his Lordship, who has now the Benefit of the said Grant, does not intend or mean otherwise.

I am not able to inform your Lordship, whether the Timber on the Premisses belonging to her Majesty be of so much Value as is represented in the Memorial, without taking a View and particular Estimate thereof; but if your Lordship pleases, the Officers of the Navy may be directed to examine what's fit for her Majesty’s Shipping, which may be applied accordingly, and that which is decaying may be sold for other proper Uses for her Majesty’s present Advantage, which will make Room for other young Trees to grow up, that may be of future Service to the Crown. All

which

Ninth Report which I humbly submit to your Lordship’s great Land* Revenue. Wi*d°m’

---- ' Sir,

The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury are pleased to direct me to transmit to you the Memorial inclosed of Thomas Earl of Westmorland; together with the Report of Robert Herbert, Esquire, upon another Memorial of the said Earl, relating to a new Grant of Rockingham , in the County of Northampton: My Lords desire you will take the same into your Consideration, and report to them the Value of the Timber growing on Sulehay Walk, within the said Forest; together with your Opinion, what may be lit to be done thereupon. I am,

Sir,

Treasury Chambers, Your most bumble Servant, the 2 2d March 1764. Thomas Whately.

Surveyor of the Woods.

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

My Lords,

In obedience to your Lordships Commands, signified to me by Letter from Mr. , the 2 2d of

March last, I have considered the annexed Memorial of the Right honourable Thomas Earl of Westmorland, relating to the Valuation of His Majesty’s Timber in Sulehay Walk, in Rockingham in the County of Northampton; and also a former Memorial of the said Earl (likewise referred to me) praying your Lordships (among other Tilings) to grant him the Office of Master Forester of Cliff within the said Forest, for Three Lives therein named; and further praying to be freed and discharged from a Clause in the present Grant, restraining him from lopping or cutting down any Timber in Sulehay Walk, within the said Bayliwick.

I find that a Grant pass’d the Third of August, in the 13th Year of Queen Elizabeth, to Sir Walter Mild may, his Heirs and Assigns, for ever, of all Woods and Underwoods belonging to the Crown

within the Hays or Walks of Sulehay and within the said Bailiwick of Cliff, in the said Forest, and of the Soil thereof, excepting and reserving to the Crown all Oak Trees which then did, or afterwards should, exceed the Scantling of Ten Inches Square, a Yard above the Ground; and 1 am informed the Memorialist is become vested in the Premises, subject to the said Clause, which he prays to be freed and discharged from in the desired new Grant of the same Office.

I have caused the said Timber to be viewed and surveyed by experienced Persons, and find there are no more than 2,750 Timber Trees standing on the Premises (there having been several Falls of Timber made not long since for the Service of the Crown) besides Saplings likely to become Timber; and that very few of these Trees are fit for the Service of His Majesty’s Navy, or likely to be so. And I am of Opinion the same may be valued to the Memorialist, exclusive of the usual and necessary Expences attending the Falls of Timber in His Majesty’s Woods, at about One thousand Seven hundred and Ten Pounds, to be now paid for the same.

I have acquainted the Memorialist with the Quantity of Timber, and the Value of it; who (as the Demand for Timber of this Kind is but small, and there being great Quantities of saleable Timber in the Neighbourhood) seems desirous that your Lordships will accept of such Annual Rent Charge as the proper Officer of the Crown shall think equivalent to the said Sum; to which I have no Objection, if your Lordships shall be pleased to direct the same.

All which is humbly submitted to April 13th your Lordships Judgment.

1764. Edmond Thomas.

A true Copy of the Original, remaining in the Office of the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands. — Examined by Wm Harrison,

Acting Surveyor General.

By the same Memorial, Lord Hyde represented that he held Cornbury Park in Fee, by virtue of a Grant of the same Date to the Earl of Clarendon, under a Rent of 20/. per Annum, which had never been paid. The Memorial of Lord Hyde was referred to the Consideration of the Auditor; and upon his Report, that the Rent had not been paid, and that no Allowance had been made for the Fees and Wages then claimed, the Lords of the Treasury gave Directions for paying what should appear to be due to Lord Hyde, which was stated by the Auditor to be a Balance of 307/. 5s. od. over and above the Sum of 1,800/ for the Rent due for Cornbury Park, for 90 Years, to Lady Day 1751.

That Sum of 307/. ,5s. od. was accordingly paid to Lord Hyde; and the Annual Payment of 21/. 5 s. 1

has ever since been continued to the Duke of Marlborough: But, as the Sum of 42/. 11 8d. allowed to

the Ranger, out of the Produce of the Coppices, is the exact Amount of the Fees granted by all the Patents prior to the Alteration of the Fee for the Laundership from Four Pence to Six Pence per Day, and was allowed in full Payment of the Fees of the Officers of this Forest, we apprehend that the Ranger was not entitled to any other Allowance; and that the Admission of Lord Hyde's Claim, in 1751, was owing to an Inadvertence of the Auditor, who does not seem to have been aware of the Effect of that Condition, in the Leases of the Coppices, which are inrolled in his Office.

This is exclusive of the Timber reserved to the Crown, the Produce of which will be stated separately.

No Reasons appear in the Proceedings for those Leases, why the Fines paid were less than the Sums proposed by the Surveyor General.

Finding the entire Government of the Forest, and the Possession of the Coppices, thus committed to the Duke of Marlborough, we directed our Precept to his Grace; with such Questions relative to the Offices he holds, and the present State of the Forest, as seenied best calculated to procure the Information necessary to enable us to fulfil the Object of our Appointment.

Appendix, From the Answers given for the Duke by Thomas N#,a. Walker, Esquire, it appears, that besides the Salaries mentioned in the Grant of the Offices, he claims, as appurtenant to the Rangership, the Right of killing Deer, Game, Fish, &c. and all other Royalties, such as Fines, Waifs, Estrays, Deodands, Mines, &c. and a Right to all that is growing in the Hollow Woods or Open Forest, such as Heath, Furze, Fern, Bushes, and Shrubs, beneath or inferior to* the Denomination of Timber or Saplings of Timber. That he claims also, under the same Patent, the Ranger's Lodge, and the other Lodges within the Part called The King's Forest, and a Right to cut Timber either in the King’s Coppices or Open Woods, for Repairs of Buildings, Gates, 8cc.; and he states that the Deer have no Provision for their Sustenance in Winter, but from

lopping of Browse, and the Keeper’s Allowance of Meadow Land.

Mr. JValker further say|, That no Swine are admitted into the Forest; that there are no specific Times for admitting the Cattle of the Commoners, or taking them out; that the Forest is cleared only from Necessity, when Want of Food obliges the Owners to remove them, and is driven as olten as the Forest Officers and Marksmen please; and that the Cattle of Strangers are impounded, and a small Fine paid to the Marksmen, and expended by them and their Assistants.

And as to the present Condition of the Forest, Mr. Walker says, " That the greatest Part of the Timber " has been cut, he has been told, at much Waste, and u Loss to the Crown; and that theflft is now very " little left." r *

This Account of the State to which the Forest is now reduced is confirmed to us as well by the Report of the Person whom We employed to survey the same, as by a Survey of the Timber lately made, under the Direction of the present Surveyor General of the Woods, and by our own Observation on a Personal View of the Forest; and yet it appears, that little Advantage to the Crown has arisen from the Timber felled in it during the present Century.
