which resulted from his first Experiment; and that, in the Year 1778, the Petitioner was enabled to resume his Labours, at length, after an indefatigable Exertion both of Body and Mind, and at a very considerable Expence, he completed another Model on a larger Scale, the Effect of which fully answered his most sanguine Expectations; and that, in 1781, the Petitioner obtained His Majesty’s Letters Patent for a Term of Fourteen Years, and soon after erected One of his Engines on a Coal Mine, but from which the Petitioner reaped no Emolument as Patentee, it being the first of the Kind introduced into Practice, and therefore considered in the Nature of an Experiment, but the many Difficulties naturally attendant on the practical Construction of such large and complicated Machines, and the numberless unforeseen Obstacles, which constantly occur on the Introduction of new Inventions, in some Measure disappointed the very high Expectations which were formed in Favour of it, and though these Difficulties were afterwards obviated, the Minds of People in general were prejudiced against the Petitioner’s Invention, which, joined with their natural Cautiousness of entering into expensive Undertakings, prevented the Petitioner from attempting again to introduce it, by building a Second Engine, till the Year 1791, when he erected one on a Copper Mine in Cornwall, which, on being set to work, fully convinced the Public of the great Utility of the Invention, and of its Superiority over every other, but even here the Petitioner was under the Necessity of again foregoing any Benefit which he might be entitled to from it as Patentee, in order to introduce it into Practice; and representing to the House, that near Eleven Years of the Term for which his Patent was granted having already elapsed, and, instead of having reaped any Advantage from his Invention, he has expended a considerable Sum of Money, which the few remaining Years of his Term will most probably be inadequate to the Reimbursement of, and, unless the Term granted by the said Letters Patent be prolonged, it will be impossible he can obtain that Recompence which was the End and Intention of the same, and to which he presumes he is entitled for the many Years intense Labour and Study, and the large Sums he has expended, in this arduous and useful Undertaking: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting him a further Term than is prescribed by his Patent for the sole Use of the Engine so invented by him, under such Limitations and Restrictions as to the House shall appear meet and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Petition A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

against D» thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and

1 ‘ others, being Freeholders, Owners or Occupiers of

Houses, Lands, and Tenements, or Burgesses, within the Borough of Derby, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That Nun's Green did formerly contain Forty-eight Acres, or thereabouts, and all the Freeholders, Owners, and Occupiers of Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Burgesses, within the said Borough, had unlimited Right of Common for their Cattle thereon at all Times of the Year, but the said Green being greatly annoyed by Nuisances, and encroached upon by divers small Buildings, spoiled or injured by digging Gravel, and improperly stocked, an Act was passed, in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for selling Part " of a Green, called Nun's Green, in the Borough of " Derby, in the County of Derby, and for applying " the Money arising from the Sale thereof in the " Improvement of the remaining Part of the said " Green, and for other Purposes therein mentioned," pursuant to which Act, a certain Portion of the said Green was sold at a high Price for Building upon, and the Residue levelled, cleared, and improved; and, by the said Act, it is expressly directed, that the remaining Part of the said Green unsold (a small Piece only excepted) shall be and remain a Common, on which the Freeholders, Owners and Occupiers of Houses, Lands, and Tenements, and Burgesses of the said Borough, shall have a Right of Common for their

Cattle under certain Regulations and Restrictions; and that the said Bill contains Clauses for Sale of the said Residue of the said Green, on which the Petitioners and others are entitled to Right of Common, as aforesaid, and for applying the Money to arise thereby in paving, cleansing, lighting, and improving the said Borough of Derby, by which Clauses, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Petitioners and others would be deprived of their Right of Common on the said Green, as reserved and secured to them in-Perpetuity by the said recited Act, to the great Injury and Inconvenience of the Petitioners and all others entitled to Right of Common on the said Green; and that the said Bill also contains divers other Clauses and Provisions which the Petitioners conceive would be highly prejudicial to them and others, as Owners of Estates, or Inhabitants within the said Borough: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, and that the same may not pass as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the Flouse shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names Petitions are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves against and others, Owners and Occupiers of Houses in the ^erb^cPav* Borough of Derby, was also presented to the House, C‘ and read; Setting forth, That the said Bill contains a Clause for raising the Money necessary for carrying the same into Execution by an Annual Assessment to be levied upon the same Property as the House Tax, to be rated in a Proportion not exceeding that in which it shall, from Time to Time, be rated to the said Tax; and that the Petitioners conceive the said Mode of Assessment is unjust and unequal, as by pursuing it all Mills, Malthouses, Warehouses, and many other Buildings in the Town, of a large Annual Amount, that will be improved by and have the Benefit of the intended Paving and Lighting, will not be liable to contribute any Thing towards the Expence, the Whole whereof will fall upon the Houses and Household Offices, to the grievous and manifest Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill as relates to the Mode of Taxation, and that the same may not pass as it now stands, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Daniel Clutterbuck being examined, said, That the Town of Brudfoi'd and its Neighbourhood are very populous, there being a very considerable and extensive Manufacture of superfine Woollen Cloth carried on within the same, and the Commercial Connections of the said Town and Neighbourhood, with the Cities of Bath and Bristol, are upon a very large Scale.

That the present Road from Bradford to Bath, is also the direct Road to Bristol, which is not only circuitous but perilous, as its Direction is up and down some remarkably long and steep Hills, that very much impede the Traveller, and are the Occasion of frequent Accidents; and that the Passage over Stoke Bridge, is very narrow, high, and dangerous.

That if a Road was made, amended, and kept in Repair, from the Bottom of a certain Lane near the Town of Bradford, called Masons Lane, to join the Turnpike Road leading from the City of Bath to Kingsdozen, at or near to Bath ford Bridge, it would be a real Accommodation to the Public, as w ell as of great Benefit to Bradford and its Dependencies.

COPY of Treasury Minute, dated 16th August 1790, on Memorial of Mr. White, on Behalf of His Majesty’s Subjects who were settled on the Mosquito Shore, praying Compensation for Losses sustained in Consequence of that Country having been given up to the Crown of Spain.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers, 16th August 1790.

PRESENT,

Mr. Pitt

Mr. Eliot,

Lord Apsley.

"Read, Memorial of Mr. White, inclosing an Application from His Majesty’s Subjects, who were settled upon ’the Mosquito Shore, praying Compensation for the Losses they have sustained in Consequence of that Country having been given up to the Crown of Spain by the Convention Treaty of 1786.

My Lords are of Opinion, That, previous to forming any Judgment on the Propriety of proposing to Parliament Measures with a View to compensate the Memorialists for Losses alledged by them to have been occasioned by their Removal from the Mosquito Shore, it is necessary to ascertain more particularly the Nature of the Articles in which such Losses may have consisted, and especially to distinguish how far the same may relate to Implements necessary for cutting Mahogany and Logwood, or for the Cultivation of Land sufficient for the Subsistence of Persons employed in that Business; or to Buildings necessary for their Habitation; or to Expences which may have been necessarily incurred in transporting their Goods and Effects to the Coast of Honduras;and how far to any supposed permanent Property in the Soil; or to any Establishments formed with a View to a regular Settlement or Colony; or to carrying on Trade; or engaging in other Pursuits besides that of cutting Mahogany and Logwood.

Write to Messrs. Marsh and Spranger, and direct them to examine the Parties, and to consider all such Information as they may be able to collect respecting the Objects above mentioned, and respecting the Nature and Extent of the said Losses, and the several Descriptions under which the same may be classed; and to report the Result thereof to this Board.

Acquaint Mr. White, That my Lords have referred his Memorial to Messrs. Marsh and Spranger, with Directions to examine into the several Allegations contained therein, and to make their Report, with as little Delay as possible, to the Board of Treasury.

Treasury Chambers,

PebrJ 24th 1792. Charles Long.

COP Y, First Report of Messrs. Marsh and Spranger, dated 22d November 1790, to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, on Losses alledged to have been sustained by Persons removing from the Mosquito Shore.

Chancery Lane, November 22d 1790.

My Lords,

According to your Lordships Directions, signified in Mr. Steele’s Letter of the 16th of September last, That we should make Enquiry respecting the Losses alledged to have been sustained by Persons by their Removal from the Mosquito Shore, in order to ascertain the Nature of the Articles in which such Losses may have consisted, and to distinguish how far the same may relate to Implements necessary for cutting Mahogany and Logwood, or for the Cultivation of Land sufficient for the Subsistence of Persons employed in that Business, or to Buildings necessary for their Habitations, or to Expences which may have been necessarily incurred in transporting their Goods and Effects to the Coast of Honduras’, and how far to any supposed permanent Property in the Soil, or to any Establishments formed with a View to a regular Settlement or Colony, or to carrying on Trade, or engaging in other Pursuits besides that of cutting Mahogany and Logwood; also, that we should examine the Parties, and consider all such Information as they may be able to collect respecting the Objects above mentioned, and respecting the Nature and Extent of the said Losses, and the several Descriptions under which the same may be classed; and to report the Result thereof to your Lordships j"

We

32 Geo. III. 24° Febru 431

We have considered the Claims that have been presented to us, and examined all such Persons as we could hear of, capable of affording Information respecting the Nature and Amount thereof.

The Number of Claims received is 63, amounting to the Sum of 41,712/. Sterling; and may be classed under the Four following Heads:

1st A large Tract of Land purchased of the Indians, by sundry Persons, with a View to a future and permanent Settlement thereon.

2d. Sugar Plantations.

3d. Lands and Houses necessary for the Use of the Settlers.

4th. Negroes, Mahogany, Craft, and Cattle.

We have in this Manner arranged the annexed Statements, N* 1 and 2, of the Amount of the Claims delivered, and what we conceive may be the probable liquidated Loss sustained under each Head: — Upon which we beg Leave submit to your Lordships Consideration the following Remarks. And with respect to " a large " Tract of Land purchased of the Indians," we have been informed by Colonel James Lawrie (who in the Year 1776 was appointed Superintendant of the Mosquito,) that in the Year 1771 he, together with Seven other Persons, for a small Consideration, purchased and obtained a Conveyance from , King of the Mosquito Shore, and Philip, Chief of the Lower Poya Indians, a Tract of Land called Abarapoya, near the principal Settlement at Black River, stated to contain 2,600,000 Acres, principally with a View to a Gold Mine apprehended to be discovered thereon. That afterwards the said Colonel Laivrie returned to England, and, in the Month of November 1771, on the Behalf of himself and others concerned, presented a Memorial to the Earl of Hillsborough, then Secretary of State for the American Department, acquainting his Lordship with the Nature of this Purchase, and requesting to be informed what Protection and Support he and others might expect from Government in working the Mine, and improving the Estate. That in Answer, his Lordship assured the said Lawrie, that whenever he was disturbed or impeded in his Rights, he might depend upon being effectually supported by Government; recommending to him the Cultivation of the Mine, and whatever other Improvement he intended to make; that the more valuable he made his Acquisitions and Improvements, the more worthy would he appear of the Protection he should at any Time have occasion to request from the Crown. — That, in consequence of this Answer, Colonel Lawrie hired Miners, and provided himself with Articles necessary for improving the Estate, and returned with them to the Mosquito Shore the latter Eijd of the Year 1773; when a Number of Negroes were purchased, and the Objects of the Mine pursued, though with little Success, on Account of Disappointments arising from the Misconduct of the Miners, until a total Stop was put thereto by the War which commenced with Spain in 1779. This Tract is represented to be very valuable, both on Account of the Mine, as well as the Nature in general of the Soil; and that it would early have answered the Expectations of the Proprietors, had the Country been in a State of greater Security against the Spaniards, prior and subsequent to the War aforementioned.

In regard to the Value of this Property, it is not in our Power to offer any Opinion. We cap only say, that the Land is estimated by the Claimants at Two Pence per Acre, and, as they conceive, very much under its Value, which amounts to the Sum of 31,360/. Jamaica Currency, or 22,400 /. Sterling. We have required from One of the Parties interested in this Tract, an Account of the Expences attending the same, which, from the Information at present received, appear to amount to the Sum of 6,391 /. like Currency, or 4,565/. Sterling.

The before mentioned alleged Answer of Lord Hillsborough, together with the Instructions in His Majesty’s Appointment of Mr. Robert Hodgson, as Superintendant of the Settlement on the Mosquito Shore, bearing Date the 31st July 1767, namely — That he should cultivate a strict Union and Friendship with his Indian and other Subjects resident on the Shore, by promoting the Prosperity and improving the Commercial Advantages thereof, seem to have justitied the Proprietors in the Steps which they had taken towards the Improvement of this Estate.

We also think it necessary, for your Lordships Information, to state that we have seen a Copy of the Declaration of Edward, King of the Mosquito Indians, dated 16 March 1739/40, whereby that Country is ceded to the Crown of Great Britain, to be settled by Englishmen, in such Manner as should be thought proper; but at the same Time we think it our Duty to add, that we do not find that Government have ever made any Grants of any Part of this country; and that it appears, by a Letter written by Lord George Germain to Sir Basil Keith, Governor of Jamaica, in June 1777, on the Subject of Applications made from the Shore, by the then Superintendant, Colonel Laurie, for Supplies of Cannon and Troops, " That it was not " the Wish or Purpose of the Crown to establish a Colony or erect a Legislature on the Mosquito Shore, as " Mr. Lawrie and others appeared to entertain Notions of, as might be collected from the Applications to

" Sir Basil Keith for Grants of Land upon the Coast, and from the Advice the Council of Jamaica gave him " to transmit, for his Majesty’s Approbation or Disallowance, several Regulations agreed upon by the Superintendant and certain of the Inhabitants with the Title of Acts."

How far your Lordships may be of Opinion, under all the Circumstances of the Case, that the Proprietors of this Tract have a reasonable Claim for Compensation for the Land, or to be reimbursed the Amount of the Expences they may prove to have been at, we submit to your Lordships Consideration; at the same Time we beg Leave to observe, that, under this Head of Claim, in the annexed Statements, we have only placed the alleged Amount of the latter.

It is also stated to us, that other very considerable Tracts of Land, distant from the principal Settlement at Black River, were in the like Manner taken up from the Indians, but without any Settlement being made thereon; but no Applications have been made to us respecting the m. — All Lands so taken up, we are informed, were surveyed and recorded on the Shore.

The Second Class of Claims is for " Sugar Plantations;" whereon we have to observe, that, whatever might have been the Wish or Intention of Government previous to the Writing of the afore-mentioned Letter from Lord George Germain to the Governor of Jamaica, many Persons, with a View of a permanent Settlement, had cultivated such Lands. — These were nearly all destroyed by the Spaniards in the Year 1779 and 1780; but, the Soil not being rendered useless for the same Culture (the Sugar Canes remaining in the Ground) the Land was deemed of more Value than others.

The Third Class is for " Houses and Lands necessary for tire Settlers;" whereon nothing material occurs to us to state for your Lordships Information.

VoL 47. The

Papers respiting giving up tli© Mosquito Shore 10 the Spaniards.

Papers re- The Fourth is for " Negroes, Mahogany, Craft, and Cattle." A Number of Negroes are stated to have specting deserted to the Spaniards, after the Convention for evacuating the Mosquito Shore, and, though hopes were

giving up the entertained, from a Correspondence which was held with the Spanish Commanding Officer in the Neighbourhood, ShoreUto°the ^at t*ie Value of such Slaves would be made good to the Proprietors, we do not find that they have obtained Spauiards. any Satisfaction for them.

With regard to a Quantity of Mahogany, stated to have been left in the Country at the Time of the final Evacuation, we understand, that though the Spaniards had agreed, that the same should be removed, yet that, soon after they had taken Possession of the Shore, none of His Majesty’s Subjects were allowed to land; and it is therefore probable, large Quantities, at a considerable Distance from Black River, could not be brought away.

As to Craft and Cattle, the Numbers and Amount thereof are not very considerable.

It has been represented to us, that, besides the Claims already delivered, many other Persons, who were settled on the Mosquito Shore, and have retired to some of the West India Islands, and other Places, lost what Property they were possessed of, and that the Amount thereof may not exceed Two thousand Pounds Sterling.

A Claim has been presented to us, by Robert White, Esquire, for the Sum of 3,072/. 195. $d. Sterling, for a Balance due to him from the Settlers, on Account of a Salary of 300l. per Annum, which is stated they had agreed to allow him for his Trouble in acting as their Agent in England; and which Balance, by the Evacuation of the Shore, they became unable to discharge. This Claim we have not included in either of the Statements, conceiving it not to fall within the Limits of the Enquiry we have been directed to make. The Account on which the Claim is founded, is made up to the Year 1786; from which Time, we are informed, Mr. White has been allowed a Pension of 3001, per Annum, in Consideration of his Services as Agent for Honduras; and, under these Circumstances, we have thought proper to mention the Receipt of this Claim, submitting the Propriety of its Allowance to your Lordships Consideration.

We have only to add, that though the Claims in general have been accompanied with the Affidavit of the Claimants, and the Appraisers of their Property, made before the Commissioners appointed to superintend the Evacuation of the Country, yet all the Information we have received, from the few Persons in England acquainted with the Property, has not been given upon Oath; nor have any of their Deeds been transmitted to this Country, but are stated to be in Jamaica and Honduras, where the greatest Part of the Claimant* jnow reside.

We have the Honour to be,

My Lords,

Your Lordships

Most obedient

Humble Servants,

Signed

Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

COPY, Second Report of Messrs. Marsh and Sprmgcr, dated 19th May 1791, to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, on Losses alledged to have been sustained by Persons removing from the Mosquito Shore.

My Lords, Chancery Lane, 19th May 1791.

After we had the Honour of presenting our former Report to your Lordships, we received a further Charge and Claim from the Proprietors of the Alberapoya Tract of Land, to the Amount of 22,684 J. 8 9 d.

Sterling.

In our said Report we stated the Proprietors Account of their Expences attending this Tract at 6,391 I. Jamaica Currency, equal to 4,5601. Sterling, which Sum is included in the further Claim; and, that your Lordships may the better judge how they have increased it to its present Magnitude, we herewith transmit a Copy. A Perusal thereof, and particularly the Two last Items, will, we apprehend, render much Comment upon them unnecessary; but it may be proper to remark, that although the Claim of 1,380/. 8*. tod. for Salary due to Stewards, was included in the before-mentioned Sum of 6,3911. Jamaica Currency, we are inclined to think, that, upon a more strict Investigation, this Charge cannot be supported, and that hitherto no Accounts or Vouchers have been produced.

The Copy of the further Claim will shew your Lordships, that its present increased Amount is owing to the Charge therein of Interest, at Five per Cent, upon every Sum stated to have been expended, computed up to the 25th of December last, and the Claim of 7,6441, for Salaries or Annual Allowances to the Thirteen permanent Proprietors.

The Propriety of this Computation of Interest, or of admitting any Interest to he charged upon the Expences attending this Tract, we submit to your Lordships Determination; but the last Item in the Account, we apprehend, cannot be supported upon any just Principle; nor can we avoid remarking, that it appears by our former Report, that Mr. White, in the Character of Agent to the Settlers on the Mosquito Shore, brought forward a Claim of 3,072/. 194. 5 d.for his Trouble in that Agency, and, as he is One of the aforesaid Thirteen Proprietors, therefore in that Character he now claims a further Allowance of 42/. per Annum.

Upon the Whole, therefore, the apparent Reluctance with which the Account of the Consideration paid for, and of the Expences attending, the Alberapoya Tract was produced by Mr. White, the constant Repetition of every Argument he could suggest, both in the Conversations and Correspondence we have had with him, to dissuade us from suggesting to your Lordships the Propriety of estimating the Compensation to be made by the Amount of the Expences attending the same, or in any other Manner than that in which they did originally, and do still, insist upon, of Two Pence per Acre, amounting to the Sum of 22,400 /. Sterling, impress us strongly with the Idea that this further Statement is fabricated more for the Purpose of raising a Claim, on Account of Expences, to somewhat more than the estimated Value of the Tract at Two Pence per Acre, than to give that fair and candid Account of the Expences actually incurred, which we called for, and expected to have received.

With respect to the Plan upon which Compensation may be made to these Claimants, we beg Leave to submit it to your Lordships better Judgment; but we think it our Duty to add, that, since our former Report, we have stronger Reasons than we then had to imagine that there are many other Persons who may come forward as the Purchasers of large Tracts of Country obtained in a similar Way; and that a Claim has lately been presented for Lands, Houses, &c. to the Amount of 2,495/. Sterling, although we were then informed that the Amount of all unreceived Claims would not probably exceed 2,000l. Sterling.

Wre have the Honour to be,

With great Respect,

My Lords,

Your Lordships Most obedient

humble Servants,

John Marsh, In*

Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

Sir George Jackson reported from the Committee, to Mr Turner.s whom the Petition of James Turner, of Milbank Street, petition re-

Westminster, Gentleman, was referred; That the Com- ported, mittee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Samuel Brandram, Colour Merchant, being examined, said, That the Yellow Colour heretofore used in this Kingdom for painting Coaches, and other Purposes, was imported from Abroad — That Mr.

Turner has invented a Yellow Colour that has been found superior to the Foreign; so much so, that they now export Mr. Turners Colour to the same Parts from whence the Foreign used to be imported; and that, for the general Purposes where Yellow Colour is used, it is less expensive, and infinitely more beautiful,

*» so

32 Geo. III.

27° Februarii.

441

so that the Necessity for the Foreign must, in a great Measure, be now superseded — That it is an Object Of Importance to the Trade and Commerce of this Kingdom, and must become more so, as it is now exported to the East and West , and all

Parts of Europe — That, as Salt is used in the Preparation, it will increase the Consumption of that Article, and render the Use of the Colour called King’s Yellow, and Orpiment, in a great Measure unnecessary.

Then Letters Patent, dated 26th February 1781, granting to the Petitioner an exclusive Right and Property, for the Term of Fourteen Years, in his Invention of a Method of producing a Yellow Colour for painting* in Oil or Water, making White Lead, and of separating the Mineral Alkali from Common Salt, all to be performed in One Process, were produced to your Committee; together with a Copy of the Inrolment in the Court of Chancery of an Instrument in Writing, pursuant to a Proviso in the said Letters Patent, describing the Nature of the safd Invention, and in what Manner the same was to be performed. Then,

Mr. Brandram being further examined, said. That Mr. Turner has been deprived of the Benefit of his Invention by the Artifices of certain Chymists and Colourmen, who have taken Advantage of his Specification; and, being in Possession of the Channels of Trade, have invaded his Patent, and supplied the Dealers and Consumers with an inferior Sort of Yellow Colour, at a lower Price, by which the Sale has been diminished to a very considerable Extent.

That Mr. Turner has obtained Verdicts against several Persons, in divers Suits at Law, for invading his Patent, and an Injunction from the Court of Exchequer to prevent the like Practices in future; but that, in prosecuting such Proceedings, he has been put to much Expence, and great'loss of Time, which has not been recompensed by the Damages given, the same having been only nominal — That unless the Term of the Patent is prolonged, and the Property of the Invention secured for an additional Term, Mr. Turner cannot receive an adequate Recompense for his Labour, Expence, and Loss of Time, in bringing the Discovery to Perfection.

Mr. Brandram then stated to your Committee, That the Consumption of his (the Witness’s) House, in the Patent Yellow, was,

Then,

Mr. Robert Maberley, Coach Painter, being exa-. mined, said, That Mr. Turners Yellow Colour is superior to the Foreign, and less expensive — That the Quality of the Kings Yellow, and Orpiment, which they formerly used to produce a beautiful Yellow, was injurious to the Health of the Workmen in the greatest Degree; and in respect to its Use, it was very inconvenient in the drying, and in not preserving its Colour.

And Mr. Maberley added, That he was a Witness, Vol. 47.

in the Court of King's Bench, when Verdicts were obtained by Mr. Turner, in different Actions, against Persons who had invaded his Patent.

Mr. Lionel Lukin and Mr. Ouxn O'Keefe, Coach-makers, were then examined, who confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Maberley; and added, That, of all the Yellow Colour they had ever used, that made by Mr.

Turner is infinitely preferable, and cheaper in every Respect.

Bristol Gaols A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Common-

1 ctition. alty of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, wag presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Common Gaol of the City of Bristol, and County of the same City, and also the House of Correction, called Bridewell, within the said City, are too small, and not properly constructed for the Reception, Confinement, Separation, and Employment of Prisoners, and it would be of great Public Utility, if a new Gaol, with a Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, were erected in some other Part of the said City and County; and that the purchasing of Ground necessary for such new Gaol, Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, building the same upon a Scale sufficiently large and commodious, and maintaining and supporting the same, will be attended with very considerable Expence, which cannot be provided for, nor can proper Regulations for the due Management of the same, and for the Security and Preservation of the Health of the Prisoners, be established and enforced, without the Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for purchasing the necessary Ground for erecting a new Goal, with a Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, within the City of Bristol and County of the same City, for building the same, and for the other Purposes above mentioned, and to enable the Petitioners to raise Monies for effecting the same, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Sheffield, the Marquis of fVorcester, See.: And they are to meet To-morrowr Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Benyon reported from the Committee, to whom Peterborough the Petition of the several Persons, who have there-unto subscribed their Names, being Owners and Oc- tionreported, cupiers of Houses, Lands, and Tenements, in the City of Peterborough, and Townships or Hamlets of East field and Newark, in the Parish of Saint John Baptist, Peterborough, and the Parish of Eye, in the County of Northampton, and Occupiers of Houses,

Lands, and Tenements, in the Town and Parish of Thorncy, in the Isle of Ely, and County of Cambridge, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. William Bowker being examined, said, That the Road leading from Swanspool Bridge, in the City of Peterborough, through the Townships or Hamlets of Eastfield and Newark, and Parish of Eye, to Thorney, in the Isle of Ely, is greatly out of Repair, and narrow, low, and incommodious to Travellers, and cannot be properly repaired and widened by the ordinary Course of Law; and that the said Road may be made more commodious, if the narrow Lanes were, in certain Parts, avoided, and made to pass on higher and more open Ground.

And the Witness further said, That some Part of the said Road, leading through a Street called Boongate, in the said City, is very narrow, and dangerous to Travellers, and that, in order to open the same, and to make it safe and commodious, it will be necessary to take down a Cottage, and some Buildings belonging thereto, the whole being of small Value; and to lay the Site, or Part thereof, into the Road; and also to add a small Part of a Close and Garden, in Boongate aforesaid, into the Road.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from Swanspool Bridge, in the City of Peterborough, to the Town of Thorney, in the Isle of Ely, in the County of Cambridge, and for altering the Course of some Part of the said Road: And that Mr. and Mr. Lionel Darner, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go, with the Mace, to the Places adjacent, and require the Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Two Members being present;

The Counsel and Agents were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration, was read;

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (before prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Name of Lieutenant Colonel Gould being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, the Reasons, which he before stated to the House on Thursday last; and he was excused accordingly.

And the Name, of the Honourable George Cranfeld Berkeley being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, the Reasons, which he before stated to the House on Thursday last; and he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Thirty-two Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir James St. Clair Erskine,

Baronet, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioners.

And the Names of Eight other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir Elijahbeing drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel fop the Sitting Members.

And the Names of Seven other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir Charles Gould being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, That, as Judge Advocate General, his Attendance was absolutely necessary on a General Court Martial holden for the Trial of Captain Shipley, of the Corps of Engineers; and the Substance of what was so alledged by him, being taken down by the Clerk, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon; and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

And the Names of Two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Thirty-eight other Members, then present, were drawn and set aside, Eight on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards (before sworn);

Eleven against tyhose Election Petitions were depending; One as being a Petitioner complaining of an undue Election and Return;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Kitching being examined, said, That the several Roads described in the Petition, are in most Parts ruinous, narrow, and incommodious for Carriages and Travellers — That many Parts of the Road lead through uncultivated Wastes and Moor Lands, and other Parts thereof are subject to be Overflowed by several' Brooks or Rivulets, which, by reason of the mountainous Country through which they run, are frequently flooded and rendered impassable — That if the said Roads were to be properly repaired, widened, and raised, and the said Brooks made passable for Carriages in the Time of Floods, by sufficient Tunnels, Arches, or other Erections, it would be of great Advantage and Convenience to all Persons residing near the same, and would likewise facilitate the Carriage of Coals, Lead, Timber, Corn, and other Produce of the adjacent Country, and also be of great Public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending, widening, raising, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from The Hoodgate, at the West End of the Town of Middleton , in the County of Durham, to the Town of Egleston, in the same County, and from Egleston Bridge to the Head of the said Town of Egleston, and from thence to the Collieries or Coal Works called West Pitts, in the Parish of Saint Andrews Auckland, in the same County: And that Mr. Burdon and Mr. do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Sanderson being examined, said, That the Skippers and Keelmen employed in navigating Keels upon the River Wtar, are very numerous, and from the Nature of their Employment are obliged to reside mostly in the same Parish, so that when they or their Families become Objects of Parochial Relief, the Parish wherein they reside is either most grievously Vol. 47.

burthened, or an inadequate Fund is raised for their Support; in order therefore to avoid these Evils, the Petitioners are induced, by a Contribution amongst themselves, and a regular small Deduction from their Wages, to raise a Fund for the Relief and Support of themselves and Families when they shall become necessitous, but that they are unable to carry their good Intentions into Effect without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for establishing a permanent Fund for the Relief and Support of Skippers and Keelmen, employed on the River Wear, who, by Sickness, or other accidental Misfortunes, or by Old Age, shall not be able to maintain themselves and their Families, and also for the Relief of the Widows and Children of such Skippers and Keelmen: And that Mr. Burdon and Mr. Milbanke do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Corn, Manure, Timber, Bricks, Tiles, and Gravel; and that many of the common Highways and Roads near the Course of the said River are unavoidably bad and founderous in the Winter, for Want of proper Materials, within a reasonable Distance, to repair the same, which Inconvenience will in a great Measure be remedied by the proposed Navigation, as Gravel and other necessary Materials for the Repair oi such Roads may, by Means thereof, be procured at a much easier Expence to the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Pa-. rishes; and that an adequate Sum of Money has been already subscribed for the Purpose of making the said proposed Navigation and Drainage: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making navigable the River Foss, from its Junction with the River Ouzc, at or near the City of York,

Subscriptions for an additional Capital or Joint Stock of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, and no more, in which Book every Person or Persons, possessed of a Share or Shares of the Original Capital Stock of the said Bank of Scotland, should be entitled to subscribe for as much of the said new or additional Stock, as he, she, or they, should be possessed of the old or original Stock at the Time of his or their subscribing, and no more, or for a lesser Number of Shares, if such Person or Persons should so think proper; and that, by another Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to enable 41 the Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland u farther to increase the Capital Stock of the said u Company," it was enacted, that, within One Month after the passing of the said Act, or as soon thereafter as might be, the Court of Ordinary Directors of the said Bank should appoint a Book to be opened and kept at the Office of the said Bank of Scotland, for receiving Subscriptions for an additional Capital or Joint Stock, to the Extent of Tw elve hundred thousand Pounds Scots, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling Money, and no more, in which Book every Person or Persons, possessed of Two or more Shares of the Capital Stock of the said Bank of Scotland at the Time, should be entitled to subscribe for a proportional Share of the said new or additional Stock, corresponding to the Share so possessed by such Person or Persons at die Time of his, her, or their subscribing, and no more, or for a lesser Number of Shares, if such Person or Persons should so think proper; and that the said Bank of Scotland being of great National Advantage, a further Increase of its Capital Stock would still tend greatly to the Advancement of Commerce, Agriculture, and Manufactures, and be otherwise highly beneficial to the Public: And therefore praying. Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand pour hundred and One Pounds Four Shillings and Eight Pence Half-penny, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued to the Representatives of Henry Bradley, and Janus , Esquires,

for the Expence of maintaining and guarding Convicts in Langstone and Portsmouth Harbours, and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seventeen thousand and Twenty-three Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Two Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued to Duncan Campbell, Esquire, for the Expence of confining, maintaining, and employing Convicts on the River Thames, and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-two thousand One hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued for defraying the Expence of sending Provisions and sundry Articles to the Settlement in New South Walts, and of the Amount of Bills drawn by Governor Philip and Lieutenant Ball, and of other Expences incurred on Account of the Convicts transported to that Settlement, and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued to the Secretary of the Commissioners, appointed in pursuance of an Act, made in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to amend and continue, for a limited " Time, several Acts of Parliament for regulating the " shipping and carrying Slaves, in Vessels,

" from the Coast of Africa and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six thousand Three hundred and Forty-seven Pounds Eleven Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued in consequence of the Expences incurred in carrying on the Prosecution against Warren Hastings, Esquire, and which has not

been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Nine hundred Twenty-six Pounds Nine Shillings and Ten Pence Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, to make good the like Sum which has been issued to Cotton, Esquire, to pay Bills of Exchange, and other Purposes, by the Direction of the Commissioners of the Treasury, and which has not been made good by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Four thousand One hundred and Forty-one Pounds Eleven Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, to make Compensation to the Owners of Ships engaged in the African Trade, for the Losses sustained in Consequence of an Act, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to regulate the shipping and carrying Slaves, in British Vessels, from the Coast of Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirteen thousand

Annoyances, and are in some Parts narrow and incommodious, and the cleansing, watering, and lighting, of the said Streets, Lanes, and Passages, in a proper Manner, and removing and preventing Encroachments, Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances therein, and rendering the same, in all Parts, sufficiently wide and commodious for Passengers and Carriages, would be of great Benefit and Convenience to all Persons residing in, or resorting to, the said Towns; and that the said Towns of Great and Bolton are very insufficiently supplied with Water, and it would tend greatly to the Health, Safety, and Convenience, of the Inliabitants thereof, if Powers were given for forming proper Reservoirs, and other necessary Works, for supplying the said Towns with good and wholesome Water, as well for domestic Uses as for the extinguishing of Fires that may happen therein, and if Powers were also given for providing Engines, and a sufficient Number of Men, to be used and employed in the extinguishing of such Fires; and that the several Streets, Lanes, and Passages in Great Bolton aforesaid, are not properly paved, and the said Earl of Derby, Sir I Ferny Bridgman, John Blackbume, James Lever, and Samuel Crook, Esquires, are joint Lords of the Manor of Great Bolton, and entitled to the Soil of the Commons and Waste Grounds, and to the Royalties within the said Manor, and the said Earl of Derby, Sir Henry Bridgman, John Blackburne, James Lever, Samuel Crook, John Ridgxcay Ann Crompton, and several

Norfolk, especially in the Towns of Winterton and Horsey in Norjolk, and like Breaches have also been made in some Parts of the County of Suffolk, and a great Number of Acres of Arable as well as Marsh Ground, many Miles round, have been Overflowed, and the Salt Water remaining thereon for several Days, the same are greatly injured, and will continue unprofitable for many Years to come, and such Breaches are continually increasing; and that the Powers granted by the said recited Act are found insufficient to authorize the said Commissioners to make effectual Provision for repairing the said Breaches, and for making proper Banks and other Works for effectually securing and protecting the said Lands, and, unless some more effectual Provision be made for that Purpose, there is great Reason to apprehend that the whole Level of Marshes and other Lands, extending as far as the Towns of Great Yarmouth and Beeeles, and even to or near the City of Norwich, will be Overflowed and rendered useless: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for amending the said Act, and for making effectual Provision for embanking against the Sea, and protecting the said Marshes and other Lands from being Overflowed by the Sea, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, Aldermen, and Burgesses, and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it appearing, by the Votes, that Applications have been made for a Tax to be imposed on all Persons keeping Dogs, to be applied in Aid of Parish Rates, the Petitioners, sensibly affected with the Evils produced by the great Number of Dogs kept within the said Borough, submit to the House, that a Tax imposed on Dogs, in Aid of the Parish Rates, for the Relief of the Poor, would be of Public Utility: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Stairs Mr. Honeyxcood reported from the Committee, to

ur whom the Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the

" Hamlet of Broad Stab's, in the Parish of Peter,

in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, and of several of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Richard Collat'd being examined, said, That the Harbour of Broad Stairs is conveniently situated for the Reception of Ships and other Vessels, and will admit those of 1.50 Tons Burthen, and that great Numbers come into the said Harbour as well for the Purpose of Trade as for Shelter and Security in Times ot Storm or Distress — That the Pier, by which the said Harbour is formed, is now in a very ruinous and decayed State, and, unless the same be forthwith put into good and substantial Repair, or wholly taken down and re-built, there is great Reason to apprehend the said Harbour will, in a short Time, become of little or no Use, and that it will require a considerable Sum to defray the Expences thereof — That the only Fund at present applicable to the repairing and supporting the said Pier arises from certain Rates, Droits, or customary Dues, payable by the Owners and Masters of Ships and Vessels coming into the said Harbour; but the same are Voi. 47.

not sufficiently ascertained, nor do they produce a sufficient Sum for that Purpose, and that the Payment thereof cannot at present be effectually enforced, and some additional Rates will be required for the Purposes before mentioned — That great Nuisances and Encroachments have, from Time to Time, been committed and placed within the said Harbour, and it would be of Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the Hamlet of Broad Stairs, and all Persons resorting thereto, if such Nuisances and Encroachments were removed and prevented for the future; and if some Regulations were made respecting the taking of Mud from the said Harbour, for the Purpose of Manure.

Mr. John Hurst being examined, said, That from Ten to Fourteen Vessels, belonging to Broad Stairs, are employed in distant and Foreign Fisheries, besides Vessels in the Chal Trade — That Vessels of about 150 Tons, drawing Eleven Feet Water, can enter the Harbour at High Water, which is dry at Low Water.

Mr. Collard being again examined, said. That the Rates and Droits were granted by a Decree from the Court of Dover, under the Sanction of the Lord Warden of The Cinque Ports — That no other Powers are now existing to compel Payment, but Custom and that Decree — That regular Accounts have been kept of the Money expended on the Pier and Harbour, which are in the Hands of the Pier Wardens — That many Nuisances have been created, by People laying Cart Loads of Flints near the Pier, which have been washed into the Harbour, and Encroachments have been made by building Jetties and Ways upon the Piers, for which the Witness knows no Method of gaining Redress — That Flints, Lime, and other Goods, are exported from the Harbour.

Mr. John Hurst being again examined, said, That several Vessels have taken Shelter in the Harbour the last Stormy Weather, particularly a Swede of about 100 Tons loaded, a Vessel of 150 Tons loaded with Potatoes and other Goods, and a Ship of about 200 Tons partly loaded — That he has known People entering the Harbour refuse to pay the Droits, because they knew there was no Power to enforce the Demand.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing or re-building the Pier adjoining to the Harbour of Broad Stairs, in the Isle of in the County of Kent, and for the better preserving the said Harbour, and for removing and preventing Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances, and regulating the Mooring of Ships and Vessels within the said Harbour: And that Mr. Honywood and the Lord North do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House resumed the adjourned Debate, upon the Motion made Yesterday, That no Arrangement respecting Oczakoze, and its District, appears to have been capable ot affecting the Political or Commercial Interests of this Country, so as to justify any hostile Interference, on the Part of Great Britain, between Russia and The Porte.

And the House was moved, That His Majesty’s most Gracious Message to this House, of the 28th Day of March, in the last Session of Parliament, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

The House was also moved, That the Entry in the

Journal of the House, of the 29th Day of March, in

the last Session of Parliament, of the Address agreed

to by tins House, to be presented to His Majesty, upon taking His Majesty's said most Gracious Message into Consideration might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

Then the Question being put, That no Arrangement respecting Oczakaw, and its District, appears to have been capable of affecting the Political or Commercial Interests of this Country, so as to justify any hostile Interference, on the Part of Great Britain, between Russia and The Porte;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Interference of Great Britain, for the Purpose of preventing the Cession of the said Fortress, and its District, to the Empress of Russia, has been wholly unsuccessful;

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That His Majesty’s Ministers, in endeavouring, by Means of an armed Force, to compel the Empress of Russia to abandon her Claim to Oczakou', and its District, and in continuing an Armament after the Object for which it was prepared had been relinquished, have been guilty of gross Misconduct, tending to incur unnecessary Expences, and to diminish the Influence of the British Nation in Europe;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

The Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Robert Preston, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Town and Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go, with the Mace, to the Places adjacent, and require the Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and One Members being present;

The Counsel and Agents were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration, was read.

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (before prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Names of Two Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of George Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioner.

And the Names of Five other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Francis Armesley, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee, by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

And the Name of Lieutenant Colonel John William Egerton being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, that he was serving on a General Court Martial, holden for the Trial of Lieutenant Lees, of the Corps of Engineers; and the Substance of what was so alleged by him being taken down by the Clerk, and the said Member having, at the Table, verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon, and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

And the Names of Forty-two other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Name of the Earl of Courtown was drawn, who having sworn that he was Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, was excused from serving on the said Committee; and the Names of Forty-one other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside; Seven on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards (before sworn); Twelve against whose Election Petitions were depending; Twenty as then serving on Select Committees; One on

A Petition of the Grocers and Tea Dealers residing Paner&jTea in the populous Streets of London, in the Parish of Paneras, was presented to the House, and read; Set- etl ICIU ting forth, That the Petitioners, in consequence of Regulations in the Act, relative to the Collection of the Duties on Tea, are deprived from receiving Permits to convey any Tea they may sell to their Customers or Friends residing within the Limits of the Chief Office of Excise, and are also deprived of Permits to send their Teas to the Quays to be shipped Coastwise to their Customers in other Towns in Britain, and are likewise deprived of Permits to send their Teas to any Waggon who quarters within the Limits of the Chief Office of Excise, by which they are prevented from supplying their Customers in the Country; and that the Petitioners have suffered much by having such Restrictions, their Trade has become limited to a few Streets, and their Exertions of Industry are checked, and they beg leave to observe, that as their Trade in Tea is under the Survey of attentive and vigilant Officers of His Majesty’s Excise, they should have Permits freely granted to convey their Goods to their Customers in the same Manner as is granted to their Fellow Citizens residing w'ithin the Parish of Mary-le-Bone: And therefore praying, That the House will take their Petition into Consideration, and ordain the Streets in Paneras Parish to be annexed to the Limits of the Chief Office of Excise, or otherwise to grant such Relief to the Petitioners as to the House may appear proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Thomas Hilly of Gresse Streel9 Rathbone Place, London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, in the Year 1787, rented a House in Gresse Street, convenient for a Tobacco Manufactory, and there carried on Business, and an Act of Parliament, which came in force on the 10th of October 1789, has prevented him from going on with his Manufactory, as he is prohibited from removing his Goods; That the Petitioner’s Case is singular and distressing, and it is only from the House he can obtain Relief, therefore he begs Leave to state the Particulars: In the Year 1783 all Ranks of Men were calling out for a more accurate Collection of the Revenue, and an Act was passed with new Regulations to prevent Smuggling; immediately after that the Petitioner used Interest to be heard, and he was permitted to present to one of the Secretaries in the Treasury a Paper, in which he set forth, that in One Port alone, for more than Thirty Years, the Revenue had been Yearly defrauded of 30,000l., which Paper was transmitted by the Secretary to the proper Revenue Board, who examined into the Matter, and Vouchers were found to ascertain the full Amount of the Frauds, and that Revenue Board immediately adopted the Check which the Petitioner pointed out, which prevented the Frauds from being carried on in the same Channel; in consequence of this Intelligence, those in Power brought forward Regulations of the greatest Public Utility, and for such an essential Service the Petitioner expected some Mark of Public Favour, such as being appointed to superintend the Check he had pointed out; no such Offer was made; he was desirous of returning to his Business and Home; that he might do so with Safety, he asked for a Copy of the Report made by the Revenue Board, and from that Board Public Thanks in the Newspapers; this was refused, and the Petitioner could not return; that for several Years the Petitioner frequently represented to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury the Distress he was reduced to in this City, by having pointed out a Fraud that for Thirty Years had escaped the Notice of the Revenue Board, and, during the Public Scrutiny, remained undiscovered, he solicited for the necessary Papers to return home, or some Allowance to subsist on here; his Applications were disregarded; in July 1789, the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury were pleased to allot 430/. to the Petitioner, as a Compensation for his Services and Expences during Six Years Attendance in London, but that Sum would only defray a very small Part of Expences incurred; the Petitioner was desirous to avoid any Argument about Pecuniary Compensation, he declined accepting the Sum offered, and requested the necessary Papers, but they were refused; a Mercantile House in the City of London, out of Pity for w hat the Petitioner suffered in Consequence of his having furnished Intelligence necessary for a Reform, were desirous to put him in a Way to obtain a Livelihood, they therefore advanced him Money to set up as a Tobacco Manufacturer in Gresse Street; and those Merchants observing that the Act had cut him off from sending his Goods to the Quays, or to any Waggon within the' Limits of the Excise Office, or selling to any Person within those Limits, and that he was refused Relief from the Lords of the Treasury and the Commissioners of Excise, they became uneasy for the Money they had advanced; the Petitioner had no Resource; his Goods were loaded with House Rent and Taxes, and going to decay; therefore he was compelled, in the Year 1791, to give the Merchants an Order for the small Sum allotted him; and that the Petitioner is fully convinced that what he suffers arises from a Mistake, for no Instance can be given of any Person being deprived of their Privileges and Property by an Act; it is certainly a Mistake to cut off the populous Streets Vo*,. 47.

in the Parish of Saint Pancras from enjoying the Liberty of the Port of London: And therefore praying the House to take his Case into Consideration, and to give him such Relief in the Premises as to them shall appear proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir William Lemon reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Jonathan of the

Borough of Penryn, in the County of Cornwall, Engineer, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Penwarne, Esquire, being examined, said, That in 1776, the Petitioner invented a Steam Engine for raising Water out of deep Mines, and for other Purposes* on a Plan greatly superior to any Steam Engines before or since made use of, exceeding the irr greatly in Power, and consuming much less Fuel, of which he at that Time made a working Model, but was prevented from pursuing and maturing his Design — That in 1778, the Petitioner resumed his Labours; and, after indefatigable Exertion both of Body and Mind, and at a very considerable Expence, completed another Model on a larger Scale, the Effect of which fully answered his Expectations.

Then Letters Patent, dated 13th 17S1, granting to the Petitioner an exclusive Right and Property, for the Term of Fourteen Years, in his Invention of a Machine or Engine for raising Water and other

_ o o

Liquids, and for other Purposes, by Means of Fire and Steam, were produced to your Committee, together with a Copy of the Inrolment in the Court of Chancery of an Instrument in Writing, pursuant to a Proviso in the said Letters Patent, describing the Nature of the said Invention, and in what Manner the same was to be performed. Then,

Mr. Pcnuarne being again examined, said, That soon after obtaining the Patent, the Petitioner erected one of his Engines on a Coal Mine; but from which he reaped no Emolument as Patentee, it being the first of the Kind introduced into Practice, and therefore considered in the Nature of an Experiment; but the many Difficulties naturally attendant on the practical Construction of such complicated Machines, and the numberless unforeseen Obstacles which constantly occur on the Introduction of new Inventions, in some Measure disappointed the high Expectations formed in Favour of it; and though those Difficulties were afterwards obviated, the Minds of People were prejudiced against the Invention, which, joined to the natural Cautiousness of entering into expensive Undertakings, prevented the Petitioner from attempting again to introduce it till the Year 1791, when he erected an Engine on a Copper Mine in Cornwall, which, on being set to w’ork, fully convinced the , Public of the great Utility of the Invention, and of its Superiority over every other; but even there the Petitioner was under the Necessity of again foregoing any Benefit, in order to introduce it into Practice — That near Eleven Years of the Term of the Patent being elapsed, and the Petitioner, instead of having reaped any Advantage from his Invention, having expended a considerable Sum, it will be impossible to obtain that Recompense for his Labour, Study, and Expence, which it was the Intention of the Letters Patent to grant him, unless the Term thereof be prolonged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for vesting in Jonathan Hornblower, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Use and Property

of certain Machines or Engines for raising Water and other Liquids, commonly called Fire Engines, of his Invention, described therein, for a limited Time: And that Sir William Lemon and Mr. Gregor do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and Privileges intended to be granted by His Majesty by Two Charters for Assurance of Ships and " Merchandizes at Sea, and for lending Money on " Bottomry, and for restraining several extravagant " and unreasonable Practices therein named," his said Majesty did, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing Date at Westminster, the 2 2d Day of June 1720, incorporate divers Persons to be a Corporation in Deed and in Name, and to have perpetual Succession and a Common Seal, by the Name of The Royal Exchange Assurance, for insuring Ships and Goods at Sea, or going to Sea, and for lending Money upon Bottomry, with Power to raise a Capital of 1,500,000l. and to make Bye-Laws and Regulations for the good Government thereof, so that such Bye-Laws were not repugnant to the Laws of the Land, which Charter is subject to Redemption and Power of Revocation, as in the said Act and Charter are mentioned; and that his said Majesty did, by other Letters Patent, bearing Date at Westminster, the Day of April 1721, incorporate the se-

veral Persons in the said other Charter, and therein named, to be a Corporation in Deed and in Name, for the Assurance of any Life or Lives, and against Casualties and Accidents by Fire, and to have perpetual Succession and a Common Seal, by the Name of The Roy al Exchange Assurance of Houses and Goods from Eire, with Power to raise a Capital of 500,000l. and to make Bye-Laws for the Government of the said Corporation, so that the same are not repugnant to the Laws and Customs of the Land, which said Charter was subject to Revocation as therein is mentioned; and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that it will be of Public Utility if the said Corporations are em-VOL. 47.

fowered to grant, sell, or purchase Annuities upon jves, which no other Corporation now is and the granting and purchasing such Annuities arc nrquently in the Hands of improper and necessitous lVrsons, who make an exorbitant Gain thereby, to the great Detriment of Individuals and the Public in general, which would be in a great Measure (if not wholly) prevented, if a known Office, long established, was empowered so to do, and that the Powers granted in and by the said Letters Patent should be extended and enlarged to the granting, selling, or purchasing of Annuities upon Lives; and that, for effectuating the Purposes aforesaid, the Petitioners apprehend it will be necessary that they and their Successors should be empowered to take and use some other Name or Names of Incorporation for the Purposes aforesaid, with Power to make, alter, and renew, a Seal, or Seals, for such Purpose, and that the falsely making, forging, counterfeiting, or altering such Seal or Seals, should be attended with sume Penalty or other Punishment: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to extend and enlarge the Powers granted in and by the said Letters Patent in the Particulars above mentioned, and also for the other Purposes above mentioned.

And Mr. Speaker having acquainted the House, That his Reasons for declining to offer the said Petition of his Highness the Nabob of The Carnatic to the House, did not arise from any Reference to the Contents of the said Petition, but from Respect to the Course of the Proceedings that is observed, when Petitions are offered to the House;

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Empire of the Moguls in has subsisted

for several Ages, dispensing, by Favour of the Almighty God, the Blessings of a regular Government to a large Division of the Inhabitants of the Earth: That one Supreme Monarch, the King of the Moguls, rules over all the Kingdoms, Provinces, and Dominions, of the said extensive Empire: 1'hat the several Kingdoms, or Provinces, are governed by Princes, who derive their Right to Authority from the King of the Moguls by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of the Empire, and a solemn Investiture, on such Conditions as may have been mentioned and ordered in such Letters Patent: That inferior Rulers hold certain Districts under the said Nabobs or Princes, by whose Saned and solemn Investiture, the Authority and Rights of such inferior Rulers are constituted: That those inferior Rulers pay immediate Allegiance and Obedience, with a stated Annual Tribute, to the said Nabobs, for their Country, besides performing Military Service in War, and, when Peace comes, paying their Proportion of the Expences incurred, estimated by the usual Amount of their respective Revenues: That, upon the dutiful Behaviour of such inferior Rulers, the Possessions of the Father are granted to the Son, or nearest legitimate Kinsman, by a regular Saned or Commission, Vo L. 47.

and a new Investiture, upon paying the accustomed Fine of Succession: That no Succession is legal, nor can the Successor execute any legal Act of Power, until he has received such Saned or Commission, and such Investiture, from his immediate Superior the Nabob, who is Lord Paramount of the Country: That, when such inferior Rulers or Vassals commit any great public Crime, refuse to pay their Annual Tribute, evade or disobey Orders in attending their Superior in War with all their Forces, when they abet Enemies, encourage Conspiracies, or in any dangerous Degree prove faithless to their immediate Lord, they are fined, imprisoned, or subjected to absolute Forfeiture, in proportion to their Crimes: That, upon the Extinction of the legitimate Male Line of such Vassals, and their lawful Male Kindred, their Territories fall of Course to the Disposal of their Liege Lord: That the present Nabob of The Carnatic, as well as his Father ul dien Cawn Bahauder, have been Nabobs or Princes of that Kingdom or Country by all the legal and regular Grants and Investitures of the Empire of the Moguls: That the present Nabob succeeded his Father in the Year of the Christian Aira 1749, by all the legal and regular Grants, as Prince of the whole Kingdom of The Carnatic, from the River Cristua to Cape Comorin: That such Grants, and such Investitures, were renewed to him, with additional Rights, Immunities, Franchises, and Privileges, by the successive Kings of the Moguls, till at length, more than Four-and-Twenty Years ago, he received an Altumgah, or Free Grant, for ever, from the present King Shah Allum: That, by this Grant of total Independence, the Allegiance of all the Inhabitants of The Carnatic, whether Natives or Europeans, was transferred to him, as it had been possessed by their former Sovereigns the Kings of Delhi: That the Nabob’s Right to the Government, Royalty, and Dominion, of the whole Carnatic, has, to the present Day, remained unimpaired, undiminished, and unimpeached, by any Act, Deed, Compact, Treaty, Conquest, or other Ground or Pretence whatsoever: That he is of Right and de facto, independent of any Claim of Sovereignty by any Prince, Power, or State, upon Earth: That he is the legal, undisputed, and acknowledged Successor of the King of the Moguls, in all his Prerogatives and absolute Rights, over the whole Carnatic: That His Highness’s Father, as well as himself, became known to the great and gracious Kings of Great Britain, King George the Second, and His present Majesty King George the Third: That his Majesty, King George the Second, in Letters under his Royal Signature, and countersigned by the principal Secretary of his Kingdom, promised his Support to the present Nabob, as an Ally who merited and should receive his Protection: That, in consequence of the reciprocal Friendship between the King of Great Britain and the Nabob, and in Consideration of the undoubted Rights of the latter, he was guaranteed in the Possession of the whole Carnatic, by His Britaruiick Majesty and the French King, by the Eleventh Article of the definitive Treaty of Peace, concluded at Paris in the Year of the Christian A£ra 1763: That His Majesty the King of Great , acknowledging and

considering the Nabob as Sovereign of The Carnatic, wrote him many gracious Letters under His own Royal Hand, treating him as an independent Prince, and promising him and his Family His Royal and August Protection: That His Majesty sent to the Nabob, as an independent Sovereign, two several Embassies under the Great Seal of Great Britain: That his Rights to an absolute Independence are so self-evident and undeniable, that the East India Company, when on the worst Terms with the Nabob, declared solemnly on their Records, that they must acknowledge him to be a Sovereign Prince: That the English East India Company settled Factories in The
