Petition from Carnatic, as Merchants, carrying on their Business as the Nabob of such under the Protection of the Nabobs of the the amatic. Country: That, conformable to their confined Situation, they addressed their immediate Superior the Nabob by Arzee or Petition: That Anwar ul Cmm Bahauder, the Father of the present Nabob, when he arrived in his Government of The found them in their Factory, surrounded by something more like a Garden Wall than a Fort: That the Injustice of the French induced Amvar ul dien Cawn Bahauder to support the English, as well as himself, against such Injustice: That Anwar ul dien being killed in Battle by the French, and his Son, the present Nabob, having succeeded him, Ahmed Shah, the King of the Moguls, ordered his Subjects, the English Factories settled in The Carnatic, to obey him the Nabob, as the mediate Power between them and their Sovereign, the King of the Moguls: That the Governors of the said Factories wrote Arzees or Petitions of Thanks to the Mogul, for appointing the present Nabob to rule over them: That, during the long War, which the Ambition and Injustice of the French raised against the Nabob, the English Company uniting themselves with him as faithful Subjects of the Mogul, their joint Exertions, which were powerfully assisted by the King of Great Britain, became at length victorious over all their Enemies: That the Company’s Servants, after this signal Success, solemnly, under the Hand of their Governor, assured the Nabob, that their Wish and Resolution were to carry on their Business under his Protection, as they had done under the Protection of former Soubadars: That the Company were so thoroughly satisfied that the Nabob wag the legal and rightful Sovereign of The Carnatic, that they wrote circular Letters to all the inferior Rulers, who governed different Districts of the Country, and who, taking Advantage of the Misfortunes of the late Times, had acted a false and undutiful Part towards their Liege Lord: That, among other Rulers of less Note, they wrote to the Rajah of to obey

Orders and Commands, signifying by such Communication, that, should that Vassal prove refractory, they, as good Subjects, would unite their Arms with those of the Nabob against the Rajah as a Rebel: That, when the Business of the Country was settled, the Presidency of Fort Saint George, as Representatives of the English Company, entered into an Agreement with the Nabob, with this Expression, " being obedient to him;" That they declared that, " by the Blessing " of God, the w'hole Carnatic was entirely and firmly " established in the Nabob and his Posterity:" That they solemnly engaged, that as long as the English Settlements shall remain in The Decan, Bengal, and Hindostan, the Company’s People are diligently to use their Endeavours in promoting and assisting the Affairs of The Carnatic, in its Obedience to the Nabob, and in maintaining firm Friendship and Regard: That the Mind of the Nabob, being swayed by reciprocal Sentiments of Regard towards the English Company, granted them a large Jaghire, which they still hold under him as Lord Paramount: That the Grant of such Jaghire not only promoted their Opulence, but raised them to their political Situation in The Carnatic, which is that of perpetual Jaghiredars: That, after the fortunate Settlement of the Public Troubles, Peace, the Wish of all good Men, became the Commencement of Misfortune to the Nabob: That the Company’s Servants having, by the powerful Aid of the King of Great Britain, been of very signal and very effectual Service in expelling the Enemies of The Carnatic, began to mix their Hands with its internal Politics: That, under the Pretence of being unable to obtain Justice by Force from the Rajah of Tanjore, for his rebellious, treacherous, and dangerous Behaviour during the War, they entered v>

into a Treaty with him: That the Nabob, deeming the Terms of the Treaty very far from being adequate, was very unwilling to sign at; and that the President of Fort Saint George put the Nabob’s Chop by Force to the said Treaty: That the Nabob will not ascribe the Treaty to the Interests of Individuals, but will only observe, that it was a glaring Encroachment on his just and independent Rights, as Sovereign of all the Inhabitants of The Carnatic: That the Company’s Servants having forgot the Object of their Institution, which was Trade, in the Length of the War turned their Thoughts to other Views: That, by pressing the Nabob to pay his Debt to the Company, which he had incurred for their Aid during the Troubles, and that in Instalments too large for his Revenue, he was forced to involve himself by borrowing Money of Individuals at,a great Interest: That thus he became to be pressed by nearly the same Persons in a double Capacity; on the one Side as Managers of the Public Funds, on the other as partly the Proprietors of the Private Debts: That Distress thus began, and was followed up by various Misfortunes: That the Company’s Government, on the Score of his Distresses, assumed a high Tone, and as Creditors of the Nabob began to lessen his Authority, by interfering with his Government: That, to render him more subservient to their own domineering Spirit, they very industriously and successfully concealed from the Nabob his being guaranteed in all his Rights by the Eleventh Article of the Treaty of Paris: That he only heard of that Treaty at last through the Humanity of an English Gentleman, after the Presidency of Fort Saint George threatened to reduce him, the Nabob, to a mere nominal Nabob, like him of Bengal: That the Company’s Servants, availing themselves of the Nabob’s Ignorance of the Treaty, and of his want of Access to the Justice of the British Government and Nation, pressed and oppressed him as Avarice x>r other Passions prevailed: That they entered into a War without his Consent, but in his Name, and charged him with the Expences of it as his War: That he was thus exposed to a double Misfortune, his Country being ravaged by the Enemy, and being forced to extort from his exhausted Subjects such Sums as the Servants of the Company chose to charge him with, on account of their Masters: That the Nabob, worn out by Oppressions, and harassed by Extortions, resolved to convey his Complaints to the Ears of his Protector and the Guarantee of his Dominions, His Majesty the King of Great Britain: That he wrote a Letter to the Earl of Chatham, then His Majesty’s Minister, and who had corresponded with him the Nabob, as an Ally of Great Britain, Ten Years before: That, in consequence of his Letter, His Majesty was pleased to appoint an Ambassador, under the Great Seal, to inquire into the Grievances of the Nabob on the Spot: That the inferior and subordinate Rulers of Provinces and Districts of The Carnatic, perceiving that the Nabob’s Authority was invaded by the Company’s Servants, became refractory, disobedient, and treacherous, evading their Annual Tribute, refusing their Military Services, corresponding with Rebels, and abetting Enemies: That the most rich, and consequently the most powerful, the Rajah of Tanjore, though highly favoured in an Agreement made in the Year 1762, became, perhaps, upon that very Account, the least attentive to his Duty, and the most obstinate in his public and constitutional Delinquency: That, small as the Tribute was which he agreed to pay by that Treaty, he evaded the Payment of it by various and false Pretences: That he encouraged and corresponded with the Rebel Jsoph Cawn: That he abetted the Invasion of AH, and gave him

Money and Provisions for his Army: That he invited The Mahrattas to The Carnatic, and carried on

Intrigues

Intrigues with the different European Factories and Settlements on the Coast: That he refused to perform his Military Services when War was in the Country, though bound to give it upon the Requisition of the Superior: That, as a Proof of his Connivance with Hyder Ali, that Chief, when Superior in the Field, in-

sisted upon his being included as his Friend in the Treaty which he forced upon the Servants of the Company at the Gates of Madras: That he refused to pay his Proportion of the Expences of the War, though possessed of a very ample Revenue, and his Country being situated in the very Heart of The Carnatic, he was protected from all Danger by the Exertions of the Nabob and the English Nation: That the Conduct of this Rajah was altogether inexcusable, will appear from the following Facts: That the Part of The Carnatic which is called Tanjore is, as has been jlist mentioned, surrounded on Three Sides by the rest of The Carnatic: That the Fertility of the Country depends on the River Cavery, which, contrary to its natural Course, is forced into the Province of Tanjore, by a Mound of Earth, in a Place beyond its Limits: That from that Circumstance, and others unnecessary to be named, Tanjore has been always dependent on its Neighbours: That when a Hindoo Sovereign reigned over The Carnatic, the Naigs of Tanjore were his Feudatories, Vassals, and Subjects: That when the Hindoo Empire declined, it became a Part of the Conquest of the Patan Kingdoms of The Decan; and that when Trouble and Invasions directed their Forces and Attention to another Quarter, Tanjore, never intended, by its Situation and Nature, to be a separate Government, became dependent on the Rajahs of Tritchinopoly: That in the Years of the Christian uEra 1686, and 1G87, that great, wise, and fortunate King of the Moguls, the illustrious Allumgeer, having reduced the Kingdoms

of The Decan, became Sovereign of The Carnatic: That Allumgeer, having constituted one of his Nobles, Zulphucar Cawn Bahauder, Nabob of Arcot and The Carnatic, ordered him to reduce the Naig of Tanjore, who had raised Troubles by abetting the Designs of the Enemies of the King; That when the said Nabob was on his March to displace the Naig, the said Naig made the most humble Submissions to him the Nabob as his immediate Superior: That, in Consequence of his Submission, he was restored to his Government, upon the usual Terms given to Feudatories and Vassals; that is, upon paying an Annual Tribute of 300,000l., besides performing Military Service, with all his Forces: That to the said Naig, whose Name was Sahu-je, succeeded Shurfa-je; and to him Babu-Saheb, both of whom paid their Annual

Tribute, performed their Military Services, besides paying the usual Fine of Succession upon their respective Investitures to their immediate Liege Lord, the Nabob of Arcot:That, after some Troubles, which were settled and composed by the Decision of the Divan, or Council of the Nabob of The Carnatic, Sahu-je, the Second of the Name, became Rajah, by the Commission, Creation, and Investiture, of the said Nabob: That Sahu-je, becoming disobedient and refractory, was afterwards imprisoned by his Liege Lord Sepadar Ali, Nabob of Arcot, who made his own Preceptor, Sheik Assud, Governor of Tanjore: That, in ’ Troubles which followed,

Sahu-je was again restored; but, being a Second Time deprived of Tanjore, one Pertaub Sing was raised to the Dignity of Rajah, by Saned of Abdalla Cawn, Nabob of The Carnatic; in which he was afterwards confirmed by the Nabob Anwar ul Dien Cawn, the Father of the present Nabob: That Pertaub Sing becoming negligent in paying his Tribute, and otherwise refractory, Anwar ul Dien Cawn, Nabob of The Carnatic, was obliged to march against him, and, having defeated and chastised him, received VoL. 47.

him to his Protection, upon paying his Arrears, and the Expence of the Expedition: That the English Company’s Government fired their Guns, and made other Demonstrations of Joy, when they heard of the Nabob’s Victory over his Vassal, and congratulated him in an Address on that Victory: That when the Nabob was unfortunately killed in Battle by the French, and other Rebels, in July 1749, much Trouble ensued in The Carnatic: That a War being kindled, in which the French assisted a false Nabob, and the English, as good Subjects of the Empire, having stood forth in Support of the legal Nabob, his present Highness of The Carnatic, Pertaub Sing, proved false to his immediate Lord: That he evaded the Payment of his Annual Tribute, and refused Compliance, upon Requisition, of the Military Services he was bound to perform by the Nature of his Tenure: That he secretly abetted the French, and corresponded with their Rulers, whilst he amused, betrayed, and deceived, his Lord Paramount, and his Friends the English: That by these Means he saved his Revenue, and became rich, and thus, by his Influence or his Power, induced the English Presidency to make the said Treaty of 17(>2: That, however, the Treaty of 1762 related only to Matters of Account, and the future Amount of the Annual Peish-cush, or Tribute; and that, consequently, it left the Constitutional Rights of the Nabob over Tanjore unimpaired and entire: That Pertaub Sing dying in December 1763, his Son Tulja-je, in consequence of the Nabob’s Promise to the Father, was raised, by Saned and Investiture, to the Putt of Tanjore, upon paying the usual Fine of Succession to his Lord: That the first Act of his Power was to assassinate all his legitimate Male Relations, making himself the last of his Family: That he was as perfidious, and more abandoned than his Father, was guilty of every public Breach of Duty, Allegiance, and Faith: That the Directors of the East India Company were so much offended at his Conduct, that they sent positive Orders to their Servants at Madras to assist the Nabob in bringing the said Tulja-je, his Vassal, to a severe Account, for his multiplied Delinquencies: That those Orders were not executed by the Presidency of Fort St. George, on account of the political State of the surrounding Powers when the Orders arrived, the Nabob himself being unwilling to drive Matters to any Extremity on the same Account: That the Rajah, continuing a System of Delinquency, presumed to take up Arms against his Neighbours and Fellow Vassals, the Subjects and Dependents of the Nabob: That the English Presidency, as well as the Nabob, when they remonstrated against the Conduct of Tulja-je, were treated by him with Inattention, Insolence, and Contempt: That the Nabob, and the Presidency, were obliged, through Necessity, to have Recourse to Arms: That their Troops, in conjunction with the eldest Son of the Nabob, attacked and besieged Tanjore, and, a Breach being made, the Rajah agreed to Terms equally dissatisfactory to the Nabob and to the Presidency: That the Besiegers had scarce removed their Troops from the Sight of the Rajah, when he began, or rather renewed, his Connection with Hyder and The Mahratlas, then the Enemies of The Carnatic: That he continued his Intrigues with the French, Dutch, and Danes: That he not only left unperformed the Articles of his late Agreement, but broke the Treaty of 1762, by evading the Payment of his Tribute, the Settlement of Accounts, and the Amount of the Annual Tribute, being the sole Objects of that Treaty: That, while he refused to pay his just Peishcush to his Superior, he aided the Enemies of that Superior with Money, Provisions, and every Species of Assistance, to induce and enable them to invade The Carnatic: That the Presidency of Fort Saint George, urged by the Necessity of preventing the dangerous Efforts of the Rajah in the very Heart of The Carnatic, again joined their Forces with

and the whole Revenue given to the Killedar and his Friends: That an ample Revenue, received without Deduction, promoted Disputes and Dissentions among themselves: That the Circles of Trouble spreading to the neighbouring Country, the Servants of the Company, as well as the Nabob, were alarmed: That the Presidency accordingly gave their Advice and Concurrence to the Nabob in resuming the Jaghire: That the Nabob accordingly resumed it, and paid a Monthly Allowance to the Killedar and his Family, till Ali, having ravaged Ami, with other Parts of The Carnatic, in the Year 1780, deprived it of all Resources: That Ami, with the rest of The Carnatic, fell under the Management of the Servants of the Company by the Deed of Assignment: That when the rest of The Carnatic was restored to the Nabob, was not restored: That such Conduct is an unjustifiable Interference with the independent Rights of the Nabob: That, besides his Loss of Revenue, he is dishonoured, by the Measure, in the Eyes of India; as the Nature of Things, as well as the Matter of Fact, proves, that the Killedar could not possibly have been permitted to have any indefeasible Right, in a Place within a few Miles of the Capital of The Carnatic: That on the 31st of January 1787, Tulja-je, Rajah of Tanjore, died, leaving none existing of the legitimate Line of his Family: That the Nabob, as Lord Paramount of the Country, made a Requisition to the Company’s Governments in India, to place Tanjore under his Administration, according to the universal Laws of the East: That the View of the Nabob’s Requisition was, not only the Preservation of the undoubted and indisputable Rights of his Government and Sovereignty, but to secure the Peace of The Carnatic, which Nature intended, and Policy required, hould be under One Government: That, adding Advantage to Justice, the Nabob made Proposiils, Vol. 47-

which could not fail to render the Affairs of the English Petition from Nation, on the Coast, prosperous: That the whole hie N;iW»oi Revenue of Tanjore is estimated, at present, at no the more than Ten Lacks of Pagodas; which may justly be ascribed to the loose, profligate, and oppressive Government of the Country, alter it was unjustly wrested from the Hands of the Nabob, in 1776: That the Company only receive, out of that Sum, Four Lacks of Pagodas, for the general Defence: That the Nabob proposed, that the whole Revenue of Tanjore (after defraying the Charges of Collection, and providing such a reasonable Subsistence for the Remains of Tuljaje's Family, as the Company’s Government should think proper) should be appropriated, and set apart, for the Military Service of The Carnatic: That to render this Offer more determinate and explicit, the Nabob engaged to realize, the First Year Eleven Lacks; the Second Year Thirteen Lacks; and from the Third Year Fifteen Lacks of Pagodas Annually, to be paid to the Company, and to be applied to the general Exper.ce: That this last mentioned Sum is One Third more than the whole estimated Revenue of the Country at present; and near Four Times as much as the Company now receive from Tanjore, towards the Public Defence: That the Company’s Governments acceding to the Nabob’s Proposals would perfectly secure The Carnatic from all Foreign Invasion:

That the Public Finances would flourish, and the Army be formidable: That the Company, instead of being almost destitute of Commerce, as at present, might apply their whole Revenue, amounting to near Twenty Lacks of Pagodas, to the Purposes of Investment: That a Subject of such Importance w ill prove an Excuse for Repetitions, that the Nabob is the Sovereign and Lord Paramount of Tanjore, which was left w ithout Heirs, by the Death of Tidjaje: That, by the Laws of India, and those of all Countries in the World where the Feudal Government exists, a Territory left without Heirs reverts to the Sovereign: That the East India Company are no more than Subjects in That in Bengal they are Dew'ans; but only Jaghirdars in The Carnatic: That neither as Dewans of Bcngaly which Country hath nothing to do with The Carnatic; nor as Jaghirdars on the Coast, where their very Tenure marks them as Subjects, they have the smallest Shadow of a Title to interfere with the Constitutional Rights of their Lord Paramount: That, however, the Constitutional Rights of the Nabob, with respect to Tanjore, were overlooked or neglected:

That the Offers of an immense Advantage to the Company and British Nation were disregarded: That a Natural Son of the late Pertaub Sing, w ho had been more than Twelve Years a Prisoner, was placed in the Government of Tanjore: That neither a Saned of Succession, nor an Investiture, were either asked from, nor given by, the Nabob; without which no legal Government can possibly exist in Tanjore: That, thus, the Nabob is grievously injured, in his nearest, dearest, and most sacred Rights: That the Company and British Nation are much injured in point of Finance: That an Example of Encroachment is exhibited to the Eyes of all India; and a Government established, in one of its Provinces, which, having its Foundation on no Right, cannot dispense Justice, the great End of all Government: That, when the Treaty of February 7 787 was negociating between the Nabob and the Madras Government, he represented to them, that the Sums demanded from him were of such a vast Magnitude as he was fully convinced his Country was by no Means able to bear; and Governor Campbell, in consequence of the Nabob's Representations, agreed, in a public Letter, previous to the Execution of the Treaty, that an Abatement of Two Lacks of Pagodas per Annum should be made in his Kists, if the Revenues were formed unequal to the Payment: That the Company's Servants have refused to allow him this Annual

Petition from Abatement; though the Nabob offered to submit the Nabob of the Accourtts of his Receipts to the Inspection of the Carnatic. such Persons as the Governor and Council should think proper to appoint for that Purpose: That by the said Treaty of 1787, it was stipulated, that in the Event of any Failure in the Kists from the want of Rain, or other unforeseen Calamities, a Deduction should be made to the Extent of the Injury which the Revenues might thereby sustain: That the Company’s Servants have also refused to conform to this Stipulation, and to allow him any Deduction in his Kists on Account of Failure in his Revenues from the want of Rain, though it was well known to them that they had suffered in a very great Degree from an unusual Drought of Four successive Years, and their own Jaghire had suffered greatly from the same Cause, and for which they had granted Remission to their own Rentors: That by the same Treaty it was agreed and stipulated, that the Nabob should be furnished Annually with an accurate Account, shewing the Number of Troops maintained, and the Names and Situations of the Garrisons supported by the Annual Contributions, and particularly the Troops and Garrisons maintained by the Nine Lacks of Pagodas Annually contributed by his Highness to the general Defence: That it is now upwards of Three and a Half Years since the Execution of that Treaty, yet the Nabob has not been furnished with any Account whatever, not even of the Dividends made to his private Creditors, and though he is to pay nearly One Half of the Expences of the late War in

Carnatic, and the Company receive Yearly about Four Lacks of Pagodas under that Head, yet they will not ascertain the Quantum of those Expences, or furnish him with any Account to shew when his Payments therein are to have an End: That, by the 15th Article of the aforesaid Treaty, it is also stipulated, that, whenever the Company shall enter into any Negocia-tions wherein the Interests of The Carnatic, and its Dependencies, may be concerned, the President in Council of Fort Saint George shall communicate the Proceedings to his Highness the Nabob of The Carnatic, as the firm Ally of the Company, and that he shall be informed of all Measures which shall relate to the declaring of War, or making Peace with any of the Princes of Hindostan, so far as the Interests of The Carnatic may be immediately concerned therein, and the Name of his Highness shall be inserted in all Treaties regarding The Carnatic: That great Preparations for War were made for several Months together, and Negociations entered into with the Nizam and the MahrattaStates, and Treaties finally made with those Powers, by the Company’s Governments in India: That, so far from conforming to that Article of the Treaty, the Nabob was not informed of any of the Proceedings regarding those Negociations, until after they had been concluded, and the Treaties executed, and even then no further than being furnished with Copies of the Treaties with the Nizam and The Mahrattas, in which neither his Name, nor The Ca, are so much as mentioned: That the Army has been assembled, and Hostilities have been commenced against Tippoo, for several Months past, without giving the Nabob any Information relative to the Operations of the War, though he is expected to pay nearly One Half the Expence thereof: That the Grain of his Country, in which the greatest Part of his Revenues consists, the Ploughing Cattle, and the Husbandmen, were seized for the Use of the Army, whereby he was deprived of the Means of realizing the actual Resources of his Country: That, after having taken these Steps, the Company’s Government at Madras drew up an incorrect and unjust Account against the Nabob, by suppressing the Reduction to be made on the new Arrangement, and the Allowance to be granted by Treaty

for Failure of Crops in bad Seasons, whereby they made appear a large Balance in Favour of the Company, and, without so much as comparing it with the Nabob’s Statement, thus transmitted it to the Government General of Bengal, which was thereby erroneously led to order the Sequestration of his Country:

That, in direct Breach of the aforesaid Treaty of 1787, and in Defiance of the Laws of Nations, they carried the said Orders of the Government General into the most rigorous Execution, seized the Administration of his Country by Force of Arms, committed Acts of Barbarity towards many of his principal Servants and Subjects, Men of Family and Distinction, throughout the Countries, and, in the Face of all the Princes and Powers, and the European Nations, in , in the Face of his Enemies, and of his own Subjects and Dependents, have indelibly injured his Honour, insulted his Dignity, and reduced him to the mere Shadow of the Prince of The Carnatic: That the Nabob has now been the most faithful and stedfast Ally of the English Nation, during a Period of near Fifty Years:

That he has gone Hand in Hand with them at all Times of Adversity as well as Prosperity, and has devoted his whole Life and Fortune to their Welfare:

That, after all, instead of enjoying Repose and Tranquillity, which he had expected would have been the Reward of his long and faithful Attachment to the English Nation, his latter Days are embittered with aggravated Misfortune and Affliction, and his grey Hairs treated with Derision and Contempt: That there are many other Grievances under which the Nabob labours, but which the establishing a general Line, that must not be transgressed, will remove:

That, in setting forth the Grievances he has explained, he has avoided to accuse or blame Individuals: That Redress is his Object, and not Revenge; and that, content with receiving Justice for the future, he wants no Retribution for past Injuries: That he is willing to ascribe some Public Encroachments upon his Rights to the Company’s being ignorant of the Limits of their own; and far be it from his Heart to lay to the Charge of a great Nation, whom he esteems, admires, and loves, those Enormities, Encroachments, and Oppressions, which Passions of various Kinds have suggested to Individuals: That the Nabob of The Carnatic sends this his Petition to the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, as the Company of Merchants of England trading to The East Indies, and their Concerns, are peculiarly under their Inspection and Controul: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to do in them as to the House shall seem fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Peter Bonders and Company, Henry paper ntDg. Isherzcood and Company, William , Abraham Hall, ing Manu--

Birch, and Ouvry, Joseph Knight, John Tootle, John fecturer* Owen, Joseph Cox, Joseph Reekes and Sharp, - Petition'

ton, John Wheeley, Joseph Tayler, and Benjamin Crompton and Son, the principal Paper Hanging Manufacturers of Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for several Years, been extensively engaged in the Business of Paper Hanging Manufacturers, and, from the great Improvements which they have made therein at a very considerable Expence, the Petitioners hoped to have at least participated the Profits derived from the increased Demand for Paper Hangings, but in which reasonable Expectation they have, from the herein after Circumstances, been disappointed; that, by a certain Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, it was enacted, that a Duty of 75 /. per Centum should, from and after the 10th Day of May 1787, be charged on all painted

Paper

32 Geo. III. 5° Martii. 487

Paper or Paper Hangings for Rooms, imported from Foreign Parts, and the said Duties being very unequal to the Duties paid by the British Manufacturers of Paper, printed, painted, or stained in Great Britain, to serve for Hangings and other Uses, and the Price of Labour in Foreign Parts being considerably less than that paid by the Petitioners, and the Importers of Foreign printed, painted, and stained Paper having it in their Power very easily to evade the Payment of the aforesaid Duty, the Revenue, as also the Petitioners, are seriously prejudiced by the same; and that, by an Act passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for better securing the Duties on Paper, printed, painted, or stained in Great Britain, certain Regulations are prescribed for protecting the Revenue from Fraud and Imposition, and by which Regulations the Petitioners have proceeded in the Conduct and Management of their several Manufactories, the same being favourable to the Interests of the Revenue, and in no material Particular inconvenient to the Individual; and that several Persons, in order to evade the Payment of the Duties imposed by the said Act on printed, painted, and stained Paper, and availing themselves of the Increase of Demand for Paper Hangings, do make and vend a Species of Blue Blossom, and Coloured Paper, for papering and hanging Rooms, and which Paper, being dyed at the Mill, is not chargeable with the Duties on Paper, printed, painted, or stained, whereby the Trade of the Petitioners is greatly injured, and the Revenue much decreased; and representing to the House, that, for want of some further Regulations for the better securing of all Duties on Foreign Paper Hangings imported into Great Britain, similar to the Regulations made for securing the Duties on Paper Hangings manufactured in Great Britain, and a proportionable Duty being laid thereon, not only the Revenue has already been, and is still liable to be, very considerably diminished, but the Paper Hanging Manufactory of Great Britain is extremely injured, and will be rendered of little or no Value: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, containing such Provisions as shall appear best calculated to meet and remove the several Inconveniences complained of.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Watson, Mr. Alderman Curtis, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Petition5* Coventry, and of the Vicars, Church-

wardens, and Overseers of the Poor of the Parishes of Saint Michael, Saint John the Baptist, and The Holy Trinity, in the said City, and of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, paying to the Relief of the Poor of and within the said several Parishes, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Poor of the said several Parishes are very numerous, and are maintained at a great and burthensome Expence; and that uniting the said Parishes with respect to the Maintenance of the Poor, and providing a convenient House for their general Reception, and obtaining proper Powers for their Government, Regulation, and Employment, would tend not only to the more effectual Relief, Assistance, and Accommodation, of such as by Age, Infirmities, and Diseases, are rendered incapable of supporting themselves by their Labour, but also to the Employment of the Industrious, and such as are able to work, to the Correction and Punishment of the Idle, Refractory, and Profligate, to the Education of the Infant Poor in Habits of Obedience, Industry, and Religion, and generally to the Advantage of themselves and the said several Parishes, whereby the Poor, instead of being wholly supported by the Inhabitants of the said Parishes, would contribute to the Assistance and Relief mutually of each other, and be of some Advantage to the said Parishes to which they have hitherto been only a heavy and grievous Burthen; and that the Church Yards or Burial Ground belonging to the Churches of Saint Michael and The Holy Trinity, in the said City, are too small for the Burial of the Dead within those Parishes: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the said several Parishes, and for purchasing Burial Ground within those Parishes, in such Manner, under such Regulations and Restrictions, and with such Powers and Authorities for the effecting the above Purposes, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Sout!mv.pt<m County of the Town of Southampton, was presented to 1W l’m-the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, ,:oD passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for better regulating the Poor, and repairing the Highways within the Town and County of the Town of Southampton, the several Parishes within the said Town were united into One District, and divers Powers were given for the Government, Employment, and Regulation of the said Poor; and that the Benefits intended to the Community by the aforesaid Act have not hitherto been experienced, nor have the good Purposes for which the same was enacted been effected, but on the contrary, from the many Defects and Omissions in the said Act, the Inhabitants of the said Town have, for several Years past, laboured under a very heavy and grievous Burthen, which is still daily increasing, inso much that the Rates for the Maintenance and Support of the Poor, are now double the Amount of what they were before the said Act was passed; For remedying whereof, and for the more just and equitable Administration of the Parochial Taxes, and for the Application of the Revenues of the said Town, in Ease of the Burthens incumbent thereon, therefore praying. That the House will take the Petitioners Case into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as shall be thought fit in that Behalf, and also such other Relief as may be deemed necessary and expedient in the Premises, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to that Effect, and for the Repeal of the former Act, preserving the Union of the said respective Parishes.

A Petition of Joseph Booth, Artist, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, after much Trouble, Labour, and Expence, hath invented a Machine or Apparatus, and certain Chemical Compositions, for the Purpose of making various Kinds of Woollen Cloths and similar Articles, in Consideration of which Invention His Majesty has been graciously pleased to grant to him, by His Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, dated the 23d of January last, the sole Benefit and Advantage thereof within England\ Wales, and Berwick upon Tweed, and also by Letters Patent, under the Seal appointed to be used in lieu of the Great Seal of Scotland, dated the 27th of January, for the Term of Fourteen Years, with a Proviso in each of the said Letters Patent, that he should, by Writing under his Hand and Seal, cause a particular Description of the Nature of his said Invention to be enrolled in the Court of Chancery of Great Britain, and also in the Court of Chancellary of Scotlandwithin Four Months after the Date of the said respective Letters Patent; and that the Petitioner has accordingly prepared such particular Description, in order that the true Intent and Meaning of the said Proviso may be complied with, and the full Benefit of the said Invention may be secured to all His Majesty’s Subjects at the Expiration of the said Term of Fourteen Years, but he is informed, that if the said Description be enrolled in the said Courts of Chancery and Chancellary, there is no Means of preventing Copies thereof from being obtained by Foreigners, and others, who will thereby have the Advantage over Vol. 47.

His Majesty’s Subjects, inasmuch as they will be enabled to make Use of the Petitioner’s said Inventions and Discoveries in neighbouring Countries, previous to the Expiration of the Term of the said Letters Patent, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner, who might otherwise supply those Countries with Woollen Cloths and similar Articles during the said Term, and to the Disadvantage of the Trade of this Kingdom, which may otherwise be very much benefited by his said Invention; and that the Petitioner conceives it to be expedient, for the Reasons and Considerations above stated, that the said particular Description so prepared by him, instead of being enrolled in the Court of Chancery of Great Britain, and Court of Chancellary of Scotland' and consequently made accessible to improper Persons, should be delivered within the said limited Time to such Principal Officers of the Court of Chancery of Great Britain, and Court of Chancellary of Scotland, as may be thought proper for their Inspection and Satisfaction, as to the Sufficiency of such Description or Specification, and that the same should be kept under their Seals, so as to be resorted to by the said Otlicers on all necessary Occasions, without being open to the Inspection of Foreigners and others, who might make an improper Use thereof, to the Injury of the Patentee, and Disadvantage of the Trade of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for authorizing such Delivery of the said particular Description or Specification within the said limited Time, instead of the same being enrolled in the said Court of Chancery of Great Britain, and Court of Chancellary in Scotland, and for effectually securing to the Petitioner and the Public the Benefit and Advantages of the said Inventions and Discoveries, or that the Petitioner may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Bernard, Mr. Steele,

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of William Wa Esquire, on Behalf r of himself and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, ever since the Establishment of a Naval Arsenal for the Use of His Majesty at Plymouth Dock, great Inconveniences hare been experienced, and considerable Expences incurred, in the Conduct of the various Branches of His Majesty’s Service there, for want of a Stream of fresh Water;

and that the Inhabitants of the Town of Plymouth

Dock, which is a large and populous Place, having

but a scanty and precarious Supply of fresh Water

from Wells, which sometimes dry in the Summer, have always laboured under great Disadvantages on this Account, and been put to considerable Expence, and the Town itself is not only much exposed to Accidents from Fire by reason thereof, but is much less healthy than it would be if a sufficient Supply of Water could be obtained to keep the same clean and wholesome; and that the Petitioner, more than Two Years since, laid before the Duke of Richmond, Master General of the Ordnance, a Plan for conveying to Plymouth Dock, at a moderate and reasonable Rate, a sufficient Stream of good and wholesome fresh Water for the Supply of all the Branches of His Majesty’s Service carried on there, and of the Inhabitants of the said Town, and also for conveying a sufficient Stream thereof to His Majesty’s Marine Barracks at Stonehouse for supplying the same, which Plan is transmitted to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purpose of accomplishing the Objects above mentioned.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Phelips, Mr. Rolle, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Ghamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Solomon Hougham, an Inhabitant of the Ward of Alders-gate Without, produced a Note from the Reverend Mr.

Garden, the Minister of the Parish, dated 23d 1787, representing the decayed State of the Church, and directed to Mr. Hougham, the Brother of the Witness, who was at that Time One of the Churchwardens; and being examined, he said, The same is Mr. Gardens Hand Writing: Then,

Mr. Joint Bristow, Surveyor, being examined, said,

That he did, in consequence of Directions from the Churchwardens (of whom Mr. Hougham was one) survey the Church of Saint Botolph without Aldcrsgate, and made a Report thereof to the Churchwardens, in Substance as follows: That the old Part of the Church was in a ruinous State, and that ft was necessary the same should undergo a thorough Repair, or be rebuilt.

Mr. Paul Postan, the Vestry Clerk of the said Pari sh, being examined, said, That on the 23d of August 1787, the Churchwardens informed the Vestry that they had received a Letter from the Reverend Mr. Garden, requesting that they would take into Consideration the then present decayed State of the Church: That the Vestry took the same into Consideration, and resolved unanimously that the Church should be repaired —

That on the 28th of August, at another Vestry held, the Report of the Proceedings of the former Vestry having been read, it was resolved that the Church should undergo a general Repair and Improvement — That on the 11th of September following, another Vestry was held, at which the Proceedings of the former Vestry were read and" confirmed, and the Particulars of the general Repairs ascertained; and, in Addition, it was resolved, That the Church should be fitted up and made as commodious as possible, and that the Churchwardens should apply to Doctors Commons for a Faculty for that Purpose, and which Faculty was

afterwards

afterwards obtained; and further, that the Churchwardens should borrow for the Repairs of the Church a Sum of 3,000l., on Life Annuities; and by the Votes of several subsequent general Vestries, that Sum was increased to 12,750 /. of which the Sum of 12,225/. was raised, and for which Annuities were granted to several Persons, and Bonds executed accordingly by the Churchwardens, Overseers, and other Inhabitants. Then,

Mr. William Powell, the Master of the Workhouse of the said Parish, being examined, said, That the old Workhouse was in a ruinous State in the Years 1786 and 1787, and was also too small to contain the Poor of the said Parish; and that by an Order of Vestry a new one was built upon a larger Scale, and in a different Situation; the Expence of which he does not know, but says the Money was directed to be raised on Annuities for Lives. Then,

Mr. Solomon Hougham being further examined, said, That the Sum of 4,650 /. was raised for building the Workhouse, and that Annuities were granted in like Manner as for the Church — That the Money raised for the Church was laid out upon the Church, and the Money raised for the Workhouse was laid out upon the Workhouse, and Accounts were kept distinct from each other — That the Annuitants were regularly paid their several Annuities out of the Parish Rates or Assessments up to Lady Day 1791, but from that Time, from some legal Doubts which have arisen, the Payments in respect thereof have been since discontinued.

William Blake, Esquire, one of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, being examined, said, That many of the principal Inhabitants of the Ward, as well as himself, are desirous that Relief should be granted to the Annuitants. Then,

James Ramsbottom, Esquire, another Inhabitant of the said Parish, confirmed Mr. Blake's Evidence.

Petition. City of London, Coal Merchant, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That at a Manufactory of considerable Extent in the Neighbourhood of London, for the Preparation of Volatile Alkali, Glauber Salts, and a Variety of Chemical Operations, the Petitioner has built a great Number of Coke Furnaces, the Heat arising from which is employed in the above Purposes, but the high Duty laid on Coals prevents the Coke burnt in them from being vended but at a great Loss, as the Coke which is burnt at Newcastle upon Tyne is from Coals which pay no Duty, and the Coke when imported into the Port of London pays very little more than Half the Duties laid on Coals; and that till of late the Whole of the Sal Ammoniac used in this Country was imported from Egypt, but if the Coke burnt in the Furnaces at the Manufactory thereof could be vended without Loss, the whole Consumption of this Country would not only be provided for by Manufactures at home, but foreign Markets might be supplied from hence, tq the great Advantage of this Country: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Encouragement of the Manufactory of Sal Ammoniac, by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do

examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Hill being examined, said, That the Town and County of the said Borough is ill supplied with Water, whereby the Inhabitants are liable to great Mischiefs in Cases of Fire — That the Streets, Lanes, and public Passages within the said Borough, and Liberties and Precincts thereof, are very ill paved and cleansed.

and incommodious to Passengers, by reason of various Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions; and many Disorders and Irregularities are frequently committed in the Night Time, for want of the said Streets and other Places being properly lighted and watched.

The Witness further said, That the Gaol of the County of the said Borough is very much confined, and insufficient for the Purpose, being unwholesome and dangerous to the Healths of Persons confined therein, and a Nuisance to the Neighbourhood, inso much that the same has lately been presented in His Majesty’s Court of Great Sessions for the said County Borough. He also said, That, although required by Law, there is not at present any House of Correction within the said County Borough, from the Want of which great Inconveniences have arisen; it has therefore become necessary and expedient that the present Gaol should be taken down, and a new Gaol and House of Correction built in a more convenient Situation.

And the Witness added, That the remedying the several Inconveniences above mentioned will not only be of Benefit, Safety, and Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Town and County Borough, but will also be of great public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a new Gaol and House of Correction for the Town and County Borough of Carmarthen, and for supplying the said Town and County Borough, and the Liberties thereof, with Water, and for paving, watching, lighting, cleansing, and regulating the Streets, Lanes, Ways, Roads, and public Passages, and for widening and making the same more commodious, and removing and preventing Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions therein, and for other Purposes: And that Mr. Rice and Mr. Philipps do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the Town of Bedford, and also of several of the Trustees for putting in Execution an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for enlarging the charitable Uses, extending the Objects, and regulating the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates given by Sir William Harpur, Knight, and Dame Alice his Wife, for the Benefit of the Poor, and other Objects of Charity, of the Town of Bedford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Trustees appointed by the said Act have proceeded to carry the same into Execution, but, for the better governing, managing, regulating, and applying of the said Charity, and the Estates belonging thereto, it is necessary to alter and amend the said Act; and that the Revenues arising from the said Estates will be much increased in a short Space of Time, wherefore it will be proper and expedient to extend and enlarge the Uses and Purposes to which the Income of the said Estates is, by the said Act, directed to be applied: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to alter, amend, and extend the said Act, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. St. John, the Earl of Upper Ossory, kc.:And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

on the High Road leading from the City of Glasgow to the Town of Hamilton, and from thence leading to Carlisle, is inconveniently situated for the Line of Road, and, from the Length of Time the said Bridge was built, has become insufficient, and is too narrow for the large and heavy Carriages that now pass betwixt the City of Glasgow and Carlisle, and which will also pass betwixt the said City and the Town of Lanerk so soon as the aforesaid new Road is made, and it would be of great Utility that a new Bridge was built over the said River of Clyde below the present Bridge, with proper Roads and Avenues to and from the said new Bridge: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for more effectually making and repairing the aforesaid Roads, and building the said Bridge.

A Petition of the Freeholders, Commissioners of Supply, Justices of the Peace, and Landholders of the County of Ross, whose Names'are thereto annexed, assembled at the Alichaclmas Head Court of the said County, on Wednesday the nth Day of October 1786, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by some unaccountable Oversight, the Acts of Yol. 47.

Parliament, which have fixed the Head Burghs and Places of County Meetings in all the other Counties in Scotland, omit to do the same with respect to Ross* shire, and the above Omission has been the Cause of much Difference in Opinion in the said County; and that the Head Courts have been for a considerable Time past held, with some Exceptions, at Tain, which is situated at the utmost Extremity of the said County, and is a great Hardship on far the greater Part of the Inhabitants; and that the Courts ot Commissioners of Supply were held alternately at all the Royal Burghs in the County, till lately that they have been held at Tain only, which greatly increases the above-mentioned Hardship, many Commissioners being seldom able to attend and exercise their Franchises, owing to the great Fatigue and Inconvenience of such Attendance in so remote a Situation: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to appoint some Central Burgh which may best accommodate the whole County, to be in all Time coming the Place for holding the public Meetings, and to be Head Burgh of the said County.

Ordered, That the said Petition he referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Adam, Sir Charles Ross,

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Ordered, That it he an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do examine and report to the House why the said Petition, which purports to have been signed on the nth Day of October 1786, was not sooner presented to the House.

Bewley, Co- A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, for Helmsdale themselves, and on Behalf of the other Land Owners Bridges and Inhabitants of the Counties of Inverness, Ross,

Petition. Cromarty, Sutherland, Caithness, and the Orkney Islands, and Boroughs therein, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty’s Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the large and rapid Rivers, called Bewley, Cotton, and Helmsdale, run across the Country immediately to the Northward of Inverness from the Mountains to the East Sea, and it is the singular Condition of those Three Rivers to be absolutely without a Bridge, from their Sources down to their respective Friths, from which uncommon Circumstance the large and populous Northern District above mentioned is sometimes utterly inaccessible, and always reached through dangerous Fords and Ferries, with great Inconveniency, and not unfrequently with the Loss of Lives; and that the Funds and Abilities of the said District have been totally exhausted by making long Tracts of good Roads, and constructing numerous Bridges, some on large, and others on smaller Streams, without the Assistance, hitherto, of any Public Aid to effect those laborious and expensive Undertakings in the Counties to the Northward of the said Rivers; and that Two of the said Rivers, viz.

Bewley and Conon, run partly through, and partly contiguous to, Two of the most considerable of the late forfeited Estates, now restored to the Heirs of the former Proprietors; and that, during the Time the said Estates were in the Hands of the Public, the Commissioners appointed for their Management entered, at different Times, upon various Proceedings for building Bridges on the said Rivers of Cotton and Bewley, and paying the Expences out of the Rents of the said Estates, but those Rents having been, from Time to Time, otherwise applied, neither were the said Bridges, nor any other Public Work, carried on upon the said Northern Estates, nor in that Quarter of the Highlands where they lie, although their Rents were regularly levied for the Public, and were intended by Parliament for general Improvements in those Parts, as well as in other Quarters of Scotland; and that the late Grants of the forfeited Estates are charged with Payment, into the Exchequer in Scotland, of certain Sums subject to the future Disposition of Parliament, and, it being understood to be the liberal Intention of Parliament to dispose of those Sums in useful and necessary Public Improvements in Scotland, the Bridges above mentioned are conceived to be primary Objects of that Description, as nearly serving to complete the only Part that now remains unfinished of a Line of Communication from one End of the Island to the other, and the Expence of building the aforesaid Bridges is, by Estimates, computed at about 12,0001.; And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for appropriating the Sum of 12,000l. of the unexhausted Balance which is subject to the Disposition of Parliament, directed, by an Act of the Twenty-fourth of His present Majesty’s Reign, to be paid into the Court of Exchequer in Scotland, by the several Persons to whom the forfeited Estates in Scotland are granted, towards building Bridges over the Rivers , Conon, and Helmsdale,

in North Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Report from The Earl of Mornington, according to Order, re-ooMmnch ported from the Committee of the whole House, to of King'* whom it was referred to consider of so much of His Majesty’s most Gracious Speech to both Houses of Speech as re-Parliament, upon the 31st Day of January last, as latestothe relates to making a suitable Provision for the Establishment of their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Dut- York, chess of York, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That His Majesty be enabled to grant a Yearly Sum or Sums of Money, out of the Consolidated Fund, not exceeding, in the Whole, the Sum of Eighteen Thousand Pounds, to take place and be computed from the 5th Day of July 1791, towards providing for the Establishment of their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Dutchess of York.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum of Eight Thousand Pounds per Annum be settled on Her Royal Highness the Dutchess of York, in case Her Royal Highness should survive His Royal Highness the Duke of York, to be issuing and payable out of the Consolidated Fund.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that the Earl of Mornington, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Secretary Dundas,

Mr. Ryder, Mr. Villiers, Mr. Steele, Mr. Attorney General, and Mr. Solicitor General, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Robert Paris Taylor, a Prisoner in His Mr. TayWi Majesty’s Prison of The Fleet, was presented to the PellUou’ House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner was appointed, by the Right honourable Henry Fox, in the Years 1757 and 1758, as Deputy Paymaster on an Expedition to the Coast of France, and in the Year 1759 in the same Station to pay the Extraordinaries and Contingencies to the Allied Army during the last War in Germany; and that the Petitioner on returning to England, in consequence of Directions received from the Paymaster General in the Year 1764, delivered his Books of Accompts, with Vouchers to support the same, into the Pay Office and Auditor’s Office, for Examination, and which were examined accordingly, and being called upon by the Auditors of Imprest, in the Year 1776, to attend the final Settlement of his Accompts, and to deliver his subsequent Accompts and Vouchers, the Petitioner was obliged to engage the Assistance of fresh Agents, and with them attended- accordingly; and that being informed, at the latter End of the Year 1779, of a Judgment having been obtained by Mr. John Powell against the Executors of the late Mr. Peter Taylor (who was one of the Petitioner’s Sureties to Lord Holland) for 27,700l., and upwards, as a Balance of the Petitioner’s Accompts with Lord Holland, or the Public, the Petitioner took every Means in his Power to convince Mr. Powell that no such Balance could be due by the Petitioner as Deputy to Lord Holland, or as a Public Accomptant, and, finding every Evasion made use of to procrastinate an impartial Investigation of his Claims, the Petitioner, early in the Year -1780, applied to the Commissioners of Public Accompts for their Support, and prayed them to summon Mr. Powell before them, with the Pay Office Books of Accompts, to prove the true State of the Petitioner’s Accompts and Balances; and that, to his great Astonishment and Prejudice, the Petitioner found that Mr. Powell evaded such Elucidation, and in the same Year preferred a Petition to the High Court of Chancery, insisting on that being the proper Place for the Investi-

gation of the Accompts in Dispute; that the Petitioner, from that Period to the present, has attended Master Holford, and is now informed that the Accompts cannot be taken in that Court; that the Petitioner having a Suit in the same Court depending between him and the Executors of Mr. Peter Taylor, deceased, the Property of the Petitioner is withheld from him, and the Judgment obtained by Mr. Powell set up as a Bar in Equity to the Claim of the Petitioner on the Effects of the deceased Mr. Peter Taylor, and the Petitioner is therefore constrained to solicit the Interposition of the House, in order that a speedy Investigation of his Dealings and Transactions with Lord Holland, as his Deputy, or as a Public Accomp-tant, may take Place, the Petitioner having been for many Years deprived of his Liberty, and otherwise in great Distress, in consequence of contrived and vexatious Delays in the final Settlement of his Accompts: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same into Consideration, and grant him such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Thomas Mudge, Watchmaker, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner being brought up a Watchmaker, and having naturally a strong Turn for Mechanical Pursuits from a very early Period of Life, devoted much of his Attention to the Improvement of Time Keepers, and, from several Discoveries he made while so employed, he was induced to think that, by giving up the Whole of his Time to this object, he should be able to bring them to such a Degree of Perfection as would render them highly useful to the Public, and particularly for ascertaining the Longitude at Sea; and that the Petitioner, under this Idea, gave up his Business, which was at that Time very considerable, and retired into the Country, where he was unremittingly employed for Eighteen Years in the Accomplishment of his Design, and having, after some Years Retirement, finished One Time Keeper, he committed it to the Care of the Reverend Doctor Hornsby, Savillian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, who having found it go with great Accuracy for the Space of Four Months, it was afterwards submitted to be tried by the Board of Longitude, and the Commissioners, after a competent Trial, were so well pleased with it, that they requested the Petitioner to prosecute his Invention, that, by having Two Time Keepers of the same Construction, he might become properly a Candidate for the Rewards offered by the Act, and as the Expence was likely to prove greater than he could sustain without Injury to his Fortune, granted him 500l. to assist him; and that the Petitioner’s Time Keeper, after this Trial, was, in the Years 1784 and 1785, carried Two Voyages to Newfoundland by the late Vice Admiral Campbell, who had then the Command of His Majesty’s Ships upon that Station, and was found by him to go with so much Accuracy, and to determine the Longitude within so trifling a Distance during both Voyages, that he afterwards repeatedly declared it had answered every Purpose that could be desired from such an Invention, and that he was convinced the Introduction of such Time Keepers into the Navy would be of great Service to the Public, adding, that he would never go to Sea without One when it was by any Means to be procured; that the same Time Keeper was afterwards committed to the Care of his Serene Highness the Duke of Saxe Gotha, whose Astronomer, Doctor Zack, took it with him several long Journies by Sea and Land, in the Course of which he was enabled to ascertain the Longitude of several Places with much greater Exactness than had been before done: That the Principles upon which the Petitioner’s said Time Keeper is constructed are so permanent, that it has now gone for more than Sixteen Years with unequalled Excellence in the Hands of many different Persons, all of them Men of great Respectability; that the Petitionerhaving, in the Month of June 1789, completed Two more Time Keepers on the same Construction, he placed them in the Hands of the Astronomer Royal to be tried, pursuant to the Act of Parliament passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, and in the Month of July 1790, a Year’s Trial expired; that, on the 4th Day of December following, the Commissioners of Longitude* upon the Vol. 47.

Report made by the Astronomer Royal, declared themselves of Opinion that they hud not gone within the Limits prescribed by the Act, but it appears, from the Register kept by the Astronomer, and delivered by him to the Petitioner, that, if the most proper Method of Calculation had been adopted for ascertaining the Going of the Petitioner’s Time Keepers, it would have been evident that they had gone much within the Limits which the Act prescribes: That the late Mr. Harrison, about Twenty-five Years since, having made a Time Keeper by which he became entitled to 10,000l. under an Act of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, the same was paid him accordingly, but, having afterwards petitioned for a further Reward, Parliament, in Consideration of the Length of Time he had employed in the Improvement of Time Keepers for the Public Benefit, granted him such an Additional Sum, as, together with what he had received from the Public before, amounted to 20,000 /. in the Whole; and that Mr. Harrisons 'pme Keejiers, though possessed of great Merit, require an extraordinary Degree of Care to preserve them from Accident, and have never been brought into general Use, but the Petitioner’s Time Keepers, besides their measuring Time with much greater Exactness than Mr. Harrison's, require no particular Attention to preserve them from being injured, have not been found to be affected by the Motion of a Ship at Sea, and are so permanent in their Principles, that they may be relied upon for going with Accuracy for a very considerable Length of Time: And therefore praying the House, upon his making a Discovery of the Principles of his Time Keepers to such Persons as may be appointed for receiving it, to grant him such a Reward for the Invention of them, and for the laborious Employment of great Part of his Life, for the Benefit of the Public (the Petitioner being now in the Seventy-seventh Year of his Age) as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Nicl Mac Lean, late a Captain in the late 84th Regiment, a Loyalist, of the late Province of New York, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner served in His Majesty’s Forces under the Command of the late General Gage, in Boston, on the first Report of Hostilities, at the Beginning of the late unfortunate War in America, and his Excellency sent him immediately, on His Majesty’s Service, to Nova Scotia, where he executed his Commission with the utmost Zeal, and with all possible Succes^: That, returning to Boston, and finding Sir William Jloue, then Commander in Chief, not inclined to employ him any further, he obtained his Leave to go to Canada, to serve under the Command of Sir Guy Carleton, now my Lord Dorchester: That he went from Boston by Halifax, in the Depth of W inter 1776, to Canada, and in attempting to get into the Garrison of Quebec, had the Misfortune to fall into the Hands of the Enemy, then blockading that Place, and although thus grievously disappointed in his first Object, his extreme and earnest Concern for the Interest and Honour of his Country engaged him to attempt a Service of the highest and of the utmost Importance to the State, and his high, and warm, and determined Zeal enabled him to accomplish it: That of Course he became the devoted Victim of the Enemy’s most spiteful and ungenerous Revenge, and suffered, through a long Course of close and cruel Imprisonment, every Species of Distress, Insult, and Indignity, that the malignant Spirit of such Revenge did instigate them to inflict, to the total Ruin of his Health and Constitution, often to the most imminent Danger of his Life, until he found Means to break out from one of their Gaols at Baltimore, in That

the Petitioner even afterwards suffered a great Variety of painful Fatigues, Distresses, and Dangers, during several Months, sculking and hiding in the lower Counties upon Delaware, before he could effect his Escape on Board the Roebuck Man of War in Delaware Bay, from which Place Commodore Hotham gave him a Passage to New York: That being, some considerable Time thereafter, informed that the Governor of Canada had appointed him to a Commission in the 84th Regiment; he embraced the first favourable Opportunity to join that Corps, but finding his Health and Constitution utterly destroyed by his Sufferings in the Hands of the Enemy, and some other

Circumstances Concurring to render his Situation disagreeable, he applied for, and very readily obtained,

Leave to resign his Commission for the regulated Price, at the End of the Wari'or Cessation of Hostilities: That, coming to Europe in 1782, the Petitioner, soon after his Arrival, presented a Memorial to the Commissioners of American Loyalists, claiming Value, according to Act of Parliament, for Property that he had been possessed of in the Province of New York, and that he had lost, in consequence of his constant and inviolable Attachment to the Interest and Services of his Sovereign, and of the British Empire, through the whole Course of the War; but the said Commissioners, after holding him in a tedious and pain-stil Suspense of Eight or Nine Years Attendance, have most unjustly rejected his said Claim, without assigning to the Petitioner any Cause or Reason whatever for so rejecting his said Claim, to his great Loss and very cruel Distress: And therefore praying, That the House will give him a full and patient Hearing before the Bar of the House, in Support and Defence of his said Claim, as a most singularly meritorious, and long and cruelly suffering American Loyalist, according to Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of an Act, made in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the further Support and " Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on in the " Greenland Seas and Davis's Slreights," the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bounty of Twenty-five Shillings per Ton be allowed for Three Years, to commence from the 25th Day of December 1792, and from the Expiration of that Term, a Bounty of Twenty Shillings per Ton be allowed for the further Term of Three Years, on all Ships employed in the Greenland and Whale Fishery, under certain Regulations and Restrictions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Whalefins, Oil, or Blubber of Whales, Seal Oil, and Seal Skins, or any other Produce of Seals, and other Fish or Creatures taken or caught in the Greenland Seas or Davis's Sti'eights, or in the Seas adjacent, by British Subjects, be permitted to be imported, Duty free, in British Ships, built, owned, and navigated according to Law, although not fitted out in the Manner required by an Act of the Twenty-sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Henry Hobart, Mr. Ryder, and Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Beer Har- Mr. Bastard reported from the Committee, to whom bour Petition the Petition of several Persons residing or having reported. Estates in the County of Devon, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Thomas Jones, a Surveyor, being examined, said, That he has lately made a Survey of the Cove of Beer, within the Parish of Seaton and Beer, in the County of Devon; and it is practicable, by erecting a new Pier or Piers, to make the same a safe and commodious Harbour for Ships and Vessels of considerable Burthen, which may be done at a moderate Expence; but that there is not at present any Fund applicable to that Purpose.

That the Improvement of the said Harbour will be of great Benefit to the Coasting Trade, and to all Ships passing near the same, by affording them safe Shelter in limes of Danger — That it will also be a Means of enlarging the Fishery carried on there, and tend to the Increase of Seamen — That a considerable Trade might be carried on to and from the said Harbour, which w ould be of great Advantage to the different Manufactures in the Neighbourhood, and also of Public Utility.

And the Witness added, That there is at present about Sixty Fishing Boats belonging to the Cove of Beer, of about Four I ons each, which, from the bad State of the Harbour, are obliged to be taken up into the Town every Time they come in — That the Vessels proper for such Fishery ought to be as large as Sixty Tons, which, by the proposed Improvement, might be accommodated, and lie in Safety, within the Harbour, and be able, at all Times, to come in and go out.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in & Bill for making a Harbour in the Cove of Beer, in the County of Devon: And that Mr. Bastard, Mr. Secretary at War, and Sir John William Dela Pole, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

and that the Petitioners are also Owners of a certain Mill, called Langley Mill, which is supplied with Water out of the said River Erexvash, and which will be materially injured if the Quantity of Water in the said River shall be by any Means diminished; and that the said intended Canal is to be made nearly parallel with the Petitioners Canal for the Space of about Six Miles, and in that Space the greatest Distance of the new Canal from the Petitioners Canal will not exceed One Mile, and in some Places will be within 440 Yards, and in others only no Yards of it, by which Means many of the Sources from which the Erexvash Canal is now supplied with Water will be intercepted, and the Communication between the said Erexi}ash Canal, and divers Mines and Collieries, will be cut off, to the great and manifest Injury of the said Company, both with respect to their Supply of Water and the Trade carried on by their Canal; and that the Petitioners have, in full Confidence of the Security of their particular Act of Parliament, and at their own equal Expence, completed their very extensive and useful Canal, by which the Neighbourhood and the Public have been, and are, essentially benefited and accommodated, and which, for the Reasons above stated, will be injured in a very great Degree, if any Act of the Nature prayed for by the said Petition should be passed: And therefore praying, That, if any Bill should be brought into the House for the Purposes prayed by the said Petition, they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the same, and that it may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, from the Cromford Canal, in the County of Nottingham, to or near to the Town of Nottingham, and to the River Trent, near Nottingham Trent Bridge, and also certain Collateral Cuts therein described from the said intended Canal, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.
