Mr. Alderman Watson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Peter Boners and Company, Henry Isherwoodand Company, Gough,

Abraham Hall, Birch and Ouvry, Joseph Knight, John Tootle, John Owen, Joseph Cox, Joseph and Sharp,

George Britton, John Wheeley, Joseph and Ben-

jamin Crompton and Son, the principal Paper Hanging Manufacturers of Great Britain, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Pickering, a Paper Stainer,- of Cheapside, being examined, said, That he is acquainted with the Petitioners, w ho have, for several Years, been extensively engaged in the Paper Staining Business, and believes that they carry on Three-Fourths of the Trade of the whole Metropolis.

And it appeared, by an Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of His present Majesty, That a Duty of 75 /. per Cent, ad valorem, is charged and payable on all painted Paper, or Paper Hangings, imported from Foreign Parts.

And the Witness informed your Committee, That the said Duty is very unequal to that paid by the British Manufacturers, and the Price of Labour in Foreign Parts is also considerably less than that paid by the Petitioners; and the Importers of Foreign printed, painted, and stained Papers, having it in their Power very easily to evade the Payment of the Duty, the Revenue, as also the Petitioners, are seriously prejudiced by the same — He further said, That the Wages of a Workman in the Paper Staining Business, in France, is from One Shilling to Two Shillings Sterling per Day; in Ireland, the highest Wages given, in the same Business, is Three Shillings and Six Pence Sterling per Day; in England, the Workmen are paid by the Piece, and can earn, according to their different Skill and Abilities, from Three Shillings to Twelve Shillings per Day; upon an Average, the Workmen employed by the Trade in general earn Seven Shillings a Day each; and, from the best Information the Witness can procure, he thinks a Frenchman can do as much Work in a Day as an Englishmen. Then,

An Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of His said Majesty’s Reign, for better securing the Duties on Paper, printed, painted, or stained, in Great Britain, was also read; w hereby certain Regulations are prescribed for protecting the Revenue from Fraud.

And the Witness said, That by these Regulations, the Petitioners have proceeded in the Conduct of their several Manufactories, the same being favourable to the Interests of the Revenue, and in no Material inconvenient to the Individual — He further added.

That there is a Species of Paper made in called blue, blossom, and coloured Paper, w'hicli is used for papering and hanging Rooms, and being dyed in the Mill, is not chargeable with the Duties on Paper, printed, painted, or stained, whereby the Trade of the Petitioners is greatly injured, and the Revenue much decreased, to the Amount of 1/. 10 Ream — That painted Pape; is imported both from France and Ireland, which although liable to a Duty by no Means meeting the Duty paid by the British Manufactun r, yet the Duty to which it is liable, is evaded for Want of its being subjected to the Excise, with such Stamps on each Sheet, and such other Regulations, as the British Manufactory is subject to.

Then,

Mr. John Boover Brooks, who conducts the Manufactory of Messrs. Bower and Co. Paper Hanging Manufacturers of Bond Street, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole Flouse, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. William M‘Dowall reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Freeholders and Owners of Land, in the County of Renfrew, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follow eth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed your Committee, That the Laws now subsisting in Scotland, for the making of Roads and building Bridges, have been found ineffectual for answering those Purposes in the County of Renfrerw, and that other and further Powers are necessary in order to carry the Intention of the said Laws into Execution; and Doubts have arisen in some Cases who are chargeable with repairing the Highways; and that it is at present attended with much Difficulty and Trouble to make effectual and properly apply the Statute Work in the said County — That a reasonable Composition in Money, instead of Labour, is in many Places found to be more useful and effectual, for the Purpose of making and repairing the Roads, as well as more easy and convenient for the Persons liable in Statute Services, than the actual Performance of the same; and that it will be of real Advantage to the County, in certain Cases, to convert the said Services into Money, and to fix and ascertain the Rate and Mode of levying thereof, and also to authorize a further Sum, than is at present levyable, for Road and Bridge Money in the said County.

Vo l. 47.

Then another Member present informed your Committee, That the Road to and from Elieston Bridge, in the said County of Renfrew, having been in a ruinous Condition, and so steep and inaccessible as to prevent any Improvement of the same, a new Bridge, called Garthland Bridge, was erected at a small Distance therefrom, and a new Road has been completely made thereto, at the sole Expence of William of

Garthland, Esquire, which supersedes the Use of the said Road to and from Elieston Bridge; and that therefore it would be of Advantage to the Public, that the said Road

Election. And the Door of the House being locked;

The Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions respecting the Right of Election for the Borough of Steyning, in the County of Sussex, into Consideration, was read.

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (before prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Name of Sir Baronet, was

drawn:

And the said Member having stated to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, That he had served on the former Committee, which had determined the Right of Election for the said Borough, and that therefore he ought not to be required to serve on the Committee now to be appointed for the Purpose of trying the Merits of the Petitions now taken into Consideration;

Thereupon the said Counsel and Agents were directed to retire some Way from the Bar.

The House was moved, That so much of an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Trials " of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members " to serve in Parliament," as relates to the Allegations of Special Excuses for not serving on Select Committees, on which the Opinion of the House is directed to be taken, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That Sir John Ingilby, Baronet, having served on the former Committee which had determined the Right of Election for the said Borough, and therefore coming within the said Provisions of the Act of the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, be excused from serving on the said Select Committee;

The House divided.

Yeas to the Right: Noes to the Left.

Teller for the Yeas, — The Lord North, - 52.

Teller for the Noes, — Nr. John Smyth, - 60.

So it passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel and Agents were again called to

o o

the Bar.

And the Names of Six other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Honourable Lieutenant Colonel Henry Phipps being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioners admitted to defend the Right of Election as determined by the former Committee.

And the Names of Twenty-one other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir Charles Gould being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, that, as Judge Advocate General, his Attendance was absolutely necessary on a General Court Martial, holden for the Trial of Lieutenant Lees, of the Corps of Engineers; and the Substance of what was so alleged by him being taken down by the Clerk, and the said Member having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon, and he was excused from serving on the said Committee*

And the Names of Twenty-two other Members, then present, w ere drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Twenty-eight other Vol. 47.

Members, then present, were drawn and set aside; Nine on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards (before sworn); Four against whose Election Petitions were depending; One as being a Petitioner, complaining of an undue Election and Return; Seven as then serving on Select Committees; and Seven on Account of having in this Session served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Names being complete;

The Counsel for the Petitioners admitted to oppose the Right of Election as determined by the former Committee, nominated the Right honourable Charles James Fox to serve on the said Committee.

And Lists of the Forty-nine Names being delivered to the Counsel; the Door of the House was opened, and the Counsel and Agents withdrew.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made in the Year if>Q5, intituled, "An Act for erecting a Bank in " Scotland" was read, whereby a Joint Stock, amounting to Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots Money, that is, One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, was allowed to be raised by the Company thereby established, for carrying on and managing a Public Bank, and certain Persons therein mentioned were authorized to appoint a Book for receiving the Subscriptions of such Persons as were willing to become Adventurers in the said Joint Stock; and by the said Act it was declared, That all and every the Persons subscribing and paying to the said Joint Stock, in Manner therein directed, should be One Body Politic and Corporate, by the Name of The Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland, under which Name they should have perpetual Succession, and should have a Common Seal, and certain Rules were thereby prescribed for the better ordering and managing the Affairs of the said Bank; and under the said Act, and Rules and Orders therein mentioned, the said Bank w as soon after established, and has ever since continued.

Then an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act to " enable the Governor and Company of the Bank of " Scotland to increase the Capital Stock of the said " Company," was read, whereby it is enacted, That within One Month after the passing of the said Act, or as soon after as might be, the Court of Ordinary Directors of the said Bank should appoint a Book to be opened and kept at the Office of the said Bank of Scotland, for receiving Subscriptions for an additional Capital or Joint Stock of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, and no more, in which Book every Person or Persons possessed of a Share or Shares of the original Capital Stock of the said Bank of Scotland should be entitled to subscribe for as much of the said new or additional Stock as he, she, or they, should be possessed of the old or original Stock at the Time of his, her, or their subscribing, and no more, or for a lesser Number of Shares, if such Person or Persons should so think proper.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, in the Year 1681, and also an Act passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, relative to the Salmon Fishery in the Water of Nith, were read: And,

A Member present informed your Committee, That the Laws in being for regulating the Fisheries in the River Nith have hitherto proved inadequate for checking the Abuses they were intended to correct; and that the Salmon Gilses, Salmon or Sea Trouts, and Hidings, and the Spawn or Fry thereof, are frequently taken and destroyed at improper Seasons in the said River Nith, and the Rivers or Streams which run into the same, and also within the Mouth or Entrance of the said River, to the great Detriment of the Owners and Occupiers of the Fisheries, and Disadvantage of the Public.

Colonel Lennox reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, acting in and for the Eastern Division of the Vol. 47.

County of Sussex, met and assembled at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held at Leues, in and for the said County of Sussex, the 6th Day of October was referred; That the Committee had examined, the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Ellis being examined, said, That, by virtue of an Act of the Seventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the better ordering the Militia of this Kingdom, the Justices of the Peace acting for the Eastern Division of the County of Sussex, in their General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, assembled, ordered the Sum of 2,097/. 10 s. — d. $to be raised upon the said Eastern Division, for the Purposes of the said Act; but, by reason of some Difficulties arising thereupon, no more than the Sum of 886/. 12s. 2d. i was collected, and paid into the Hands of Mr.

Charles Gilbert, the Treasurer of the said Division; as appeared by an Account produced to your Committee.

The Witness further said, That, by virtue of another Act, passed in the Ninth Year of His said Majesty’s Reign, respecting the Militia, the said Justices ordered the like Sum of 2,097/. 10^. — d. I to be raised upon the said Eastern Division, of which no more than the Sum of 440/. lSs. 11 d.\ was collected, and paid into the Hands of the said Treasurer — And he added, That both the said Sums, making together 1,327/. ns. 1 d. i, have remained in the said Treasurers Hand since their respective Payments, as a separate Fund unappropriated;

and that, by several Acts of Parliament, the said County Stock is heavily charged, and it would tend to the Relief and Improvement of the same, and to the Ease of the Inhabitants of the said Eastern Division, if the said Sum of 1,327/. 11 s. 1 d. £ was paid into, and made Part of, the general Stock of the said Division, subject to be disposed of and applied in the same Manner, and by the same Authority, as the said County Stock in general is subject and liable to.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the w hole House.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Fydell reported from the Committee, to w hom

the Petition of several Owners and Proprietors of Estates, and Inhabitants within the Borough and Parish of Boston, in the County of Lincoln, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Paving Bills, had been complied with (except that the Person employed to give the Notices had, by Mistake, affixed the Notice Three Times upon the Door of the Parish Church, in the Month of September last, instead of affixing it upon the Door of the Sessions House, and had also caused Notice to be published for Three Sundays in the said Parish in the same Month; and that it is not intended to erect any Turnpike, or take any Toll, for paving the said Streets); and that the Vox,. 47.

Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Thirkill being examined, said, That the Streets, and other public Passages and Places, within the said Borough and Parish, are not properly paved and cleansed, and are subject to various Encroachments, Nuisances, and Annoyances, and are, in some Parts, narrow and incommodious for Travellers and Carriages, and some of the public Roads therein are not in good Repair, and the Inhabitants of the Parish are not obliged to perform any Statute Duty thereon — That it would be a great Convenience and Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Borough and Parish, and to all Persons resorting thereto, if the Streets, and other public Places therein, were properly paved, repaired, cleansed and widened, and rendered sate and commodious, and if all Encroachments, Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances therein were removed and prevented for the future, and the Roads properly amended and repaired.

Mr. Fydell reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the Commissioners for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, of the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better Regulation and Government of the Pilots conducting Ships and Vessels into and out of the Port ot Boston, in the County of Lincoln, and for affixing and setting down Mooring Posts upon the Banks or High Marshes, within or adjoining to the Haven and Harbour of the said Port, and for affixing and laying down Bridges over the Creeks upon the High Marshes, within or adjoining to the said Haven and Harbour, and for preventing Mischiefs by Eire in the said Haven and Harbour, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: W here the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. William Robinson being examined, said, That

since the passing of the said Act, the Trade and Commerce of the said Port are greatly increased, but that no F'ower is thereby given for appointing a Harbour Master of the said Port, for the Purpose of directing and regulating the Mooring and removing of the Ships and other Vessels within the said Haven or Harbour, for Want of which considerable Delay and Damage frequently happen to Ships and other Vessels, and great Inconvenience to the Owners or Masters thereof.

And being further examined, he said, That there are, within the said Haven and Harbour, certain Marshes, Sand Banks, and Shoals of Sand or Mud, which frequently obstruct and prevent Ships, and other Vessels, coming into the said Haven and Harbour, and that no Provision is made by the said Act for removing such Obstructions. — And the Witness added, That the appointing a Harbour Master of the said Port, with sufficient Powers for directing and regulating the Mooring and removing of Ships and Vessels therein, and cutting through, removing, or lessening the said Marshes, Sand Banks, and Shoals, and making some necessary Alterations in the said Act,

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Neighbourhood of Custompton, Devon: And also,

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Minister, Capital Burgesses, and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Bradninch, in the County of Devon;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, having long lamented the prodigious Increase of Dogs as a serious Evil to the Community, as well on Account of the great Consumption they make of many of the Necessaries of Life as the dreadful Calamities they frequently occasion, but more particularly alarmed, at this Time, by some recent and fatal Instances of Canine Madness, beg Leave to join the many Applications made to Parliament for taking the Matter into Consideration, and earnestly hope that a Tax may be laid on Dogs, to be applied in Aid of the Poors Rates, or such other effectual Measures devised as, by lessening the Number of those Animals, will contribute very essentially to the Peace and Safety of His Majesty’s Subjects in general, as well as the Welfare and better Support of the Poor.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That it appears, that the Resources of Bengal, even at the Beginning of the present War, were so exhausted, by various Drains, through a long Series of successive Years, as to be perfectly incompetent to support the Expences of a War, for any Length of Time, without being reduced to the greatest Extremity of Distress, and that, by the Length of the War, that Distress has already taken Place;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it appears, by the latest Dispatches from Lidia, that the War was then carrying on with a View to diminish the Power and decrease the Territory of Tippoo Sultan v

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by adding, at the End thereof, the Words in consequence of his unprovoked Attack on an u Ally of the Company, and that the War had been " conducted with distinguished Ability and Success."

And the Question being put, That those Words be there added;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That it appears, by the latest Dispatches from India, that the War was then carrying on with a View to diminish the Power and decrease the Territory of Tippoo Sultan, in consequence of his unprovoked Attack on an Ally of the Company, and that the War had been conducted with distinguished Ability and Success.

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed, That the Agreement entered into by Earl Cornwalliswith the Nizam, in his Letter of the 7th of July 1789; the establishing an offensive Military Post in the Travancore Country; the seizing the Dominions of the Nabob of Ai'cot, and of the Rajah of Tanjore, in direct Violation of Treaty; and, the carrying on a War in India, with a View to Acquisition and Addition of Territory; are in direct Violation of the wise, moderate, and politic Views established, by the Parliament of Great Britain, as the Rule of Conduct to be observed in the British Settlements in India.

And the said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Mr. Rice reported from the Committee, to whom Carmuthta the Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, ^oad* and others, of the County of Carmart, was referred; That the Committee bad examiaed, and found that the Standing Orders of the House relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with, in respect to the Roads leading from Golden Grove Park; from Cae-Cappel-Issa; from the Cross Road in the Parish of Llarrvihangel Abcrbythych; and from the Cross Inn, in the Parish of Liangathen, (except that the Notices, required to be inserted in the public Newspapers in the Months of August or September, were inserted on the 28th of September, and the 3d and 5th of October; but, with respect to the several other Roads mentioned in the Petition, the said Standing Orders had not been complied with, the Utility of repairing those Roads not having been discovered till it was too late to comply with the said Orders; and it appeared to the Committee, that the principal Inhabitants of the Parishes, through which the said Roads pass, are desirous that the same may be made Turnpike); and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Roderick being examined, said, That he is well acquainted with the Roads described in the Petition —

That the same are very much out of Repair, and extremely inconvenient, narrow, and founderous — That the River Tony, at Rhyd-y-cappel and in the

Parish of Liangathen, is at Times dangerous, by reason of large Stones and rapid Currents, and often rendered impassable by Floods, so that Travellers and Carriages are often impeded, and cannot conveniently pass or travel along the Roads, or cross the said River at those Places with Safety.

And the Witness added, That it would be of great Benefit, Convenience, and Utility to the Petitioners, and all other Persons residing in or having Occasion to travel on the said Roads, if the same were properly formed, diverted, widened, and made commodious, and proper Bridges built on the River Tcricy, and Ferry Boats established until such Bridges should be completed.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Orred being examined, said. That the Buildings and Inhabitants of the Town of Liverpool have of late Years greatly increased, and are still increasing; and it has become necessary that One or more additional Church or Churches should be provided for the Accommodation of the Inhabitants of the said Town.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Council of the Petition from Borough of Brechin, was presented to the House, and ^*^fm0for read; Setting forth. That by certain Laws now in Ministers, Force, the Pastors or Ministers and Lay Persons of the &c. of the Episcopal Communion in Scotland are laid under pe- Episcopal culiar Restrictions in the Exercise of their Religious Worship, and subjected to Penalties and Forfeitures which, at the Time of passing those Laws, w ere judged necessary for the Security of his late Majesty’s Person and Government; and that the Circumstances which gave Occasion to those Penal Statutes do now no longer exist, and the Persons subjected to them have given every Proof of their Loyalty which the Law has put in their Power, and are well known to entertain Principles most friendly to the Constitution and Government of this Country, and tending to promote its Peace and Welfare, of which the Petitioners have Experience in the Conduct of those of the Episcopal Communion within their Jurisdiction: And therefore the Petitioners, moved with Sympathy for a respectable Body of their Fellow Citizens who are deprived of that Toleration which is so freely enjoyed by all other Protestant Dissenters in that Part of the Kingdom, beg Leave to request that the Clemency of the British Legislature may be extended to the Persons above mentioned, and such Relief granted from the Hardships and Restraints which they at present lie under as may seem expedient to the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Bernard reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Joseph Booth, Artist, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as fofloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioner said, That he had invented a Machine r Apparatus, and certain cliemical Compositions,' for Vol. 47.

the Purpose of making various Kinds of Woollen Cloths, and similar Articles, for which he hath obtained Patents under the Seal of Great Britain and of Scotland, for the Term of Fourteen Years, with a Proviso to enroll a Specification of his said Invention in the Court of Chancery of Great Britain, and also in the Court of Chancellary of Scotland, within Four Months after the Date of the said respective Letters Patent — That he has accordingly prepared such particular Description, but is informed that if the same be enrolled in the said Courts, there is no Means of preventing Copies from being obtained by Foreigners and others, who will thereby have the Advantage over His Majesty’s Subjects, and be enabled to make use of the said Inventions and Discoveries, to the manifest Injury of your Petitioner, and to the Disadvantage of the Trade of this Kingdom. — And being further examined, he said, That his Reasons for apprehending that the Specification of his Invention will he obtained by Foreigners, and carried Abroad, are, that being a Draughtsman by Profession, he was, in the Year 17S1, employed by Mr. Delius, of Hamburgh, Agent for some Manufacturers on the Continent, to copy certain Drawings of Machinery, which he has since discovered to have been those of Sir Richard Arkwright, for carding and spinning of Cotton, and that he has since heard those Engines have been established in Prussia, and some Parts of Germany.

Mr. James Turner being examined, said, That, owing to the Specification of his Patent having been accessible and liable to be copied, Copies thereof have been obtained and carried Abroad, and the Patent Yellow manufactured in Foreign Parts, to his great Injury; and that he has suffered so much by this and other Infringements of his Patent, that, notwithstanding the acknowledged Merit of his Invention, he has actually been a Loser thereby; in particular, Mr. Authur, a Paper Maker, has obtained a Patent for this Yellow in France, where the Specification is not liable to Inspection. — And the Witness further stated, That Mr. Samuel Brandrum, of London, has, at this Time, Commissions from his Correspondents in the United States of America, to send them Copies of Specifications of Patent Medicines, and other useful Inventions; and that Mr. Magellan, a Portuguese (who is lately dead) was for many Years employed by Foreign States to obtain Information of all new Inventions and Discoveries, and to procure Copies of the Specifications of Inventions, with a View of establishing them Abroad.

Then Mr. Charles Simpson being examined, said, That having, on Tuesday last, applied at the Enrolment Office in Chancery, for a Copy of the Specification of Lord Dundona/d's Invention for the extracting or making Tar from Pit Coal, he has this Morning obtained the same, on paying a Fee of Fifteen Shillings.

William Morland, Esquire, being examined, said, That the House in which he is a Partner pay to Foreigners Money on Letters of Credit given on them, many of which are to Persons sent to inspect the Manufactories and Inventions established in this Country — That such Persons frequently inquire where such are established, and ask for Letters of Recommendation from them to different Residents, who live in those Places where they are set up; and he believes it to be a Matter of great Notoriety that such Practices exist, and, he believes, miteh to the Prejudice of the Manufacturers of this Country.

John Grubb, Esquire, Clerk of the Patents, being then examined, said, That he has been in that Office upwards of Twenty Years; and that, after Specifications are enrolled, Copies thereof may be obtained by any Person whomsoever, 6n applying to the proper Officers at the several Offices of Enrolment, on paying tfoi customary Fees, the Amount of which are

And he produced to your Committee an Office Copy of a Specification obtained by him from the Office of Petty Bag, which Copy contains Drawings of the Invention for which a Patent was granted — That he understands, far the greater Number of Persons who apply for Copies of such Specifications are Foreigners, or employed on the Behalf of Foreigners, with a View to introduce the Inventions into Foreign Countries — That this has been a Subject Matter of great Complaint, and has been looked upon as a great Grievance by the Authors of Inventions invariably, ever since he has been in Office — That, during the last War, a Discovery was made for sheathing of Ships with a Material freed from the Inconveniences which the Mode then in use was subject to, and it was then thought an Object to prevent its being practised by the Countries with whom we were then at War; but the Patentee being restricted in Point of Time for enrolling his Specification, he was precluded from obtaining Redress — That it appears to him, that the only Reasons for the Specification being liable to Inspection, are in order that it may be seen whether the Invention is supportable as a Monopoly in Point of Novelty, and whether the Principle of any new Invention, for which any Person is soliciting, or intending to solicit, may not clash with the Principle of any prior Patent, and further to secure to the Public the free Exercise and Advantage of such Invention, after the Expiration of the Term of Fourteen Years; and he thinks that neither of these Reasons render it necessary to give Copies to any Person; and that if the Specification was delivered in to an Officer appointed for that Purpose, and properly qualified, and no Copies allowed to be taken (except in Cases of Trials at Law, or after the Expiration of the Term granted by the Patent) the existing Inconvenience would be remedied without Prejudice to the Interests of any Individual, or the Public. — And,

Mr. James Chalmers being examined, said, That after the Specifications of Inventions are enrolled in the Chancellary of ScotlandExtracts or Copies thereof may be obtained by any Person who applies for the same, on paying the usual Fees, which are of small Amount.

Mr. Cawthorne reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Owners, Proprietors, and Occupiers of Lands and Tenements, and other Inhabitants, within the Parishes of Ford and and other adjacent Parishes, in the County of thumberland; and also, the Petition of the Duke of Buccleuch, and Lord Delaval, and the humble Petition of several Freeholders, Owners, Proprietors, and Occupiers of Land and Tenements, within the several Parishes and Chapelries of Ford, Loivick, Kirknewton, Carham, and Bmnkston, in the County of Northumberland, and of Kyloe and Cornhill, in the County of Durham, and other adjacent Parishes in the said Counties, and in North Britain, ware severally referred; That

the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with (except that no Notices were given for the Application in the second mentioned Petition, it not having been determined to apply for repairing the Roads therein mentioned, until it was too late to give the Notices as required by the said Standing Orders); and that the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the same, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. John Carr being examined, said. That he knows the Roads extending from Cornhill Bum to Millfield March Bum, and from Lane, west-

ward, towards Howtell, to Ford Bridge, and from thence through Baremoor and Lowick to Hunting-hall Burn, and from Ford Bridge, through Etal, to Duddoe Burn, adjoining to the Berwick Turnpike Road — That, from the great Intercourse and Traffic on the said Roads, and the many heavy Carriages passing thereon, the same are become broken and founderous, and cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair by the ordinary Course of Law. — He further said, That it would tend greatly to the Benefit of the Public, and to the Neighbourhood, if the said Roads were kept in Repair; for which Purpose, it will be necessary that certain Tolls should be granted; and, in order to render the same effectual, it will be also expedient that the main Road should pass over Ford Bridge, and that several Bye Roads lying contiguous thereto should be shut up.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Carr being further examined, said, That the Roads leading from Flodden Lane to the Borders of Scotland, and from Cornhill Burn to the East End of the Village of Cornhill, and from the West End thereof to Coldstream Bridge, across the River Tweed, and from Lowick to the Eastern Turnpike Boad leading from Bdford to Berwick, at or near Fenwick Wood Head, are narrow, incommodious, and out of Repair; and that it would tend greatly to the Improvement of Agriculture in the Country adjacent to the said Roads, and be beneficial to the Neighbourhood, by opening a Communication with Collieries and Lime Stone Quarries, and be of great Convenience to the Public in general, if the said Roads were properly amended, widened, and kept in Repair.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and improving the Roads leading from Cornhill Burn, by BaUinsburn and Flodden Lane, to Millfield March Burn, and by Foi'd Bridge to Lowick; and also from Ford Bridge, through Etal, to Duddoe Burn, otherwise Homey Bum, adjoining to the Berwick Turnpike Road, and also for shutting up and stopping certain Bye Roads therein mentioned, all in the County of Northumberland: And that Mr. Cawthorne and Mr. Grey do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That, in consideration of the Circumstances mentioned in the said Report, Leave be granted that Notices may be given, at the next General Quarter Sessions of the Peace to be holden for the County of Northumberland, and in Three Newspapers to be printed or circulated in the said County in this present Month of March, and in the Month of April, or in either of them, of the Application to Parliament for making Provision in the said Bill, for repairing and improving the Roads leading from Flodden , by a Farm called The Encampment, to the Borders of Scotland, and also the Road leading from Cornhill Burn to the East End of the Village of Cornhill, and from the West End thereof to Coldstream Bridge, across the

IORD Viscount Bay/iam, from the Select Com-s mittee who were appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of Sir Godfrey IV , Baronet, and John Tarleton, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussinformed the House, That it appeared to the said Select Committee, That the Merits of the Petition did in Part depend upon the Right of Election; and that, thereupon, the said Committee required the Counsel for the several Parties to deliver to the Clerk of the said Committee, Statements in Writing of the Right of Election for which they respectively contended.

That, in consequence thereof, the Counsel for the Sitting Members, John Sargent and Richard Paul drell, Esquires, delivered in a Statement as follows:

" That the Right of Election is in the Bailiff, Jurats, and Freemen, and in the Populacy, according " to the last Determination of the House of 1 oth " bruary 1670, by which Word Populacy are meant " Inhabitants Housekeepers paying Scotland Lot, as " explained by the Resolutions of the House of 15th " December 1761."

That, upon the said Statement, the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Right of Election, as set forth in the said Statement, is not the Right of Election for the said Town and Port of Seaford.

That the Counsel for the said Petitioners, Sir Godfrey Webster, Baronet, and John Tarleton, Esquire, delivered in a Statement as follows

" The Counsel for the Petitioners state, that the " Right of Election for the Town and Port of Seaford, " according as the same was decided by the last Determination in the House of Commons on the 10th il February 1670-1 is " In th accord-

Martii. . 1792.

" ing to the Interpretation of the Word Populacy, by the Resolution of the said House on the 15th of " December 1761, " In the Inhabitants Housekeepers of " the said Town and Port paying Scotland Lot," and in " such Inhabitants Housekeepers only."

That, upon the said last mentioned Statement, the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants Housekeepers of the said Town and Port paying Scotland Lot, and in such Inhabitants Housekeepers only.

That the said Select Committee have also determined,

That John Sargent, Esquire, is duly elected a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex:

And also, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That Richard Paul Jodrell, Esquire, is not duly returned a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford:

determined,

And also. That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the said John Tarleton, Esquire, ought to have been returned a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford:

And also, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Petition of the said Sir Godfrey Webster,

Baronet, and John Tarleton, Esquire, did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious:

That the Opposition of the said John Sargent and Richard Paul Jodrell, Esquires, to the said Petition, did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious.

A Petition of Robert Shuttleworth, of Barton Lodge, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is Owner of a very valuable Water Mill, situate in Burnley, in the County of Lancaster, upon the River of West Colder, which Mill is used both in the Woollen Manufactory, and in grinding of Corn, and is worked by the Water of the River West Colder; and that the Petitioner finds a Bill has been brought into the House for making a Canal from or near Sowerby Bridge Wharf, in the County of York, to or near Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, and several Navigable Branches, amongst others, to or near Coin, Rochdale, and Oldham, all in the County of Lancaster, with convenient Reservoirs and Towing Paths; and that the said Navigable Branch, to or near Coin, cannot be supplied with Water without diverting the Water of the River West Colder, or some considerable Brooks, Streams, and Feedings of Water, which supply that River, and a Diminution of the Water of the said River will occasion frequent, if not a total Stoppage to the said Mill, and thereby render the same of little or no Value to the Petitioner: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that he may be heard against the same.

A Petition of Martha Halsted, of Eaves,

in the Chapelry of Burnley, and County of Lancaster, Spinster, John Hargreaves of Fulledge, in the Chapelry and County aforesaid, Clerk, and Topper of

Burnley, in the said County, Clothier, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, Martha Halsted, is Owner of several valuable Water Mills, situate in Habergham Eaves, upon the Confluence of the Rivers Brown and West Colder, which Mills are employed in the Woollen and Cotton Manufactories, and worked by the Waters of the said Rivers, and the Petitioner, John Hargreaves, is Owner of a considerable Colliery at Fulledge aforesaid, which he now is and has been working for several Years, being enabled so to do by Means of certain Water Engines for draining and raising the Water from the same Colliery, which Engines are worked by the Water of the River of West Colder, and the Petitioner, John Topper, is Owner of a Water Mill in Burnley aforesaid, upon the River of West Colder, which Mill is used both in the Woollen and Cotton Manufactories, and is worked by the Water of the River of West Colder; and that the Petitioners find a Bill has been brought into the House for making a Canal from or near Sowerby Bridge in the County of York, to or near Manchester, in the County of Lancaster, and several Navigable Branches, amongst others, to or near Coin, Rochdale, and Oldham, all in the County of Lancaster, with convenient Reservoirs and Towing Paths; and that the said Navigable Branch, to or near Coin, cannot be supplied with Water without diverting the Waters of the Rivers Brown and West Colder, or some considerable Brooks and Streams of Water which supply those respective Rivers, and a Diminution of the Water of the said Rivers will occasion a total Stoppage to such of the said Mills and Engines as are upon or worked by the said Rivers respectively: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, and that they may be heard against the same.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Colder Navigation, at or near Sowerby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Hal fax, in the West Riding of the County of York, to Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also several Collateral Cuts from the said Canal, be read a Second Time; and the Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves, against the said Bill, upon their Petitions, if they think fit. A Petition of the Gentlemen, Farmers, Manufac- Petition from turers, and others, of the several Townships of g &r

Bulwell, Arnold, and other Places adjacent thereto, a^aiust’Noi-within the County of Nottingham, whose Names are imgham thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, anil Canal Bill, read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Canal for the Navigation of Boats, and other Vessels, from the Cromford Canal, in the County of Nottingham, by, through, or near the Town of Nottingham, to join and communicate with the River Trent, near Nottingham Trent Bridge, and also for making several Navigable Collateral Cuts from, and to communicate with, such intended Canal; and that the Petitioners conceive that if such Canal should be made by the Authority of Parliament, the Operation of it will be to enhance the Price of Coals, not only to the Petitioners, and to the Bleachers and other Manufacturers, and their Neighbours, but to the whole Town and Neighbourhood of Nottingham, to a very considerable Degree, in as much as that the Coals, now' procured by them from the neighbouring Collieries at a reasonable Rate by Land Carriage, will be liable to and in all Probability taken away by Water to Newark', and other distant Markets, by Vessels, who will not only have the Opportunity of selling such Coals at an advanced Price, but reap an Advantage by Back Carriage, and consequently the Petitioners, and the Inhabitants of Nottingham and Neighbourhood thereof, will be obliged to give as much for their Coals as will make it equivalent to the extra Price now obtained for the same at Newark and other Markets, and the Advantage to be derived by Back Carriage, though it may make them somewhat cheaper at Grantham, and other adjacent Places, where no Manufactures exist; and further, that Coals are an Article of great Consequence to the Bleachers, Trimmers, and Dyers, the Price of whose Labour and Business must ultimately fall on the Manufactory of the Tow ns of Nottingham,

Leicester, and Derby, as the principal Bleachers for Manufacturers in those Towns reside at Basford, Bulwell, Arnold, and other neighbouring Villages; and that the Consumption of Coals in Cotton Mills is likewise daily increasing, and there arc several in Nottingham, Basford, Bulwell, Arnold, and their Vicinities, and other Mills are now constructing, and, at present, the Working of them by Steam Engines is, on the Whole, thought to be the cheapest Mode: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

of Helligan, in the same County, Clerk, and John Rashleigh, of Penquiie, in the same County, Esquire, Persons who have a Right to choose, nominate, and appoint, the Returning Officer of the said Borough; and also, the Petition of Sir Ralph Payne, Knight of the Bath, and William Morshe Esquire, respecting the Right of choosing the Returning Officer for the said Borough, informed the House, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Persons entitled to elect the Portreeve of the Borough of Fowey are those who are capable of holding that Office, that is, such Prince’s Tenants only as have been duly admitted on the Court Rolls of the Manor of the said Borough, and have done their Fealty, and such Persons only are duly admitted whose Lands, being Freehold, were anciently, and continue to be, held immediately of the Duke of Cornwall as Parcel of his said Manor of the said Borough, and whose Titles to those Lands have been presented at a Court Baron by a sworn Homage or Jury of the Freeholders of the said Manor.

Petition A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

agaiustBroad thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of Land, Farm-Uour ers> Landholders, and Occupiers of Tythes, in the several Parishes of Saint Peter, Saint John, and Saint Lawrence, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for repairing or re-building the Pier adjoining to the Harbour of Broad Stairs, in the Isle of Thanet, in the County of Kent, and for the better preserving the said Harbour, and for removing and preventing Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances, and regulating the Mooring of Ships and Vessels within the said Harbour; and Setting forth, That, should such Bill pass into a Law as it now stands, it will greatly injure the Petitioners, by taking from them their ancient and immemorial Rights, long enjoyed, in the taking and carrying away, from out of the said Harbour, Sand, Soil, Sea Weed, and other Manure, for the Improvement of their Land, together with Flints and Stones for the Purpose of Building, and Beach and Gravel for mending the Highways: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law as it now stands, and that they may be heard, by themselves and Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect the Petitioners in such Exercise of their ancient Rights.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, or Chunsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the several Owners and Occupiers of Mills, situate on the Rivers Colder and in the

West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending in the House for making a Navigable Canal from the Town of Manchesteby , in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to Todmorden, and from thence to Soxcerby Bridge Wharf, in the said County of

York, and the Petitioners conceive, that the passing such Bill into a Law would not only be very prejudicial to the Estates and Interest of the Petitioners, but also to the Woollen Manufactory of that Part of the West Riding of the County oiYork; and that there are at present on the said Rivers upwards of Thirty Mills, within the Distance of less than Forty Miles, for the Milling of Woollen Cloths, scribbling and spinning of Wool and Cotton, and grinding of Corn, which produce to the Proprietors upwards of 10,000l. per Annum, and those Mills, in Times of Drought, experience considerable Loss for want of Water, many of them at those Times are not able to work more than Twelve or Fourteen Hours in the Day, and, should a Diminution of Water, sufficient to supply a Canal, take place, the Petitioners apprehend many of those Mills will be nearly rendered useless in the Summer Months, and the Manufacturers be obliged (as has been the Case within Four or Five Years) to carry their Cloths to distant Mills, on other Rivers, to be milled; and that the Trade and Manufactories of that Part of the Country have of late Years greatly increased, and there is Reason to hope are in a State of progressive Increase; that the Rivers Colder and Hepton, in their present State, are not equal to the Powers wanted by the several Mills situate thereon, and if a Diminution of Water in those Rivers take place, those Mills must inevitably be very materially injured, as well as the Trade and Manufactures of that Neighbourhood: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against so much of the said Bill as affects the said Rivers Colder and

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Colder Navigation, at or near Svwerby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Halifax, in

the West Riding of the County of York, to Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also several Collateral Cuts from the said Canal, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Manu- Petition facturers, and Traders in Cloth and other Woollen a*ffns\s<w‘ and Cotton Goods, in and near Halifax, in the West Mancha Riding of the County of York, whose Names are Navigation thereto subscribed, was presented to the House, and Bill, read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending in the House for making a Navigable Canal from Manchester, by Rochdale and Todmorden, to Sawerby Bridge Wharf, near Halifax, and the passing such Bill into a Law would, as the Petitioners conceive, be highly injurious to the Trade of the Country, particularly to the Woollen Manufacture within the Parish of Halifax, for that upon the River Colder (wherewith the Canal is intended to be made parallel for Twenty Miles or thereabouts) and a Rivulet called j Beck, the most material Feeder thereof, there are upwards of Thirty Mills, chiefly used in Fulling and Milling Cloths, and other Woollen Goods, and in scribbling, spinning, and manufacturing Wool and Cotton, which Mills, from the great Increase of Trade, are constantly fully employed, and in Times of Drought and Scarcity of Water are not in their present State capable of dispatching in due Time the Business allotted to them; and that the intended Canal must, of necessity, deprive those Mills of the greatest Part of their Water, and render them useless, or nearly so, to the Trade of the Country, consequently would materially injure, if not totally ruin, the Woollen and Cotton Manufacture, through a large populous District, gradually and of late Years very rapidly increasing in Commerce by Means of the Mills, which, as the Petitioners conceive, are essentially requisite to its Support and Continuance:

And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by Counsel, against the said Bill, or so much thereof as is likely to affect the said Mills, and the Trade of the Country wherein they are situate.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Colder Navigation, at or near Sowerby Bridge Wharf, in the Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, to Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and also several Collateral Cuts from the said Canal, be read a Second 'lime; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

And the Names of the Members were taken out of the Box (belore prepared) put into Six Glasses, and drawn and read in the usual Manner.

And the Name of Sir Charles Gould being drawn, he offered to the House, as an Excuse for not serving on the said Committee, That he was under the Necessity of attending, as Judge Advocate General, on a Court Martial, holden for the Trial of Three Officers of the .54th Regiment of Foot; and the Substance of what was so alleged by him being taken dowm by the Clerk, the Opinion of the House was taken thereon; and he was excused from serving on the said Committee.

And the Names of Eight Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of William Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

And the Names of Four other Members, then present, were drawn who were not objected to.

And the Name of Sir James Murray, Baronet, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioner.

And the Names of Sixteen other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Seventy-six other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside; Twelve on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards (before sworn); Nine against whose Election Petitions were depending; Tea as then serving on Select Committees; Forty-three on Account of having in this Session served on Select Committees j and Two as having voted at the Election.

And the Names of all the Members of the House having been drawn from the Glasses, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House; and it appearing that there wanted Twenty-one Names to complete the List of Forty-nine Members to be delivered to the Counsel at the Bar;

Mr Speaker adjourned the Order for taking the said Petition into Consideration, till Tomorrow, Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

And then the House was adjourned, by Mr. Speaker, till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Sir James Steuart Denham reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act, made in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Roads from Livingstone, by the Kirk of Shotts, to the City of and by the

Town of Hamilton to the Town of , and for

repairing and widening the Roads from the Confines of the County of Ayr, at or near Lochgate, to the Town of Strathaven, and for repairing the several Roads leading into the City of Glasgow, so far as the same relate to the Road leading from the Town of Airdrie towards the City of Glasgow, through the Village of Sheltleston, till it falls into the Great Road from Murric* hall to the said City, and for repairing the Road from the said Great Road, by Drygate and to

Camlyne, and for repairing and widening several other Roads, and for building a Bridge over the River Clyde at or near Theevesford, and for opening and making certain Streets in or near the City of Glasgow, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Black being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed several considerable Sums of Money on the Credit thereof, which still remains due, and cannot be repaid, and the said Roads rendered more level and convenient, unless several Alterations be made.

That by several Acts of Parliament a Road has been formed from the City of Edinburgh to the Bridge over Almond Water, being the Confines betwixt the Counties of Edinburgh and Linlithgow.

That a Road has also been formed and made from the City of Glasgow to the Town of Airdrie.

That Parts of the said Road between Livingstone and the City of Glasgow, where the same passes over the Shotts, and Hirst Hills, and Colder Brae, are very inconvenient for Carriages, from the severe Pulls in ascending the said Hills and Brae, which might be avoided by carrying the said Road to the Southward of the present Line.

That there are certain Parts of the Road between the City of Glasgow and the Town of , which

are also inconvenient from severe Pulls and otherwise,

which might be remedied by altering the present Line of Road, and carrying a new Line in a more level and convenient Direction.

That the Bridge over the River Clyde, called Both-well Bridge, on the Road from the City of Glasgow to the Town of Hamilton, and from thence to Carlisle, is inconveniently situated for the Line of Road, and, from the Length of Time since it was built has become insufficient, and is too narrow for the heavy Carnages that now pass between Carlisle and Glasgow, by the said Bridge, and may require to be rebuilt.

That when the Alteration of the Line of Road from Glasgow to Livingstone, by the South of Colder Brae, and the Shotts and Hirst Hills, is accomplished, it will be requisite to vary the present Line of Road from the Town of Hamilton, by Hamilton Bridge, to New Inn, on the present Great Road from Glasgow to Livingstone, and to carry the said Road by Hamilton Bridge, in the most convenient Direction, to join the New Line of Road from Glasgow to Livingstone, and also to make a Branch Road from the said New Line of Road from Glasgow to Livingstone, in the most convenient Direction, through the Lands of Coltness and others, to join the present Turnpike Road from Carlisle to the City of Glasgow.

That, in order to render the said Roads more commodious, it will be necessary to grant some further and other Powers to the Trustees appointed by the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for altering and enlarging the Powers of an Act, passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Roads from Livingstone, by the Kirk of Shotts, to the City of Glasgow, and other Roads therein mentioned, and for building a Bridge over the River Clyde at or near Theevesford, and for opening and making certain Streets in and near the City of Glasgozv, for altering a Part of the High Road betwixt Edinburgh and Glasgow, by carrying a new Line of Road to the North of the Hills, and another Line of Road by the South, and for straightening and making the Roads more convenient, as also for altering the Road from the City of Glasgow to the Town of Hamilton, and building a Bridge over the River Clyde below the present old Bridge, called Bothwell Bridge, as also, for altering the Road from the Town of Hamilton Eastward, until it joins the Great Road between Edinburgh and Glasgow: And that Sir James Denham and Mr. William McDowall do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Lewis, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Common Gaol of the said City and County of the City of Bristol, and also the House of Correction, are too small, and not properly constructed for the Reception, Confinement, Separation, and Employment of Prisoners; and that it would be of great Public Utility if a new Gaol, with a Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, were erected and built in some other Part of the said City and County.

That the purchasing of Ground necessary for such new Gaol, Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, building the same uport a Scale sufficiently large and commodious, and maintaining and supporting the same, will be attended with very considerable Expence, which cannot be provided for, nor can proper Regulations for the due Management of the same, and for the Security and Preservation of the Health of the Prisoners, be established and enforced without the Aid and Authority of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a new Gaol, a Penitentiary House, and House of Correction, within the City of Bristol: And that the Lord Sheffield and the Marquis of Worcester do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The Witness further said, That the Petitioner, with the Consent of the Patrons and Vicar of the Parish Church of Leeds aforesaid, as also of his Grace the Lord Archbishop of York, hath begun to erect the said Church, and intends to finish the same as soon as it can be conveniently done, and to have the said Church and Piece of Ground consecrated, and an Annual Stipend to be settled for the Minister thereof, by a Rent Charge to be fixed and ascertained on the Pews, Seats or Stalls to be made in the said Church, in Consideration of the Petitioner having the First

Sir William Heathcote reported from the Committee, G rt to whom the Petition of Robert Forbes, of Gosport, Bridge Peti in the County of Southampton, Merchant, was re- tion referred; That the Committee had examined, and Portt(1-found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for building Bridges, had not been complied with, the Party making the Application not being apprized of the Necessity of giving the Notices therein required; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Nathaniel Gilmore being examined, said, That great Inconvenience having been experienced by the Public in general, and more particularly by the Officers and others belonging to His Majesty’s Hospital at Haslar, in the County of Southampton, for Want of a Bridge over a certain Salt Water Lake branching from the Harbour of Portsmouth to the Village of Alverstoke, the Petitioner stated this Matter to the Commissioners for Sick and Hurt Seamen, to whom he made a Proposal to build a Bridge over the said Lake, and to permit the Officers and others belonging to the said Hospital to pass over the same, on being paid the like Salary that was allowed to the Ferryman employed for that Purpose; to which Proposal the said Commissioners agreed; and, in consequence of the said Agreement, the Petitioner began to erect, and has now nearly completed, a good substantial Brick Bridge, sufficient for the Passage of Carriages, as well as Foot Passengers, over the said Lake.

And the Witness further said, That the said Bridge will be of great public Benefit and Convenience to those belonging to the said Hospital, and also to all Persons having Occasion to resort thereto, the only Method hitherto of Conveyance for Foot-Passengers over the said Lake having been in Boats, which are frequently prevented passing by the Lowness of the Water, or from bad Weather; and Carriages have always been under the Necessity of going round from Gosport, through Alverstoke, in order to get to the Hospital, which is a Distance of near Three Miles. — And he added, that the building and finishing of the said Bridge will be attended with a very considerable Expence.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the Circumstances mentioned in the said Report, Leave be granted, that Notices may be given at the next General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the County of Southampton, and in Three Newspapers, to be printed or circulated in the said County in this present Month of March, and in the Month of April, or either of them, of the Application to Parliament for a Bill for enabling Robert Forbes, of Gosport, in the County of Southampton, Merchant, to erect and finish a Bridge across the Lake called Stoke or Haslar Lake, in the Parish of Alverstoke, in the County of Southampton.

Mr. Joseph Booth being examined, said, That, in pursuance thereof, the Towns of Manchester and Salford have, from Time to Time, been regulated; but that the Powers thereby granted are insufficient for the Purposes intended, and it is expedient that the said Act should be repealed, and new Powers granted to effectuate the several Objects of the present Application.

That the said Towns have very much increased in Population and Extent of Buildings, and many of the Streets and other public Passages are 'narrow, inconvenient, and unsafe for Travellers and Carriages, and are subject to various Nuisances and Annoyances, on Account of which Accidents frequently happen; and there is no Provision in the said Act for, widen* ing and repairing the Streets, or removing Obstructions and Annoyances:

That it will be of Convenience and Advantage to the Inhabitants, if Powers were granted for watching and watering the Streets, and for providing Fire Engines and other Requisites, with a sufficient Number of Firemen properly appointed; and if Regulation* were made for the Prevention of Accidents by Fire: And it would also be of Advantage if Hackney Coaches and Chairs were to be licensed and regulated, and proper Rules provided for the Regulation of Carmen and Porters: — That there are certain public Weighing Engines, which, if regulated, would likewise be of Advantage to the Inhabitants: — That the Town is liable to bfe burthened by Vagrant Poor coming to lodge there, and great Benefit would arise from the licensing public Lodging Houses: — That it would tend to the Peace of the Inhabitants, and facilitate the Execution of the Police, if a proper Place was

to

Bolton Paving, & c. Petitions re< ported.

to be provided for the Deputy Constable, and also a House and Guard Rooms for the Military, which may from Time to Time reside in the Town; and if such further Powers were granted as shall be necessary for the effectual Regulation of the said Towns.

And the Witness added, That, in widening the Streets, it will be necessary and expedient to take down the Exchange, and to lay open the Site thereof for the Use of the Public.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " cleansing and lighting the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the Towns of Manchester and Salford, " in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and for providing Fire Engines and Firemen, and for preventing Annoyances within the said Towns," and for granting other Powers for those Purposes; and for watching the said Towns, for licensing and regulating Hackney Coaches and Chairs, and regulating Carmen and Porters, for widening and rendering more convenient several of the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, for opening Communications with some of such Streets, and for regulating Party Walls within the said Towns, and for other Purposes therein mentioned: And that Mr. Blackburne and Mr. Thomas Stanley do prepare, and bring in, the same.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. William Maire being examined, said, That the Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the said Towns of Great and Little Bolton, are not properly cleansed and lighted, and are subject to various Encroachments and Annoyances, and in some Parts are narrow and incommodious; and that it would be a great Benefit to all Persons resorting to the said Towns, if the said Streets, Lanes, and Passages, were properly cleansed, lighted, and rendered commodious, and the Encroachments and Annoyances removed — That the said Towns are very ill supplied with Water, and it would tend greatly to the Health, Safety, and Convenience of the Inhabitants thereof, if Powers were given for forming proper Reservoirs and other necessary Works for supplying the said Towns with good and wholesome Water, as well for domestic Purposes as for extinguishing of Fires that may happen therein; and also for providing Engines and Eiremen — And he added, That the Streets, Lanes, and Passages in Great Bolton are very ill paved: And further said, That there are several Commons and Waste Grounds with-

in the Manor of Great Bolton, which, at present, afford little or no Profit or Advantage to the Persons entitled thereto, but are capable of great Improvement; and if the same were divided and inclosed, and if, after allotting certain Parts thereof to the Lords of the Manor, the rest was sold on a perpetual Annual Chief Rent, and the Money thereby to be raised, and the Yearly Rent thereof applied towards improving and regulating the said Town of Great Bolton as aforesaid, and iu Aid of the Poor Rates there, and also, in widening, paving, lighting, watching, cleansing, and watering the said Town, and for better regulating the Market, and for providing Fire Engines and Firemen, and if a Rate or Assessment was made upon the Inhabitants of both the said Towns, for carrying into Execution and supporting the same, it would be of great Utility and Benefit, as well to the Lords of the Manor aforesaid, as also to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands within the several Manors of Great and Little Bolton.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Maire being further examined, said, That it would be a great Accommodation to the said Towns of Great and Little Bolton, if Power was given lor licensing Hackney Coaches within and for certain Distances round the said Towns; and for providing a proper and convenient Home for the Deputy Constables of the said Towns, where they might keep their Offices, and manage the Business of their Places; and also for removing and regulating Pipes or Funnels placed on the Outsides of Houses for the Conveyance of Smoke, and to regulate the Construction of Chimnies and Fire Places, of Fire and Steam Engines, and other Manufactories, within the said Towns; and also, to pave and watch the Streets withiiv the said Town of Little Bolton.

A Petition of the Parishioners and Inhabitants of Petition the Parish of Saint Michael in Bedzvardine, in the County of Worcester, who are assessed to the Rate for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill has been brought into the House for the Purpose of uniting the several Parishes in the City of Worcester, and to enable them to borrow Money to erect a large Building for a House of Industry for the Poor of the said Parishes, and the said Parish is included in the said Bill; and that the Parish of Saint Michael in Bedicardine, hath ever been separate from, independent of, and unconnected with, the City of Worcester, in all its Laws and Government, and only subject, in common with the rest of the County of Worcester, to the Regulations of the Justices of the said County, the Parish is small, and the Paymasters chiefly Tenants at Rack Rent, the Poor not exceeding in Number Twelve Persons (Accidents excepted) a Levy of Two Pence in the Pound per Month, for Three Years last past, has been more than sufficient to defray the necessary Expence of the said Parish, including the Relief of the Poor, Quarter Rates, and other incidental Expences, and no Increase thereof is, or can be, apprehended in future, the Poor are well provided for, and well satisfied, having no Complaint to make, the Paymasters do not complain of any heavy Burthens or extravagant Expenditure, but, on the contrary, are well satisfied with their Poor Rates, and only desire to remain as they are, and the Parishioners universally acknowledge that they are the least burthened with Poor Rates of any Parish in the Neighbourhood, as they have and enjoy many local Advantages and Cha- rities; and that the Petitioners, on the 12th Day of February, were informed of the Intention of uniting the said Parish with the said City, for the Purpose of establishing a General House of Industry, at which Time Notice was given that a Meeting of the Parishioners would be held at the Parish Church of Saint Michael, to take into Consideration the Propriety of establishing a General House of Industry for the Poor of the said City, and of uniting the said Parish with the said City, at which Meeting it was resolved unanimously, that such House of Industry, so far as respected the said Parish of Saint Michael, was altogether unnecessary and useless, and, if carried into Execution, would be injurious and ruinous to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, and increase the Taxes to an immoderate Burthen; and that the Petitioners submit, that the raising of 12,000l. for the Purposes of the said intended Act, for which the Poors Rates are to be mortgaged, is a very large Sum of Money, that the erecting a House of Industry is a Matter of Speculation, as it is by no Means certain such a House wiil answer the End proposed, it having been tried Twice for the said City, and failed each Time for want of a sufficient Number of Persons to be employed therein who were able to work, and, that the Statute of the Twenty-second of His present Majesty, Cap. 83, gives all requisite Powers to carry the good Intentions of the Humane into Execution, therefore there is no Necessity for the present Bill: And therefore praying, That the said intended Bill may not be permitted to pass into a Law, or that every Word and Clause therein contained, tending to affect the said Parish of Saint Michael in Bcduardine, be expunged therefrom, and the said Parish left independent of, and unconnected with, the said City, or the said intended Bill.

appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Samuel Turner being examined, said, That there is a Tract of Low Land or Fen Grounds within the said Parish, containing 1,220 Acres and upwards, which Lands, for Want of a proper Drainage, are liable to Inundation in wet Seasons; and that if the same were effectually drained they would become much more productive, and greatly increase in Value, to the immediate Benefit of the Proprietors, and to the ultimate Advantage of the Community.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for more effectually draining certain Fen Lands and Low Grounds, in the Parish of Great Carlton, in the County of Lincoln: And that Mr. Anderson Pelham and Sir John Thorold do prepare, and bring in, the same.
