8. Whether it does not frequently happen, that Q. Take them on an Average, how long have they Persons are removed by Habeas Corpus from the Bench been confined ? y

to the Fleet, and from the Fleet to the Bench f One Eight Years, One Six, One Three, and all

This Question doth not relate to the Compters. others upon an Average Twelve Months.

g. How much do the Donations amount to, and how are they disposed of among the Prisoners ?

The Donations amount to 54/. 2 5 d. per Annum;

some of them paid Quarterly, some Half-yearly and Yearly; but for many Years the Keeper has advanced the Prisoners a Weekly Sum according to their Expences; and, as they keep their own Accounts, they repay him when the Money comes into their Hands; it is chiefly laid out in Coals, Candles, Provisions for the Sick, paying for fetching in the Victuals from different Taverns, Public Halls, &c. which is generally very valuable, and keep them from Want; and before the present Method they used to divide the Money amongst them every Quarter, which they soon spent in Drunkenness, &c. and were afterwards greatly distressed, and perishing through Cold and Hunger.

10. Whether there is not a Sum of Money paid, called High Bar Money, and how is it disposed of among the Prisoners ?

Know not what High Bar Money means; have no such Fund come to this Prison.

11. Rule respecting the Rules, and to state the Regulations to the Committee?

Have no Rules to Prisoners here, but Rules to govern them by.

12. To give an Account of those who have Families, See?

27 Men have Wives, and 68 Children.

2 Men, Widowers - - 4 Children.

1 Woman, Widow - - 1 Child.

Q. What Variations in the Number confined in your Prison has there been within the Time you have been in Custody, and how long has been?

A. During the Time of my Confinement, which has been Seven # Years, though fluctuating, the Variation has been but little.

Q. How many appear to live in extreme Poverty ?

A The whole of them.

Q. How many do you see, from their general Manner of living, appear to have any Property of their own besides their bare Necessaries ?

A. The Whole of them are in very necessitated Circumstances.

Q. How many, from their general Reputation in the said Prison, are supposed to be able to pay the Whole of their Debts, or any considerable Proportion?

A. From their general Appearances they can pay but little, and many nothing at all.

Q. How would you divide the Number as to their Rank and Life ?

A. Three Merchants, Six Traders, Twenty-one Mechanics, One Attorney, Three Seamen, and One Labourer.

Q. Have you collected an Account of the Number of Wives and Children belonging to the Debtors in your Prison; and w hat is their Number ?

A. Twenty-three Wives, and Fifty Children,

C Hodgson, Steward.

13. To state, as near as possible, how many there are who do any Thing towards supporting themselves, by working at their Trades ?

On the Master Side Persons employed in Trades are — One Attorney, a Carver, a Taylor, a Pattern Drawer, and a Cabinet Maker. On the Mens Common Side, none work at Trades: The Women wash and work.

14. How many surrendered upon the Act passed in the Year 1780?

There were only Three who escaped in the Year 1780: One of them the Keeper re-took before the Act, and the other Two surrendered.

Appendix, N' 7.

Martis, 140 die Februarii, 1792.

Committee to inquire into the Practice and Effects of Imprisonment for Debt.

Mr. Joseph Birchell, examined.

Do you hold an Official Situation in the Office of the Sheriff of Middlesex.

I do; and am an Attorney. I act as Under Sheriff of Middlesex. I have been in that Office Twelve Years.

How many bailable Writs, that is, Writs on which the Defendant must be arrested if he does not find Bail, are, upon an Average, issued into Middlesex Annually.

About 9,500 on Mesne Process.

How many Arrests, on an Average, are actually made Annually in that County on Mesne Process?

Between 5 and 6,000; possibly there may be more.

How do you ascertain these Facts ?

By the Entries made in the Sheriff’s Office.

What do you take to be the Average Number of Writs for Debts under 50 /. ?

Seven thousand Annually.

How many under 20. /?

About One Half.

How many Defendants, on an Average, are actually sent to Prison Annually ?

About 900, speaking as to the County of Middlesex only. In all these Sams I speak of Middlesex only, exclusive of London.

Of

32 Geo. III.

Of those who go to Prison, what Proportion do you find whose Debts are under 20 /. ?

More than One Half.

What are the usual Expences attending an Arrest, and of completing the Appearance of the Defendant by Special Bail ?

At the least about 8 /.

Do the Expences of such Proceedings vary?

They do; and depend on the Amount of the Debt, in proportion to which a Fee is usually paid to the Bailiff making the Arrest.

Does it frequently happen that the Defendant is detained in Custody on more than One Action ?

They are frequently detained on several Actions.

Are the Expences increased on that Account?

The Expences accumulate in proportion to the Number of Actions; but should he be detained on Three Actions for 10/. each, the Expences of the Arrest, and of completing his Appearance by Special Bail, will amount to 24/. or 25/. I compute this as the least possible Expence upon Three Actions of 10/. each.

What appears to you to be the Average Number of Debts which are Annually settled immediately on the Arrest ?

I do not think that One in Five pay their Debts, or settle with their Creditors on the Arrest.

Does the Sheriff usually take Bail, or what Security, for the Appearance of the Defendant?

The Debtor is usually discharged on giving a Bail Bond executed by himself and Two Friends, or an At* torney’s undertaking for his Appearance.

Is the Sheriff ever requested by the Defendant to take a Deposit of Money as a Security for his Appearance ?

‘ The Sheriff has sometimes been offered Money, but this is refused as contrary to Law; but I have Reason to believe that the Bailiffs do sometimes take Money.

Are any Fees paid on Discharge of Defendants and Debtors from Gaol?

The Sheriff usually take a Fee of 4$. 8 on the Discharge of a Debtor either in Execution or Mesne Process, and I think a Fee of 8 s. 10 is taken by the Keeper of the Prison.

Are Defendants or Debtors ever detained in Custody for Non-payment of such Fees?

By the Sheriffs never.

Are Bails frequently found to be insufficient on Examination, and therefore rejected?

They are.

What is the Consequence of Bail being so rejected ?

The Debt and Costs are generally paid by the Sheriff, in Consequence of Process of Contempt against him for the Debtor’s Non-appearance.

Are those Proceedings attended with a considerable additional Expence?

About Three or Four Pounds; which falls ultimately on the Debtor — and in the Event of his Insolvency upon the Creditor.

In case new Bail is offered and rejected, what is the Consequence?

Attended with additional Expence, payable in like Manner, by the Sheriff in the First Instance, and then by the Debtor, if he is able, or his Bail.

Does it frequently happen, that after all these Proceedings the Defendant surrenders himself into Custody, or is surrendered by the Bail, whereby they are discharged ?

VOL. 47.

660

When the Bail are apprehensive of Danger, they RePort oa generally surrender the Debtor to Prison in their Discharge; and it will sometimes happen, that after the Debt. Return of the Process on which the Debtor has been arrested, perhaps at the Distance of Six Weeks or Two Months, if the Sheriff's Officer who made the Arrest has Reason to apprehend that the Debtor cannot procure Bail who will justify according to the Rules of the Court, Bail is put in at the Expence of the Sheriff's Officer, merely for the Purpose of surrendering the Debtor to Prison in ofder to discharge the Sheriff from his Responsibility?

Is the Number of bailable Writs, or Writs for the Purpose of Arrest for Debts under 20/. gradually increasing?

They are increasing rapidly;

Did you ever know an Instance, when a Divisiort actually took Place of the Effects of an Insolvent Debtor, on his being discharged under the Authority of the Act commonly called the Lords Act?

I never heard of the Division of an Insolvent Debtor’s Effects under the Lords Act, nor of any Debtor having been brought up under the compulsory Clause which entitles the Creditor to compel a Surrender of the Debtors Property.

Can you give the Committee any Account of Persons arrested in Execution where the original Debt without Costs was below to/.?

Several, and with the Costs under 10/.

Have you known Instances of Persons insane being arrested?

Yes — and I think that in One or Two Instances the Court have refused to discharge the Party.

When you state the Number who actually go to Gaol, is it exclusive of those who go to Lock-up or Spunging Houses?

Most certainly, because they must amount to some Thousands who go to Lock-up Houses.

Is not this attended with great Expence?

I have never made any Enquiry in my Official Situation, having never had any Complaint made to me; but I have an Opportunity of knowing, in Point of Fact,

' that it is attended with very considerable Expence.

May every Prisoner in a Lock-up House call for what expensive Provisions and Liquors he pleases ?

I know of no Objection.

Are the Articles used by Prisoners in Spunging or Lock-up Houses charged to them by the Persons keeping such Houses at an exorbitant Rate ?

I have understood so, but I cannot state it as a Fact within my own Knowledge.

Committee on Effects of Imprisonment for Debt.

Mr. Birchcll again examined.

Does it frequently happen, after a Defendant has lain many Months in Prison, the Plaintiff’ is nonsuited, of discontinues the Action ?

The Plaintiff is sometimes nonsuited; but Debtors are daily discharged by reason of their Discontinuance of the Action, or because the Plaintiff does not judge it prudent to be at any further Expence.

Does it frequently happen, that the Defendant is discharged for Want of proceeding against him ?

Very often, and after being several Months in Prison.

Is the Sheriff, after having taken Bail, bound for the Appearance of the Debtor ?

The Sheriffs, having arrested the Debtor, are bound, at all Events, for his Appearance; and therefore they are compelled to be very scrupulous in taking Bail, which puts the Debtor under considerable Difficulties, and especially as Two are necessary. When sufficient Bail cannot be procured, the Plaintiff may proceed either against the Bail or the Sheriff. The Difficulty of procuring Bail is very much increased, by reason that none but Housekeepers are qualified to justify in; Court.

TawnleyWard, Esquire, examined.

Is in the Profession of the Law.

Has it occurred to you, in the Course of your Practice, to observe on the Effects of Arrests and Imprisonment for Debt?

It has frequently. — I have known Instances where Persons arrested for considerable Sums, and the Causes have afterwards proceeded to Trial, that Verdicts have passed in Favour of Persons so arrested. — With respect to Imprisonment where Debtors are imprisoned, and the Plaintiffs do not proceed against them accord-in g to the Practice of the Courts of Law, such Debt-

o a m ' #

ors must procure their own Discharge at their own Expence, unless the Plaintiffs think proper to give such Discharge.

Must a Debtor, on an Arrest, be committed to Prison if he cannot find Bail?

The Sheriff has a Right, if he thinks proper, to detain the Body of the Debtor till the Return of the Writ; but in all such Cases that Indulgence cannot be obtained without a considerable Expence to the Debtor. — I apprehend it is owing to the Indulgence of the Sheriff or his Officer, that such Debtor is not sent to Prison after the Expiration of Twenty-four Hours from the Time of the Arrest.

How long may a Debtor remain in Confinement from the Time of his being first arrested to the Time of Trial?

If a Debtor should be arrested any Day in Trinity Vacation, the Plaintiff in that Action is not bound to file a Declaration against the Defendant till the last Day of the succeeding Hilary Term, which contains a Period of more than Seven Months, — The Plaintiff has Two Terms to proceed to Trial or Judgment, so that the Debtor may be kept in Confinement Twelve Months before the Cause is tried.

If upon the Trial the Debt should not be proved, and the Defendant of Course entitled to his Discharge, does he obtain Costs from the Plaintiff?

In such a Case the Defendant is entitled to taxed Costs, but which bear no Proportion to the Expence he must necessarily have been put unto, in Consequence of that Arrest, nor can he maintain any Action for false Imprisonment against the Plaintiff, unless the Jury on the Trial of that Cause shall be of Opinion that he wras maliciously held to Bail.

Has it often happened within your Knowledge, that a Defendant has succeeded in an Action for malicious Imprisonment?

Very few Instances have occurred in which the Debtors have succeeded in such Actions, as it is necessary, in order to maintain such Action, to show that the Arrest was malicious.

Has it often happened within your Knowledge, that the Debtor has been discharged upon Trial?

A Debtor is not entitled to have his Discharge im-mediatley upon the Trial,* and it may so happen that

a Cause is tried at the Sittings after Trinity Term, wherein a Verdict shall be found for the Debtor, yet* that Debtor cannot obtain his Discharge from such Imprisonment before the succeeding Michaelmas Term, which may make a Period of Four Months.

Upon his Discharge is he entitled to any Consideration for his Loss of Time and Labour during his Confinement ?

No.

Do you know that Persons are frequently arrested on Oath of the Plaintiff where the Defendant goes to Prison for Want of Bail, and the Plaintiff shall delay his Proceeding for Two Terms, and on the Trial Verdict shall pass against the Plaintiff?

No such Instances can occur, because the Defendant is entitled to his Discharge in Consequence of the Plaintiff' not having proceeded to deliver his Declaration before the End of the next Term after the Return of the Process.

Have you had an Opportunity of observing that Debtors have remained in Prison, who have been able to discharge their Debts?

I know of One particular Instance, which is the Case of Benjamin Pope, who is now in the Fleet Prison at my Suit, as surviving Administrator of Sir Alexander Leilk, Boronet, upon Execution of Capias ad -j'acicndumfor io, oooo/. and upwards.

Have you Reason to believe that M\ Pope is in Possession of Property equal to the Discharge of that Debt ?

I have Reason to believe, at the Time Mr. Pope n as-committed to Prison he had Property to a much greater Amount than was sufficient to discharge such Debt; and I believe he is still possessed of Property more than sufficient for that Purpose.

State the Circumstances on which you ground that Belief?

On the Trial of the Action against Pope by Sir A. Leith, and for the Damage and Costs given on that Action he is now in Custody, it was proved that Pope was possessed of Property to the Amount of more than 40,000l. and it was the then general Opinion of the World, that he was possessed of 100,000l. Pope being in Execution, it was not in my Power to seize any Part of his Effects, Real or Personal, the Law having considered that I had made my Election by taking his Body. Information has been repeatedly given me, since he has been in Execution, of his having Property to a very great Amount.

How long has he been in Prison?

I believe about Nine Years — but the Return will show.

Do you know any Thing of his Manner of living in Prison?

I have been frequently informed that he lives in a very frugal, oeconomical Manner, and that his Expences do not amount to 50/. per Annum — that being entitled, in consequence of his Length of Confinement, to a Room in the Prison, which lets for a considerable Rent, a Guinea per Week, he has disposed of that — and that lie resides in a Room lor which he pays only One Shilling per Week.

What has been the Expence to you of the Arrest and other Prosecutions against Mr. Pope, since the Verdict ?

I have paid to the Sheriff of Middlesex Poundage on 10,000l. and upwards, at the Rate of One Shilling in the Pound for the first 100l. and Six Pence on every 100l. exceeding 100l. for which the Sheriff' commenced an Action against me, and I was compelled to pay it, under a Judgment of the Court of

671

Bench; no Part of which can I recover from Mr. Pope, nor the Interest on the Money, since the Judgment, and which Interest is a Saving to the Defendant Pope of 500l. and upwards Annually.

Do you know any other Instances of the same Sort?

I cannot at present state the Names of otiier Debtors, but I have known, in the Course of my Practice, a great Number of Debtors, who have remained in Prison, and were possessed of Property sufficient to discharge their Debts.

Mr. Richard Grassxccll, Secretary to the Society for the Discharge and Relief of Imprisoned Debtors, commonly called The Thatched House Society, examined.

I low long have you been so ?

Near Six Years.

Is it the established Rule and Practice of the Society to make very'strict Enquiry into the Character and Conduct of imprisoned Debtors who apply for Relief?

It is the constant Practice of the Society to relieve none but such whose Characters have been strictly enquired into.

[A Paper delivered by the Witness, containing an Account of the Society.]

To obtain Benefit from this Charity, each Petitioner is obliged to name Two reputable Housekeepers as Vouchers for his Integrity, Sobriety, and Industry, to whom the Society constantly refer for their Enquiries, and by this Means preclude even a Possibility of Imposition.

Is it a Rule of this Society to prefer the most aged and infirm of those who apply for Relief?

It is the Rule of the Society to prefer those who are in the most indigent Circumstances.

When was this Society instituted ?

In February 1772.

Does it extend its Enquiries and Relief to Debtors in County Gaols?

The first Institution appeared to be confined only to the Metropolis, but it gradually extended its beneficial Effects to several County and City Gaols, and stands at this Time unlimited in its Operation within the Kingdom.

Can you state the Number of Debtors relieved, from the first Institution of the Society to the present Time, and the Sums paid for their Relief, with the Number of their Wives and Children ?

[Delivers in a written Account, from which it appears, that the Sum Total of Debtors discharged and relieved by the Charity of the Society, is 12,590, who had 7, S42 Wives, 23,268 Children, amounting in all to 43,700 Persons — the Average of the Money expended for the Debtors, about 45 s. each, to procure their Discharge; and for those who have been relieved, about 135. each — The whole of the Expence of the Society from its first Institution, by which the Numbers above stated have been discharged or relieved, amounts to 29,384/. 10s. 2 id.]

Do you find, from the Enquiries of the Society, that in general the greater Part of the Debts so settled consists in Law Charges and Costs ?

The greater Part of small Debts appear to be frequently Double the original Debt, often Treble, and semetimes Six Times the Amount, and more.

Vol. 47.

Of the 12,590 Debtors, stated in the written Paper delivered in to the Committee to have been discharged and relieved, can you state what Number have been actually discharged ?

Not separately — but upon the Calculation I have given of those discharged Annually, the Number will be about 11,600l.

Of what Description of Persons is the greater Part of the Debtors relieved?

About Two-thirds Manufacturers and Labourers — the Remainder Seamen, Dealers and Chapmen, and various Professions.

Do you find, by the Enquiries and Proceedings of the Society, that many Debtors are long confined by their Creditors without any apparent Ability to pay, and yet without being accused by their Creditors of fraud ?

Yes; it appears on the Books that the following Case occurred: — A young Man, about 25 Years of Age, had a Wife and Five Children, who had an Employment in one of the Public Offices, was arrested for several different Sums, to the Amount of 100l. or upwards; — as he had nothing to pay, he remained 15 Months in Prison, totally deprived of Employment — then all his Actions were superseded by the Society for 6/. — Another Instance in my ov.n Recollection, was the Case of Robert who was

detained in Maidstone Gaol near Three Years, after being entitled to the Groats from January 1788 to December 1790 — the Amount of the Debt was 200l. for which the Society paid a Composition of Eight Guineas, and obtained his Discharge.

Do you know that Debtors are long confined on their Groats under the Lords , alter surrendering their Effects as prescribed?

I know an Instance in which the Groats were paid for Five Years and upwards, to an aged Man, who bad a Wife and Eleven Children, for a Debt of only 21 /.

In stating these particular Instances, do you mean to say that they are the only Instances of the Sort which have come within your Knowledge?

Not by many.

Have you known several Instances of Persons confined for a long Time for Small Debts, without any Charge of Fraud?

I have.

What is the Expence of obtaining the Discharge of a Debtor under the Lords Act ?

To a Debtor, if he applies to his own Attorney, I have generally understood it to cost him between Two mid Tltree Guineas — if in a County Gaol, as it often Imppens, his Plaintiff lives at a considerable Distance, on whom Notices must be served — but the Society contract for that Business with their Solicitor, at a much less Expence.

Does any Division of the Debtor’s Effects actually take Place, as the Act prescribes ?

I never heard of any.

Committee on the Effects of Imprisonment for Debt.

Philip fVyat Crowther, Esquire, examined.

I hold the Office of Secondary of the City of London — have been in the Office of Secondary Two Years — am also Solicitor to the City of London.

How many bailable Writs are, on an Average, issued into London Annually ?

Three thousand and Fifty-five.

How many Arrests are, on an Average, according to the best of your Knowledge, actually made in the City of London Annually on Mesne Process ?

There must be at least One thousand Five hundred. — The Sheriff has no actual Return of all the Arrests made, so as to make this Answer more correct.

Can you state the Average Number of Writs for Debts under 50/.?

In the Course of the last Year Two thousand Two hundred and Ten Warrants were issued upon bailable Process to that Amount; but I cannot ascertain how many actual Arrests took Place in consequence.

How many under 20/.?

One thousand One hundred and Forty.

Can you state how many Defendants actually go to Prison Annually?

For the last Year Two hundred and Sixty-two.

Of those how many for Debts under 20/.?

One hundred and Twenty-one.

What is the usual Expence attending an Arrest, and of completing the Appearance of the Defendant by Special Gail?

About 61. or gl.

What appears to be the Average Number of Debts which are Annually settled immediately on the Arrest ?

I cannot speak with Certainty — but from the best Information I can collect from the Clerks in the Office, I should take it to be about One Fifth.

Does the Sheriff usually take Bail, or what Security, for the Appearance of the Defendant?

He takes a Bond executed by the Defendant with Two Sureties — but in Cases where the Attorney is a Man of Respectability, a Practice has prevailed with the Sheriff’s Officer of accepting the Undertaking of the Defendants Attorney.

Is the Sheriff ever requested by the Defendant to take a Deposit of Money, or any other Security, for his Appearance?

Application to that Effect has been made, but refused as contrary to Law.

Is it ever known that the Sheriffs Officer does ever in Fact accept such Offer ?

Indirectly I believe it is so, but it is without the Knowledge of the Sheriff.

Are any Fees paid on the Discharge of Defendants and Debtors from Gaol ?

(The Witness delivered in an Account of Fees, from which it appears that the total Amount of Fees at the Poultry and New Compters are 15 s. 6 d. and at Ludgate 7 s.8//.]

Are Defendants or Debtors ever detained in Custody for Non-payment of such Fees?

Most certainly never for the Sheriffs Fees or Poundage, and I believe never for the Gaol Fees, because Vo 1. 47.

there are Charities in the City of London, from which Persons of that Description have applied for the Discharge of the Fees, and they are always relieved.

Are Bails frequently found to be insufficient on Examination, and therefore rejected?

Most certainly, though they tendered themselves, and were ready to swear, as required by Law, that they were worth double the Sum for which the Action was brought.

What is the Consequence of Bail being so rejected?

That the Court will sometimes, on Application, give them Time to add another Bail; but if refused, which is frequently the Case, then Attachment issues against the Sheriff — on which he is immediately compelled to pay the Debt and Costs.

Does not the Expence of these Proceedings in general fall ultimately on the Defendant?

If the Defendant is in a Situation to pay, they certainly all fall on him; if he is Insolvent, then the Loss certainly falls on the Plaintiff. When the Attachment i96ues against the Sheriff, he pays the Money. He then resorts to the Bail Bond; and it frequently occurs that they are the same Bail who have been rejected in Court. If they are insufficient, then the Sheriff sustains the Loss.

Does it frequently happen that the Defendant surrenders himself into Custody, or is surrendered by his Bail, whereby they are discharged ?

Yes.

What is the additional Expence of this Proceeding?

About 3/. for every Action.

Do you find that in the City of London the Number of bailable Writs, for the Purpose of Arrests for Debts under 20/. is increasing?

They certainly are, but not to any large Amount.

Did you ever know an Instance where a Division actually took Place of the Effects of an insolvent Debtor, under the Authority of the Act commonly called the Lords Act ?

No: I thought it had been so, but on Enquiry I found it was not so.

Do you know of any Instance where the Debtor has been brought up under the Clause of that Act which entitles the Creditor to compel Surrender of the Debtor’s Property;

I do not.

Withdrew.

A PETITION of the Grand Jury of the County Petition fro# of Middlesex, in the Quarter Sessions held for the Grand the County, at the Sessions House, Clerkenwell Green, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Lotteries. That the Petitioners feel it their indispensable Duty to represent to the House the dreadful Consequences which result to the Community at large from the alarming Spirit of Gambling, excited and encouraged among all Classes of the lower Orders of the People by the Establishment of Lotteries; and the Petitioners beg to observe the Increase of illegal Insurances, the dreadful Distresses occasioned to sober industrious Families, who, but for those Temptations to Vice and Immorality, would probably have supported themselves and their Families by honest Industry; That Servants have been tempted to engage in a Series of Depredations on their Masters to furnish the Supplies necessary to enable them to adventure in that dreadful Species of Public Gambling; the Petitioners have heard (and have every Reason to believe) that Parents have been torn from their Children, and dearest Relations of Society outraged and violated, in consequence of the said increasing and wide spreading Evil: That the Petitioners will not shock the Feelings of the House, by enumerating the frequent Instances of unfortunate Persons who, unable to bear up under the Accumulation of Distress brought upon themselves by such Species of Gambling, have ventured to lay Hands upon themselves, and, in Opposition to the first Laws of God and Man, by violent Means, put an End to a miserable Existence: And therefore requesting the House to provide such a Remedy for those alarming Mischiefs as may appear to them adequate to the Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Petition do tie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Magistrates acting for the Eastern Division of the County of Essex, the Mayor and Inhabitants of the Borough of Colchester, and other Inhabitants of the said Division, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Petition <« thereunto subscribed, Electors of the City and Liberty ao Enquiry of Westminster, w as presented to the House, and read; *Dt0 A*5"5" Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe with Regret, by the Votes of the House, that a Motion was sterElection, made on Tuesday, the 13th of March 1792, for an Enquiry into all Abuses committed by Persons in Office at the Election for a Member to serve in Parliament for the City of Westminster, in the Month of July 1788, as far as the same related to Penalties incurred under the Excise Law and Lottery Act, which Motion was rejected: That George Smith, a Publican in Westminster, was in the Year 1788 convicted, on the Prosecution of the Attorney General, in* the Sum of 50/. for brewing Beer for Sale without a Licence, and that the Prosecution was officially conducted by John Vivian, Esquire, Solicitor to the Board of Ex-

cise: That in the Month of October 1788, the said George Smith was employed by George , Esquire, Secretary to the Treasury, as an Emissary and Agent, in Favour of Lord Hood, one of the Lords of the Admiralty, at that Time prosecuting a Petition in this House against Lord John Townshend, the successful Candidate at the Election for Westminster in 1788, and that the said Petition was tried before a Committee of this House in the Months of April, May, and June 1789: That in the Month of January 1789, George Smith applied to the said George Rose, stating the particular Circumstances of his Case in a Petition, and praying to have the Penalty he had incurred remitted; that the said George Rose, Esquire, did forward the said Petition to the Chairman of the Board of Excise, and did afterwards send a Letter to the Secretary,

. desiring

t

32 Geo. III. 4° Aprilis.

687

desiring as a Favour that all Proceedings on Smith's Penalty might be stopped till the Chairman, who was at that Time absent, returned to Town: That on the 8th of April 1789, the said George Rose did write to the said George Smith in these Words; " Mr. Rose desires " Mr. Smith will call on him in Old Palace Yard Tomorrow Morning at 8 o’Clock, as Mr. Vivian will " then be thereThat the Secretary of the Treasury, in thus procuring a secret Interview early in the Morning, at his own House, between the Solicitor to the Board of Excise and the convicted Defendant, acted in a Manner highly suspicious: That, from the Nature of the Transaction, it is difficult to know what passed at such a clandestine Meeting, but it appears, by Receipt from the Excise Office, signed John Vivian," that no Part of the Penalty incurred by the said George Smith was levied before the 14th of May 1790, being a Respite of above Thirteen Months ’ from the Time of the private Interview at Mr. Rose's House: That during the first Part of those Thirteen Months the said George Smith was extremely useful to the Treasury in forwarding the Interest of Lord Hood, the unsuccessful Candidate, and, during the latter Part of the Period, extremely troublesome to the Treasury in demanding to be paid for his Services: That the Excise Penalty appears to have slept while he was an Election Agent, and only became active when he shewed himself in the Shape of an unsatisfied Creditor: That the said George , being unable to procure from the Secretary of the Treasury Payment of his Bill for his said Election Services as his Agent, brought an Action against him to recover the Amount: That the said Action was tried, in the Month of July 1791, before the Lord Chief Justice of the Court of King’s Bench, by a Special Jury who, by giving a Verdict for the whole Demand of the Plaintiff, did thereby declare themselves satisfied that Smith had performed Election Services against Lord John Townshend at the Request of the Secretary of the Treasury; and that the said Action was defended by the Solicitors to the Treasury: That in the Course of the Trial of the said Action, the following material Evidence was given upon Oath by the Solicitor for Lord Hood; viz. " That Mr. Rose had, while the Petition against Lord " John Townshend was depending, assured him he

" might trust Smith, because there was a Prosecution " going on against him in the Excise, and, as a Mark " of the Trust and Confidence they had in him, they " had interfered, and stepped in to serve himand that the said Evidence was uncontroverted upon the Trial, and has been since circulated in a printed Statement for above Eight Months, without Refutation: That the above-mentioned Proceedings do appear to the Petitioners to warrant their Opinion, that Mr. Rose, by using that influence with the Board of Excise, and its Solicitor, which his Situation as Secretary to the Treasury afforded him, has endeavoured, as far as in‘him lay, to apply the Penalties, provided by Act of Parliament for the Punishment of Frauds upon the Revenue, to the corrupt Purpose of establishing an undue Influence in the Election of a Member of Parliament: That the Petitioners, considering the great and increasing Extension of the Excise Laws, and the Number of Individuals subject to their Operation, cannot but entertain the most alarming Apprehensions of Danger to the Freedom of Election, should the Influence, which Administration must necessarily have in the Execution of those Laws, be made Use of for the Purpose of corrupting or intimidating the Minds of the Electors of this Kingdom: — That John Hoskins, having been arrested on the Affidavit of the Solicitor of the Lottery, and being a Prisoner in the King's Bench Prison for Penalties to the Amount of 700l. incurred under the Lottery Act, did offer to the said Solicitor, who at the Time was acting as Agent to Lord Hood, to procure

Vol. 47.

Sixty Votes for the said Lord Hood, in Consideration of his Release from Prison: That the Solicitor of the Lottery declined complying with the said Proposition until he had consulted higher Authority, and that, after a short Interval of Time, the Proposal was accepted, and, on the said Hoskins having procured Sixty Persons to vote for Lord Hood, the said Hoskins was actually discharged from Prison on Bail notoriously insufficient; that the Expence attending the putting in and justifying such Bail so notoriously insufficient, was, in Part, defrayed by Lord Hood, a Candidate at the said Election, and one of the Lords of the Admiralty: That the Petitioners have Reason to believe that this Transaction would have been traced to Persons of higher Authority, and that other Instances of equal Enormity on the Part of the Servants of the Crown, in the said Election, would have been proved, had an Enquiry been granted: — That the said Petitioners, taking into their Consideration the above Circumstances, anxious to maintain the Freedom of Election thus daringly invaded, to prevent a Misapplication of the Public Money, and to preserve from Abuse Powers which, even in the purest Exercise of them, must be considered as dangerous, but which, if misapplied, would become absolutely destructive to the Liberties of the People, do consider a Parliamentary Enquiry as necessary to secure the Constituent Body of this Kingdom in the free Enjoyment of their Constitutional Privileges, and to preserve the Independence of the House of Commons: And therefore praying the House to take the several Matters above mentioned into their most serious Consideration, and to institute a solemn Enquiry into the Truth thereof, and to grant unto the Petitioners such Relief therein as to the House, in its Justice and Wisdom, shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition to lie upon the Table.

Coast, which they ever enjoyed exclusively from any other Nation; that their Stoves on their Salmon Rivers were by Force of Arms broke open, plundered, and their Men driven therefrom by the French, all which had been represented to His Majesty's Secretary of State, without any Satisfaction given for the very heavy Losses sustained, and now that valuable Tract, of more than One Half the whole Coast, with all the valuable Salmon Rivers thereon, alrondoned to our natural Rivals in the said Fishery, the French; and that, under the various Acts since that of William and Mary, and the great Bounties and other Encouragements given to our rival Fishery, our Newfoundland Fishery has gradually declined, many of those who flourished under the former Act are become insolvent, or reduced so low as not to be able to carry it on, many, very many, opulent Boatkeepers are reduced to Beggary, and become burthensome to their Parishes, and those now concerned in the Fishery must decline the same, if not relieved by this House; and that, under the specious Pretence of Encouragement to the Fisheries, a new Bill is brought into the House contrary to the general Wishes of the Trade, laying an additional Burthen on the poor Fishermen of a new Duty on Rum, calculated, they presume, for the very Purpose of countenancing the Custom-house, which is now a Burthen by Salaries to this Country, litigious and troublesome to the Traders, and productive of no one Good whatever; that it will establish a Court of Civil Jurisdiction on arbitrary and destructive Principles, leaving the Traders entirely under the Will of the Judge and Assessors, without Appeal to the Courts of Westminster, and thereby depriving them of that valuable Privilege of Trial by Jury, a Situation which they presume must very soon destroy that valuable Trade, for Experience has shewn them what can be done by Official Men in the Island of Newfoundland, and makes them very justly dread any further Power being vested without free Appeal to the Courts of Law at Westminster; and that the Petitioners are ready to prove the Injuries they hereby set forth, with many others sustained arising from the Acts now complained of, and the Bill now ' before the House, should it pass into a Law; And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, that the various Acts so injurious to the Fishery may be repealed, and such other Encouragement given as may restore the Fishery to its former State, and that the Petitioners may be heard, at the Bar of the House, to support this their Petition.

Report on Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported ing"theeim-C from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it portation and was referred to consider of the Laws respecting the Exportation Importation and Exportation of Sugar, and the Duties, of Sugar, &c. Drawbacks, and Bounties thereon, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed); viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every sworn Broker, residing within the City of London, or the Bills of Mortality, who shall, after the 1st Day of May 1792, buy or sell any Brown or Muscovado Sugar, shall deliver to the Clerk of the Grocers Company, on or before Wednesday in every Week, an Account of the Quantities of Brown or Muscovado Sugar, bought or sold by him in the preceding Week, and of the Price paid for each Quantity; and that the said Clerk shall make up, on or before the Third W ednesdin June next, an Account of the Average Price of such Sugar, to be computed according to the Quantities and Prices of such Sugar bought or sold in the Six Weeks preceding, and in like Manner on or before the Third Wednesday in October next, according to the Quantities and Prices of the Six Weeks then preceding, and in like Manner, in every succeeding Year, on the Third Wednesday in February, the Third Wednesday in June, and the Third Wednesday in October, according to the Quantities and Prices of the Six Weeks then preceding such Days respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Exportation of Sugar of the British Plantations from Great Britain to any Country or Place whatever, except to Ireland, or any other Part of the British Dominions, shall be prohibited for Four Months, from the 23d Day of June next, in case the Average Price of Brown and Muscovado Sugar, taken on the Six Weeks preceding, shall then exceed Sixty Shillings for every Hundred Weight, exclusive of the Duty of Customs, and from the 20th Day of October next, for Four Months, in case such Average Price, taken on the Six Weeks preceding, shall then exceed Fifty-five Shillings for every Hundred Weight, exclusive of the Duty of Customs, and in like Mannar in every succeeding Year, the Exportation of Sugar shall be prohibited as aforesaid for Four Months, from and after the Saturday next following the Third IV°d-nesday in February, June, and October, in case the Average Price, at any of the said Periods respectively, taken on the Six Weeks preceding, shall exceed Fifty Shillings for every Hundred Weight, exclusive of the Duty of Customs.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, as long as the Exportation of Sugar of the British Plantations from Great Britain shall be so prohibited, it should not be lawful to grant any licence for transporting Sugar directly from any BYiiish Colony or Plantation to any Country in Europe belonging to any Foreign Sovereign or State.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that Sugar and Coffee, not of the British Plantations, imported into Great Britain in British-built Ships from any Country not in Europe,

be allowed, upon the Importation thereof, to be Warehoused, under certain Regulations, at the Expence of the Importer, and to be again exported without Payment of any Duties whatsoever; but that, if the same be taken out for Home Consumption, they be subject respectively to the Duties then payable on the Importation of such Articles, not being of the British Plantations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that Sugar and Coffee be allowed to be imported into the Port of Nassau, in the Island of Ncio Providence, or some other convenient Port in the Bahama Islands, in Foreign Ships, subject to the Regulations contained in an Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for establishing certain Free Ports in the West India Islands, and another Act, made in the Thirtieth Year of His present Majesty, for amending the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sugar and Coffee imported into Great Britain, or any of the Dominions of Great Britain, from the said

697

said Port of Nassau, or such other Port in the Bahama Islands as shall be fixed upon, should be deemed Sugar and Coffee not of the British Plantations.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Speech of Mr. Speaker, this Day, upon pre- Mr. Speak-senting to His Majesty the Bill to enable His er’s Speech to Majesty to make Provision for the Establishment the King-of Their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Dutchess of York and Albany, and also to settle an Annuity on Her Royal Highness during the Term of Her natural Life, to commence from the Decease of His said Royal Highness, in case Her said Royal Highness shall survive Him; and also, the Bill for granting to His Majesty the Sum of Four hundred thousand Pounds, to be issued and paid to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, to be by them placed to the Account of the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt; when they received the Royal Assent.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

It is my Duty to tender to Your Majesty Two Bills, in the Name, and on the Behalf of, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled.

In pursuance of Your Majesty’s Recommendation,

Your Commons cheerfully proceeded to make a Provision for the Establishment of Their Royal Highnesses

the Duke and Dutchess of York;and, they trust that

8 P the

608 5e — 17°

A. 1792.

the Bill which they have passed for this Purpose will fully manifest their just Sense of what is due to the Rank and Dignity of their Royal Highnesses, as well as the Satisfaction they derive from an Event which, whilst it promotes the Comfort and Happiness of Your Majesty and Your illustrious Family, is also materially conducive to the Interests and Honour of Your People.

Other Objects, no less interesting to Your Majesty’s Mind, constantly directed as it is to the Welfare of Your Subjects, have also engaged the Attention of Your Commons. The prosperous and improving Condition of the Public Revenue, and the Reductions which have been found practicable in the Naval and Military Establishments, afforded the Means, of which Your Commons thought it their Duty to avail themselves, of making a large Addition to the Fund, to be applied in the Course of the present Year, to the Reduction of the Public Debt: Their Conduct upon this, as upon other Occasions, was governed by the Conviction, that the Efficiency and Success of the Plan, which has been established by Parliament for this important Purpose, must essentially tend to the future Ease, and permanent Security of these Kingdoms. In the Adoption of these Measures, Your Commons have felt peculiar Satisfaction, by finding themselves enabled, at the same Time, to give some immediate Relief to Your Majesty’s Subjects, whose Firmness in sustaining the Burthens, rendered necessary by a due Regard to the Maintenance of Public Credit, and whose Spirit of En-terprize, and useful Industry, have so effectually contributed to advance to the Pre-eminence they have attained, the general Interests and Prosperity of the Empire.

Your Commons, Sire, contemplate with just Satisfaction the continued and progressive Improvement in the internal Situation of the Country: To preserve, augment, and diffuse the Blessings, of which we are in Possession, they consider as the most important of their Duties; and, actuated by this Principle, which comprehends a zealous and firm Attachment to the Form of Government under which we live, and a faithful and vigilant Attention to the Interests and Happiness of all Classes of their Fellow Subjects, they are persuaded that those Measures, which are the Result of it, cannot fail to receive Your Majesty’s most Gracious Approbation.

The Bills, which I have in my Hand, are severally intituled,

" An Act to enable His Majesty to make Provision

for the Establishment of Their Royal Highnesses " the Duke and Dutchess of York and , and

* also to settle an Annuity on Her Royal Highness " during the Term of Her natural Life, to commence from the Decease of His said Royal Highness, in case Her said Royal Highness shall survive " Him:

" An Act for granting to His Majesty the Sum of " Four hundred thousand Pounds, to be issued and " paid to the Governor and Company of the Bank of " England, to be by them placed to the Account of " the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National ' " Debt."

To which Your Commons, with all Humility, entreat Y*our Majesty’s Royal Assent.

That, on Account of the Flatness of the Country through which the River Witham takes its Course, the Floods of the Winter, especially in dry Seasons, are scarcely sufficient to scour out the Outfall of the said River, and of the Haven of Boston, from the Sullage of the Tides deposited in Summer Time, when the Backwater is insufficient to carry away the same, although they are confined for more than Ten Miles between lofty Banks, in order that they may act upon the Sullage with the greater Force and Efficacy; and that the Petitioners, aware that any Diminution of the Waters committed to their Charge would considerably endanger their Works, and the Drainage, of the adjoining Lands, amounting to more than 100,000 Acres, appointed One of their Number to attend the Proceedings of the Advocates for an intended Navigable Canal from the Town of Grantham to the River Trent; and that, in consequence of various Representations made to the Advocates for the said intended Canal, they resolved not to interfere with the Waters of the River Witham, or of any of the Brooks that feed it, and inserted in their Bill a Clause to protect the same from being applied to the Use of the intended Navigable Canal, but the said protecting Clause was struck out of the said Bill, immediately before it was presented to the House, without the Consent of the Proprietors of the said intended Canal, as the Petitioners have been informed, and certainly without any Notice thereof having been given to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners have good Reason to fear, that the Persons who struck out the said Clause in so unprecedented a Manner, intend to make use of some Part of the Waters of the River Witham, for the Purpose of filling the intended Canal, to the manifest Injury of those who have lent Money, to the Amount of 53,000l. or upwards, on the Faith of the Witham Act, and to the evident endangering of the Works

In- whom the Petition of the Owners and Proprietors of Drainage" Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, within the Petition re- Open, Arable, or Tillage Fields, Commons, Ings, ported. Meadows, Pastures, and Waste Grounds, within the several Townships or Hamlets of Anlaby, and

Tranby, in the County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and of the Owners and Proprietors of ancient inclosed Lands, within the several Townships or Hamlets above mentioned, and also in in

the same County, whose Names are thereunto respectively subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills of Inclosure and Drainage, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Codd being examined, said, That within' the said Townships there are several Open, Common, Arable, or Tillage Fields and Lands, and several Common Pastures, Ings, Meadows, and Waste Grounds, in which the Lands of the Proprietors lie intermixed, and the said Ings, Meadows, and Pastures-are frequently Overflowed, and are in their present State capable of little or no Improvement — That if the said Fields and Lands were divided and inclosed, and tire said Commons, Ings, Meadows, Pastures, and Waste Grounds were drained, divided, and inclosed, great Advantage would accrue to all Persons interested therein — That there are certain ancient in-

closed Lands within the said Townships which pay Tythes in Kind, and the Proprietors are desirous the same should be exonerated therefrom, and a Money Payment charged upon the said Lands in lieu thereof.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for dividing, inclosing, draining, and improving the Open Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commons, and Waste Grounds, within the several Townships or Hamlets of Hessle, Anlaby, and , in the County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, for making a Compensation in lieu of Tythe for certain ancient inclosed Lands within the said several Townships of Hamlets, and also within the Township or Hamlet of Woojerton, in the same County: And that Mr. Henry Hobart and Mr. Samuel Thornton do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the General Commissioners for Navigation by the River Witham, on Behalf of themselves, the Creditors of the said Trust, and other Persons interested in the said Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade carried on by Means of the Navigation on the River Witham is of considerable Consequence to the Petitioners, to a large Extent of Country through which it passes, and to divers Persons who have lent

Tract of Country, contiguous to the said River, would be much depreciated, was it deprived of the immemorial Use of what is so necessary to the Occupation of it; and that, even-in Winter (except in wet Years) the Quantity of Water is found insufficient to cleanse the Outfall, and consequently every Diversion or Diminution of that Quantity must be extremely injurious to the Country: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by Counsel, against a Bill now pending before the House, for Leave to make a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, to the River Trent, at or near Ratcliff e, in the County of Nottingham, and to supply it with Water, by seizing, without any Appearance of Right or Justice, on some of those Streams which now, and immemorially have, by emptying themselves into the said River Witham, their natural Outfall, contributed materially to the Convenience and Preservation of the Country.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for taking into Consideration the Matter of the several Petitions, Accounts, and other Papers, presented to this House in the last Parliament, relating to the internal Government of the Royal Burghs in Scotland, he now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The House was moved, That the Entry in the Journal of the House, of the 27th Day of May in the last Session of Parliament, of the Resolution of the House, " That this House will, early in the next " Session of Parliament, take into Consideration the " Matter of the Petitions, and other Papers, presented " to this House in the last Parliament, relating to u the internal Government of the Royal Burghs in 41 Scotland," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed , That this House, having received Petitions from Forty-six of the Royal Burghs of Scotland complaining of various Grievances in the Government of the said Burghs, and the House, after taking the same into Consideration, having, on the 17th of February 1788, ordered, that Notarial Copies and Setts of the Royal Burghs should be laid before this House, and then having made several other Orders for Accounts of the Cess, Stent, or Land Tax levied in the said Burghs, and of the Sums of Money paid to the Receiver General on Account of the same, and for Accounts of the Revenues of the said Burghs, and for Accounts of the Lands of the said Burghs alienated since the Union; and, in Obedience to the said Orders, such Accounts having been laid before this House, it is incumbent on this House to proceed to the Examination of the said Papers and Accounts, in such Mode as shall best ascertain whether the Grievances complained of are true, and what Remedy the House ought to apply to such Grievances.

And the said Motion was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the several Petitions, and other Accounts and Papers, presented to this House in the last Parliament, relative to the internal Government of the Royal Burghs in Scotland, be referred to the Consideration of a Committee;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

A Petition of the Merchants, and of the few remaining Boat Keepers, trading to, and concerned in, the Newfoundland Fishery, from the Towns of Teingmouth, Newton Bushell, the Parishes adjacent, the Towns and Villages in and near Torbay, &c. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are much alarmed at the Contents of a Bill now in the House, which contains Matters that they fear will, if not utterly ruin, very much diminish, the Newfoundland Trade in which they are engaged; and Representing to the House, that the said Trade is now in a very reduced and declining State, from the many Burthens and Restrictions imposed thereon of late Years, and they are convinced, that, if the House would take it into due Consideration, and inquire into the Causes of such Reductions, and into- the whole State and Nature of the said Trade, instead of passing new Laws and Restrictions, which will inevitably tend to the Ruin of the Trade, the House would be induced to ease them of the Burthens and Difficulties under which they already labour: And therefore praying, That the Bill now in the House may not pass into a Law, and that the House would, themselves, institute an Inquiry into the State and Means of the said Trade, and pass such Laws as would be found necessary for its Relief and Protection.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to amend an Act, passed in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the Encouragement of the " Fisheries carried on from Great Britain, Ireland, and " the British Dominions in Europe, and for securing " the Return of the Fishermen, Sailors, and others, " employed in the sffid Fisheries, to the Ports thereof, Vol. 47.

A Petition of the Traders, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants of the Town of BrLvham, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Set-01 the Fi'lhe- h°g forth, That the Petitioners are much alarmed at j,o: uifs. the Contents of a Bill now in the House, which coni'..- tains Matter that they fear will be injurious to, and

ft. Vol. 47.

further reduce, the Newfoundland Fishery, on which the Existence of the Petitioners, their Families, and Thousands besides in this Country, very much depends; and that the Burthens and Restrictions laid on the said Fishery, by Laws passed of late Years, have materially lessened the Business and Occupations of the Petitioners and others: And therefore praying the House to fake into Consideration the Causes of such Reduction, and that the Bills before the House may not be passed into a Law, and that the House would of themselves institute an Inquiry into the State and Means of the said Fishery and Trade, and would pass such Laws as would be found necessary for its Relief and Protection.

A Petition of the Merchants of Poole, carrying on the Fishery, and.trading to the Island of Newfoundland, was also presented to the House, and read;

Settbg fortl], That the Petitioners are much alarmed at -the Contents of a Bill now in the House, which ' contains Matter that they conceive will, if not totally ruin, very much injure the Newfoundland Trade, in which they are engaged; and Representing to the -House, that the said Trade is now in a very reduced and declining State, from the many Burthens and Restrictions imposed thereon of late Years, and they are convinced that, if the House will take into Consideration, and inquire into, the Causes of such Reduction, and into the whole State and Nature of the said Trade, instead of passing new Laws and Restrictions, which will inevitably tend to its Ruin, the House would be induced to ease them of the Burthens and Difficulties under which they labour: And therefore praying, That the Bill now in the House may not pass into a Law, and that the House would themselves institute an Inquiry into the State and Men of the said Trade, and give it such Relief as shall appear necessary.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill to amend an Act, passed in the Fifteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for the Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on from Great Britain, Ireland, and the " British Dominions in Europe, and for securing the Return of the Fishermen, Sailors,

" and others, employed in the said Fisheries,

" to the Ports thereof, at the End of the Fishing Season;" and for laying an additional Duty on Rum, and other Spirits, imported into the Island of Newfoundland, be read a Second Time.

The House being informed that Mr. Pearson, from the Inspector General of the Exports and Imports of Great Britain, attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Order.

An Account of the Number of Vessels, their Tonnage, and Number of Men, that have arrived from Africa in the British West India Islands, between the 5th of January 1789 and the 5th of January 1792, with the Number of Slaves imported therein, distinguishing each Year, from what Part of the Coast taken on Board, and at what Island in the West Indies landed, also distinguishing the Men from the Women, and the Boys from the Girls; together with the Number of Negroes that died from the Time of their being taken on Board until their Arrival" in the West Indies, distinguishing the Males from Females, and the Boys from the Girls; together with the Number of Negroes re-exported in each Year from each Island respectively, and the Number retained each Year in each Island respectively, so far as the same can be made up.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Account was read.

Ordered, That the said Account be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of Measures to be taken for the Abolition of the Trade carried on by British Subjects, for the Purpose of procuring Slaves from Africa.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Account be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The said Account is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Petition re-thereunto [subscribed, Inhabitants, Householders, Re- *P«ju»g th* siants within the Borough of Pontefract, in the County for

of York, and, as such, Electors of Representatives to Pontefract, serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, upon the 9th Day of March, in the Year 1791, the Select Committee, who were appointed to try and determine the Merits of a Petition of Charks Mcllish and John Anstruther, Esquires, and also, the Petition of several other Persons, Freeholders of Burgage Tenure, within the Borough of Pontefract, and, as such, claiming to be Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, severally complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, reported to the House, That it appeared to the said Select Committee, that the Merits of the Petitions did wholly depend upon the Right of Election, and that therefore, the said Committee had required the Counsel for the several Parties to deliver, to the Clerk of the said Committee, Statements in Writing of the Right of Election, for which they respectively contended — That, in consequence thereof, the Counsel for the said Charles Mellish and John Anstruther, and the said other Persons, delivered in a Statement respecting the Right of Election for the said Borough, as follows: " That the Right of Election for Members to serve in Parliament for the " Borough of Pontefract, in the County of York, is in " Persons having, within the said Borough, a Freehold " of Burgage Tenure, paying a Burgage Rent" — That the Counsel for the Sitting Members, John Smyth and William Sotheron, Esquires, delivered in a Statement as follows: " The Counsel for the Sitting Members state the Right of Election for the Borough of Pontefract to be in the Inhabitants " Householders Resiants " — That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the said several Petitioners, the said Select Committee reported, That they had determined, " That the Right of Election,

" as set forth in the said Statement, is not the Right " of Election for the Borough of Pontefract, in the " County of York" — That, upon the Statement delivered in by the Counsel for the Sitting Members, the said Select Committee reported, That they had determined, " That the Right of Election, as set " forth in the said Statement, is the Right of Election for the said Borough of Pontefract; " and that John Walsh, Esquire, and also several other Persons, pretending to be Electors of Representatives to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Pontefract, having presented their respective Petitions to the House to prevent the said Judgment of the said Select Committee from becoming final and conclusive, praying that they might be admitted as Parties, according to the Form of the Statute in that Case made and provided, to oppose that Right of Election in Favour of which the said Select Committee had reported as above set forth, and that they respectively might have such further and other Relief in the Premises as to the House should seem meet, and the Nature of their Case might require, and the Petitioners insisting that the Right of Election which hath been deemed valid in the Judgment of the said Select Committee, is the ancient and true Right of Election for the said Borough of Pontefract, therefore praying, That they may be admitted as Parties to defend such Right of Election so reported to the House as aforesaid, according to the Form of the said Statute, and that they may have such further and other Relief as to the House shall seem meet, and as the Nature of their Case may require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 1st Day of May next, at the same Time that the Petition of John Walsh, Esquire, who claims to be an Elector of Representatives

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, commonly called The Turkey Company, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That it would tend very much to the Benefit and Convenience of the Petitioners, and other British Subjects, to extend and render more effectual an Act, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, "An Act for enlarging and regulating the " Trade into the Levant Seas," by authorizing Persons Abroad to administer the Oath in the said Act mentioned, and by enabling the Treasurer of the said Company to supply the Place of the Governor or Deputy Governor thereof, in case of their necessary Absence; and that the Petitioners intended, and were prepared, to petition the House within the Time prescribed for receiving Petitions for private Bills, but were prevented from offering the same to the House from their not having been able to obtain, within such Time, sufficient Informatian and Advice relating the reto: And therefore praying, that they may now have Leave to petition the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Governor and Company of Merchants of England, trading into the Levant Seas, commonly called The Turkey Company.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Rose, Mr. Smith of Ludgershall, and Mr. Samuel Thornton, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House being informed, That Sir George son, one of the Members of the Select Committee appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of Robert Preston, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Town and Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, had some very important Business to transact, on Friday and on Saturday next, which required his Personal Attendance at the Distance of at least Ninety Miles from London, having made Appointments to meet several Persons at such Place, some of whom likewise are to come from a considerable Distance, and that it would be attended with very material Injury to his Affairs if not permitted to attend such Engagements;

The House was moved, That the Entry in the Journal of the House, of the 18th Day of June 1789, of the Proceedings of the House, in relation to the Leave given to Sir Samuel Hannay to be absent from the Select Committee, appointed to try and determine the Merits of certain Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the City and Liberty of Westminster, might be read.

And the same was read accordingly;

And the Matter so alleged by Sir George Jackson being taken down in Writing, the said Sir George Jackson was sworn at the Table to the Truth thereof.

Ordered, That the said Sir George Jackson have Leave to absent himself from his Attendance on the said Select Committee, on Friday and on Saturday next, on his private Affairs.

Lord Viscount Parker, from the said Select Committee, acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee (in case the House should give Leave to Sir George Jackson to be absent on Friday and on Saturday next) to move the House, That they might have Leave to adjourn, at the Rising of the Committee Tomorrow, until Monday Morning next, at Eleven of the Clock, such Adjournment being with the Consent of all Parties.

And Lord Viscount Parker moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Leave, for the special Cause assigned, to adjourn as desired.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Common- Petition alty of the City of Exeter, was presented to the House, against tie and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe that Bills are now depending in the House for making tur« Bfll, ti further Regulations in the Government of Bill for L

land, and the Newfoundland Fishery, the Provisions of couraS" which will lay additional Restrictions on the Trade to *ke Newfoundland from this Country; that such Trade to Newfoundland being carried on to a very considerable Extent from different Places within the Port of Exeter, and the Trade of the said City being much connected with it, the Petitioners conceive it to be their Duty to represent to the House, that for many Years past the said Trade has been in a declining State, arising in a great Measure, as the Petitioners are informed, from the Restrictions and Burthens already laid upon it, and they are apprehensive the Provisions proposed by the said Bills w ill still increase the Difficulties and Embarrassments under which it labours, and operate as a great Discouragement to the Enter-prize and Exertions of all Persons concerned therein, and by this Means a Trade which has been, and in its ordinary Course might continue to be, of the most essential Advantage to this Country, must be considerably diminished, if not totally ruined: And therefore the Petitioners hope, That, before any further Progress is made in a Matter of so much Importance, the Hoase will institute an Enquiry into the present State of the Newfoundland Trade, the Causes of its present Decline, and the probable Esse.cts of the proposed Regulations, and that the Bills, now depending in the House for the Purposes aforesaid, may be suspended, until a full Investigation has taken Place for the Information of the House, with respect to the present reduced State of the said Trade, and that such Measures may be taken for its Relief and Protection as to the House, upon such Enquiry, shall seem meet.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, and other Commonable Places in the Parish of Aynho, in the County of Northampton, without any Amendment: And also,

Petition from Mr. Adam reported from the Committee, to whom Proprietors, gie Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are FdUor"of thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors, Printers, News papers, and Editors of Newspapers, Magazines, and other &c. reported. Daily or Temporary Publications, on Behalf of themselves, and all others concerned in the like Branches of the Printing Trade, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Acts, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King George the First, the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, and in the Twenty-second and Twenty-seventh Years of His present Majesty, whereby certain Penalties are inflicted on Persons Printing, Advertizing, or Publishing Proposals or Schemes relative to Chances of Prizes in Public Lotteries, or other illegal Transactions relating thereto, were read. And,

Mr. Thomas Wright, a Newspaper Printer, being examined, said, That the said Acts of Parliament, and the Penalties thereof, were not understood by the Petitioners, or the Trade in general, to extend to them, until Michaelmas Term last, when the Judgment of the Court of King’s Bench was given, for the First Time, in an Action brought for Recovery of Penalties under the said Acts, or One of them, against the Printer of a public Newspaper, for an Advertisement contained in such Paper.

That, previous to such Decision, the Petitioners and others had unfortunately printed, published, and circulated certain Schemes, Plans, and Proposals relative to public Lotteries; but since the Judgment of the Court of King’s Bench, in November last, no such Schemes have been published, as the Doubts, which had before been entertained on those Subjects, were then removed.

That, soon after such Judgment was given, Actions were commenced against several of the Petitioners, demanding Penalties to the Amount of between 50 and 60,0001.: and, unless an Indemnity is granted, the Consequences, must be attended with inevita-

ble Ruin to most of the Persons against whom such Actions are brought

And the Witness added, That several of the Actions now depending are brought in the Name of George Goodwin, and prosecuted by George Crosley, an Attorney in the Court of King’s Bench — That when some of those Actions were originally brought in the Name of George Goodwin, they were found to be defective in Form, and were quashed by the Court; since when new. Actions have been commenced, but that no Declarations were filed in those Actions, until Saturday last, the 21st Instant.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to indemnify and save harmless all Persons being Proprietors, Printers, and Editors of Newspapers, Magazines, and other Daily or Temporary Publications, who may have incurred Penalties or Forfeitures under an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, "An Act for continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and " Perry, to raise Money, by Way of a Lottery, for " the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-two, and for transferring the De-' ficiencies of a late Malt Act to the Land Tax for u the said Year; and for giving Time for inserting " the Money given with Apprentices in their Indentures, and touching lost Bills, Tickets, or Orders,

" and for exchanging the Tickets in the Exchequer " for Certificates, and for suppressing Lotteries denominated Sales, and other private Lotteries, and " for enlarging the Time for the Accountant General of the Bank of England to return Duplicates of " Annuities into the Exchequer;" and also, an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act " for the more effectual preventing of excessive and " deceitful Gaming;" and also, an Act, passed in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act " for licensing Lottery Office Keepers, and regulating the Sale of Lottery Tickets;" and also, an Act, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of His said present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act to render more effectual the Laws " now in being for suppressing unlawful Lotteries:"

And that Mr. Adam and Mr. Erskine do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Benjamin New, one of the Proprietors of Estates in the Division of Postcomb, in the Manor and Parish of Lewknor, in the County of Oxford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner being applied to, to sign a Petition to the House for dividing and inclosing certain Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, Waste, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, within the Divisions of Lewknor and Post-comb, in the Manor and Parish of Lewknor, in the County of Oxford, he was induced to sign it by being told Mr. Cooper and all the other Proprietors, except himself, had signed; but the Person who brought it to him refused to read it, stating he was in a hurry: That he would by no Means have signed it, had he not been imposed on, and, finding that a great Number of the Proprietors are averse to the Act’s taking Place, and as he would be prejudiced by the said Bill should it pass into a Law, therefore praying, That he may be at Liberty to withdraw the Petition signed by him and that he may be heard by himself, or Counsel, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioner may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
