A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore mentioned, bad been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Steward of His Majesty’s Household, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; which Bills are as followeth, viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty a certain Sum of Money, to be raised by a Lottery:

An Act for rectifying Mistakes in the Names of several of the Commissioners appointed, by an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, to put in Execution an Act, made in the same Session, intituled, Vot. 47.

" An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a " Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the " Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred " and Ninety-one," and for appointing other Commissioners, together with those named in the first-mentioned Act, to put in Execution an Act of this Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-two; and for indemnifying such Persons as have acted as Commissioners for executing the said Act, for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Britain, for the

Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-one:

An Act for defraying the Charge of the Pay and Clothing of the Militia in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-two:

An Act to indemnify such Persons as have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments; and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, or others, who have omitted to register or deliver in their Qualifications within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for those Purposes; and to indemnify Members and Officers in Cities, Corporations, and Borough Towns, whose Admissions have been omitted to be stamped according to Law, or, having been stamped, have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped, to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the Execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors; for indemnifying Deputy Lieutenants and Officers of the Militia, who have neglected to transmit Descriptions of their Qualifications to the Clerks of the Peace, within the Time limited by Law, and for giving further Time for that Purpose; and for allow ing further Time to such Persons as have omitted to pay the Duties on the Indentures and Contracts of Clerks, Apprentices, or Servants:

An Act for the more effectual Prevention of Frauds in the Revenue of Excise, with respect to the Manufacturing of Sope:

An Act to enable the Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland further to increase the Capital Stock of the said Company:

An Act to continue and amend several Laws relating to the Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on in the Greenland Seas and Davis's and to amend the Laws now in Force for the Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on in the Seas to the Southward of the Greenland Seas and Davis's Streights:

Wharf at Maidstone aforesaid; and that the said Company of Proprietors have, at a very great Expence and Hazard, completed the Navigation of the said River from Tunbridge to Maidstone, for all Vessels of Forty Tons, which is the Burthen required by the said recited Acts, and the said Company of Proprietors have also expended several Sums of Money in scouring, cleansing, and deepening such Part of the said River Medway as lies above the lower Part of the late Mrs. Edmonds's now Shepherd's Wharf, at Maidstone aforesaid; and that a Bill has been lately brought into the House for improving the Navigation of the said River below the said Town of , by which it appears, that the principal Object of the Persons who promote the same is to make the said River navigable for Vessels of a larger Burthen than can be navigated upon such Part of the said River as is under the Jurisdiction of the Petitioners; and that, in the present State of the said River, the Petitioners can always navigate their Vessels down the same, and therefore, as the Improvement of the Navigation of the said River, as proposed by the said Bill, will be of no essential Benefit to the Petitioners, they hope they shall not be burthened with an Expence on Account of any such Improvement in the said Navigation; and that the Petitioners observe, that the said Bill includes some Part of the said River which is at present within the Jurisdiction of the Petitioners, and without their Consent, and also subjects the Petitioners to the Payment of several heavy Tolls, Rates, and Duties, for all Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, passing along the said River, and gives them no Security that they shall receive any Compensation for those Payments, and there are several other Parts of the said Bill w'hich they conceive will be highly injurious to their Property: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as shall appear to affect their Rights and Interests, and that such Provision may be made in the said Bill for their Relief, as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for improving the Navigation of the River from the Town of Maidstone through the several Parishes of Maidstone, Boxley, Allington, and Aylesford, in the County of Kent, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices who come to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Stoke Cha- Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, to whom pel Petition the Petition of several of the principal Inhabitants of reported. the Chapelry of Lane End, in the Parish of Stoke upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, was referred; That the Committee bad examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Sparrow being examined, said, That in the Year 1761, John Bourne, of Newcastle under Lyme, erected and endowed, chiefly at his own Expence, a small Chapel at Lane End, which, together with a Burial Ground adjoining, was duly consecrated, and made use of by the Inhabitants of the said Chapelry; and the Rev. IsaacMorcton, now deceased, was by the said Mr. Bourne, with the Consent of the Rector of the said Parish, who was also Patron of the Church, and the Consent of the Diocesan, presented to the said Chapel, and he and his Successors have ever since officiated as Patrons or Curates thereof.

The Witness further said, That the said Chapel being now gone greatly to Decay, and being too small, and wholly insufficient to contain the Number of Persons who of late Years have resorted thereto, owing to the great Increase of Inhabitants within the said Chapelry and its Neighbourhood, which is situated in the Staffordshire Potteries, the Petitioners are willing and desirous that a new Chapel, on a larger Plan, should be erected in a more convenient Situation within the said Chapelry, and a more extensive Burial Ground be provided.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for re-building die Chapel, and enlarging the Chapel Yard, of Lane End, within the Parish of Stoke upon Trent, in the County of Stafford: And that Mr. Gilbert and Sir Ednjnntl Littleton do prepare, and bring in, the same.

" Resolved, That, from and after the 1st Day of

" Resolved, That, from and after a Time to be

" Resolved, That, from and after a Time to be limited,

it shall not be lawful for any Ships to clear out from " any Port of Great Britain, for the Coast of Africa,

" for the Purpose of taking on Board Negroes, unless " such Ships shall have been previously employed in the " African Trade, or contracted for, for that Purpose,

" previous to such Time.

" Resolved, That from and after a Time to be " limited, the Owner or Owners, or Master of every " British Vessel, which shall be entered Outwards in " any Port or Place in this Kingdom, or in His Majesty’s Islands or Plantations in America, shall " declare to the principal Officers of His Majesty’s " Customs of the Port or Place from whence the Vessel " is about to depart, for the Purposes of taking on " Board Negroes on the Coast of Africa, the general " Destination of the Voyage, and the particular Island " or Islands, in His Majesty’s Plantations, to which he " or they propose to carry the Negroes so purchased; " and that One or more of the Owners, together with " the Master or Person having the Command of such " Ship or Vessel, shall, with Two sufficient Sureties, enter into Bond to His Majesty, in the Sum of One " Thousand Pounds for every Hundred Tons Burthen " of such Ship or Vessel, and in a similar Proportion

"where the Tonnage shall fall short or exceed the " above Burthen, to proceed directly from the Coast " of Africa to some One of His Majesty’s Plantations " in the West Indies, or to the Island of New Providence

" in the Bahamas, and there land the Negroes taken " on Board on the Coast of Africa, unless the Master " of such Vessel shall, by Stress of Weather, or other " unavoidable Accident, be obliged, for the Safety of " the Vessel and the Crew, to carry such Ship or Vessel " into the nearest Port of Safety.

" Resolved, That from and after a Time to be limited, " it shall not be lawful to import into any of His Majesty’s Islands or Plantations in America, any " African Negro, or any African, Creole, or Mulatto " Slave, - from any Foreign Island, Colony, Territory, " or Dominion in America.

" Resolved, That, from and after a Time to be " limited, the Tonnage of Shipping Annually cleared " out from the different Ports of this Kingdom to the " Coast of Africa, for the Purpose of purchasing " Negroes, shall not exceed a Number of Tons to be " limited."

A Petition of the thereunder written General Com- Petition missioners for Drainage by the River Witham, in the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That about 100,000 Acres of 3Da Low Lands, lying on both Sides of the River Witham, had been Overflowed and rendered unprofitable by the Outfall of the said River having been obstructed, and in a great measure stopt up, by the Sand and Silt brought in by the Tide; and that an Act of Parliament was obtained in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to restore the Outfall of ttie said River, and thereby to drain the said Low Lands, upon the 1’aith of which Act upwards of 50,000l. have been borrowed to defray the Charge of the necessary Works of Drainage, and the said Lands, now drained and cultivated, are also charged with a heavy Tax on that Account, exclusive of large Sums of Money which have likewise been borrowed on Credit of the Navigation of the 9aid River; and that the Petitioners have been elected by the Country to act as General Commissioners, for the Purpose of carrying into Effect the Regulations, and exercising the Powers conveyed by the said Act, in which they are specifically required and strictly enjoined (as a Matter of absolute Necessity) to preserve the living Waters, and confine the Flood Waters which fall into the Channels flowing into the said River; and Experience has most clearly evinced the Wisdom of that Law, and that the Drainage of the Country absolutely and wholly depends on a strict Observance of it, the Subply of Water in Summer being usually so scanty^hut the utmost Care is necessarily taken to preserve it, and even in Winter (except in wet Years) the Quantity is insufficient perfectly to cleanse the Outfall; and that the Petitioners cannot therefore observe with Indifference that a Bill is now depending before the House for making a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Grantham, in the said County of Lincoln, to llatcUffe, in the County of Nottingham, and for

supplying it with Water, by diverting, and (without any Semblance of Right or Justice) seizing upon, some of those Streams which now and inmicmorially have flowed into the 'River Witham, and are firmly persuaded that every Diversion of those 'Waters will essentially injure the Drainage of a very extensive and valuable Tract of Country: And therefore praying,

That the House will take these Circumstances into Consideration, and that the Petitioners may be heard, by Counsel (on Behalf of themselves and the Trust delegated to them) against the Bill for making the said proposed Cunal, and supplying it with Water from any of those Streams which are essentially and absolutely necessary for the Preservation of the Drainage and Outfall of the River Witham.

A Petition of the Proprietors of Lands drained by the River Witham, in the County of Lincoln, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That more than 200,000 Acres of Low Lands are drained and made very profitable by the Outfall of the River Witham, and it is proved, by Experience, that the said Outfall would be obstructed, and in a great Measure stopped up with Sand and Silt brought in by the Tide, if it was not scoured out from Time to Time by the Living and Flood Waters, which are carefully preserved and confined for that Purpose; and that the Quantity of Water flowing down the Witham, and from all the Rivulets and Streams running into it, is barely sufficient to preserve the said Outfall, on which the said very extensive and valuable Tract of Country wholly depends for its Drainage; and that the Petitioners are informed, that an Application is made to Parliament for an Act to make a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Gr, in the said County of Lincoln, to Ratcliffe, in the county of,

and to supply the said Canal with Water by diverting (without any Colour of Right) the Course of some of those Streams which now flow, and have flowed imme-morially, into the River Witham, and which are essentially necessary to the Preservation of the Drainage thereby: And therefore praying. That the House will take these Circumstances into Consideration, and that they may be heard, by Counsel, against this Attempt so injurious to their lawful Property.

A Petition of the Commissioners for Navigation by the River I Tit ham, in the County of Lincoln, on Behalf of themselves, of the Creditors under that Trust, and of all other Persons interested therein, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That an Act was made, in the Second Year of His Majesty’s Reign, for draining and preserving certain Low Lands called The Fens, lying on both Sides the River Witham, in the County of Lincoln, and for restoring and maintaining the Navigation of the said River, from the High Bridge, in the City of Lincoln, through the Borough of Boston, to the Sea, and under the said Act, Money to the Amount of 6,800l. has been borrowed, and remains due, on the Credit of the Tolls to be taken on the said River; and that the said Navigation is of great Importance to the Country through which it passes, and w ill absolutely be ruined if deprived of its customary Supply of Water, which is now scarcely sufficient to support it, though every Care is taken to prevent Waste; and the Petitioners are therefore justly alarmed by an Attempt to obtain an Act of Parliament for making a Navigable Canal from the Town of Grantham, in the said County of Lincoln, to Ratcliffe, in the County of Nottingham, and for supplying the said Canal with Water by diverting (without any Colour of Right) some of those Streams which now flow, and have flowed immemorially, into the said River Witham; and they are convinced that every Diversion and Subtraction of Water must essentially VrOL. 47.

injure the said Navigation i And therefore praying,

That the House will take these Circumstances into Consideration, and that they may be heard, by Counsel, on Behalf of themselves and of the Trust committed to them, against so much of the Bill for making the said proposed Canal as appears to be injurious to the Petitioners and to the said Navigation on the River Witham.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being of the Committee of the Sugar Refiners of London, appointed to manage all Public Matters relating to their Trade, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for regulating the Exportation of Sugar, and allowing the Importation of Sugar and Coffee into the Bahama and Bermuda Islands in Foreign Ships; and Setting forth, That there are large and extensive Works held, and considerable Capitals embarked, by the Petitioners and others in their Manufactories, the Nature of which is tedious and complicated, their Stocks heavy and burthensome, requiring much Time to perfect in the Process; that high Bounties and Drawbacks to encourage the Exportation of Sugar, either raw or refined, raises the Article in its Price, the Reduction of which to fair and equitable Terms is an Object as desirable to the Petitioners as the Consumer; and that the said Bill contains certain Regulations, in respect to the Exportation of Sugar, which, as the Petitioners apprehend and trust they shall -be able to prove to the House, will be productive Vo/,. 47.

of great Embarrassment in the Management of their Trade, and tend to the grievous Oppression and Distress of those concerned in it, if not to the total Ruin of many of them, without producing any permanent Advantage or Relief to the Public, as the Prices of Sugar will not thereby be brought to their proper Level: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against such Parts of the said Bill as may be prejudicial to themselves, and the said Trade in general, and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is re-committed: And that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think tit.

A Petition of William Sanday, of Holme in the County of Nottingham.

And the said Petition was brought up and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is possessed of a Wharf at Ratclffe upon Trent, in the said County of

Nottingham, situate on the River Trent, with Warehouses, Sheds, and other Conveniencies, for the Purpose of landing and depositing Coal, and housing Coke and other Articles, for the Supply of the Vale of Behoir, and for depositing Corn, Wool, and Other Articles, intended to go up or down the River Trent, and the said Wharf and Warehouses, and other Conveniencies, have been constructed by the Petitioner at a very great Expence; and that there is a Bill depending in the House for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, to the River Tixnt, at or near Ratcliffe, in the County of Nottingham, and, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, and the Navigation thereby intended should be made and perfected, the said Wharf, Warehouses, and other Conveniencies, constructed by the Petitioner, will be rendered useless, and of little or no Value, to the great Loss and Damage of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Provision may be made in the said Bill for making Compensation to him for the Loss and Damage he must sustain as aforesaid, or that he may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next, Ten of the Clock.

a Bill is intended to be moved, the Object of which is to grant Relief to His Majesty’s Protestant Subjects of the Episcopal Communion in Scotland from certain Pains and Penalties under which they suffer, find themselves sincerely inclined to wish Success to a Measure which they presume to think so just, humane, and liberal, and which, moreover, they are persuaded will give Satisfaction to the Community at large: Under this Impression they beg Leave to request that the Wisdom of Parliament may see it equitable to pass into a Law the Bill for the Relief of those of the Scots Episcopal Persuasion from certain Pains and Penalties affecting their public Religious Worship, and they are induced to make this Request from the Consideration that they certainly know the Scots Episcopalians are dutifully and cordially attached to His Majesty’s Person and Government, and pay all dutiful Respect to the Laws of their Country, and, as their Religious Principles tend to peaceable Submission to all in Authority, the Petitioners cannot refuse wishing a respectable Number of their Fellow Subjects may be relieved from unnecessary Hardships.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the said Samuel Whitbread, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Steyning:

And also, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Petition of the said Samuel Whitbread, Esquire, did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious:

And also, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Petition of the said Electors of the Borough of Steyning, in the County of Sussex, did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious:

And also, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the Opposition of the said James Martin Lloyd, Esquire, to the said several Petitions, did not appear to the said Select Committee to be frivolous or vexatious.

And the said Determinations were ordered to be entered in the Journals of this House.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do Steynii; attend this House, Tomorrow Morning, with the last ReU,rnl5t< Return for the Borough of Steyning, in the county of amendti Sussex, and amend the same, by rasing out the Name of James Martin Lloyd, Esquire, and inserting the Name of Samuel Whitbread, Esquire, instead thereof.

Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of proper Bounties to be allowed, in certain Cases, to Masters and Surgeons of Ships employed in the Conveyance of Slaves from the Coast of A) rica, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bounty of One hundred Pounds be allowed to each Master, and Fifty Pounds to each Surgeon, of every Ship employed in conveying Slaves from the Coast of Africa, upon Proof being made that not more than Two Slaves, in each Hundred that shall have been taken on Board such Ships, have died; and of Fifty Pounds to each Master, and Twenty-five Pounds to each Surgeon, where not more than Three Slaves in each Hundred have died, within a certain Period.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are appointed to prepare and bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Resolutions which, upon Tuesday last, were reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of Measures to be taken for the Abolition of the Trade carried on by British Subjects for the Purpose of procuring Slaves from Africa, ;and which upon Tuesday and Wednesday last were agreed to by the House, That they do make Provision therein, pursuant to the Resolution now reported, and agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Gentlemen,' That they do make Provision in the said Bill, for regulating the carrying and transporting of Slaves from the Coast of Africa, during a Time to be limited. Vol. 47.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Freeholders, Justices of Peace, and Commissioners of Supply of the County of Kincardine, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Clergy and Laity of the Scotch Episcopal Church are, by several Statutes, restrained from the free Exercise of their Religious Worship, and subjected to such Penalties, Forfeitures, and Disabilities, as oblige them either to sacrifice their Religion, or to expose their Persons to hazard, and abandon the Civil Privileges to which, as Citizens, they are entitled in common with other Dissenters, and the Petitioners are thoroughly convinced, that those Statutes are no longer necessary to the Security of His Majesty’s Person and Government: And therefore praying. That such Relief may be granted to the Pastors or Ministers, and Lay Persons, of the Episcopal Communion in Scotland, as may seem expedient to the House.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Council of the Montrose for Borough of Montrose, was also presented to the House,

D* and read; Setting forth, That, by certain Laws now

in Force, the Pastors or Ministers, and Lay Persons, of the Episcopal Communion in Scotland, are laid under peculiar Restrictions in the Exercise of their Religious Worship, and subject to Penalties and Forfeitures, which, at the Time of passing those Laws, were judged necessary for the Security of his late Majesty’s Person and Government; and that the Circumstances which gave Occasion to those Penal Statutes do now no longer exist, and the Persons subjected to them have given every Proof of their Loyalty which the Law has put in their Power, and are well known to entertain Principles most friendly to the Constitution and Government of this Country, and tending to promote its Peace and Welfare, of which the Petitioners have Experience in the Conduct of those of the Episcopal Communion within their Jurisdiction; and therefore the Petitioners, moved with Sympathy for a respectable Body of their Fellow Citizens, who are deprived of that Toleration which is so freely enjoyed by all other Protestant Dissenters in that Part of the Kingdom, beg Leave to request that the Clemency of the British Legislature may be extended to the Persons above mentioned, and such Relief granted, from the Hardships and Restraints which they at present lie under, as may seem expedient to the House.

A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of the Burgh of Inverbervie, in Council assembled, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, it having been judged necessary to the Security of His Majesty’s Person and Government to prohibit the Clergy and Laity of the Episcopal Communion in Scotland, from assembling for the Exercise of Divine Worship, under most severe Penalties, and the Forfeiture of every Civil Privilege, which otherwise, as Citizens, they were entitled to enjoy, the Petitioners are persuaded, that, by appearing worthy of Favour, the Members of that Communion will receive, from the Wisdom and Justice of the Legislature, the Relief of which they stand in so great need; the Petitioners think it therefore their Duty, in Justice to a respectable and deserving Body of their Fellow Subjects, to bear Testimony in Favour of the Ministers and Lay Persons of the Scotch Episcopal Church, of whose Loyalty to His Majesty, and Attachment to the Constitution, they are fully convinced: And therefore praying, That such Relief may be granted to them from Vol. 47.

Petition from Inverbervie for D\

the Penal Laws, now existing against them, as may seem proper to the House.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Mr. Thomas Stanley reported from the Committee, who were appointed to take into Consideration the Standing Orders of the House respecting Bills for making Navigable Canals, and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That when any Application is intended to be made to this House for a Bill to make any Navigable Cut or Canal, or to make any River Navigable, or to vary or alter any such Cut, Canal, or Navigable River, Notice of such intended Application shall be inserted Three Times in The London Gazette, in the Months of August and September, or either of them, previous to the Session of Parliament to which such Application is proposed to be made, as well as in the Newspapers, and at the Quarter Sessions, agreeably to the Directions of a former Standing Order of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Notices shall contain the Parishes and Townships in, to, or through which any such Cut, Canal, or Navigable River is intended to be made, altered, or carried.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Map or Plan of such proposed Cut, Canal, or Navigable River, with a Book of Reference, shall be deposited for public Inspection, at the Office of Clerk or Clerks of the Peace of every County, Riding, or Division, through which such Cut, Canal, or Navigation, is intended to be made, varied, or altered, on or before the l ith Day of November, previous to the Ap-Yot. 47,

residing in Ireland.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Edward Burrow, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Trade and Navigation to and from the Town, Port, and Harbour of Whitehaven, in the County of Cumberland, have of late Years much increased, and are at present in a very improving State; but that the Harbour is too small for the Ships resorting thereto, and that it would be advantageous to the Trade and Commerce of the Country if the same was to be enlarged, and properly regulated, improved, and maintained:

Then,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and respecting Commons of the City of London, in Common Council the Duty on assembled. Coals.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That, by the Act of the Ninth of Ann, Cap. 22, and several subsequent Acts, a local Duty of Three Shillings per Chaldron or Ton was imposed upon all Sorts of Coals and Culm imported and brought Coastwise into the Port of London, or the River Thames, within the Liberty of the said City upon the same River, and was appropriated for the building certain Churches in or near the Cities of London and Westminster, and for other Purposes enumerated in the said Acts, and there is no Charge, Claim, or Incumbrance on the said Duty, other than an Annuity to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, granted in Consideration of their having advanced the Sum of 1,750,000l. for the Purpose of discharging certain Sums of Money which had been raised, from Time to Time, upon the said Duty; and that, besides the said local Duty of Three Shillings, there were other local Duties laid on the said Commodities by the Operation of Overcharges in the National Imposts 1779 ar>d *782* the Officers in computing those Branches having taken Five per Cent, of all the preceding Branches indiscriminately, although One of them was the aforesaid local Duty of Three Shillings, and the Consolidation Act, of the Twenty-seventh of His present Majesty, having added Eight-twentietlxs of a Penny to the total Duty on Coals, in order to raise the Fraction to an- Integer, and it appears, by Computations now made, that the Surplus arising from the said local Duties, after paying the Annuity to the Bank of England, is more than sufficient for paying off the Whole of the said Debt

802 17° M A. 1792.

of 1,750,000l.; and that, by the Act, of the Thirteenth of George the First, Cap. 21. it was provided, that so soon as the whole Debt and Interest should be paid, the Duty should be understood to be redeemed, and by the Act of the First of George the Second, Stat. 2. Cap. 8. it was enacted, That, on Payments being made to the Bank, not less than 500,000l. each, the Annuity should be proportionably reduced: And therefore submitting the Premises to the Consideration of the House, in Hopes that the said local Duties may be repealed, or that such other Relief may be granted to the Petitioners in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Petition A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

thereunder written, on Behalf of themselves and other Suffolk Em- Owners of divers Marshes, and other Grounds and He-bankment reditaments, lying on each Side of the River Yare, in bill. the several Parishes of,

Brammerton, Surlingham, Rockland, Carlton,

Langley, Hardley, Norton, Thorpejuxta

wich, Postwick, Brundel, Buckingham,

singham, Cant ley, Limpcnho Thorpe,

hampton, Halvergate, and in the County of

Norfolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending before the House for more effectually preserving certain Lands and Grounds, within the said County of Norfolk, from Injury or Damage by the Sea, and for repealing an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King James the First, intituled, "An Act for the speedy Recovery " of many Thousand Acres of Marsh Ground, and other Ground, within the County of lately

" surrounded by the Rage of the Sea in divers Parts "of the said County, and for the Prevention of the " Danger of the like surrounding hereafter;" in the Preamble of which Bill it is stated, That various Inroads or Breaches have lately been made by the Sea upon the Coast of the County of Norfolk, at and

Winterton, in the said County, and that sundry Marshes, and Lands adjacent thereto, have been Overflowed and much damaged by the Sea Water; and further Setting forth, That, from the Distance of the several Parishes above-mentioned from Horsey and Winterton aforesaid, and by Reason of divers Walls and Embankments made since the passing of the said Act, in the several Marshes in the said Parishes above-named, at the Costs and Charges of the Owners and Proprietors of the Lands therein, the same Marshes are so defended that no Salt Water has, within the Memory of Man, flowed, or is likely to flow, over the same, by Means of the Breaches of the Sea at Horsey and Winterton aforesaid, and that therefore the said Marshes are not liable, in any Respect, to be injured by the said Breaches, and ought not, as the Petitioners submit, in any Degree to be assessed towards the Repairs thereof; and that, for Want of regular Notices having been sent to the aforesaid Parishes, or other usual and proper Notices given them, many Proprietors in the said Parishes are entirely uninformed of such a Bill having been brought forward, and such of the Petitioners as have been lately informed thereof, in Consequence of no printed Copies of the said Bill having been made and dispersed in the usual Manner, and by Reason of the great Privacy with which the said Bill hath been hurried on, have not had sufficient Time to form a competent Judgment of the Extent of the operative Clauses therein contained: And therefore, on Behalf of themselves and the said other Owners and Proprietors, for the Reasons aforesaid, and in order that the Petitioners may have Time to employ One or more experienced and skilful Engineers to take the Levels of the different Marshes, and to draw Plans of such Marshes, and of the Walls and Embank*

ments thereof, and to obtain such further Information as may be wanting as to the Effects (if any) winch the' said Sea Breaches have, or are likely to have, upon; the Marshes and Lands in1 the above; named' Pat-rishes, and to make his or their Report: thereon, praying, That the further Reading of the said Bill may be put off for Three Months, or for such further Time as the House may think proper; and that the Petitioners may then produce such Evidence, as they may have obtained, before the House, and may be heard, by themselves, their Agents or Counsel, as they shall think fit, against such Part of the said Bill as may affect them or their Property, or have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for more effectually preserving certain Lands and Grounds, within the Counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, from Injury or Damage by the Sea, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves, their Agents or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it-be an Instruction1 to the said Committee, That theydo admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said; Petition.

That the Petitioners, and all other Owners and Occupiers of Land in the Parish of Battersea, are entitled to Right of Common upon the said Common, and observe, by the said Bill, that it is intended to divide the said Common among only a few Persons having Land adjoining thereto, which will be injurious to all the other Owners and Occupiers of Land in the Manor and Parish of Battersea having a Right of Common: And therefore praying, That the said Common may not be inclosed and divided without considering the Petitioners Rights and Proportions of the said Common, and that they may be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

An ingrossed Bill for dividing and inclosing certain Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, Waste and other Commonable Lands or Grounds, within the Divisions of Lewknor and Postcomb, in the Manor and Parish of Lewknor, in the County of Oxford, was read the Third Time.

The Committee appointed to enquire how far the Laws for preventing illegal Insurances, and other Evils, which have been found to attend the Drawing of State Lotteries, are effectual to the Object proposed by them, have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matters to them referred: And,

Your Committee have thought that they should better execute the Commands of the House, by pointing their Examination to the Generality and Magnitude of the Evils occasioned by Lotteries, rather than by investigating the innumerable Distresses which the House must see are the necessary Consequences of the Evil itself. Your Committee are convinced that Lotteries were productive of Two general Evils: One, that of Public Offices, without Licence, openly selling Tickets, Shares, and Chances, and making illegal Insurances; the other, making illegal Insurances privately and clandestinely.

With respect to the First Evil, your Committee find, That since a Determination of the Court of King’s Bench, in Michaelmas Term last, it has been wholly eradicated.

And as to the Second, your Committee find, That by the Vigilance of the Magistrates in the Country it has been totally suppressed; but that in the Metropolis the Practice still prevails among the Community at large, but more particularly among the lower Classes of People, to a very extensive and pernicious Degree.

Not to tire the House with too long a Detail, your Committee have subjoined an Appendix, containing the full Evidence that was given before them; by which the Extension of the Evil, together with its Consequences, the Fraud and Violence with which it is carried on and supported, and the Conduct of the

The House divided. The Noes w’ent forth.

Tellers for the Yeas,

or Payments in lieu of Tythe or Tythes, Magistrates, and that of the Stamp Office, will fully

~ appear.

Your Committee therefore, upon the Whole, are of Opinion, That as to the First Evil, the Laws have been fully effectual; and as to the latter, which your Committee consider as the most important, the Laws, within the Metropolis, have had little or no Effect.

tnised him that they would not renew the Licence of the House at the next Licensing Day.

That there were fewer illegal Lottery Offices and Insurance Offices, during the Drawing of the Irish than the English Lottery.

That with respect to illegal Lottery Offices, by which he meant Offices for the Sale of illegal Shares or Chances — before he had been Three Days appointed Inspector, he seized One of the Clerks in the Office of Shergold and Co. as a Vagrant, and carried him before Mr. Alderman Clark, who took Two Days to consider the Case, and then discharged him, as not being within the Statute of 27 Geo. III.; after which the other Aldermen, until the present Lord Mayor came into Office, had declined to act in such Cases.

That the Decision of the Court of King’s Bench, in Michaelmas Term last, in the Case of the King against Oldman, had the Effect of totally suppressing these Offices for the Sale of illegal Shares and Chances; and that towards the Middle of the last English Lottery there was not One such Office in the whole Kingdom — Before that Decision, there had been about Twelve such Offices in London and Westminster, and many of them in the Country. That the Practice of making clandestine Insurances does not begin above a Day before the Drawing of the Lottery commences.

That he has no Salary annexed to his Office, but is paid as the Commissioners of the Stamp Office think he deserves.

Mr. Robert Sharman was next examined; who said, That he lived at N° 50, in Lombard Street — That he knew Insurances had been made in the last Lottery, where the Premium was against the Insurer, from Five to Twenty per Centum — He knew that the Practice of Insurance had been very general; and he thought never more so than in the late Lottery — In a great Line it was, he observed, carried on in great and respectable Houses, mostly unlicensed; but in a lower Degree, in obscure Shops and Rooms, where a Green Blind and a Number are put up, which is perfectly understood by the People; it was also carried on in Houses where no external Signs were shewn — He had seen Insurances done himself in some of the Houses above described, though not in many — The Insurances were made sometimes in Books, sometimes on Paper only — The Clerk took down the Numbers wished to be insured, and then received the Money — At some of the Places Duplicates ,of the Numbers were given, but hardly ever where the larger Sums were insured.

Mr. Sharman, on being asked as to the Amount of the Sums to be insured, observed, that between Three and Four hundred Pounds had been the highest, and Half a Guinea the lowest — That Four Pence or Five Pence was paid as the Premium for the Half Guinea on the First Day of Drawing, and that it regularly increased every Day. — He produced to your Committee a small Numerical Book, and said that the Use of it was to enter the Numbers as drawn every Day, and that without such a Book, Insurances (at least to any Extent) could not be carried on — That the small Book above mentioned, being more portable, was better adapted to the carrying on of illegal Insurances; and that they were the same as those carried about to Public Houses — Mr. Sharman then observed, that the Persons who take the Insurances carry the Accounts to the several Offices, and procure the highest Poundage they can, in order to cover those they have made — That many of the Inferior Offices very often closed without paying; and that he never knew so many in that Predicament as there were in the last Lottery — And finally, he observed, on being asked, Whether, and in what Degree, the Encrease of Insurance in the Course of the last English Lottery ought to be ascribed to the Prevention of the Sale of illegal Policies? That he did not believe there had been a single legal Insurance made during the whole Drawing of it.

Vol. 47.

Mr. John Copperthrvaite was next examined, who

said, That his Residence in general was at Walworth, in Surrey; but being bred in a Merchant’s Counting House, he was often employed by Tradesmen and others in the adjusting of difficult Accounts, and was in the Habits of frequenting Coffee Houses, and other Houses of public Resort, near the Royal Exchange, and in different Parts of London and Westminster, where he had an Opportunity of being a Witness to the Mode in which illegal Insurances were made — He stated that he had seen various Persons carrying Numerical Books from House to House, where, immediately on their Arrival, they withdrew into a private Room, followed by those who wished to insure; and he has seen the same Persons afterwards come out with the Ticket, or rather with the Duplicate, in their Hands; and that he had himself been applied to, to take a small Numerical Book round to Coffee Houses and Public Houses, for which he was to have a Per Cenlage — Two of the Persons who made this Application to him had regular Licences, the other he believes had not

Mr. James Hawkins being examined, said, That he is a Stationer in Wells Court, Queen Street, Cheap-side — That he was in the Habit of selling Numerical Books for the Lotteries; but the particular Purpose for which they were used he knew not — that there were Two Sorts, One of the largest, and one of the smaller Size — That his were of the same Species as that shewn to him, though the Size was smaller — That he supplied Lottery Office Keepers, and other Persons, indifferently, with these Books — he thought he sold about Eighty in the Course of the Year, small and large together — He observed the same People frequently bought both small and large.

Mr. Thomas Cooke being examined, said, That he is an Engraver and Printer, and lives in Little Britain — That he sold Numerical Books of Four different Sizes, indiscriminately to all Customers. — In Licensed Offices they were used for registering Tickets; but whether they would answer any other Purpose he could not tell — he knew the small Books were used by the Clerks attending the Drawing of the Lottery — he thought he sold, during the Drawing of the English and Irish Lotteries, about 350 of these Books — and that he printed about Fifty more for the English than for the Irish Lottery.

Mr. Garnet Terry being examined, said, That he is an Engraver and Bookseller, in That he had formerly sold Numerical Books, though he had quitted that Line of Business this last Year — he knew that these Numerical Books were used by the Clerks to the Lottery Offices, and by Deputy Insurers for taking Numbers in Private Houses, but more particularly in Public Houses and Coffee Houses — That for his Part he left off selling them, because it had brought latterly such a Vagabond Set to his House — While he continued in that Line of Business, he had Customers, as well during the Drawing the Irish as the English Lottery — That he sold in One Year about 300, the greater Part of which were of the Size of the One then shewn to him; but that he knew there were a smaller Size than that.

Mr. Benjamin Bunn being examined, said, That he is a Pawnbroker, and lives in — That he

had been in that Branch of Business many Years — that he served about 100 Customers Daily; but that during the Drawing of the English and Irish Lotteries (excepting in the last Week) his Number was increased to about 130 — he thought the English Lottery brought upon an Average more Customers than the Irish; and he observed, that the Jews, to whom he chiefly lent Money, were more addicted to Gaming, than any other Set of People — he also remarked, that many

Illegal Insurances, cvC on Lotteries

812 2r Mail. A. 1792.

Illegal in- of the People who dealt with him, declared it was for surances&c. purpose of procuring Money for Insurance; and on Lotteries, generajiy were with him between Seven and

Nine, in the Morning, and very late in the Evening — and he thought no greater Proof could be given of the Truth of what they said — He likewise mentioned, that the Sales in his Branch of Business during this Period were always very dead, and but few Things redeemed, in Proportion to what were at other Times.

Mr. William Windsor being examined, said, That he is a Pawnbroker, and lives in the Minories — and upon Mr. Bunn's Evidence being read to him, he confirmed the same in every Part.

Mr. John Beck Heather being examined, said, That he is a Pawnbroker, and lives in Long Acre, where he has carried on his Business these 25 Years — He said, be served Daily, on an Average, between Seventy and Eighty Customers; but that during the Drawing of the Lottery he generally had Thirty more each -Day, excepting as to the last Week of it, when he found but little Difference from his usual Business — With regard to his Sales, he scarcely took a Shilling a Day; and he believed One hundred Pounds would not answer the Loss he always sustained from the Drawing of the Lottery; he likewise observed, that not Half the usual Quantity of Things were redeemed at this Season.

Mr. William Parker being examined, said, That he is a Pawnbroker, and lives in Princes Street, Soho — That during the Drawing of the Lottery, he found no great Difference as to the Number of his Customers, but that his Sales were quite dead during that Time, nor did Persons redeem what they had pawned — that he has often remarked, that when People came into his Shop to pledge Goods, the whole Conversation was about Insurances.

Mr. John Salkeld being examined, said, He was a Pawnbroker — that he lives in Fleet Street, and has been in Business many Years. — During the Drawing of both the English and Lotteries, particularly the

English, he serves more Customers than at other Times, but that his Sales are dead, and very few redeem during that Period — that he has often heard People mention that they pawn their Goods for the Purpose of having Money to insure with.

William Rix, Esquire, Town Clerk of the City of London, attending according to Order, produced to the Committee Two Resolutions of the Court [of Common Council of the said City, of the 5th of April last; which are as follow:

" Resolved, That the Drawing of the State Lottery

" in the Guildhall of this City, is a great Interruption " to the Peace and Commerce of this Metropolis, " and renders the Attendance upon public Business in "the said Hall inconvenient and dangerous.

" Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Court, " That the State Lottery ought not in future to be " drawn in the Guildhall of this City."

Ebenezer Maitland, Esquire, Foreman of the Grand Jury of the City of London, attending the Committee, said, That the Reasons which induced the Grand Jury of London to call the Attention of the Court at the Old Bailey to the Practice which so much prevails of making illegal Insurances, were, that the Practice is so notorious, that the Jury in their individual Capacities were acquainted with many Instances of Evil having arisen from it; and the Evidence of the Witnesses examined in Support of the Prosecution of many of the Prisoners being of such a Nature as to satisfy them, that Insurance of Numbers in the last Lottery was the Cause of their committing the Crimes which brought them before the Jury.

Henry Barford, Esquire, Foreman of the Grand Jury

for the County of Middlesex, being examined, confirmed the Whole of the Evidence of Mr. Maitland.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to continue, for a Time to be limited, several Acts of Parliament, for regulating the shipping and carrying Slaves in British Vessels from the Coast of Africa: And that Sir William Dolben and Mr. Henry Hobart do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House was moved. That the Resolution which upon the 7th Day of this Instant May was reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of proper Bounties to be allowed, in certain Cases, to Masters and Surgeons of Ships employed in the Conveyance of Slaves from the Coast of Africa, and was then agreed to by the House, might be read.

And the same was, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and is as folio weth; viz.

" Resolved, That a Bounty of One hundred Pounds " be allowed to each Master, and Fifty Pounds to " each Surgeon, of every Ship employed in conveying " Slaves from the Coast of Africa, upon Proof being " made, that not more than Two Slaves, in each Hundred that shall have been taken on board such Ships, " have died; and of Fifty Pounds to each Master, " and Twenty-five Pounds to each Surgeon, where " not more than Three Slaves in each Hundred have " died within a certain Period."

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, the said Bill, That they do make Provision therein, pursuant to the said Resolution.

Mr. Secretary Dundas presented to the House, by His Majesty’s Command,

Copy of a Proclamation, dated at the Queen’s House, this 21st Day of May 1792.

And the said Proclamation was read; and is as folio weth; viz.

By the KING,

A Proclamation.

GEORGE R.

Whereas divers wicked and seditious Writings have been printed, published, and industriously dispersed, tending to excite Tumult and Disorder, by endeavouring to raise groundless Jealousies and Discontents in the Minds of Our faithful and loving Subjects, respecting the Laws and happy Constitution of Government, Civil and Religious, established in this Kingdom, and endeavouring to vilify and bring into Contempt the wise and wholesome Provisions made at the Time of the glorious Resolution, and since strengthened and confirmed by subsequent Laws, for the Preservation and Security of the Rights and Liberties of Our faithful and loving Subjects: And whereas divers Writings have also been printed, published, and industriously dispersed, recommending the said wicked and seditious Publications to the Attention of all Our faithful and loving Subjects: And whereas We have also Reason to believe, that Correspondencies have been entered into with sundry Persons in Foreign Parts, with a View to forward the criminal and wicked Purposes above mentioned: And whereas the Wealth, Happiness, and Prosperity of this Kingdom do, under Divine Providence, chiefly defend upon a due Submission to the Laws, a just Confidence in the Integrity and Wisdom of Parliament, and a Continuance of that zealous Attachment to the Government and Constitution of the Kingdom, which has ever prevailed in the Minds of the People thereof: And whereas there is nothing which We so earnestly desire, as to secure the Public Peace and Prosperity, and to preserve to all Our loving Subjects the full Enjoyment of their Rights and Liberties, both Religious and Civil; Wre therefore being resolved, as far as in Us lies, to repress the wicked and seditious Practices aforesaid, and to deter all Persons from following so pernicious an Example, have thought fit, by the Advice of Our Privy Council, to issue this Our Royal Proclamation, solemnly warning all Our loving Subjects, as they tender their own Happiness, and that of their Posterity, to guard against all such Attempts, which aim at the Subversion of all regular Government within this Kingdom, and which are inconsistent with the Peace and Order of Society; and earnestly exhorting them at all Times, and to the utmost of their Power, to avoid and discourage all Proceedings tending to produce Riots and Tumults; and We do strictly charge and command all Our Magistrates, in and throughout Our Kingdom of Great Britain, that they do make diligent Enquiry, in order to discover the Authors and Printers of such wicked and seditious Writings as aforesaid; and all others who shall disperse the same: And We do further charge and command all our Sheriffs, Justices of the Peace, Chief Magistrates in our Cities, Boroughs, and Corporations, and all other Our Officers and Magistrates throughout Our Kingdom of Great Britain, that they do, in their several and respective Stations, take the most immediate and effectual Care to suppress anil

g X prevent

Bill to continue Acts for regulating the shipping of Slaves presented.

prevent all Riots, Tumults, and other Disorders which may be attempted to be raised or made, by any Person or Persons; which, on whatever Pretext they may be grounded, are not only contrary to Law, but dangerous to the most important Interests of this Kingdom: And We do further require and command all and every Our Magistrates aforesaid, that they do, from Time to Time, transmit to One of Our principal Secretaries of State, due and full Information of such Persons as shall be found offending as aforesaid, or in any Degree aiding or abetting the rein; it being Our Determination, for the Preservation of the Peace and Happiness of Our faithful and loving Subjects, to carry the Laws vigorously into Execution against such Offenders as aforesaid. Given at our Court at the Queen’s House, the Twenty-first Day of May, One thousand Seven hundred and Ninety-two, in the Thirty-second Year of our Reign.

God Save the KING.

Ordered, That the said Proclamation do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Ordered, That the said Proclamation be taken into Consideration upon Friday Morning next.

Mr. Henry Hobart, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for regulating the Exportation of Sugar, and allowing the Importation of Sugar and Coffee into the Bahama and Bermuda Islands in Foreign Ships, was re-committed, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read.

And the House being informed that some further Amendments are necessary to be made to the said Bill;

Resolved, That the said Bill be again re-committed.

Resolved, That the said Bill be again re-committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

reign of all the Russias, and his Imperial Majesty the Grand Signior, their Heirs and Successors to the Thrones, as well as between their Empires and Subjects; as also all Enmity, which shall be buried in eternal Oblivion; and there shall be from henceforth a perpetual Peace by Land and Sea; a constant Friendship and unalterable Harmony shall be re-established, and maintained with the most sincere, attentive, and strict Observance of the Articles of the Treaty of Peace now stipulated; so that neither of the Two Parties shall hereafter attempt against the other, either secretly or openly, any unfriendly Act or Proceeding; and in virtue of the Renewal of so sincere a Friendship, the Two contracting Parties grant a reciprocal Amnesty and general Pardon to all those of their Subjects, without any Distinction, who have committed any Crime against either of the Two Parties, setting at Liberty those who are in the Gallies or in Prison, permitting all Persons in Exile, or banished, to return to their Homes, with Promise to restore to them, after the Peace, all the Honours and Estates which they before possessed, without committing or suffering others, with Impunity, to commit against them any Insult, Damage, or Offence, under any Pretext whatever} but that each of them may live under the safeguard and Protection of the Laws and Customs of his Country equally with his Countrymen.

Article II.

The Treaty of Peace concluded the 10th of July 1774, in the Year of the Hegira 1188, the 14th of the Moon Zemaxiel Evvel; the Explanatory Convention of the 10th of March 1779, that is to say, the 20th of Zcmaziel Ahir 1193; the Treaty of Commerce of the 10th of June 1783, that is to say, the 20th 1197; and the Act touching the Incorporation of the Crimea and Taman to the Empire of Russia, which declares the River of Cuban to be the Frontier, concluded the 28th December 1783, that is to say, the 15th Safer 1198, are confirmed, by this new Treaty of Peace, in all their Articles, excepting only those which have been by the present or by former Treaties successively changed; and the Two high contracting Parties engage to observe them religiously and unalterably, and to fulfil them with good Faith and Punctuality.

Article III.

In consequence of the Second Article of the Preliminaries, declaring that in future the Dniester shall be the Boundary between the Two Empires, so that from henceforth the Frontiers of the Empire of Russia shall extend to that River; the Two contracting Parties have agreed with each other, and ordain by these Presents, that the River Dniester shall constitute the Frontier for ever between the Empire of Russia and the Sublime

Porte; so that the whole Territory situated on the left Shore of the Dniester, shall remain in Perpetuity under

the full and incontestable Dominion of the Empire of

Russia; an<4 the whole Territory situated on the right Shore of the said River, shall be restored and remain in Perpetuity, under the full and incontestable Dominion of the Sublime Porte.

Article IV.

In consequence of this Regulation fixed, touching the Limits of the Two Empires, and in virtue of the Fourth Article of the Preliminaries, declaring that all the other Frontiers shall remain the same as they were at the Commencement of the present War, and that the Countries occupied by the Troops of the Empire of Russia during this War, shall be restored to the Sublime Porte, with all the Fortresses therein, and in the State in which those Fortresses now are; her Imperial Majesty restores to the Sublime Porte, Bessarabia, conquered by her Armies, with the Fortresses of

Akierman, Kilia, and Ismail, and with the Burghs, Villages, Habitations, and every Thing included in that Province.

Vol. 47.

In like Manner her Imperial Majesty restores the Treaty Province of Moldavia, with all the Towns, Habita- betweea tions, and every Thing included in it, and the Sublime ®J^Spo^d Ottoman Porte receives them on the following Condi- r tions, under a solemn Promise of perfectly observing the m.

1. To observe and accomplish religiously every Thing that was stipulated in Favour of the Two Provinces of JVallachia and Moldavia, in the Treaty concluded in 1774, that is to say, in the Year of the Hegira 1188, the 14th of the Moon Zemaziel Evvel-, in the explanatory Convention concluded in 1779, that is to say, the 20th of Zemaziel Ahir 1193; in the Act of the 28th December 1783, or the 15th of the Moon Suffer 1198, signed by the Grand Vizir in the Name of the Sublime Ottoman Porte.

2. Not to demand or exact from those Countries any Payment for old Accounts, of what Nature soever.

3. Not to exact from those Countries any Contribution or Payment in the whole Period of the War; but in Consideration of the great Variety of Losses and Devastations which they have sustained during the Course of this War, to exempt them from all Imposts and Charges for Two Years, to be computed from the Date of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty.

4. To grant to the Families who shall desire to quit their Country and remove elsewhere, free Egress with all their Property; and, in order that the said Families may have sufficient Time to give to their near Relations,

Subjects of the Ottoman Empire, or to whomsoever they may think proper, equally Subjects of the Ottoman Empire, and to sell their moveable and immoveable Property to Subjects of the same Empire, according to the Laws of the Country, and for the Settlement of their Affairs, the Term of Fourteen Months is granted to them for such Emigration from their Country, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty.

Article V.

In Testimony of the Sincerity with which the Two high contracting Parties seek to re-establish Peace and good Harmony with each other, not only for the present, but also to secure it in a lasting Manner for the future, by removing every Thing which might hereafter give the slightest Pretext for Dispute or Coolness; the Sublime Porte promises, in renewing at present the Firman formerly issued, to send Orders to the Pacha of Ahaltzik or Ahiska, commanding the Frontiers, and others, forbidding them, most strictly, to disturb or molest hereafter, under any Pretext, either secretly or openly, the Countries and Inhabitants which are under the Government of the Czar of Cartalinia, expressly enjoining them not to disturb the good Harmony and good Neighbourhood in any Part

Article VI.

Having confirmed, by the 11th Article of the present Treaty, amongst other anterior Stipulations, the Act of the 28th of December 1783, concerning the Incorporation of the Crimea and Taman to the Empire of Russia, and fixing the River of the Cuban as the Boundary between the Two contracting Parties in those Countries, the Sublime Ottoman Porte, as a Proof of its sincere Desire to prevent in future every Thing that might disturb the Peace, Tranquillity, and good Harmony between the Two Empires, promises and engages solemnly to employ its whole Authority, and all the Means proper, to restrain and check the People bordering on the left Shore of the Cuban, so that they make no Incursions into the Territory of the Empire of Russia, nor do any Damage, Injury, Waste, or<iRob-bei-y whatever, to or upon the Russian Subjects, or their Settlements, or the Lands or Inhabitants, either openly or secretly, under any Pretext whatsoever; and that they

The Porte, most positive Orders to whom it may concern, together with the strongest Prohibitions, under the most rigorous Penalties, which are to be absolutely proclaimed in those Places after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Peace. If, after the Stipulations made in the present Treaty, and the Prohibitions declared to the said People, any One of them should still presume to make Incursions into the Territory of the Empire of Russia, to cause any Damage Or Injury whatever, steal Cattle, or any Thing else, or carry away Russian Subjects into Slavery, in such Case, after having made Complaint thereof, Justice shall be done without the least Delay, by restoring what may have been pillaged or stolen. Above all, no Difficulty shall be made relative to the Restoration of, and Search for, Russian Subjects who shall have been carried off, making Compensation likewise for all Expences which may have been incurred, and rigorously punishing the Offenders, in the Presence of the Russian Commissary appointed by the Chief who shall command on the Frontier. Supposing that, contrary to all Expectation, such Justice shall not be done in the Space of Six Months, to be computed from the Day of making the Complaint, the Sublime Porte engages to pay out of its own proper Treasury, all the Expences which those Offenders shall have occasioned, in the Space of One Month after Claim shall have been made by the Russian Minister: Provided, that the Punishments above specified, for disturbing the Repose of good Neighbourhood, are nevertheless to take place without the least Delay.

Article VII.

Commerce being the true Pledge and the most solid Bond of reciprocal Harmony, the Sublime Ottoman Porte, renewing Peace and Friendship with the Empire of Russia, in Testimony of the Sincerity with which it desires that a secure and advantageous Trade between the Subjects of the Two Empires may flourish in the best Manner possible, promises, by these Presents, to observe and follow the 6ist Article of the Treaty of Commerce with the Empire of relative to the

Corsairs of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli; and namely, that if a R,ussian Subject should meet with Corsairs of Algiers, Tunis, or Tripoli, and should be taken Prisoner by them, or if those Pirates should seize a Ship, or any Effects whatsoever from Russian Traders, in such Case, the Sublime Ottoman Porte engages to employ its Authority with the said Cantons for the Release of every Russian Subject, who, in such case, should have been reduced to Slavery, and for the Restitution of the Ship, Merchandize, and Effects which may have been taken, and for making Compensation to the injured Party for all the Damages which might result therefrom: And when Intelligence should arrive, certifying the Nonexecution of the Firmans by the said Cantons of

giers, Tunis, and Tripoli, the Sublime Porte, upon the Requisition of the Minister or Charg£ d’Affaires of the Empire of Russia, engages to pay and satisfy the injured Party from the Imperial Treasury, in the Space of Two Month*, or sooner, if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the aforesaid Requisition.

Article VIII.

All the Prisoners of War, and other Slaves, of either Sex, and of what Quality and) Rank soever, who may be found in either of the Two Empires, excepting those who in the Russian Empire, being Mahometans, may have voluntarily embraced the Christian Religion; and those who being Christians, may have also voluntarily embraced the Mahometan, Religion in the Ottoman Empire; all such, immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty, without any Pretext whatsoever, are to be reciprocally delivered up, surrendered, and restored, without any Ransom or

Payment. Irt like Mahner all other Christians reduced to Slavery; that is to say, Polanders, Moldavians, tVat-lachians, the Inhabitants of Peloponnesus, Islanders, Georgians, and all others, without any Exception, are also to be delivered up, without any ftafisom or Payment. All such Russian Subjects as by any Accident whatever, after the Conclusion Of this salutary Peace, shall be reduced to Slavery, and be found in the Ottoman Empire, shall also be restored and given up; which the Empire of Russia promises to observe, with perfect Equality and Reciprocity, towards The Ottoman Porte and its Subjects.

Article IX.

Although, after the Cessation of Hostilities on the Occasion of the happy Negotiation of the Peace now concluded, no Misunderstanding can arise relative to hostile Operations, yet, after the Signature of the Treaty of Peace, the supreme Plenipotentiary and actual Privy Councillor of the Empire of Russia, shall give Notice thereof to the Commanders in Chief of the Armies and Fleets of the Empire of Russia; and in like Manner, the Supreme Vizir of The Ottoman shall notify

to the Ottoman Armies arid1 Fjjfets, that Peace ana Friendship between the Two great Empires are entirely re-established. 1; "

Article X.

In order that the happy Peace and sincere Friendship between the Two Empires maybe the more solidly confirmed, Ambassadors Extraordinary shall be solemnly sent on each Part, at such Time as the Two Courts shall determine with One Accord.

The respective Ambassadors shall be received and treated upon the Frontiers with art equal Etiquette, and with the same Honours and Ceremonies as are observed in the respective Embassies between the Powers the most honoured by the Two Empires. As a Mark of Friendship, Presents suitable to the Dignity of the Two Empires, shall be reciprocally sent by the said Ambassadors.

Article XI.

After the Conclusion of the Treaty of Peace between the Two great Empires, and the Exchange of the respective Ratifications of the Sovereigns, the Imperial Russian Troops and the Galley Fleet shall proceed to the Evacuation of the Territory of the Ottoman Empire.

But as it is necessary to combine the said Evacuation by the Troops and the Galley Fleet with the Circumstances of the Season, the Two high contracting Parties have agreed to fix, as the latest Term, the 15th of the Month of May, Old Stile, of next Year 1792, by which Time all her Imperial Majesty’s Troops shall pass to the left Shore of the Dniester, and the Whole of the Galley Feet shall entirely quit the Mouths of the Danultc.

As long as the Imperial Russian Troops-shall remain in the conquered Countries and Fortresses, which, conformably to the Treaty of Peace, will be restored to The Ottoman Porte, the Administration and Order of Affairs shall continue as it now is, under their Government, and The Ottoman Porte shall not intermeddle therewith in any Shape, till the Time of the Retreat of all the Troops. The Imperial: Russian Troops, to the last Day of their Retreat, shall receive in those Countries all Things necessary, and Provisions, as are now furnished to them.

The actual Privy Councillor and Supreme Plenipotentiary on the Part of her Imperial Majesty, the Aui* tocratrix of all the Russiasy and the Supreme Vizir, on the Part of the Sublime Ottoman Porte, after the Signature of the present Treaty of Peace, by the respective Plenipotentiariea, shall exchange at in the

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed. Assureds by the Royal Exchange Assurance Companies, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Royal Exchange Assurance Company and their Successors, to grant, purchase, and sell Annuities upon Lives; and Setting forth, that his late Majesty King George the First was pleased, by Letters Patent, dated the 2 2d Day of June, 1720, to incorporate certain Persons therein named to he a Corporation by the Name of The Royal Exchange Assurance for insuring Ships and Goods at Sea, or going to Sea, and for lending Money upon Bottomry, and afterwards by other Letters Patent, dated the 29th of Apri 1721, incorporated the same Persons to he a Corporation for the Assurance of any Life, or Lives, and against Casualties and Accidents by" Fire, by the Name of The Royal Exchange Assurance of Houses and Goods from Fire, and both the said Corporations consist of one and the same Governor, and of the same Directors and Persons, and they are possessed of Sums of Money laid out in the Public Funds and other Securities, upon the Trusts, and for the Intents and Purposes, mentioned in such respective Charters; and that the Petitioners have severally made Insurances with the said Companies, and are materially interested in their respective Capitals, and in the Sums of Money so invested by them as aforesaid, and the said Companies are not, nor is either of them, now possessed of any other Capital or Sum of Money, than as aforesaid, for the purchasing of Annuities, rvor are or will be possessed of any other Capital or Sum of Money, for securing and paying any Annuities that they may grant and sell (except such Sum and Sums of Money as shall, from Time to Time, be received by them for the granting and selling of such Annuities) and the Petitioners are therefore apprehensive that the Bill, now depending, to empower the said Companies to grant, purchase, and sell, Annuities upon Lives, and to become another Corporation also, by the Name of The Royal Exchange Annuity elusive of their

Two former Corporate Names) will he injurious to the Public in general, and to the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel, against the same, and that the said Bill may not pass info a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard*, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Twelfth Report of the Commissioners appointed
